Surat al-Nur is Medinan by scholarly consensus (ijma').

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory, and in which We have sent down clear signs, that you may remember.﴾ (24:1)

The purpose of this surah is to mention the rulings concerning chastity (al-'afaf) and covering (al-sitr). ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote to the people of Kufa: "Teach your women Surat al-Nur." ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Do not let women dwell in upper chambers, do not teach them writing, but teach them Surat al-Nur and spinning."

As for "wa-faradnaha" (and We made it obligatory): it was recited with a light (takhfif) pronunciation of the rāʾ, meaning "We made obligatory upon you and upon those after you what is in it of rulings." And with a heavy (tashdid) pronunciation, meaning "We sent down in it various obligations." Abū ʿAmr recited "wa-farraḍnaha" with the heavy pronunciation, meaning "We divided it in its revelation, piece by piece" (najman najman). Al-fard (obligation) means cutting, and from it comes furḍat al-qaws (the notch of the bow), and farāʾiḍ al-mirath (the shares of inheritance) and farḍ al-nafaqah (the obligation of maintenance). It is also reported from him: "faradnaha" meaning "We detailed it and made it clear." It has also been said that the form indicates intensification, because of the abundance of obligations in it.

The word "sūrah" in the language is a name for a noble rank (manzilah sharifah), and for this reason a portion of the Qur'an is called a sūrah. Zuhayr said [the verse is recorded as such in the originals, though it is well known that this verse belongs to al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, from a poem in praise of al-Nuʿman and seeking his pardon]:

"Did you not see that Allah has given you a sūrah, / Every king is seen swaying beneath it?"

The matter has already been discussed in the introduction of the book (see vol. 1, p. 65).

It has also been read as "sūrah" with a nominative (raf') ending, on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "anzalnaha," as said by Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Akhfash. Al-Zajjaj, al-Farraʾ and al-Mubarrad said: "sūrah" is in the nominative because it is the predicate of an implied subject, since it is indefinite and one does not begin with an indefinite in every context; i.e., "this is a sūrah." It is possible that his saying "sūrah" is the subject, and what follows it is a qualifier that removed it from pure indefiniteness, so beginning with it became acceptable for that reason, and the predicate would then be in his saying "al-zaniyatu wa-l-zani" (the adulterous woman and the adulterous man).

It has also been read as "sūratan" with an accusative (nasb) ending, on the assumption of the verb "anzalna" (We sent down): "sūratan anzalnaha" (a sūrah which We sent down). A poet said [it is al-Rabiʿ ibn Dubayʿ ibn Wahb, according to al-ʿAynī's Sharh al-Shawahid al-Kubra]:

"I fear the wolf if I pass by it alone, / And I fear the winds and the rain."

Or it may be in the accusative by supposing an implied verb, i.e., "send down a sūrah." Al-Farraʾ said: it is a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun (the hāʾ and alif), and a circumstantial state of a pronoun may precede it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

It contains twenty-two issues.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator﴾. Zina (unlawful sexual intercourse) was known in the language before the Shari'ah, like the names for theft and killing. It is the term for a man's insertion of his penis into a woman's vagina without marriage or a semblance of marriage, with her consent. If you wish, you may say: it is the insertion of one genital organ into another, which is naturally desired and forbidden by the Shari'ah. When this occurs, the hadd (prescribed punishment) becomes obligatory. The discussion of the hadd for zina, its reality, and the positions of the scholars on it has already passed. This verse abrogates (naskh) the verse of confinement and the verse of harm in Surat al-Nisa' by consensus. [[See vol. 5, p. 82 onward and p. 361 onward.]]

**Second:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿one hundred lashes﴾. This is the hadd for a free, adult, unmarried male fornicator, and likewise for a free, adult, unmarried female fornicator. The Sunnah established a year of exile (taghrib) for the general case, with differences of opinion on this. As for slaves, the obligation is fifty lashes, based on His saying: ﴿So if they commit immorality, they shall receive half the punishment of free chaste women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25]. This applies to a female slave, and a male slave is in the same position. As for a free married man (muhsan), his punishment is stoning (rajm) rather than lashing. Some scholars say: he is lashed one hundred times and then stoned. All of this has already been explained thoroughly in al-Nisa', so there is no need to repeat it, and praise be to God.

**Third:** The majority read ﴿al-zaniyatu wa-al-zani﴾ with the nominative (raf'). 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi read al-zaniyata with the accusative (nasb). According to Sibawayh, the accusative is the more eloquent reading, because in his view it is like your saying: "Zaydan, strike." The nominative, in his view, is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), [[There is some looseness in this expression, since the reasoning that requires it to be a subject with an omitted predicate is what several exegetes have mentioned.]] and its estimated meaning is: "What is recited to you concerning [the ruling of] [[An addition from the books of tafsir.]] the fornicatress and the fornicator." The people agreed on the nominative, even though, according to Sibawayh, analogy favors the accusative. As for al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, the nominative is the more eloquent in their view, and the predicate is in His saying: ﴿then lash﴾, because the meaning is: "The fornicatress and the fornicator are to be lashed by the judgment of God." This is a good view and the view of most grammarians. If you wish, you may estimate the predicate as: "They should be lashed." Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wa-al-zan﴾ without the yā' (the final long vowel).

**Fourth:** God, glorified and exalted, mentioned both the male and the female, although al-Zani alone would have sufficed. It has been said: He mentioned both for emphasis, as He said: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. [[See vol. 6, p. 159.]] It is also possible that He mentioned both here so that no one would suppose that because the man is the one who penetrates, and the woman is a place that does not penetrate, she therefore bears no hadd. So He mentioned her to remove this difficulty, which led a group of scholars, among them al-Shafi'i, into error. They said: there is no expiation (kaffarah) upon the woman for intercourse during Ramadan, because the man said: "I had intercourse with my wife during the day in Ramadan," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Expiate!" He ordered him to give expiation, and the woman is not one who has had intercourse and is not one who penetrates.

**Fifth:** The "fornicatress" is mentioned first in the verse because in that era the zina of women was widespread, and the Arabs' women and the prostitutes of the time had banners (signs) and openly displayed this. It was said: zina by women is more shameful, and it is more harmful because of pregnancy. It was also said: because desire is stronger in women and dominates them more, so He placed her first as a severe warning to restrain her desire. Although modesty (haya') was instilled in her, once she commits zina all of her modesty departs. Furthermore, shame attaches more to women, since their station is seclusion (al-hajb) [[In the originals: "al-hajbah."]] and protection. So their mention was given precedence as a sign of severity and concern.

**Sixth:** The alif and lam in His saying ﴿al-zaniyatu wa-al-zani﴾ are for the category (li-al-jins), and this indicates that the ruling is general to all fornicators. Whoever says that lashing is to be combined with stoning says: the Sunnah has added a ruling, so it is carried out together with the lashing. This is the view of Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, did so with Shurahah. Its explanation has already passed in al-Nisa'. [[See vol. 5, p. 87.]] The majority said: it is specific to the two virgins (al-bikrayn), and they cited as evidence that it is not general the exclusion of male and female slaves from it.

**Seventh:** God, glorified and exalted, stated what is obligatory upon the two fornicators when testimony is given against them, as will come, and the scholars agreed on this. They differed about what is obligatory upon a man found with a woman under one garment. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: each of them is to be struck one hundred lashes. This is reported from 'Umar and 'Ali, but it is not established as authentic from them. 'Ata' and Sufyan al-Thawri said: they are to be disciplined (yu'addabani). Malik and Ahmad also said this, according to the degree of their positions on discipline. Ibn al-Mundhir said: most of those whom we have seen hold that the one found in this state should be disciplined. The selection of what is correct in this issue has already passed in Hud, [[In pp. 88–89 of vol. 9, he mentioned some rulings on discipline, and perhaps the author thought he had mentioned the details. See also vol. 5, p. 86.]] and praise be to God alone.

**Eighth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-ijlidu﴾ [then lash]. The fa' (then) entered because this is a place of command, and the command in the imperfect form functions as a condition. Al-Mubarrad said: it carries the meaning of a consequence (jaza'), i.e., if a fornicator commits zina, then do such-and-such to him, and for this reason the fa' entered. Likewise: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. [[See vol. 6, p. 159.]]

**Ninth:** There is no disagreement that the addressees of this command are the imam (ruler) and whoever stands in his place. Malik and al-Shafi'i added: the masters (al-sadah) concerning their slaves. Al-Shafi'i said: for each there is lashing and amputation. Malik said: lashing but not amputation. It has also been said: the address is to the Muslims, because upholding the symbols of religion is obligatory upon the Muslims, and then the imam acts on their behalf, since it is not possible for them to gather together to carry out the hudud.

**Tenth:** The scholars agreed that lashing with a whip is obligatory. The whip with which one must be lashed should be one between two whips: neither harsh nor soft. Malik transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that a man confessed to zina against himself during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called for a whip, and a broken whip was brought, and he said: "Above this." Then a new whip was brought whose tip had not been cut (i.e., its edge was still sharp and had not been worn down), and he said: "Below this." Then a whip was brought that had been used, and it was supple. [[The thamarah (tip) means: the end, meaning its end is sharp, its edge has not been broken and it has not been worn. "Rukiba bihi" means its edge has been broken and it has been worn, and it has not become so soft that the one struck by it feels no pain. (See Muwatta', Kitab al-Hudud.)] Then he ordered it, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was lashed… [the hadith]. Abu 'Umar said: this hadith has been transmitted as mursal (with a missing link) by all the narrators of the Muwatta', and I do not know of it being connected (musnad) in any way with this wording. Ma'mar transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from the Prophet (ﷺ) something similar in exact wording. It has been mentioned in al-Ma'idah that 'Umar lashed Qudamah for wine with a complete whip, meaning a middle one. [[In the originals: "al-Jarud," which is an error, because the one whom our master 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, lashed was Qudamah ibn Maz'un. The author, may God have mercy on him, mentioned his story in vol. 6, p. 297, so refer to it there, and see his biography in the books on the Companions.]]

**Eleventh:** The scholars differed about stripping the one being lashed for zina. Malik, Abu Hanifah and others said: he is stripped, but the woman is left with something that covers her, though not something that protects her from the blows. Al-Awza'i said: the imam has the choice: if he wishes he strips him, and if he wishes he leaves him. Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: he is not stripped, but he is left with a shirt. Ibn Mas'ud said: it is not permissible in this case to strip or to stretch out [the one being lashed]. Al-Thawri also said this.

**Twelfth:** The scholars differed about how men and women are to be struck. Malik said: men and women are equal in all the hudud. Neither of them is to be made to lie down, and in his view it is only valid on the back. Ashab al-Ra'y (the Hanafis) and al-Shafi'i hold that the man should be lashed while standing, and this is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him. Al-Layth [ibn Sa'd [[From b, j, t and k.]]], Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: the striking in all the hudud and in discretionary punishment (ta'zir) is done with the person stripped and standing, not stretched out, except for the hadd of slander (qadhf), where he is struck while wearing his clothes. Al-Mahdawi related this in al-Tahsil from Malik. The padding and the fur are removed from him. Al-Shafi'i said: if stretching him out is beneficial, he is stretched out.

**Thirteenth:** They differed about the places on a person's body that are struck in the hudud. Malik said: all the hudud are struck only on the back, and likewise discretionary punishment. Al-Shafi'i and his companions said: the face and the genitals are avoided, and the other limbs are struck. This is reported from 'Ali. Ibn 'Umar pointed to striking the legs of a slave woman whom he had lashed for zina. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: there is consensus on protecting the face, the private parts and the vital organs. They differed about striking the head. The majority said: the head is avoided. Abu Yusuf said: the head is struck. This is reported from 'Umar and his son, and they both said: the head is struck. 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, struck Subaygh [[He is Subaygh (on the pattern of Amir) ibn 'Usul, who used to trouble people with obscure questions and inquiries, so 'Umar exiled him to Basra.]] on the head, and this was discretionary punishment (ta'zir), not a hadd. Among Malik's proofs is what the people found in practice, and the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The evidence, or else the hadd on your back," which will come.

**Fourteenth issue:** The beating that is obligatory is one that is painful but does not wound or break the skin, and the one administering it should not raise his hand above his armpit. This is the view of the majority, and it was the view of ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, may God be pleased with them both. ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, was brought a man who was to receive a prescribed punishment (ḥadd), and a whip that was between two whips was brought. He said to the one administering the punishment: "Strike, but do not let your armpit be seen, and give each limb its due." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, was also brought a drinker of wine, and he said: "I will send you to a man who will not show you any leniency." So he sent him to Muṭīʿ ibn al-Aswad al-ʿAdawī, and said: "When you wake tomorrow, administer the ḥadd to him." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, came while he was beating him severely, and said: "You have killed the man! How many did you strike him?" He said: "Sixty." He said: "Reduce it by twenty."

Abū ʿUbayda [his statement [[in b and k]]] said: "Reduce it by twenty" means: make the severity of this beating that you have struck him with a retribution (qiṣāṣ) for the twenty that remain, and do not strike him the twenty.

In this report there is jurisprudence (fiqh) that the beating of a drinker is a light beating.

The scholars have differed regarding which prescribed punishments are the most severe in beating, and they are:

**Fifteenth issue:** Mālik and his companions and al-Layth ibn Saʿd said: the beating in all the prescribed punishments is equal, a beating that is not severe, between two beatings. This is also the view of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions said: discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) is the most severe beating, and the beating for fornication is more severe than the beating for wine, and the beating for the drinker is more severe than the beating for slander (qadhf). Al-Thawrī said: the beating for fornication is more severe than the beating for slander, and the beating for slander is more severe than the beating for wine.

Mālik argued from the fact that the stipulation (tawqīf) regarding the number of lashes was transmitted, and nothing was transmitted from any of them, from one whom submission is obligatory to, indicating either a lessening or an increase. Abū Ḥanīfa argued from the action of ʿUmar, for he beat in discretionary punishment more severely than he did for fornication. Al-Thawrī argued that since fornication has a greater number of lashes, it is impossible that slander should be more effective in inflicting pain. The same applies to wine, because the ḥadd was established only through independent reasoning (ijtihād), and the course of matters of independent reasoning does not have the strength of matters of stipulation.

**Sixteenth issue:** The prescribed punishment that God has ordained for fornication, wine, slander and other offences should be carried out in the presence of the rulers (ḥukkām), and none carries it out except the most virtuous and best of people, whom the leader (imām) chooses for that. The Companions, may God be pleased with them, did likewise whenever such matters occurred to them. The reason for this is that it is an execution of a legal principle and an act of worship (qurba taʿabbudiyya), and it is obligatory to safeguard its performance, its measure, its place and its condition, such that none of its conditions or rulings is exceeded. The blood and sanctity of a Muslim are great, so it is obligatory to observe them to the fullest extent possible.

It is related in the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) report from Ḥuḍayn [with an unpointed ḥāʾ, a damma and a dotted ḍād] ibn al-Mundhir Abū Sasān, who said: "I witnessed ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, and al-Walīd was brought, having prayed the dawn prayer two rak'as, then he said: 'Shall I add more?' Two men testified against him, one of them Ḥumrān, that he had drunk wine, and another testified that he saw him vomiting. ʿUthmān said: 'He did not vomit until he had drunk it.' Then he said: 'O ʿAlī, stand up and flog him.' ʿAlī said: 'Stand up, O Ḥasan, and flog him.' Ḥasan said: 'Give the hot one (ḥārrahā) to the one who takes charge of its cool one (qārrahā)' [al-Nawawī said in his commentary on this ḥadīth: 'al-ḥārr is the severe and disliked, and al-qārr is the cold, pleasant and good. This is one of the proverbs of the Arabs, and its meaning is: let whoever takes charge of its harshness and its filth be the one who takes charge of its sweetness and pleasures. The pronoun refers to the caliphate and rule; that is, just as ʿUthmān and his close relatives take charge of the sweetness of the caliphate and monopolise it, they should take charge of its distress and its filth. Its meaning is: let ʿUthmān himself, or some of his closest and nearest relatives, take charge of this flogging.'], then he said: 'O ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, stand up and flog him.' So he flogged him, while ʿAlī was counting..." The ḥadīth has been mentioned earlier in (the commentary on) Sūrat al-Mā'ida. So observe ʿUthmān's words to the imām ʿAlī: "Stand up and flog him."

**Seventeenth issue:** God, exalted is He, specified the number of lashes for fornication and slander. For wine, the stipulation of eighty was established through the action of ʿUmar in the presence of all [i.e., in their presence] of the Companions, as mentioned earlier in Sūrat al-Mā'ida [see vol. 6, p. 297], so it is not permissible to exceed the prescribed punishment in any of these.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This applies so long as people are not persistent in evil, and sins have not become sweet to them such that they make them a habit, and incline towards them with leniency, so that they do not desist from a wrong they have committed. Then severity becomes required, and the punishment is increased [in b, j, t and k: 'the flogging'] because of the increase in the sin. ʿUmar was brought a man who was drunk in Ramaḍān, and he beat him a hundred lashes: eighty for the ḥadd of wine and twenty for violating the sanctity of the month. Thus punishments must be composed in proportion to the gravity of the offences and the violation of sanctities. A man once played with a child, and the governor beat him three hundred lashes, and Mālik did not object when it reached him [the addition of Ibn al-ʿArabī's uncle]. How then would he feel if he saw our time, with the violation of sanctities, the recklessness towards sins, the public display of wrongdoing, the selling of prescribed punishments, and slaves being entrusted with carrying them out in the office of judges! He would die of grief and would not sit with anyone. And God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian."

I say: For this meaning, God knows best, the punishment for wine was increased until it reached eighty. Al-Dāraquṭnī related: "al-Qāḍī al-Ḥusayn ibn Ismāʿīl narrated to us: Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm al-Dawraqī narrated to us: Ṣafwān ibn ʿĪsā narrated to us: Usāma ibn Zayd narrated to us, from al-Zuhrī, who said: 'ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar informed me, saying: I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Ḥunayn, moving among the people, asking about the dwelling of Khālid ibn al-Walīd. A drunkard was brought to him.' He said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to those with him, and they beat him with what was in their hands.' He said: 'And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) threw dust upon him.' He said: 'Then Abū Bakr, may God be pleased with him, was brought a drunkard,' he said: 'So he took into account what they had done in beating him on that day, and he beat forty.' Al-Zuhrī said: 'Then Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān informed me, from Ibn Wabra al-Kalbī, who said: Khālid ibn al-Walīd sent me to ʿUmar.' He said: 'I came to him, and with him were ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, and they were reclining with him in the mosque. I said: Khālid ibn al-Walīd sent me to you, and he sends you greetings, and says: The people have indulged excessively in wine, and they have treated the punishment for it with contempt!' ʿUmar said: 'These men are with you, so ask them.' ʿAlī said: 'We see that when he is drunk he raves, and when he raves he slanders, and the slanderer deserves eighty.' He said: 'ʿUmar said: Convey to your companion what he said.' He said: 'So Khālid flogged eighty and ʿUmar flogged eighty.' He said: 'And when ʿUmar was brought a weak man who had committed a lapse, he beat him forty. He said: ʿUthmān also flogged eighty and forty.'"

From this same meaning is his (ﷺ) saying: "Had the new moon been delayed, I would have increased [the fasting] for you," as a deterrent to them when they refused to desist. In another narration: "Had the month been extended for us, we would have continued in continuous fasting (waṣāl), such that those who go to extremes would abandon their excess." [This ḥadīth is mentioned in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim in the Book of Fasting, chapter on the prohibition of continuous fasting, and in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī in the Book of Adherence to the Sunna, chapter on what is disliked of excess and dispute, etc.]

Ḥāmid ibn Yaḥyā related from Sufyān, from Mis'ar, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Marwān, that ʿAlī beat al-Najāshī for wine a hundred lashes. Abū ʿAmr mentioned it and did not mention its cause.

**Eighteenth issue:** God's saying: ﴿Let not pity for them overtake you in the religion of God﴾, meaning: do not refrain from carrying out the prescribed punishments out of compassion for the one being punished, and do not lighten the beating without causing pain. This is the view of a group of the exegetes (ahl al-tafsīr). Al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: "Let not pity for them overtake you" refers to the beating and the flogging. Abū Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, said: "Carrying out a prescribed punishment in a land is better for its people than forty nights of rain," then he recited this verse. Ra'fa (pity) is the most tender mercy. It has been read as "ra'fa" with an open alif, on the pattern fa'la, and as "ra'āfa," on the pattern fa'āla. These are three dialects, and all of them are verbal nouns, the most famous being the first, from ra'ūf when he is tender and merciful. It is said: ra'fa and ra'āfa, like ka'ba and ka'āba. I have shown pity to him (raʾftu bihi) and I have been pitied for him (ruʾftu bihi). Al-Raʾūf is among the attributes of God, exalted is He: the compassionate and merciful.

**Nineteenth issue:** God's saying: (i.e., in the judgment of God), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He could not take his brother under the law of the king﴾ [Yūsuf 12:76], meaning: under his judgment. It has also been said: "in the religion of God" means in obedience to God and His law, in what He has commanded you regarding the carrying out of the prescribed punishments. He established this for them, by way of firmness and encouragement, with His saying: ﴿If you believe in God﴾. This is like when you say to a man whom you are urging: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such!" meaning: these are the deeds of men. [See vol. 9, p. 235 onward.]

**Twentieth issue:** God's saying: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾. It has been said: none should witness the punishment except one who does not deserve the disciplining [in j, t and k: "except one who deserves"; in b: "except one who deserves". The latter is probably more correct.] Mujāhid said: "A man or more, up to a thousand." Ibn Zayd said: "There must be the presence of four, by analogy with testimony regarding fornication, since this is a branch of it." This is the view of Mālik, al-Layth and al-Shāfiʿī. ʿIkrima and ʿAṭāʾ said: "There must be two," and this is the well-known view of Mālik, since he regarded it as a place of testimony. al-Zuhrī said: "Three, since that is the minimum of plurality." al-Ḥasan said: "One or more," and he is also reported to have said: "Ten." al-Rabīʿ said: "More than three."

The argument of Mujāhid is God's saying: ﴿Why did not a band from every group of them go forth [Tawba 9:122]﴾ and His saying: ﴿If two groups [ṭāʾifatān] [Ḥujurāt 49:9]﴾, and this was revealed concerning the fighting of two men. Likewise is His saying: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾. The single individual is called a group (ṭāʾifa) up to a thousand. This is also stated by Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibrāhīm. Abū Barza al-Aslamī ordered a slave girl of his who had committed fornication and given birth to have a garment cast over her, and he ordered his son to beat her fifty lashes, not severely nor lightly, but painfully. He summoned a group, then recited: ﴿And let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾.

**Twenty-first issue:** There is disagreement regarding the purpose of the presence of the group. Is the aim of it to bring humiliation upon the fornicators and reproach in the presence of people, and that this deters the one punished, and whoever witnesses and attends it takes a lesson from it and is restrained by it, and its account spreads so that those after him take heed from it? Or is it a supplication for them both for repentance and mercy? These are two opinions among the scholars.

**Twenty-second issue** [It should be noted that the principal issues are twenty-one, apart from you, so that is twenty-two, as is indicated]: It is reported from Ḥudhayfa, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O assembly of people, beware of fornication, for it has six characteristics: three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for those in this world, it removes radiance, brings poverty, and shortens life. As for those in the Hereafter, it necessitates divine wrath, a bad reckoning, and eternal abiding in the Fire." And from Anas that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The deeds of my community are presented every Monday and Thursday, and the wrath of God intensifies against fornicators." And from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "When it is the night of the middle of Shaʿbān, God looks upon my community and forgives every believer who does not associate anything with God, except five: a sorcerer, a soothsayer, one who is undutiful to his parents, one who persists in drinking wine, and one who persists in fornication."

There are seven issues in this verse.

The first issue: the scholars differed about the meaning of this verse, and there are six interpretations. The first is that the purpose of the verse is to denounce fornication (zina) and to make its wrongness clear, and that it is forbidden for the believers. Its connection with what precedes it is fine and eloquent. By His words "does not marry" (lā yankiḥu) He means "does not have intercourse with" (lā yaṭa'u), so that nikāḥ (marriage) here means sexual intercourse (jimāʿ). The matter is repeated for emphasis and to address both parties. Then He added the pairing of the idolatress and the idolater, because polytheism (shirk) is more general than fornication in sins. The meaning is: the fornicator, at the time of his fornication, has intercourse only with a fornicatress from among the Muslims, or with one who is better than her among the idolatresses. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and his companions that nikāḥ in this verse means intercourse (waṭʾ). Al-Zajjāj denied this and said: "Nikāḥ in the Book of Allah is only known to mean marriage (tazwīj)." This is not so, for in the Qur'an there is ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqara 2:230], and the Prophet (ﷺ) explained that it means intercourse. This has already been discussed in al-Baqara (see vol. 3, p. 146). Al-Ṭabarī mentioned something close to this interpretation from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima, but it is neither clear nor complete. Al-Khaṭṭābī related from Ibn ʿAbbās that its meaning is intercourse, that is: there is no fornication except with a fornicatress, and this implies that it is fornication on both sides. This is one opinion.

The second: what Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that Murthid ibn Abī Marthad used to carry prisoners in Makkah. There was a prostitute in Makkah called ʿAnāq, who was his friend. He said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I marry ʿAnāq?' He remained silent with me, and then this was revealed: ﴿The fornicatress—none marries her except a fornicator or an idolater﴾. He called me, recited it to me, and said: 'Do not marry her.'" This is the wording of Abū Dāwūd, and the hadith of al-Tirmidhī is more complete. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: "This is specific to this woman, since she was a disbeliever. As for a believing fornicatress, the contract with her is not annulled."

The third: it is also specific to a man among the Muslims who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to marry a woman called Umm Mahzūl, who was among the prostitutes, and she stipulated that he would support her. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. This was said by ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and Mujāhid.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning the People of the Ṣuffa, who were a group of the Emigrants (Muhājirūn). They had no dwellings or tribes in Madinah, so they stayed in the ṣuffa (the raised platform) of the mosque. They were four hundred men who sought provision during the day and took shelter in the ṣuffa at night. In Madinah there were prostitutes who openly practised immorality and were well provided with clothing and food. The People of the Ṣuffa intended to marry them, so that they could live in their houses and eat from their food and wear their clothing. So this verse was revealed to protect them from that. This was said by Ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ.

The fifth: al-Zajjāj and others reported from al-Ḥasan that he said: "What is meant is the fornicator who has been subjected to the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), and the fornicatress who has been subjected to it." He said: "This is a ruling from Allah, so it is not permissible for a fornicator who has received the ḥadd to marry anyone except a woman who has received the ḥadd." Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī said something similar. In the Muṣannaf of Abū Dāwūd, from Abū Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A fornicator who has received the ḥadd does not marry except one like him." It is also narrated that a man who had received the ḥadd married a woman who had not, and ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) separated them. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "This view is not sound in reasoning, just as it is not established by transmission. Is it valid to make the marriage of a man who has received the ḥadd dependent on the marriage of a woman who has received it? By what report would that be, and on what principle of the Sharīʿah would it be analogised?"

I say: Ilkiyā related this view from some later companions of al-Shāfiʿī, that if a fornicator marries a woman who is not a fornicatress, they are to be separated because of the apparent meaning of the verse. Ilkiyā said: "If one acts on the apparent meaning, it would necessarily follow that a fornicator may marry an idolatress, and a fornicatress may marry herself to an idolater. This is extremely far-fetched, and it is a complete departure from Islam." Perhaps these people also said that the verse is abrogated only in the case of the idolater, not the fornicatress.

The sixth: that it is abrogated (mansūkha). Mālik narrated from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is married by none but a fornicator or an idolater." He said: "It was abrogated by the verse that follows it: ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ [al-Nūr 24:32]." This was also said by Ibn ʿAmr, who said: "The fornicatress has entered among the single (ayāmā) of the Muslims." Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās said: "Most scholars hold this view." The jurists say: whoever has committed fornication with a woman may marry her, and others may marry her too. This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, Sālim, Jābir ibn Zayd (the established report from Jābir ibn Zayd is that the one who fornicated with her is forbidden to her, and that is verified), ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Mālik ibn Anas, and it is the view of Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions. Al-Shāfiʿī said: "The matter concerning it is as Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said; God willing, it is abrogated." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The mention of polytheism in this verse weakens these approaches." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "What seems right to me is that nikāḥ either refers to intercourse, as Ibn ʿAbbās said, or to the contract. If it refers to intercourse, its meaning is: there is no fornication except with a fornicatress. This is an expression that the sexual act of the man and of the woman occurs from both sides, and the meaning of the verse would be: intercourse with a fornicatress happens only from a fornicator or an idolater. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and it is a sound meaning."

If it is said: when a mature man commits fornication with a girl who is not yet mature, or a sane man with a madwoman, or an awake man with a sleeping woman, that is fornication on the part of the man, so this is a fornicator who has married someone who is not a fornicatress, and then the meaning goes outside its intended scope. We say: it is fornication from every side, except that the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) is waived for one of them and applies to the other. If the meaning is the contract, then it means: one who marries a fornicatress who has committed fornication and has consummated it without ensuring her istibrāʾ (the waiting period to confirm she is not pregnant by another) is in the position of a fornicator, except that there is no ḥadd upon him because the scholars differ on this. As for one who concludes the contract with her and does not consummate it until he has ensured her istibrāʾ, that is permissible by consensus (ijmāʿ).

It was also said: the meaning of the verse is not that a fornicator never marries anyone except a fornicatress, since it can be imagined that he marries a woman who is not a fornicatress. Rather, the meaning is that whoever marries a fornicatress is himself a fornicator. It is as if He said: "No fornicator marries a fornicatress except a fornicator," so the sentence is inverted, because he does not marry a fornicatress except while being content with her fornication, and he is only content with that if he also fornicates.

The second issue: this verse is evidence that marriage to a fornicatress is valid. If the wife of a man commits fornication, the marriage is not thereby annulled, and if the husband commits fornication, his marriage with his wife is not annulled either. This is on the basis that the verse is abrogated. It was also said that it is muḥkama (not abrogated). This will come later.

The third issue: it is reported that a man committed fornication with a woman in the time of Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and he flogged them both one hundred lashes, then married one of them to the other in his place, and exiled them for one year. Similar things were reported from ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd and Jābir (may Allah be pleased with them all). Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Its beginning is illicit intercourse (sifāḥ) and its end is marriage (nikāḥ)." This is like a man who stole fruit from a garden and then went to the owner of the orchard and bought his fruit from him: what he stole is forbidden and what he bought is lawful. On this view Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī acted, holding that water (semen) has no sanctity. It was reported from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "If a man commits fornication with a woman and then marries her afterwards, they are both fornicators forever." On this view Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him) acted, holding that he may not marry her until she has been cleansed of his corrupt water, because marriage has sanctity, and part of its sanctity is that it not be poured onto the water of illicit intercourse, so that the forbidden is not mixed with the lawful and the water of humiliation is not mixed with the water of honour.

The fourth issue: Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: whoever is known for fornication or other sinful conduct and openly practises it, and marries into a family of decency while deceiving them about himself, they have the choice of remaining with him or separating from him. This is like a defect among defects. He argued from the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "A fornicator who has been flogged (al-majlūd) does not marry except one like her." Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said: he mentioned the flogged one only because of his notoriety in wickedness, and it is he from whom one must be separated from others. As for one who is not known for wickedness, no.

The fifth issue: some of the earlier scholars said: the verse is muḥkama (unabrogated, of firm ruling), and not abrogated. According to these, if a man commits fornication, the marriage between him and his wife is annulled, and if the wife commits fornication, the marriage between her and her husband is annulled. Some of these said: marriage is not dissolved by that, but the husband is commanded to divorce her if she commits fornication, and if he keeps her he is sinful. It is not permissible to marry a fornicatress, nor to marry a fornicator, unless repentance becomes evident, and then marriage is permitted.

The sixth issue: "And that is forbidden to the believers" (wa-ḥurrima dhālika ʿalā al-mu'minīn), that is, the marriage of those prostitutes. Some of the interpreters claim that Allah the Exalted forbade the marriage of those prostitutes to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and among the most famous of them was ʿAnāq. [This is based on the abrogation of the verse; its basis is not clearly established.]

The seventh issue: Allah the Exalted forbade fornication in His Book, so wherever a man commits fornication, the ḥadd is incumbent upon him. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Thawr. The people of opinion (Aṣḥāb al-Ra'y) said concerning a Muslim man who was in the land of war under safe conduct (amān) and committed fornication there and then left: he is not punished. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the land of war and the land of Islam are the same, and whoever commits fornication is liable to the ḥadd, according to the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nūr 24:2].

There are twenty-six issues (masa'il) in this passage.

**The first:** This verse was revealed concerning those who make false accusations (qadhafah). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Its occasion was what was said about 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her." It was also said: "Rather, it was revealed on account of accusers in general, not that particular incident." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We have not found in the reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) any report that explicitly states the cause of the accusation. The apparent meaning of the Book of Allah the Exalted is sufficient in indicating the accusation that requires the hadd (the prescribed punishment), and the scholars are in agreement on this."

**The second:** His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse﴾ means those who revile. The term "throwing" (ramy) is borrowed for this, because it harms with speech, as al-Nabigha said:

*"And the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."*

Another said:

*"He accused me of a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and on account of the well (al-Tawi) he threw it at me."*

[[The verse is by Ibn Ahmar. Al-'Alawi means the well.]]

It is also called qadhf (accusation), and from it is the hadith: "Ibn Umayya accused (qadhafa) his wife with Shurayk ibn al-Sahma'," meaning he threw (ramaha) it at her.

**The third:** Allah the Exalted mentioned women in the verse, as they are the more important (ahamm) [[In the original manuscripts: "from the point of view that it is more important." The wording in al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan is clearer, which is: "He specified women with this, although men share them in the ruling, because accusation concerning them is more abominable and more painful to souls, and because women are the object of men's desire," etc.]], and throwing them with immorality is more shameful and more painful to the souls. The accusation of men is included in the ruling of the verse by meaning, and the consensus of the Ummah is upon this. This is like His explicit prohibition of the flesh of swine, which includes its fat and cartilage and similar things, by meaning and consensus.

Al-Zahrawi related that the meaning is: "And the chaste souls (al-anfus al-muhsanat)," so by its wording it includes men and women, and His saying supports this: ﴿And the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. Others said: He meant by al-muhsanat the private parts (al-furuj), as the Exalted said: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], so the private parts of men and women are included in it.

It was said: He only mentioned the foreign woman when she is accused, so that the accusation of a man against his wife would be included with it. And Allah knows best.

Jumhur (the majority) read "al-muhsanat" with a fatha on the sad, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. Al-muhsanat here means the chaste (al-'afa'if). The meaning of ihsan (chastity/marital protection) and its levels has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'." And praise be to Allah.

**The fourth:** For qadhf there are nine conditions according to the scholars. Two conditions concern the accuser: sanity (al-'aql) and puberty (al-bulugh), because they are the foundations of legal responsibility (taklif), since legal responsibility does not apply without them. Two conditions concern the thing by which one accuses: that the accusation be of an act of intercourse for which the hadd is obligatory, which is zina (fornication) and liwat (sodomy), or of denying paternity, and not of other sins. And five conditions concern the one accused: sanity, puberty, Islam, freedom, and chastity from the immorality with which she was accused, whether or not she is chaste from other things.

We stipulated sanity and puberty for the accused just as we stipulated them for the accuser, even though they are not among the meanings of ihsan, because the hadd was only established to deter harm inflicted on the accused, and there is no harm upon one who lacks sanity and puberty, since liwat with them is not described as zina, nor is it described as such from them.

**The fifth:** The scholars agreed that if one explicitly mentions zina, it is qadhf and a throwing (ramy) that requires the hadd. If one speaks by allusion (ta'ridh) and does not state explicitly, Malik said: "It is qadhf." Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: "It is not qadhf unless he says, 'I meant by it qadhf.'" The evidence for what Malik said is that the purpose of the hadd for qadhf is only to remove the disgrace which the accuser inflicted upon the one accused. So when the disgrace occurs through allusion, it must be qadhf like explicit statement, and reliance is upon understanding. The Exalted has related about Shu'ayb: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87], meaning the foolish, the astray. They alluded to him with reviling through words that appear as praise, according to one interpretation, as was mentioned earlier in "Hud." [[See vol. 9, p. 87.]]

The Exalted said about Abu Jahl: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. He said, relating about Maryam: ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman (baghiyya)﴾ [Maryam: 28]. So they praised her father and negated baghaa' (unchastity, i.e., zina) from her mother, and by this they alluded to Maryam. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And for their disbelief and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nisa': 156]. Their disbelief is well known, and the tremendous slander is the allusion to her, meaning: your father was not a man of evil and your mother was not unchaste, so you are contrary to both of them, and you have brought this child. [[See vol. 6, p. 7 onwards.]]

The Exalted said: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah. And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. From this statement it is understood that what is meant is that the disbelievers are not upon guidance, and that Allah the Exalted and His Messenger are upon guidance. Thus what is understood from this allusion is what is understood from its explicit form. [[See vol. 14, p. 298.]]

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, imprisoned al-Hutay'ah when he said:

*"Leave off the noble deeds, do not journey in pursuit of them, and sit down, for indeed you are the one who eats and clothes himself."*

Because he likened him to women, who are fed, given drink, and clothed.

And when he heard the saying of al-Najashi:

*"His tribe do not betray a covenant, and they do not wrong people by the weight of a mustard seed."*

He said: "Would that the address were like that. The poet only meant the weakness of the tribe, and there are many like it."

**Sixth issue:** The majority of scholars hold that there is no hadd (the fixed prescribed punishment) for one who slanders a man or woman of the People of the Book. Al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Abi Layla said: the hadd is due if she has a child by a Muslim. A third view is that if one slanders a Christian woman married to a Muslim, he is flogged the hadd. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Most scholars agree and hold the first view. I have not encountered anyone who disagrees with it. If a Christian slanders a free Muslim, he receives what a Muslim would receive: eighty lashes. I know of no disagreement on this. [In the manuscript k: "ikhtilafan" (a disagreement).]

**Seventh issue:** The majority of scholars hold that if a slave slanders a free person, he is flogged forty lashes, because it is a hadd that is halved by slavery, like the hadd for fornication. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb that he is flogged eighty lashes. Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad flogged a slave who slandered a free person eighty lashes, and al-Awza'i also held this view.

The majority argued from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿If they commit an outrageous act, then upon them is half the punishment of free women﴾ [al-Nisa: 25]. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 136.]

Others said: We understood there that the hadd for fornication belongs to Allah, and that it may be lighter for one upon whom Allah's blessings are few, and more severe for one upon whom Allah's blessings are great. As for the hadd for slander, it is a right of a human being, due for the offence against the honour of the one slandered, and the offence does not differ by slavery or freedom. They sometimes said: If it differed, it would have been mentioned as it was mentioned for fornication.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: What the common scholars of the regions hold is the first view, and I hold it too.

**Eighth issue:** The scholars agreed that a free person is not flogged for a slave who slanders him, because their ranks are different, and because of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever slanders his slave with fornication, the hadd will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection, unless it is as he said." Recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim. In some of its chains: "Whoever slanders his slave with fornication and it is not established, the hadd of eighty will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection." Recorded by al-Daraqutni.

The scholars said: That happens in the Hereafter because ownership is lifted there, and the noble and the lowly, the free and the slave, are equal, and no one has superiority except by piety. Since that is so, people are equal in the hadd and in sanctity, and retaliation is taken from each for the other, unless the wronged person pardons the wrongdoer. They were not made equal in this world so that the intrusion would not enter upon the owners through the equality they grant them, and so that no sanctity or superiority in standing would remain for them, and the purpose of subjugation would be defeated. It is the wisdom of the All-Wise, the All-Knowing; there is no god but Him.

**Ninth issue:** Malik and al-Shafi'i said: If one slanders a person whom he considers a slave but who is free, he incurs the hadd. Al-Hasan al-Basri said this too, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Malik said: If one slanders an umm walad (a slave mother of a child by her master), he is subject to the hadd. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, and it is the analogy of al-Shafi'i's view. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: There is no hadd on him.

**Tenth issue:** The scholars differed concerning one who says to a man: "O you who had intercourse between the thighs!" Ibn al-Qasim said: He incurs the hadd, because it is an allusion. Ashhab said: There is no hadd in it, because it is an attribution to an act that is not counted as fornication by consensus.

**Eleventh issue:** If one accuses a girl who can be penetrated before puberty of fornication, it is slander according to Malik. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: It is not slander, because it is not fornication, since there is no hadd for her, and he is subject to ta'zir (discretionary discipline). Ibn al-'Arabi said: The question is open and difficult, but Malik sought to protect the honour of the one slandered, and others considered protecting the back of the slanderer. Protecting the honour of the one slandered is preferable, because the slanderer has uncovered her concealment with the tip of his tongue, so the hadd is binding on him.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad said concerning a girl of nine: Her slanderer is flogged. Likewise, if a boy reaches ten, his slanderer is beaten. Ishaq said: If one slanders a boy who could be penetrated like him, there is the hadd upon him, and likewise for a girl who has passed nine.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: One who slanders someone who has not reached puberty is not subject to the hadd, because that is a lie, but he is disciplined for the harm.

Abu 'Ubayd said: In the hadith of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), a woman came to him and mentioned that her husband was having intercourse with her slave girl. He said: "If you are truthful, we will stone him; and if you are lying, we will flog you." She said: "Send me back to my family, I am being driven by jealousy (ghayra nagira)." [Footnote: The discussion of this phrase will follow shortly.]

Abu 'Ubayd said: In this hadith is the jurisprudence that a man who has intercourse with his wife's slave girl incurs the hadd. And in it also: if someone slanders him with that, the slanderer incurs the hadd. Do you not hear his words: "If you are lying, we will flog you"? The basis of all this is that the doer was not ignorant of what he was doing and what he was saying. If he was ignorant and claimed a doubt, the hadd is averted from him in all of that.

Also in it: if a man slanders another man in the presence of a judge while the one slandered is not present, nothing is due upon the slanderer until the one slandered comes and seeks his hadd, because one does not know that perhaps he would have confirmed it. Do you not see that 'Ali, peace be upon him, did not take up the matter with her?

Also in it: if a man is slandered before a judge, and then the one slandered comes and seeks his right, the judge enforces the hadd on the basis of his hearing it, do you not see that he says: "If you are lying, we will flog you"? This is because it is one of the rights of people.

I say: It has been disputed whether it is one of the rights of Allah or one of the rights of human beings, and this will come.

Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Asma'i said: Shu'ba asked me about the phrase "ghayra nagira." I told him: It is derived from the boiling (nagr) of the pot, which is its bubbling and surging. It is said of it: "nagirat tanghar" and "nagarat tanghir" when it boils. Its meaning is that she meant her insides were boiling from anger and jealousy when she did not find with him what she wanted. He said: It is said of it: "I saw so-and-so boiling (yatanaghgharu) against so-and-so," meaning his insides boil with rage against him.

**Twelfth issue:** One who slanders one of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) incurs two hadds. This was said by Masruq. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The sound view is that it is one hadd, because of the generality of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ (the verse), and the nobility of their station does not require an increase in the hadd for one who slanders them, because the nobility of rank does not affect the hadd, and its diminishment does not affect the hadd by disparagement. And Allah knows best. The discussion of whether one who slandered 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) is to be killed or not will come.

**Thirteenth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then they do not bring four witnesses﴾. What requires four witnesses, unlike other rights, is fornication, out of mercy to His servants and to conceal them. This was already discussed in Surat al-Nisa. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 72.]

**Fourteenth issue:** Among the conditions for the testimony of witnesses being delivered, according to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that it be in one session. If they separate, it is not testimony. 'Abd al-Malik said: Their testimony is accepted whether they are together or separate. Malik held that their gathering is an act of worship, and Ibn al-Hasan said the same. 'Abd al-Malik held that the purpose is the delivery of testimony and its being together, and that has been achieved. This is the view of 'Uthman al-Batti and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then they do not bring four witnesses﴾ and His words: ﴿so when they do not bring the witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 13], and He did not mention separated or together.

**Fifteenth issue:** If the testimony is complete but the witnesses are not upright (ʿadl), al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Sha'bi held that there is no hadd upon the witnesses or upon the one testified against. This was also the view of Ahmad, al-Nu'man and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Malik said: If four testify against him for fornication, and one of them is one whose testimony is rejected (maskhut) or a slave, they are all flogged. [In the manuscripts b, t, k: "maskhut." In j, a: "masquṭ."] Sufyan al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq said concerning four blind men who testify against a woman for fornication: they are beaten.

**Sixteenth issue:** If one of the witnesses retracts after the one testified against has been stoned for fornication, one group said: He pays a quarter of the blood-money, and nothing is due from the others. This was also said by Qatada, Hammad, 'Ikrima, Abu Hashim, Malik, Ahmad and the people of opinion. Al-Shafi'i said: If he says "I intended to have him killed," then the heirs have a choice: if they wish, they kill him; if they wish, they pardon and take a quarter of the blood-money, and he incurs the hadd. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He is killed, and the others owe three-quarters of the blood-money. Ibn Sirin said: If he says "I made a mistake and meant someone else," then he owes the full blood-money. And if he says "I intended to kill him," then he is killed. Ibn Shubruma said the same.

**Seventeenth issue:** The scholars differed concerning whether the hadd for slander is one of the rights of Allah, or one of the rights of human beings, or whether it has a mixture of both. The first view is that of Abu Hanifa. The second is that of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The third was said by some later scholars.

The benefit of the disagreement is this: if it is a right of Allah the Exalted and it reaches the imam, he enforces it even if the one slandered does not seek it. The repentance of the slanderer benefits him between himself and Allah the Exalted, and the hadd is halved by slavery as with fornication. If it is a right of a human being, the imam does not enforce it except upon the demand of the one slandered, it lapses by his pardon, and the slanderer's repentance does not benefit him until the one slandered absolves him.

**Eighteenth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿with four witnesses﴾. The reading of the majority is with the number four construed with (idafa to) "witnesses." 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar and Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir read "bi-arba'atin" (with tanwin) "shuhada'." In this there are four possibilities: it may be in the genitive position as a qualifier of "arba'a," or as an apposition. It may also be a circumstantial (hal) from an indefinite noun, or a specification (tamyiz). But there is a question about the circumstantial and the specification: the circumstantial would be from an indefinite noun, and the specification is plural. Sibawayh holds that it is tanwin of the number, and leaving its idafa is only permitted in poetry. Abu al-Fath 'Uthman ibn Jinni praised this reading and preferred it over the reading of the majority. Al-Nahhas said: It may also be that "shuhada'" is in the accusative position, meaning: "they did not bring four witnesses."

**Nineteenth issue:** The ruling on the testimony of the four is that it must be by direct observation, as they see it like the stick in the kohl-pot, as was discussed earlier in al-Nisa in the text of the hadith. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 73.] And that it be in one session, according to the view of Malik. If one of them becomes confused, all three are flogged, as 'Umar did in the matter of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. That is because Abu Bakra Nufay' ibn al-Harith and his brother Nafi' testified against him for fornication. al-Zahrawi said: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, and Ziyad, their brother by the same mother, who was attributed to Mu'awiya, and Shibl ibn Ma'bad al-Bajali. When they came to deliver the testimony and Ziyad hesitated and did not deliver it, 'Umar flogged the three mentioned.

**Twentieth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then flog them﴾. Al-jald is striking. Mujalada and mudaraba are striking with or upon hides; then "al-jald" was borrowed for other things, such as a sword or other. From this is the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

I fight them on the day of al-Hadiqa bareheaded,
as if my hand with the sword were a flame of a player.

"Eighty" is put in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar). "Lashes" is a specification (tamyiz).

(And do not accept their testimony ever after.) This implies for the duration of their lives. Then they are judged to be "fāsiqūn" (defiantly disobedient), meaning they have stepped outside obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

The twenty-first issue: Allah's words, ﴿Except those who repent﴾ [24:5]. It is in the accusative position as an exception (istithnāʾ). It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position as a substitute (badal). The meaning: "And do not accept their testimony ever, except those who repent and make amends after the slander, [then] indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

The verse thus contains three rulings concerning the slanderer: flogging him, rejecting his testimony forever, and his being a fāsiq. The exception does not apply to his flogging, by consensus, except for what al-Sha'bi is reported to have said, as will come. It applies to his being a fāsiq, by consensus. People differed over whether it applies to the rejection of his testimony. Shurayh the judge, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa said: the exception does not apply to the rejection of his testimony; rather, his fisq is removed in the sight of Allah Almighty alone. As for the testimony of the slanderer, it is never accepted at all, even if he repents and retracts his statement, and under no circumstances.

The majority (al-Jumhur) said: the exception applies to the rejection of the testimony. So when the slanderer repents, his testimony is accepted, and rejection was only because of the cause of fisq; when that is removed by repentance, his testimony is accepted absolutely, both before and after the hadd punishment. This is the view of the majority of jurists.

Then they differed about the form of his repentance. The view of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Sha'bi and others is that his repentance is only by his retracting his own statement in that slander for which he was punished with the hadd. And so ʿUmar did: he said to those who testified against al-Mughira, "Whoever retracts his statement, I will accept his testimony in what is to come; and whoever does not do so, I will not accept his testimony." So al-Shibl ibn Maʿbad and Nafiʿ ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah retracted their statements and repented, while Abu Bakrah refused to do so, and so he (ʿUmar) did not accept his testimony. al-Nahhas related this view from the people of Madina.

Another group, among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others, said: his repentance is that he reforms and his condition becomes good, even if he does not retract his statement by denial; it is sufficient for him to regret his slander, seek forgiveness for it, and abandon returning to its like. This is the view of Ibn Jarir. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: the exception applies to the three rulings. When he repents and his repentance becomes evident, he is not flogged, his testimony is accepted, and the designation of fisq is removed from him, because he has become one of those whose testimony is approved, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic has said: "And indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents" [20:82] — the verse.

The twenty-second issue: Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed as to when the testimony of the slanderer lapses. Ibn al-Majishun said: by the very act of slander. Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab and Sahnun said: it does not lapse until he is flogged; if someone prevents his flogging, whether by pardon or otherwise, his testimony is not rejected. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: his testimony during the period of the term is suspended, and the view that repentance is only by retraction of the slander is preferred; otherwise, what return to justice is there for one who slandered, was flogged, and remained in his former justice?

The twenty-third issue: They also differed, on the view that his testimony is accepted after repentance, as to in what matters it is accepted. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is accepted in everything absolutely, and likewise everyone who has been punished with a hadd in any matter. This was transmitted by Nafi' and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam from Malik, and it is the view of Ibn Kinanah. Al-Waqqar (a title of Zakariyya ibn al-Faqih al-Misri) mentioned from Malik that his testimony is not accepted in the matter for which he was punished specifically, but is accepted in other matters. This is the view of Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun. al-Utbi related the same from Asbagh and Sahnun. Sahnun said: whoever is punished with a hadd in any matter, his testimony is not accepted in a matter like that for which he was punished. Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: whoever is punished with a hadd for slander or fornication, his testimony is not accepted in any aspect of fornication, nor in slander, nor in li'an, even if he is just; they related this from Malik. They all agreed that the testimony of an illegitimate child is not accepted concerning fornication.

The twenty-fourth issue: An exception that follows a series of conjoined sentences returns to all of them according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions. According to Abu Hanifa and most of his companions, the exception returns to the nearest mentioned item, which is fisq; for this reason his testimony is not accepted, since the exception returns to fisq alone and not to the acceptance of testimony. The source of disagreement on this principle has two causes. The first: are these sentences, because of the conjunction in them, in the status of one single sentence, or does each sentence have its own independent ruling, with the conjunction particle serving merely to link and not to share? The latter is the sound view regarding the conjunction of sentences, since it is permissible to conjoin differing sentences one upon another, as is known in grammar. The second: is the exception compared to the condition in returning to the preceding sentences, so that it returns to all of them according to the jurists, or is it not compared to it, because that is analogy in language, which is invalid as known in the principles of jurisprudence? The principle is that all of this is possible and there is no preponderance, so the position of the judge of suspension is determined. The problem is reinforced by the fact that both matters have come in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: the verse of hirabah has the pronoun returning to all by agreement, and the verse of killing a believer by mistake has the exception returned to the last item by agreement, while the verse of slander is open to both readings, so suspension without preference is determined. Our scholars said: this is a universal, principled analysis. The view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both, is preferred from the standpoint of detailed jurisprudential reasoning, namely that the exception returns to fisq and to the prohibition of accepting testimony together, unless one distinguishes between them by a report that must be accepted. The Ummah agreed that repentance erases kufr, so what is below that must be more deserving of it, and Allah knows best. Abu ʿUbayd said: the exception returns to the preceding sentences. He said: the one who is accused of fornication is not more grave in crime than the one who commits fornication; then the fornicator, if he repents, his testimony is accepted, because "the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin." And if Allah accepts the repentance of a servant, the servants are more deserving of accepting it, and such an exception exists in several places in the Qur'an, among them the saying of Allah, "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger..." [5:33] up to His words, "except those who repent" [5:34]. There is no doubt that this exception returns to all. al-Zajjaj said: the slanderer is not graver in crime than the disbeliever, so his right, if he repents and makes amends, is that his testimony be accepted. He said: His words "ever" mean as long as he is a slanderer, just as it is said, "the testimony of a disbeliever is never accepted," meaning as long as he is a disbeliever. al-Sha'bi said to the one who differed on this issue: "Allah accepts his repentance, and you do not accept his testimony!" Then, if the exception returns to the last sentence according to certain usulis, then His words, "And those are the defiantly disobedient," are a causal clause and not an independent sentence, meaning: do not accept their testimony because of their fisq; so when the fisq is removed, why would their testimony not be accepted? Then the repentance of the slanderer is retraction of his statement, as ʿUmar said to the slanderers of al-Mughira in the presence of the Companions without any objection, along with the publicizing and fame of the affair from Basra to the Hijaz and other regions. Had the interpretation of the verse been what the Kufans interpreted, it would not have been possible for knowledge of that to be lost to the Companions, and they would have said to ʿUmar, "It is not permissible to accept the repentance of the slanderer ever," and they would not have been able to remain silent about the judgment by distorting the interpretation of the Book. So their view falls, and Allah is the One sought for help.

The twenty-fifth issue: al-Qushayri said: there is no disagreement that if the slanderer is not flogged, either because the one slandered died before demanding the hadd from the slanderer, or the matter was not brought to the authority, or the one slandered pardoned him, then the testimony is accepted, because according to the opponent in this issue, the prohibition of accepting testimony is conjoined to the flogging. Allah the Exalted said: "Flog them eighty lashes and never accept their testimony ever." At this point al-Shafi'i said: his condition before being flogged is worse than his condition when he is flogged, because hudud are expiations; so how would his testimony be rejected in his better state rather than in his worse of the two? I say: he spoke thus, and there is no disagreement. It has already preceded from Ibn al-Majishun that his testimony is rejected by the very act of slander. This is the view of al-Layth, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i: his testimony is rejected even if he is not flogged, because by slander he becomes defiantly disobedient, since it is among the major sins, so his testimony is not accepted until his innocence is established either by the confession of the one slandered that he committed fornication or by the establishment of proof against him.

The twenty-sixth issue: Allah's words, "and make amends" [24:5], mean manifesting repentance. It has been said: "and make amends" means amending the deed.

(Then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful) — since they repented and Allah accepted their repentance.

There are twenty-six issues (masa'il) in this passage.

**The first:** This verse was revealed concerning those who make false accusations (qadhafah). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Its occasion was what was said about 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her." It was also said: "Rather, it was revealed on account of accusers in general, not that particular incident." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We have not found in the reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) any report that explicitly states the cause of the accusation. The apparent meaning of the Book of Allah the Exalted is sufficient in indicating the accusation that requires the hadd (the prescribed punishment), and the scholars are in agreement on this."

**The second:** His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse﴾ means those who revile. The term "throwing" (ramy) is borrowed for this, because it harms with speech, as al-Nabigha said:

*"And the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand."*

Another said:

*"He accused me of a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and on account of the well (al-Tawi) he threw it at me."*

[[The verse is by Ibn Ahmar. Al-'Alawi means the well.]]

It is also called qadhf (accusation), and from it is the hadith: "Ibn Umayya accused (qadhafa) his wife with Shurayk ibn al-Sahma'," meaning he threw (ramaha) it at her.

**The third:** Allah the Exalted mentioned women in the verse, as they are the more important (ahamm) [[In the original manuscripts: "from the point of view that it is more important." The wording in al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan is clearer, which is: "He specified women with this, although men share them in the ruling, because accusation concerning them is more abominable and more painful to souls, and because women are the object of men's desire," etc.]], and throwing them with immorality is more shameful and more painful to the souls. The accusation of men is included in the ruling of the verse by meaning, and the consensus of the Ummah is upon this. This is like His explicit prohibition of the flesh of swine, which includes its fat and cartilage and similar things, by meaning and consensus.

Al-Zahrawi related that the meaning is: "And the chaste souls (al-anfus al-muhsanat)," so by its wording it includes men and women, and His saying supports this: ﴿And the chaste women among the women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. Others said: He meant by al-muhsanat the private parts (al-furuj), as the Exalted said: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91], so the private parts of men and women are included in it.

It was said: He only mentioned the foreign woman when she is accused, so that the accusation of a man against his wife would be included with it. And Allah knows best.

Jumhur (the majority) read "al-muhsanat" with a fatha on the sad, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a kasra. Al-muhsanat here means the chaste (al-'afa'if). The meaning of ihsan (chastity/marital protection) and its levels has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'." And praise be to Allah.

**The fourth:** For qadhf there are nine conditions according to the scholars. Two conditions concern the accuser: sanity (al-'aql) and puberty (al-bulugh), because they are the foundations of legal responsibility (taklif), since legal responsibility does not apply without them. Two conditions concern the thing by which one accuses: that the accusation be of an act of intercourse for which the hadd is obligatory, which is zina (fornication) and liwat (sodomy), or of denying paternity, and not of other sins. And five conditions concern the one accused: sanity, puberty, Islam, freedom, and chastity from the immorality with which she was accused, whether or not she is chaste from other things.

We stipulated sanity and puberty for the accused just as we stipulated them for the accuser, even though they are not among the meanings of ihsan, because the hadd was only established to deter harm inflicted on the accused, and there is no harm upon one who lacks sanity and puberty, since liwat with them is not described as zina, nor is it described as such from them.

**The fifth:** The scholars agreed that if one explicitly mentions zina, it is qadhf and a throwing (ramy) that requires the hadd. If one speaks by allusion (ta'ridh) and does not state explicitly, Malik said: "It is qadhf." Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: "It is not qadhf unless he says, 'I meant by it qadhf.'" The evidence for what Malik said is that the purpose of the hadd for qadhf is only to remove the disgrace which the accuser inflicted upon the one accused. So when the disgrace occurs through allusion, it must be qadhf like explicit statement, and reliance is upon understanding. The Exalted has related about Shu'ayb: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning﴾ [Hud: 87], meaning the foolish, the astray. They alluded to him with reviling through words that appear as praise, according to one interpretation, as was mentioned earlier in "Hud." [[See vol. 9, p. 87.]]

The Exalted said about Abu Jahl: ﴿Taste it! Indeed, you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. He said, relating about Maryam: ﴿O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman (baghiyya)﴾ [Maryam: 28]. So they praised her father and negated baghaa' (unchastity, i.e., zina) from her mother, and by this they alluded to Maryam. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And for their disbelief and their saying against Maryam a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nisa': 156]. Their disbelief is well known, and the tremendous slander is the allusion to her, meaning: your father was not a man of evil and your mother was not unchaste, so you are contrary to both of them, and you have brought this child. [[See vol. 6, p. 7 onwards.]]

The Exalted said: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah. And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24]. From this statement it is understood that what is meant is that the disbelievers are not upon guidance, and that Allah the Exalted and His Messenger are upon guidance. Thus what is understood from this allusion is what is understood from its explicit form. [[See vol. 14, p. 298.]]

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, imprisoned al-Hutay'ah when he said:

*"Leave off the noble deeds, do not journey in pursuit of them, and sit down, for indeed you are the one who eats and clothes himself."*

Because he likened him to women, who are fed, given drink, and clothed.

And when he heard the saying of al-Najashi:

*"His tribe do not betray a covenant, and they do not wrong people by the weight of a mustard seed."*

He said: "Would that the address were like that. The poet only meant the weakness of the tribe, and there are many like it."

**Sixth issue:** The majority of scholars hold that there is no hadd (the fixed prescribed punishment) for one who slanders a man or woman of the People of the Book. Al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Abi Layla said: the hadd is due if she has a child by a Muslim. A third view is that if one slanders a Christian woman married to a Muslim, he is flogged the hadd. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Most scholars agree and hold the first view. I have not encountered anyone who disagrees with it. If a Christian slanders a free Muslim, he receives what a Muslim would receive: eighty lashes. I know of no disagreement on this. [In the manuscript k: "ikhtilafan" (a disagreement).]
