**Seventh issue:** The majority of scholars hold that if a slave slanders a free person, he is flogged forty lashes, because it is a hadd that is halved by slavery, like the hadd for fornication. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb that he is flogged eighty lashes. Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad flogged a slave who slandered a free person eighty lashes, and al-Awza'i also held this view.

The majority argued from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿If they commit an outrageous act, then upon them is half the punishment of free women﴾ [al-Nisa: 25]. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 136.]

Others said: We understood there that the hadd for fornication belongs to Allah, and that it may be lighter for one upon whom Allah's blessings are few, and more severe for one upon whom Allah's blessings are great. As for the hadd for slander, it is a right of a human being, due for the offence against the honour of the one slandered, and the offence does not differ by slavery or freedom. They sometimes said: If it differed, it would have been mentioned as it was mentioned for fornication.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: What the common scholars of the regions hold is the first view, and I hold it too.

**Eighth issue:** The scholars agreed that a free person is not flogged for a slave who slanders him, because their ranks are different, and because of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever slanders his slave with fornication, the hadd will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection, unless it is as he said." Recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim. In some of its chains: "Whoever slanders his slave with fornication and it is not established, the hadd of eighty will be enforced upon him on the Day of Resurrection." Recorded by al-Daraqutni.

The scholars said: That happens in the Hereafter because ownership is lifted there, and the noble and the lowly, the free and the slave, are equal, and no one has superiority except by piety. Since that is so, people are equal in the hadd and in sanctity, and retaliation is taken from each for the other, unless the wronged person pardons the wrongdoer. They were not made equal in this world so that the intrusion would not enter upon the owners through the equality they grant them, and so that no sanctity or superiority in standing would remain for them, and the purpose of subjugation would be defeated. It is the wisdom of the All-Wise, the All-Knowing; there is no god but Him.

**Ninth issue:** Malik and al-Shafi'i said: If one slanders a person whom he considers a slave but who is free, he incurs the hadd. Al-Hasan al-Basri said this too, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Malik said: If one slanders an umm walad (a slave mother of a child by her master), he is subject to the hadd. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, and it is the analogy of al-Shafi'i's view. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: There is no hadd on him.

**Tenth issue:** The scholars differed concerning one who says to a man: "O you who had intercourse between the thighs!" Ibn al-Qasim said: He incurs the hadd, because it is an allusion. Ashhab said: There is no hadd in it, because it is an attribution to an act that is not counted as fornication by consensus.

**Eleventh issue:** If one accuses a girl who can be penetrated before puberty of fornication, it is slander according to Malik. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: It is not slander, because it is not fornication, since there is no hadd for her, and he is subject to ta'zir (discretionary discipline). Ibn al-'Arabi said: The question is open and difficult, but Malik sought to protect the honour of the one slandered, and others considered protecting the back of the slanderer. Protecting the honour of the one slandered is preferable, because the slanderer has uncovered her concealment with the tip of his tongue, so the hadd is binding on him.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad said concerning a girl of nine: Her slanderer is flogged. Likewise, if a boy reaches ten, his slanderer is beaten. Ishaq said: If one slanders a boy who could be penetrated like him, there is the hadd upon him, and likewise for a girl who has passed nine.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: One who slanders someone who has not reached puberty is not subject to the hadd, because that is a lie, but he is disciplined for the harm.

Abu 'Ubayd said: In the hadith of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), a woman came to him and mentioned that her husband was having intercourse with her slave girl. He said: "If you are truthful, we will stone him; and if you are lying, we will flog you." She said: "Send me back to my family, I am being driven by jealousy (ghayra nagira)." [Footnote: The discussion of this phrase will follow shortly.]

Abu 'Ubayd said: In this hadith is the jurisprudence that a man who has intercourse with his wife's slave girl incurs the hadd. And in it also: if someone slanders him with that, the slanderer incurs the hadd. Do you not hear his words: "If you are lying, we will flog you"? The basis of all this is that the doer was not ignorant of what he was doing and what he was saying. If he was ignorant and claimed a doubt, the hadd is averted from him in all of that.

Also in it: if a man slanders another man in the presence of a judge while the one slandered is not present, nothing is due upon the slanderer until the one slandered comes and seeks his hadd, because one does not know that perhaps he would have confirmed it. Do you not see that 'Ali, peace be upon him, did not take up the matter with her?

Also in it: if a man is slandered before a judge, and then the one slandered comes and seeks his right, the judge enforces the hadd on the basis of his hearing it, do you not see that he says: "If you are lying, we will flog you"? This is because it is one of the rights of people.

I say: It has been disputed whether it is one of the rights of Allah or one of the rights of human beings, and this will come.

Abu 'Ubayd said: al-Asma'i said: Shu'ba asked me about the phrase "ghayra nagira." I told him: It is derived from the boiling (nagr) of the pot, which is its bubbling and surging. It is said of it: "nagirat tanghar" and "nagarat tanghir" when it boils. Its meaning is that she meant her insides were boiling from anger and jealousy when she did not find with him what she wanted. He said: It is said of it: "I saw so-and-so boiling (yatanaghgharu) against so-and-so," meaning his insides boil with rage against him.

**Twelfth issue:** One who slanders one of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) incurs two hadds. This was said by Masruq. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The sound view is that it is one hadd, because of the generality of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ (the verse), and the nobility of their station does not require an increase in the hadd for one who slanders them, because the nobility of rank does not affect the hadd, and its diminishment does not affect the hadd by disparagement. And Allah knows best. The discussion of whether one who slandered 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) is to be killed or not will come.

**Thirteenth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then they do not bring four witnesses﴾. What requires four witnesses, unlike other rights, is fornication, out of mercy to His servants and to conceal them. This was already discussed in Surat al-Nisa. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 72.]

**Fourteenth issue:** Among the conditions for the testimony of witnesses being delivered, according to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that it be in one session. If they separate, it is not testimony. 'Abd al-Malik said: Their testimony is accepted whether they are together or separate. Malik held that their gathering is an act of worship, and Ibn al-Hasan said the same. 'Abd al-Malik held that the purpose is the delivery of testimony and its being together, and that has been achieved. This is the view of 'Uthman al-Batti and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then they do not bring four witnesses﴾ and His words: ﴿so when they do not bring the witnesses﴾ [al-Nur: 13], and He did not mention separated or together.

**Fifteenth issue:** If the testimony is complete but the witnesses are not upright (ʿadl), al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Sha'bi held that there is no hadd upon the witnesses or upon the one testified against. This was also the view of Ahmad, al-Nu'man and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Malik said: If four testify against him for fornication, and one of them is one whose testimony is rejected (maskhut) or a slave, they are all flogged. [In the manuscripts b, t, k: "maskhut." In j, a: "masquṭ."] Sufyan al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq said concerning four blind men who testify against a woman for fornication: they are beaten.

**Sixteenth issue:** If one of the witnesses retracts after the one testified against has been stoned for fornication, one group said: He pays a quarter of the blood-money, and nothing is due from the others. This was also said by Qatada, Hammad, 'Ikrima, Abu Hashim, Malik, Ahmad and the people of opinion. Al-Shafi'i said: If he says "I intended to have him killed," then the heirs have a choice: if they wish, they kill him; if they wish, they pardon and take a quarter of the blood-money, and he incurs the hadd. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He is killed, and the others owe three-quarters of the blood-money. Ibn Sirin said: If he says "I made a mistake and meant someone else," then he owes the full blood-money. And if he says "I intended to kill him," then he is killed. Ibn Shubruma said the same.

**Seventeenth issue:** The scholars differed concerning whether the hadd for slander is one of the rights of Allah, or one of the rights of human beings, or whether it has a mixture of both. The first view is that of Abu Hanifa. The second is that of Malik and al-Shafi'i. The third was said by some later scholars.

The benefit of the disagreement is this: if it is a right of Allah the Exalted and it reaches the imam, he enforces it even if the one slandered does not seek it. The repentance of the slanderer benefits him between himself and Allah the Exalted, and the hadd is halved by slavery as with fornication. If it is a right of a human being, the imam does not enforce it except upon the demand of the one slandered, it lapses by his pardon, and the slanderer's repentance does not benefit him until the one slandered absolves him.

**Eighteenth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿with four witnesses﴾. The reading of the majority is with the number four construed with (idafa to) "witnesses." 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar and Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir read "bi-arba'atin" (with tanwin) "shuhada'." In this there are four possibilities: it may be in the genitive position as a qualifier of "arba'a," or as an apposition. It may also be a circumstantial (hal) from an indefinite noun, or a specification (tamyiz). But there is a question about the circumstantial and the specification: the circumstantial would be from an indefinite noun, and the specification is plural. Sibawayh holds that it is tanwin of the number, and leaving its idafa is only permitted in poetry. Abu al-Fath 'Uthman ibn Jinni praised this reading and preferred it over the reading of the majority. Al-Nahhas said: It may also be that "shuhada'" is in the accusative position, meaning: "they did not bring four witnesses."

**Nineteenth issue:** The ruling on the testimony of the four is that it must be by direct observation, as they see it like the stick in the kohl-pot, as was discussed earlier in al-Nisa in the text of the hadith. [Footnote: See vol. 5, p. 73.] And that it be in one session, according to the view of Malik. If one of them becomes confused, all three are flogged, as 'Umar did in the matter of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. That is because Abu Bakra Nufay' ibn al-Harith and his brother Nafi' testified against him for fornication. al-Zahrawi said: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, and Ziyad, their brother by the same mother, who was attributed to Mu'awiya, and Shibl ibn Ma'bad al-Bajali. When they came to deliver the testimony and Ziyad hesitated and did not deliver it, 'Umar flogged the three mentioned.

**Twentieth issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then flog them﴾. Al-jald is striking. Mujalada and mudaraba are striking with or upon hides; then "al-jald" was borrowed for other things, such as a sword or other. From this is the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

I fight them on the day of al-Hadiqa bareheaded,
as if my hand with the sword were a flame of a player.

"Eighty" is put in the accusative as an absolute object (masdar). "Lashes" is a specification (tamyiz).

(And do not accept their testimony ever after.) This implies for the duration of their lives. Then they are judged to be "fāsiqūn" (defiantly disobedient), meaning they have stepped outside obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

The twenty-first issue: Allah's words, ﴿Except those who repent﴾ [24:5]. It is in the accusative position as an exception (istithnāʾ). It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive position as a substitute (badal). The meaning: "And do not accept their testimony ever, except those who repent and make amends after the slander, [then] indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

The verse thus contains three rulings concerning the slanderer: flogging him, rejecting his testimony forever, and his being a fāsiq. The exception does not apply to his flogging, by consensus, except for what al-Sha'bi is reported to have said, as will come. It applies to his being a fāsiq, by consensus. People differed over whether it applies to the rejection of his testimony. Shurayh the judge, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa said: the exception does not apply to the rejection of his testimony; rather, his fisq is removed in the sight of Allah Almighty alone. As for the testimony of the slanderer, it is never accepted at all, even if he repents and retracts his statement, and under no circumstances.

The majority (al-Jumhur) said: the exception applies to the rejection of the testimony. So when the slanderer repents, his testimony is accepted, and rejection was only because of the cause of fisq; when that is removed by repentance, his testimony is accepted absolutely, both before and after the hadd punishment. This is the view of the majority of jurists.

Then they differed about the form of his repentance. The view of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Sha'bi and others is that his repentance is only by his retracting his own statement in that slander for which he was punished with the hadd. And so ʿUmar did: he said to those who testified against al-Mughira, "Whoever retracts his statement, I will accept his testimony in what is to come; and whoever does not do so, I will not accept his testimony." So al-Shibl ibn Maʿbad and Nafiʿ ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah retracted their statements and repented, while Abu Bakrah refused to do so, and so he (ʿUmar) did not accept his testimony. al-Nahhas related this view from the people of Madina.

Another group, among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others, said: his repentance is that he reforms and his condition becomes good, even if he does not retract his statement by denial; it is sufficient for him to regret his slander, seek forgiveness for it, and abandon returning to its like. This is the view of Ibn Jarir. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: the exception applies to the three rulings. When he repents and his repentance becomes evident, he is not flogged, his testimony is accepted, and the designation of fisq is removed from him, because he has become one of those whose testimony is approved, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic has said: "And indeed I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents" [20:82] — the verse.

The twenty-second issue: Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed as to when the testimony of the slanderer lapses. Ibn al-Majishun said: by the very act of slander. Ibn al-Qasim, Ashhab and Sahnun said: it does not lapse until he is flogged; if someone prevents his flogging, whether by pardon or otherwise, his testimony is not rejected. Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Lakhmi said: his testimony during the period of the term is suspended, and the view that repentance is only by retraction of the slander is preferred; otherwise, what return to justice is there for one who slandered, was flogged, and remained in his former justice?

The twenty-third issue: They also differed, on the view that his testimony is accepted after repentance, as to in what matters it is accepted. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is accepted in everything absolutely, and likewise everyone who has been punished with a hadd in any matter. This was transmitted by Nafi' and Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam from Malik, and it is the view of Ibn Kinanah. Al-Waqqar (a title of Zakariyya ibn al-Faqih al-Misri) mentioned from Malik that his testimony is not accepted in the matter for which he was punished specifically, but is accepted in other matters. This is the view of Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun. al-Utbi related the same from Asbagh and Sahnun. Sahnun said: whoever is punished with a hadd in any matter, his testimony is not accepted in a matter like that for which he was punished. Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: whoever is punished with a hadd for slander or fornication, his testimony is not accepted in any aspect of fornication, nor in slander, nor in li'an, even if he is just; they related this from Malik. They all agreed that the testimony of an illegitimate child is not accepted concerning fornication.

The twenty-fourth issue: An exception that follows a series of conjoined sentences returns to all of them according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions. According to Abu Hanifa and most of his companions, the exception returns to the nearest mentioned item, which is fisq; for this reason his testimony is not accepted, since the exception returns to fisq alone and not to the acceptance of testimony. The source of disagreement on this principle has two causes. The first: are these sentences, because of the conjunction in them, in the status of one single sentence, or does each sentence have its own independent ruling, with the conjunction particle serving merely to link and not to share? The latter is the sound view regarding the conjunction of sentences, since it is permissible to conjoin differing sentences one upon another, as is known in grammar. The second: is the exception compared to the condition in returning to the preceding sentences, so that it returns to all of them according to the jurists, or is it not compared to it, because that is analogy in language, which is invalid as known in the principles of jurisprudence? The principle is that all of this is possible and there is no preponderance, so the position of the judge of suspension is determined. The problem is reinforced by the fact that both matters have come in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: the verse of hirabah has the pronoun returning to all by agreement, and the verse of killing a believer by mistake has the exception returned to the last item by agreement, while the verse of slander is open to both readings, so suspension without preference is determined. Our scholars said: this is a universal, principled analysis. The view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both, is preferred from the standpoint of detailed jurisprudential reasoning, namely that the exception returns to fisq and to the prohibition of accepting testimony together, unless one distinguishes between them by a report that must be accepted. The Ummah agreed that repentance erases kufr, so what is below that must be more deserving of it, and Allah knows best. Abu ʿUbayd said: the exception returns to the preceding sentences. He said: the one who is accused of fornication is not more grave in crime than the one who commits fornication; then the fornicator, if he repents, his testimony is accepted, because "the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin." And if Allah accepts the repentance of a servant, the servants are more deserving of accepting it, and such an exception exists in several places in the Qur'an, among them the saying of Allah, "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger..." [5:33] up to His words, "except those who repent" [5:34]. There is no doubt that this exception returns to all. al-Zajjaj said: the slanderer is not graver in crime than the disbeliever, so his right, if he repents and makes amends, is that his testimony be accepted. He said: His words "ever" mean as long as he is a slanderer, just as it is said, "the testimony of a disbeliever is never accepted," meaning as long as he is a disbeliever. al-Sha'bi said to the one who differed on this issue: "Allah accepts his repentance, and you do not accept his testimony!" Then, if the exception returns to the last sentence according to certain usulis, then His words, "And those are the defiantly disobedient," are a causal clause and not an independent sentence, meaning: do not accept their testimony because of their fisq; so when the fisq is removed, why would their testimony not be accepted? Then the repentance of the slanderer is retraction of his statement, as ʿUmar said to the slanderers of al-Mughira in the presence of the Companions without any objection, along with the publicizing and fame of the affair from Basra to the Hijaz and other regions. Had the interpretation of the verse been what the Kufans interpreted, it would not have been possible for knowledge of that to be lost to the Companions, and they would have said to ʿUmar, "It is not permissible to accept the repentance of the slanderer ever," and they would not have been able to remain silent about the judgment by distorting the interpretation of the Book. So their view falls, and Allah is the One sought for help.

The twenty-fifth issue: al-Qushayri said: there is no disagreement that if the slanderer is not flogged, either because the one slandered died before demanding the hadd from the slanderer, or the matter was not brought to the authority, or the one slandered pardoned him, then the testimony is accepted, because according to the opponent in this issue, the prohibition of accepting testimony is conjoined to the flogging. Allah the Exalted said: "Flog them eighty lashes and never accept their testimony ever." At this point al-Shafi'i said: his condition before being flogged is worse than his condition when he is flogged, because hudud are expiations; so how would his testimony be rejected in his better state rather than in his worse of the two? I say: he spoke thus, and there is no disagreement. It has already preceded from Ibn al-Majishun that his testimony is rejected by the very act of slander. This is the view of al-Layth, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i: his testimony is rejected even if he is not flogged, because by slander he becomes defiantly disobedient, since it is among the major sins, so his testimony is not accepted until his innocence is established either by the confession of the one slandered that he committed fornication or by the establishment of proof against him.

The twenty-sixth issue: Allah's words, "and make amends" [24:5], mean manifesting repentance. It has been said: "and make amends" means amending the deed.

(Then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful) — since they repented and Allah accepted their repentance.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 24, verses 6–10 (part 1 of 4)**

There are thirty issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾. The word "أَنْفُسُهُمْ" (anfusuhum, "themselves") is in the nominative case (marfu') as a substitute (badal). It may also be in the accusative (nasb) as an exception (istithna'), or as the predicate of "يَكُنْ" (yakun, "there is/be").

(﴿so the testimony of one of them﴾) The nominative "شَهَادَةُ" (shahadatu) is the reading of the Kufans, as the subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). The meaning is: the testimony of one of them that removes from him the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) is ﴿four testimonies﴾. The people of Medina and Abu 'Amr read "أَرْبَعَ" (arba'a) in the accusative, because the meaning of "فَشَهَادَةُ" (fashahadatu) is "that he testifies." The implied sense is: "it is incumbent upon them that one of them testify four testimonies," or "the matter is that one of them testify four testimonies." There is no disagreement that the second is accusative by the verb "testify" (al-shahadah).

(﴿and the fifth﴾) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). The predicate is "أَنَّ" (anna) and what follows it. The light form (al-mukhaffafah) has the same meaning as the heavy form (al-muthaqqalah), since its meaning is "that he." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Talhah, and 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "وَالْخَامِسَةَ" (wal-khamisata) in the accusative, meaning "and he bears witness, the fifth testimony." The rest read it in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate in "أَنَّ لَعْنَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ" (anna la'nata Allahi 'alayhi, "that the curse of Allah be upon him"). That is, "the fifth testimony is his saying: the curse of Allah be upon him."

**The second issue:** concerning the occasion of its revelation. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that Hilal ibn Umayyah accused his wife before the Prophet (ﷺ) of [adultery with] Shurayk ibn Sahma'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Evidence, or a punishment on your back." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, when one of us sees a man upon his wife, he seeks evidence!" The Prophet (ﷺ) kept saying: "Evidence, or else a punishment on your back." Hilal said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, I am truthful, and Allah will surely reveal in my case something that clears my back from the punishment." So this was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾, and he recited until he reached ﴿among the truthful﴾ (70). The hadith is related in full.

It has also been said: when the previous verse was revealed concerning those who accuse chaste women, its apparent meaning included wives and others. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I find a man with my wife, I will wait until I bring four witnesses! By Allah, I will strike him with the sword without turning away from him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you wonder at the jealousy of Sa'd? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me." There are different narrations of Sa'd's words; this is roughly their meaning.

Then after that came Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, and accused his wife Shurayk ibn Sahma' al-Balawi, as we mentioned. The Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to inflict on him the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf). At that point this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered them in the mosque and they performed the mutual imprecation (li'an). The woman hesitated at the fifth oath when she was admonished. It has been said that it was an oath that brings [the punishment]: that is, the fifth testimony entails the painful punishment if she was lying. Then she said: "I will not disgrace my people for the rest of the day." [The word "day" here refers to the genus, meaning days in general.] So she performed the li'an. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) separated them, and she gave birth to a boy who was like a dark-grey camel [al-awraq from camels: that which has a color between white and black], in the disliked description. Afterwards that boy became a governor in Egypt, and he did not know his own father.

Also 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani came and accused his wife and performed the li'an. The well-known view is that the case of Hilal came first, and that it was the cause of the verse. It has been said: the case of 'Uwaymir ibn Ashqar came first. This is a sound, well-known hadith that the imams have transmitted.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Safrah said: "The correct view is that the one who accused his wife was 'Uwaymir, and that Hilal ibn Umayyah is an error." Al-Tabari said: his saying in the hadith "Hilal ibn Umayyah" is objectionable; rather the accuser was 'Uwaymir ibn Zayd [In Usd al-Ghaba from al-Tabari: 'Uwaymir ibn al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Haritha ibn al-Jadd] ibn al-Jadd ibn al-'Ajlani, who witnessed Uhud with the Prophet (ﷺ). He accused her of [adultery with] Shurayk ibn al-Sahma'. Al-Sahma' is his mother; she was called that because of her blackness. He is the son of 'Abdah ibn al-Jadd ibn al-'Ajlani. This is what the historians of reports used to say.

It has also been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to the people in the sermon on Friday: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾. 'Asim ibn 'Adi al-Ansari said: "May I be your ransom! If one of us found a man upon his wife's belly and spoke about what happened, he would be flogged eighty lashes, and the Muslims would call him a sinner, and his testimony would not be accepted. How then can one of us bring four witnesses? By the time he seeks four witnesses, the man will have finished his need!" Then the Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be peace, said: "Thus was it revealed, O 'Asim ibn 'Adi." 'Asim went out listening and obeying. Hilal ibn Umayyah met him, saying "inna lillah" [in the sense of distress]. He said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil! I found Shurayk ibn al-Sahma' upon the belly of my wife Khawlah, committing adultery with her." Khawlah was the daughter of 'Asim ibn 'Adi. In this chain it is stated that the one who found Shurayk with his wife was Hilal ibn Umayyah, but the correct view is the opposite, as already explained. Al-Kalbi said: "The more apparent view is that the one who found a partner with his wife was 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, because of the abundance of what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed li'an between al-'Ajlani and his wife." They agreed that this adulterer was Shurayk ibn 'Abdah, and his mother was al-Sahma'. 'Uwaymir and Khawlah bint Qays and Shurayk were cousins of 'Asim. This incident occurred in Sha'ban in the ninth year after the Hijrah, upon the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Tabuk to Medina, as al-Tabari said.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, who said: "I was present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he performed the li'an between 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani and his wife, on the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the battle of Tabuk. He (the husband) denied the pregnancy that was in her womb and said: 'It is the son of Ibn al-Sahma'.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Bring your wife, for the Qur'an has been revealed concerning you two.' So he performed the li'an between them after the afternoon prayer, near the pulpit, upon a [woven] cloth (khamal) [khamal is the fringe of a velvet or similar woven cloth that has trailing threads like a carpet's fringe]." In its chain is al-Waqidi, from al-Dahhak ibn 'Uthman, from 'Imran ibn Abi Anas, who said: "I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far say..." and he mentioned it.

**The third issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾. It is general concerning every accusation, whether he says: "You have committed adultery," or "O adulteress," or "I saw her committing adultery," or "This child is not mine," for the verse includes all of these. The li'an is obligatory if he does not bring four witnesses. This is the view of the majority of scholars, the general body of jurists, and the community of the people of hadith. It has been related from Malik something similar. Malik used to say: he does not perform the li'an unless he says: "I saw you committing adultery," or he denies a pregnancy or a child from her. The view of Abu al-Zinad, Yahya ibn Sa'id, and al-Batti is similar to the view of Malik: the li'an is not obligatory by accusation alone, but only by seeing [the act] or denying a pregnancy together with a claim of istibra' (establishing that the womb is clear). This is the well-known view of Malik, and it was stated by Ibn al-Qasim. The sound view is the first, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an suffices to make li'an obligatory by mere accusation without seeing [the act]. So rely upon it, especially since in the sound hadith: "Have you seen a man who found another man with his wife?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go and bring her," and he did not require him to mention seeing. And they agreed that a blind man performs li'an if he accuses his wife. Had seeing been a condition of li'an, the blind man would not perform it. This is what Abu 'Umar said. Ibn al-Qassar narrated from Malik that the li'an of a blind man is not valid unless he says: "I touched his private part in her private part."

The proof for Malik and those who follow him is what Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: Hilal ibn Umayyah, who was one of the three whose repentance was accepted, came from his land at night and found a man with his family. He saw with his eye and heard with his ear, and he did not confront him until morning. Then he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I came to my family at night and found a man with them, and I saw with my eye and heard with my ear." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked what he brought and was distressed by it, so this was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾, and he mentioned the hadith. This is an explicit text that the li'an in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed judgment was concerned with seeing, so it is not necessary to extend this beyond that. Whoever accuses his wife without mentioning seeing is to receive the punishment, due to the generality of His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾.

**The fourth issue:** if he denies the pregnancy, he performs the li'an, because this is stronger than seeing. He must mention non-intercourse and the istibra' after it. Our scholars differed about the istibra'. Al-Mughirah and Malik, in one of their two views, said: one menstrual cycle suffices in this regard. Malik also said: he does not deny it except after three menstrual cycles. The sound view is the first, because the clearing of the womb from occupation is achieved by it, as in the istibra' of a slave woman. We took three menstrual cycles into account in the waiting period (al-'iddah) for another ruling, which will be explained in the chapter on divorce, if Allah wills. Al-Lakhmi narrated from Malik that he said once: "The child is not denied by istibra', because menstruation can occur during pregnancy." This was also the view of Ashhab in the Book of Ibn al-Mawwaz, and it was said by al-Mughirah. He said: "The child is not denied except after five years, since that is the maximum period of pregnancy, according to what has been mentioned earlier."

**The fifth issue:** the li'an for us occurs between every pair of spouses, whether they are free or both slaves, Muslims or disbelievers, dissolute or upright. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i. There is no li'an between a man and his slave woman, nor between him and the mother of his child (umm walad, a slave woman who bore her master's child). It has been said: the child of a slave woman is not disowned by him except by a single oath, unlike li'an. It has also been said: if he denies the child of an umm walad, he performs li'an. The first view is the correct representation of the school of Malik, and it is the right one.

Abu Hanifah said: li'an is not valid except between two free Muslim spouses, because li'an is testimony in his view, while in our view and in al-Shafi'i's view it is an oath. So everyone whose oath is valid, his accusation and li'an are valid. They agreed that both must be legally responsible (mukallaf).

In the words [of the Prophet (ﷺ)]: "He found a man with his wife" [the Arabic: "وَجَدَ مَعَ امْرَأَتِهِ رَجُلًا"] [note: this refers to the saying of 'Uwaymir or another, based on the earlier disagreement] is evidence that li'an is obligatory for every pair of spouses, because he did not specify a man from a man or a woman from a woman. The verse of li'an was revealed in accordance with this answer, when He said: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾, and He did not specify one spouse from another. This is the view of Malik and the people of Medina, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, and Abu Thawr. Furthermore, li'an necessitates the annulment of the marriage, so it resembles divorce; therefore whoever may be divorced may perform li'an.

Li'an is oaths, not testimonies. Allah the Exalted, who is the most truthful of speakers, said: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ (10) [al-Ma'idah: 107], meaning "our oaths." He also said: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: "We bear witness that you are truly the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. Then He said: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 16].

He (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for the oaths, there would have been a matter between me and her." As for the arguments put forward by al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa, they are arguments that do not stand on their own legs. Among them is the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no li'an (mutual imprecation between spouses) among four: there is no li'an between a free man and a slave woman; there is no li'an between a free woman and a slave; there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Jewish woman; and there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Christian woman." It was narrated by al-Daraqutni through chains that he declared weak in all of them. It is also related from al-Awza'i and Ibn Jurayj, two imams, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, as his own statement, and they did not raise it [[In Sunan al-Daraqutni: "yarfa'ah" (they both raised it).]] to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They also argued on the basis of reasoning: since spouses were excluded from the general category of witnesses by His words, "And they have no witnesses except themselves," it follows that only one whose testimony is acceptable may perform li'an. Furthermore, if it were an oath, it would not be repeated; and the wisdom in its repetition is that it stands in place of witnesses for adultery. We reply: this is refuted by the oath of qasama (the oath of collective accusation in cases of homicide), for it is repeated, and yet it is not testimony by consensus (ijma'), and the wisdom in its repetition is the intensification of the gravity of matters of chastity and blood. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The decisive point that it is an oath and not testimony is that the husband swears for himself, to establish his claim and to free himself from punishment. How could anyone claim in the Sharia that a witness testifies for himself in a way that imposes a ruling upon another? This is remote in principle and nonexistent in reasoning.

Sixth: The scholars differed concerning the li'an of a mute man. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: he performs li'an, because he is one whose divorce, zihar (a form of divorce by likening a wife to a forbidden relative) and ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse) are valid, when his meaning is understood. Abu Hanifa said: he does not perform li'an, because he is not among those competent to testify, and because he may speak with his tongue and deny the li'an, so we cannot carry out the hadd (prescribed punishment) against him. This meaning has already been mentioned in Surat Maryam [[See vol. 11, p. 101.]] along with its evidence, and praise be to Allah.

Seventh: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Abu Hanifa observed the generality of the verse and said: If a man accuses his wife of adultery before marrying her, he performs li'an. He forgot that this is included in His words, "And those who accuse chaste women," and this man accused a chaste woman who was not his wife. Li'an occurs only in accusation that involves lineage (nasab), and this accusation does not involve lineage, so it does not require li'an, just as if he had accused a stranger woman.

Eighth: If he accuses her after divorce, it is examined: if there is a lineage he wishes to deny, or a pregnancy from which he wishes to disown himself, he performs li'an; otherwise he does not perform li'an. 'Uthman al-Batti said: he never performs li'an, because she is no longer a wife. Abu Hanifa said: he does not perform li'an in either case, because she is not a wife. This is refuted by the accusation before marriage, as we mentioned just above; rather, this is more fitting, because the marriage had already taken place and he wishes to deny lineage and clear himself of a child who would be attributed to him, so li'an is necessary. And when there is no pregnancy expected and no lineage feared to be attached, li'an has no benefit, so it is not enforced; it is then a general accusation falling under the generality of His words, "And those who accuse chaste women," and so the hadd is obligatory for him, and al-Batti's view is invalid because its corruption is evident.

Ninth: There is no li'an between a man and his wife after the expiry of the 'idda (waiting period), except in one case: that the man is absent, his wife gives birth to a child during his absence while he does not know, he divorces her, her 'idda expires, and then he returns and disowns the child. In that case he may perform li'an with her here, after the 'idda. Likewise, if he returns after her death and disowns the child, he performs li'an for himself while she is dead, after some period of the 'idda, and he inherits from her, because she died before the separation between them took place.

Tenth: If he disowns the pregnancy and the matter fulfills its conditions, he performs li'an before the delivery, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: he does not perform li'an except after she has delivered, because it may be wind or one of the illnesses. Our evidence is the explicit text that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed li'an before the delivery and said: "If she brings forth such-and-such, it belongs to its father; and if she brings forth such-and-such, it belongs to so-and-so." Then she brought forth with the disliked attributes.

Eleventh: If he accuses his wife of intercourse through the anus [he performs li'an [[Addition required by the context.]]]. Abu Hanifa said: he does not perform li'an, and he based this on his principle that sodomy does not entail the hadd. This is invalid, because accusing with it is a disgrace, and it falls under the generality of His words, "And those who accuse their wives," and it has already been mentioned in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, pp. 242ff.]] and al-Mu'minun [[See p. 106 of this part.]] that the hadd is obligatory for it.

The twelfth issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: "One of the strange things about this man is that when he accuses his wife and her mother of adultery, [if he is flogged for the mother the punishment for the daughter falls away, and if he performs li'an for the daughter the punishment for the mother does not fall away]. This has no basis, and I have not seen anything worth relating from them on it. This is utterly false, for he has specified the general wording of the verse in the case of the daughter, who is a wife, with the punishment for the mother without any report or established principle from which he drew an analogy."

The thirteenth issue: If a man accuses his wife and she then commits adultery before the li'an, there is neither a hadd nor li'an. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and most scholars. Al-Thawri and al-Muzani said: the punishment for the accuser does not fall away, and the accused's adultery after being accused does not impair or remove her earlier chastity, because the criterion is chastity and continence at the time of the accusation, not after it. Just as if one accuses a Muslim and the accused then apostatises after the accusation and before the accuser is punished, the punishment does not fall away from the accuser. Moreover, all hudud are judged by the time of obligation, not the time of execution.

Our proof is that before the completion of the li'an and the hadd, a factor has appeared which, had it existed at the outset, would have prevented the validity of the li'an and the obligation of the hadd; so likewise if it arises later. This is like two witnesses who appear to be upright, but the judge does not rule on their testimony until their immorality becomes apparent, by their committing adultery or drinking wine; the judge may not then rule on that testimony. Moreover, the ruling of chastity and virtue is taken on the basis of outward appearance, not on the basis of certainty and conviction. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The back of a believer is a sanctuary (ḥimā)." So the accuser is not to be punished except on a conclusive proof. And success is from Allah.

The fourteenth issue: If a man accuses his wife and she is an adult who can bear a child, they perform li'an: his li'an is to avert the hadd, and hers is to avert the punishment. If she is a minor who cannot bear a child, he performs li'an to avert the hadd, and she does not perform li'an, because if she confessed nothing would be binding on her. Ibn al-Majishun said: there is no hadd for accusing one who has not reached puberty. Al-Lakhmi said: on this view, there is no li'an for the husband of a minor girl who cannot bear a child.

The fifteenth issue: If four people testify against a woman for adultery, one of them being her husband, the husband performs li'an and the three other witnesses are flogged. This is one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions. The second view is that they are not flogged. Abu Hanifa said: if the husband and the three testify from the outset, their testimony is accepted and the woman is flogged. Our proof is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [24:4], and the verse continues. It informs us that whoever accuses a chaste person and does not produce four witnesses is flogged. Its apparent meaning requires that he produce four witnesses other than the accuser, and the husband is an accuser of his wife, so he is excluded from being one of the witnesses. And Allah knows best.

The sixteenth issue: If a child appears from his wife and he leaves the denial of it, he may not deny it after his silence. Shurayh and Mujahid said: he may deny it at any time. This is an error, because his silence after knowing of it is consent, just as if he had acknowledged it and then denied it, which is not accepted from him. And Allah knows best.

The seventeenth issue: If he delays this until she has given birth and says: "I hoped it would be wind that dissipates, or that she would miscarry, so I might be relieved of the accusation," is there a time limit for denying the child after birth? Opinions differ on this. Our view is that if he has no excuse for his silence until three days have passed, he is content with it and may not deny it. This is also al-Shafi'i's view. He further said: whenever he could have denied it in the customary way, that is, by going to the judge, and did not do so, he may not deny it afterwards. Abu Hanifa said: I do not stipulate any period. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: forty days, the period of postnatal bleeding, is to be considered. Ibn al-Qassar said: the proof for our view is that denying one's child is forbidden to him, while attributing to himself a child that is not his is forbidden to him as well; therefore a latitude must be granted so that he may consider and reflect whether it is permissible for him to deny it or not. We made the limit three days because it is the first limit of plurality and the last limit of paucity, and three days have been set as the period by which the condition of the musarra (a she-camel, cow or sheep whose udders are tied and not milked for days so that milk gathers in the udder; when the buyer milks it he discovers its state. From the hadith: "Whoever buys a musarra has the choice of the two better options," meaning he may keep the item or return it) is tested, so it should be likewise here. As for Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, their consideration is no more deserving than considering the period of gestation and suckling, since they have no evidence in the Shari'ah; whereas we have cited evidence in the Shari'ah from the period of the musarra.

The eighteenth issue: Ibn al-Qassar said: if a woman says to her husband or to a stranger, "Ya zaniyah" with the feminine ending, and likewise a stranger to a stranger, I know of no explicit text from our companions on it, but in my view it is an accusation and the speaker is liable to the hadd, for he has added a letter; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said it is not an accusation. They agreed that if he says to his wife "Ya zani" it is an accusation. The proof that it is an accusation when said to a man is that when an address is understood in its meaning, its ruling applies, whether in a foreign or Arabic word. Do you not see that if he says to a woman "zanayt" (with a fatha on the ta') it is an accusation, because its meaning is understood from it? Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf argue that since it is permissible to address a feminine person with the masculine form, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And women said﴾ [12:30], the saying "ya zani" may be an accusation when addressed to a woman; but since the verb of the masculine may not take the feminine form when it precedes the subject, addressing a woman with the feminine form has no ruling. And Allah knows best.

The nineteenth issue: In a void marriage, the husband performs li'an against his wife, because she has become a bed (firash) and the lineage is attached to him in it, so li'an applies to it.

The twentieth issue: Scholars differed concerning the husband who refuses to perform li'an. Abu Hanifa said: there is no hadd upon him, because Allah made the hadd obligatory upon the stranger and li'an obligatory upon the husband; since li'an does not transfer to the stranger, the hadd does not transfer to the husband, and he is to be imprisoned indefinitely until he performs li'an, because hudud are not deferred by analogy. Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority of jurists said: if the husband does not perform li'an, he is flogged, because li'an for him is a clearing of himself, like witnesses for a stranger; if a stranger does not produce four witnesses he is flogged, and likewise the husband if he does not perform li'an. The hadith of al-'Ajlani indicates this, in his words: "If I remain silent, I remain silent over a rage; if I kill, I am killed; if I speak, I am flogged."

The twenty-first issue: Scholars also differed on whether the husband may perform li'an together with his witnesses. Malik and al-Shafi'i said he performs li'an whether he has witnesses or not, because witnesses have no function except averting the hadd, whereas the removal of the bed and the denial of the child require li'an in any case. Abu Hanifa and his companions said li'an was prescribed for the husband only when he has no witnesses other than himself, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾ [24:6].

The twenty-second issue: The beginning in li'an is with what Allah began with, namely the husband. Its benefit is to avert the hadd from him and to deny the lineage from him, based on the Prophet's words ﷺ: "Produce evidence, or the hadd falls on your back." Were one to begin with the woman before him, it would not be valid, because that reverses what Allah ordained. Abu Hanifa said it is valid. This is false, because it contradicts the Qur'an, and it has no principle to which it may be returned, nor any meaning that strengthens it; rather the meaning is on our side, because when the woman begins the li'an she denies what was not established, and this has no basis.

The twenty-third issue: The manner of li'an is that the judge says to the one performing it: "Say: I testify by Allah that I saw her committing adultery, and I saw the adulterer's member in her private part like a kohl stick in a kohl pot, and I did not have intercourse with her after my seeing." If he wishes he may say: "She has indeed committed adultery, and I did not have intercourse with her after her adultery." He repeats whichever of these two formulas he wishes four times. If he refuses these oaths or any part of them, he is flogged. If he denies a pregnancy, he says: "I testify by Allah that I have verified her chastity, and I have not had intercourse with her since, and this pregnancy is not from me," and he points to it, swearing this four times, and says in each oath: "And I am truly among the truthful in this my claim against her." Then in the fifth he says: "The curse of Allah be upon me if I am among the liars." If he wishes he may say: "If I have lied about what I have mentioned concerning her." When he says that, the hadd falls from him and the child is denied to him. When the man has finished his li'an, the woman stands after him and swears four oaths by Allah, saying in them: "I testify by Allah that he is indeed a liar, or that he is among the liars regarding what he has claimed against me and attributed to me." If she is pregnant she says: "And this my pregnancy is from him." Then in the fifth she says: "The wrath of Allah be upon me if he is truthful, or if he is among the truthful in this claim of his." Whoever requires li'an for accusation says in each of the four testimonies: "I testify by Allah that I am truly among the truthful regarding what I have accused her of, namely the adultery of so-and-so." He says in the fifth: "The curse of Allah be upon me if I am a liar regarding what I accused her of, namely adultery." She says: "I testify by Allah that he is indeed a liar regarding what he accused me of, namely adultery." In the fifth she says: "The wrath of Allah be upon me if he is truthful regarding what he accused me of, namely adultery." Al-Shafi'i said: the one performing li'an says, "I testify by Allah that I am truly among the truthful regarding what I accused my husband so-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, of," and he points to her if she is present, saying this four times. Then the imam admonishes him, reminds him of Allah the Exalted, and says: "I fear that if you have not spoken truly you will bear the curse of Allah." If he sees that he intends to proceed, he orders someone to place a hand on his mouth and says: "Your saying 'and the curse of Allah be upon me if I am among the liars' is binding." If he refuses, he leaves him, and he says: "The curse of Allah be upon me if I am among the liars regarding what I accused so-and-so of, namely adultery." It is supported by what Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered a man, when he ordered the two who perform li'an, to place his hand on his mouth at the fifth oath, saying: "Indeed it is binding."

The 24th issue: The scholars differed on the ruling concerning one who slanders his wife by naming a man, whether he is to be punished (ḥadd) or not. Mālik said: "He must perform li'ān (mutual oath-imprecation) with his wife, and the one accused is to be punished (ḥadd)." Abū Ḥanīfa also said this, because he is a slanderer (qādhif) of someone for whom there was no necessity to slander.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: "There is no ḥadd upon him, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has not placed upon one who accuses his wife of adultery except a single ḥadd, by His saying: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾, and He did not differentiate between one who mentions a specific man and one who does not. Al-ʿAjlānī accused his wife of having a partner (Sharīk), and likewise Hilāl ibn Umayya, and neither of them was punished." Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is on our side, because Allah, exalted is He, prescribed the ḥadd for slandering a stranger and a wife in absolute terms. Then the ḥadd for the wife was specified as being removed by li'ān, and the stranger remained under the absolute scope of the verse. Al-ʿAjlānī did not receive the ḥadd for Sharīk, nor Hilāl, because the claimant did not demand it, and the ḥadd for slander is not enforced by the ruler except after the demand, by consensus between us and him."

The 25th issue: When the two persons performing li'ān have both finished their li'ān, they separate, and each of them leaves by a door of the congregational mosque different from the door through which the other leaves. If they both leave through one door, that does not invalidate their li'ān. There is no disagreement that li'ān is not performed except in a congregational mosque where the Friday prayer is held, in the presence of the sultan or whoever stands in his place among the judges. A group of scholars recommended that li'ān take place in the congregational mosque after the ʿAṣr prayer. A Christian woman performs li'ān against her Muslim husband in the place that she honours in her church, with the same [[من ب وك. وفى أوج وط: مثل. (١٢ - ١٣)]] as what a Muslim woman performs it with.

The 26th issue: Mālik and his companions said: "With the completion of li'ān, separation (furqa) occurs between the two who performed li'ān, so they never reunite, nor do they inherit from each other, and it is not lawful for him to take her back (murāja'a) ever, neither before nor after a [another] husband." This is also the view of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Zufar ibn al-Hudhayl and al-Awzāʿī. Abū Ḥanīfa, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: "Separation does not occur after they finish li'ān until the judge separates them." This is also the view of al-Thawrī, based on the saying of Ibn ʿUmar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) separated the two who performed li'ān," so he attributed the separation to himself, and based on his saying, peace be upon him: "You have no authority over her."

Al-Shāfiʿī said: "When the husband completes the testimony and the li'ān, his bed with his wife is removed, whether she performs li'ān or not." He said: "As for the li'ān of the woman, it is only to avert the ḥadd from her, and her li'ān has no meaning in the removal of the bed. Since the li'ān of the husband negates the child and drops the ḥadd, the bed is lifted." ʿUthmān al-Battī used to see that li'ān does not diminish anything of the marriage bond between the spouses until he divorces. This is a view that none of the Companions preceded him in, and al-Battī recommended that the one performing li'ān divorce after the li'ān, and he did not approve of it before that, which indicates that li'ān, in his view, has produced a ruling. Jābir ibn Zayd, as mentioned by al-Ṭabarī and related by al-Lakhmī from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ṣufra, said in agreement with the view of ʿUthmān. The well-known position of the school is that the completion of li'ān between them is itself a separation.

Those who held this view argued that there is nothing in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, that makes separation obligatory when one of them performs li'ān, and by the saying of ʿUwaymir: "I have lied about her if I keep her," and he divorced her three times. He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not reject that from him, and did not say to him, 'Why did you say this, when you have no need for it, because she was already divorced by the li'ān?'" The argument for Mālik according to the well-known position and those who agree with him is his saying, peace be upon him: "You have no authority over her." This is an informing from him that the completion of li'ān removed his authority over her. His separating them is not the establishing of a new ruling; rather it was the enforcement of what Allah, exalted is He, made obligatory between them of separation, and this is the meaning of li'ān in the language.

The 27th issue: The majority of scholars held that the two who performed li'ān never marry each other ever. If he retracts his accusation (yukadhdhib nafsahu), he is flogged with the ḥadd, and the child is attributed to him, but she never returns to him. On this the Sunnah is beyond doubt and there is no disagreement. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned from ʿAṭāʾ that if the one who performed li'ān retracts his accusation after the li'ān, he is not punished, and he said: "They have already separated by a curse from Allah." Abū Ḥanīfa and Muḥammad said: "If he retracts his accusation, he is flogged with the ḥadd and the child is attributed to him, and he may be one of the suitors (khuṭṭāb) if he wishes." This is also the view of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salama, and they said: "The marriage returns as lawful just as the child is attributed to him, since there is no difference between any of these." The argument of the majority is his saying, peace be upon him: "You have no authority over her," and he did not say, "except if you retract your accusation." Ibn Isḥāq and a group related from al-Zuhrī that he said: "The Sunnah passed that when they perform li'ān they are separated, so they never reunite." Al-Dāraqutnī related it, and he related it as a marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet) report from the ḥadīth of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The two who perform li'ān, when they separate, never reunite ever." It is also related from ʿAlī and ʿAbd Allāh, who both said: "The Sunnah has passed that the two who perform li'ān do not reunite." From ʿAlī: "Ever."

The 28th issue: Li'ān requires four things: the number of the formulas, which is four testimonies as already mentioned; the place, which is that it be intended in the most noble of places in the cities: if it is in Mecca, then at the Corner (al-Rukn) and the Station (al-Maqām); if it is in Medina, then at the pulpit (minbar); if it is in Jerusalem, then at the Rock (al-Ṣakhra); and if it is in the rest of the cities, then in their mosques. If the two are unbelievers, they are sent to the place which they believe to be honoured: if they are Jews, then the synagogue (kanīsa); if they are Magians, then in the fire-temple; and if they have no religion, like the idolaters, then li'ān is performed between them in the session of the judge. The time, which is after the ʿAṣr prayer. And the gathering of people, which means that there should be four persons or more present. So the formula and the gathering of people are conditions, while the time and the place are recommended.

The 29th issue: Whoever says that separation occurs only with the completion of their li'ān, then if one of them dies before its completion, the other inherits from him. And whoever says that it occurs only with the separation by the imam, then if one of them dies before that and before the completion of li'ān, the other inherits from him. And according to the view of al-Shāfiʿī: if one of them dies before the woman performs li'ān, they do not inherit from each other.

The 30th issue: Ibn al-Qaṣṣār said: "The separation by li'ān is not a annulment (faskh) according to us, and this is the position of al-Mudawwana, for the ruling of li'ān's separation is the ruling of divorce's separation, and half of the dowry is given to the woman not consummated with." In Mukhtaṣar Ibn al-Jallāb: "She has nothing," and this is based on the view that the separation of li'ān is an annulment.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 24, verses 6–10 (part 1 of 4)**

There are thirty issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they have no witnesses except themselves﴾. The word "أَنْفُسُهُمْ" (anfusuhum, "themselves") is in the nominative case (marfu') as a substitute (badal). It may also be in the accusative (nasb) as an exception (istithna'), or as the predicate of "يَكُنْ" (yakun, "there is/be").

(﴿so the testimony of one of them﴾) The nominative "شَهَادَةُ" (shahadatu) is the reading of the Kufans, as the subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). The meaning is: the testimony of one of them that removes from him the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) is ﴿four testimonies﴾. The people of Medina and Abu 'Amr read "أَرْبَعَ" (arba'a) in the accusative, because the meaning of "فَشَهَادَةُ" (fashahadatu) is "that he testifies." The implied sense is: "it is incumbent upon them that one of them testify four testimonies," or "the matter is that one of them testify four testimonies." There is no disagreement that the second is accusative by the verb "testify" (al-shahadah).

(﴿and the fifth﴾) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). The predicate is "أَنَّ" (anna) and what follows it. The light form (al-mukhaffafah) has the same meaning as the heavy form (al-muthaqqalah), since its meaning is "that he." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Talhah, and 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "وَالْخَامِسَةَ" (wal-khamisata) in the accusative, meaning "and he bears witness, the fifth testimony." The rest read it in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate in "أَنَّ لَعْنَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ" (anna la'nata Allahi 'alayhi, "that the curse of Allah be upon him"). That is, "the fifth testimony is his saying: the curse of Allah be upon him."

**The second issue:** concerning the occasion of its revelation. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that Hilal ibn Umayyah accused his wife before the Prophet (ﷺ) of [adultery with] Shurayk ibn Sahma'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Evidence, or a punishment on your back." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, when one of us sees a man upon his wife, he seeks evidence!" The Prophet (ﷺ) kept saying: "Evidence, or else a punishment on your back." Hilal said: "By the One who sent you with the truth, I am truthful, and Allah will surely reveal in my case something that clears my back from the punishment." So this was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾, and he recited until he reached ﴿among the truthful﴾ (70). The hadith is related in full.

It has also been said: when the previous verse was revealed concerning those who accuse chaste women, its apparent meaning included wives and others. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I find a man with my wife, I will wait until I bring four witnesses! By Allah, I will strike him with the sword without turning away from him." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you wonder at the jealousy of Sa'd? I am more jealous than him, and Allah is more jealous than me." There are different narrations of Sa'd's words; this is roughly their meaning.

Then after that came Hilal ibn Umayyah al-Waqifi, and accused his wife Shurayk ibn Sahma' al-Balawi, as we mentioned. The Prophet (ﷺ) resolved to inflict on him the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf). At that point this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered them in the mosque and they performed the mutual imprecation (li'an). The woman hesitated at the fifth oath when she was admonished. It has been said that it was an oath that brings [the punishment]: that is, the fifth testimony entails the painful punishment if she was lying. Then she said: "I will not disgrace my people for the rest of the day." [The word "day" here refers to the genus, meaning days in general.] So she performed the li'an. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) separated them, and she gave birth to a boy who was like a dark-grey camel [al-awraq from camels: that which has a color between white and black], in the disliked description. Afterwards that boy became a governor in Egypt, and he did not know his own father.

Also 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani came and accused his wife and performed the li'an. The well-known view is that the case of Hilal came first, and that it was the cause of the verse. It has been said: the case of 'Uwaymir ibn Ashqar came first. This is a sound, well-known hadith that the imams have transmitted.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Safrah said: "The correct view is that the one who accused his wife was 'Uwaymir, and that Hilal ibn Umayyah is an error." Al-Tabari said: his saying in the hadith "Hilal ibn Umayyah" is objectionable; rather the accuser was 'Uwaymir ibn Zayd [In Usd al-Ghaba from al-Tabari: 'Uwaymir ibn al-Harith ibn Zayd ibn Haritha ibn al-Jadd] ibn al-Jadd ibn al-'Ajlani, who witnessed Uhud with the Prophet (ﷺ). He accused her of [adultery with] Shurayk ibn al-Sahma'. Al-Sahma' is his mother; she was called that because of her blackness. He is the son of 'Abdah ibn al-Jadd ibn al-'Ajlani. This is what the historians of reports used to say.

It has also been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to the people in the sermon on Friday: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾. 'Asim ibn 'Adi al-Ansari said: "May I be your ransom! If one of us found a man upon his wife's belly and spoke about what happened, he would be flogged eighty lashes, and the Muslims would call him a sinner, and his testimony would not be accepted. How then can one of us bring four witnesses? By the time he seeks four witnesses, the man will have finished his need!" Then the Prophet (ﷺ), upon him be peace, said: "Thus was it revealed, O 'Asim ibn 'Adi." 'Asim went out listening and obeying. Hilal ibn Umayyah met him, saying "inna lillah" [in the sense of distress]. He said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil! I found Shurayk ibn al-Sahma' upon the belly of my wife Khawlah, committing adultery with her." Khawlah was the daughter of 'Asim ibn 'Adi. In this chain it is stated that the one who found Shurayk with his wife was Hilal ibn Umayyah, but the correct view is the opposite, as already explained. Al-Kalbi said: "The more apparent view is that the one who found a partner with his wife was 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, because of the abundance of what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed li'an between al-'Ajlani and his wife." They agreed that this adulterer was Shurayk ibn 'Abdah, and his mother was al-Sahma'. 'Uwaymir and Khawlah bint Qays and Shurayk were cousins of 'Asim. This incident occurred in Sha'ban in the ninth year after the Hijrah, upon the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Tabuk to Medina, as al-Tabari said.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, who said: "I was present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he performed the li'an between 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani and his wife, on the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the battle of Tabuk. He (the husband) denied the pregnancy that was in her womb and said: 'It is the son of Ibn al-Sahma'.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Bring your wife, for the Qur'an has been revealed concerning you two.' So he performed the li'an between them after the afternoon prayer, near the pulpit, upon a [woven] cloth (khamal) [khamal is the fringe of a velvet or similar woven cloth that has trailing threads like a carpet's fringe]." In its chain is al-Waqidi, from al-Dahhak ibn 'Uthman, from 'Imran ibn Abi Anas, who said: "I heard 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far say..." and he mentioned it.

**The third issue:** the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾. It is general concerning every accusation, whether he says: "You have committed adultery," or "O adulteress," or "I saw her committing adultery," or "This child is not mine," for the verse includes all of these. The li'an is obligatory if he does not bring four witnesses. This is the view of the majority of scholars, the general body of jurists, and the community of the people of hadith. It has been related from Malik something similar. Malik used to say: he does not perform the li'an unless he says: "I saw you committing adultery," or he denies a pregnancy or a child from her. The view of Abu al-Zinad, Yahya ibn Sa'id, and al-Batti is similar to the view of Malik: the li'an is not obligatory by accusation alone, but only by seeing [the act] or denying a pregnancy together with a claim of istibra' (establishing that the womb is clear). This is the well-known view of Malik, and it was stated by Ibn al-Qasim. The sound view is the first, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the apparent meaning of the Qur'an suffices to make li'an obligatory by mere accusation without seeing [the act]. So rely upon it, especially since in the sound hadith: "Have you seen a man who found another man with his wife?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go and bring her," and he did not require him to mention seeing. And they agreed that a blind man performs li'an if he accuses his wife. Had seeing been a condition of li'an, the blind man would not perform it. This is what Abu 'Umar said. Ibn al-Qassar narrated from Malik that the li'an of a blind man is not valid unless he says: "I touched his private part in her private part."

The proof for Malik and those who follow him is what Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: Hilal ibn Umayyah, who was one of the three whose repentance was accepted, came from his land at night and found a man with his family. He saw with his eye and heard with his ear, and he did not confront him until morning. Then he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I came to my family at night and found a man with them, and I saw with my eye and heard with my ear." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked what he brought and was distressed by it, so this was revealed: ﴿And those who accuse their wives, and have no witnesses except themselves﴾, and he mentioned the hadith. This is an explicit text that the li'an in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed judgment was concerned with seeing, so it is not necessary to extend this beyond that. Whoever accuses his wife without mentioning seeing is to receive the punishment, due to the generality of His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾.

**The fourth issue:** if he denies the pregnancy, he performs the li'an, because this is stronger than seeing. He must mention non-intercourse and the istibra' after it. Our scholars differed about the istibra'. Al-Mughirah and Malik, in one of their two views, said: one menstrual cycle suffices in this regard. Malik also said: he does not deny it except after three menstrual cycles. The sound view is the first, because the clearing of the womb from occupation is achieved by it, as in the istibra' of a slave woman. We took three menstrual cycles into account in the waiting period (al-'iddah) for another ruling, which will be explained in the chapter on divorce, if Allah wills. Al-Lakhmi narrated from Malik that he said once: "The child is not denied by istibra', because menstruation can occur during pregnancy." This was also the view of Ashhab in the Book of Ibn al-Mawwaz, and it was said by al-Mughirah. He said: "The child is not denied except after five years, since that is the maximum period of pregnancy, according to what has been mentioned earlier."

**The fifth issue:** the li'an for us occurs between every pair of spouses, whether they are free or both slaves, Muslims or disbelievers, dissolute or upright. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i. There is no li'an between a man and his slave woman, nor between him and the mother of his child (umm walad, a slave woman who bore her master's child). It has been said: the child of a slave woman is not disowned by him except by a single oath, unlike li'an. It has also been said: if he denies the child of an umm walad, he performs li'an. The first view is the correct representation of the school of Malik, and it is the right one.

Abu Hanifah said: li'an is not valid except between two free Muslim spouses, because li'an is testimony in his view, while in our view and in al-Shafi'i's view it is an oath. So everyone whose oath is valid, his accusation and li'an are valid. They agreed that both must be legally responsible (mukallaf).

In the words [of the Prophet (ﷺ)]: "He found a man with his wife" [the Arabic: "وَجَدَ مَعَ امْرَأَتِهِ رَجُلًا"] [note: this refers to the saying of 'Uwaymir or another, based on the earlier disagreement] is evidence that li'an is obligatory for every pair of spouses, because he did not specify a man from a man or a woman from a woman. The verse of li'an was revealed in accordance with this answer, when He said: ﴿And those who accuse their wives﴾, and He did not specify one spouse from another. This is the view of Malik and the people of Medina, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, and Abu Thawr. Furthermore, li'an necessitates the annulment of the marriage, so it resembles divorce; therefore whoever may be divorced may perform li'an.

Li'an is oaths, not testimonies. Allah the Exalted, who is the most truthful of speakers, said: ﴿Our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ (10) [al-Ma'idah: 107], meaning "our oaths." He also said: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say: "We bear witness that you are truly the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. Then He said: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 16].

He (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for the oaths, there would have been a matter between me and her." As for the arguments put forward by al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa, they are arguments that do not stand on their own legs. Among them is the hadith of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no li'an (mutual imprecation between spouses) among four: there is no li'an between a free man and a slave woman; there is no li'an between a free woman and a slave; there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Jewish woman; and there is no li'an between a Muslim and a Christian woman." It was narrated by al-Daraqutni through chains that he declared weak in all of them. It is also related from al-Awza'i and Ibn Jurayj, two imams, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, as his own statement, and they did not raise it [[In Sunan al-Daraqutni: "yarfa'ah" (they both raised it).]] to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They also argued on the basis of reasoning: since spouses were excluded from the general category of witnesses by His words, "And they have no witnesses except themselves," it follows that only one whose testimony is acceptable may perform li'an. Furthermore, if it were an oath, it would not be repeated; and the wisdom in its repetition is that it stands in place of witnesses for adultery. We reply: this is refuted by the oath of qasama (the oath of collective accusation in cases of homicide), for it is repeated, and yet it is not testimony by consensus (ijma'), and the wisdom in its repetition is the intensification of the gravity of matters of chastity and blood. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The decisive point that it is an oath and not testimony is that the husband swears for himself, to establish his claim and to free himself from punishment. How could anyone claim in the Sharia that a witness testifies for himself in a way that imposes a ruling upon another? This is remote in principle and nonexistent in reasoning.

Sixth: The scholars differed concerning the li'an of a mute man. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: he performs li'an, because he is one whose divorce, zihar (a form of divorce by likening a wife to a forbidden relative) and ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse) are valid, when his meaning is understood. Abu Hanifa said: he does not perform li'an, because he is not among those competent to testify, and because he may speak with his tongue and deny the li'an, so we cannot carry out the hadd (prescribed punishment) against him.
