Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr related that ʿĀʾishah absolved Hassan of the false accusation and said: "He did not say anything." Hassan himself denied that he had said anything of that kind, in his verse:

"Chaste, steadfast, she is not suspected of any doubt,
and she wakes up hungry from the flesh of the heedless. [*Ḥaṣān*: chaste. *Razān*: steadfast, dignified, chaste. *Ghirthā*: hungry. *Mā tuzann*: is not suspected. *Al-ghawāfil*: plural of *ghāfilah*, i.e., she does not graze in people's honour.]

The beloved of the best of people in religion and lineage,
the Prophet of guidance and of noble and bountiful virtues.

The noblewoman of a tribe of Luʾayy ibn Ghālib,
of noble endeavours, whose glory never vanishes.

Refined, whom Allah has made good in her nature [*khīm*: nature, disposition, character, origin],
and purified from every blemish and falsehood.

If what has reached you is that I said it,
then let my fingers never lift my whip to me.

How then, when my love for her endures as long as I live, and my support
for the family of the Messenger of Allah, the adornment of gatherings?

She has a lofty rank over the people, whose excellence
the reach of the one who seeks to surpass falls short of."

It has been narrated that when he recited to her "Chaste, steadfast," she said to him: "You are not like that"; she meant that you fell into the heedless ones. This is a contradiction, and it can be reconciled by saying that Hassan did not say it explicitly and plainly; rather he made an allusion to it and hinted at it, so it was attributed to him. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 11–22 (part 2 of 3):

Scholars have differed over whether he (ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy) engaged in the slander (al-ifk), and whether he received the prescribed punishment (al-hadd, the fixed penalty set by the Law). God knows best which of these was the case.

The sixth issue: Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) flogged two men and a woman for the slander: Mistah, Hassan and Hamnah. At-Tirmidhi also mentioned this. Al-Qushayri reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) flogged Ibn Ubayy eighty lashes, and for him in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Qushayri said: What is established in the reports is that he struck Ibn Ubayy, and he struck Hassan and Hamnah. As for Mistah, no explicit slander has been established from him, but he used to listen and spread (the story) without explicit accusation.

Al-Mawardi [the seventh issue: al-Mawardi] and others said: They differed over whether the Prophet (ﷺ) inflicted the hadd on the people of the slander, and there are two views. One is that he did not inflict the hadd on any of the people of the slander, because the hadd punishments are only carried out on the basis of confession or proof, and God did not command him to carry them out on the basis of his report about them, just as He did not command him to kill the hypocrites, although He informed him of their disbelief. I say: This view is corrupt and contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an, for God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses — lash them with eighty lashes﴾, meaning, as evidence for the truth of their claim. The second view: The Prophet (ﷺ) inflicted the hadd on the people of the slander: ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, Mistah ibn Uthathah, Hassan ibn Thabit and Hamnah bint Jahsh. Concerning this a Muslim poet said:

Hassan has tasted what his people had,
and Hamnah, when they spoke foolishly, and Mistah.
And Ibn Salul tasted disgrace in the hadd,
as he plunged into a lie that speaks plainly.
They undertook to hurl baseless accusations at the wife of their Prophet,
and to provoke the wrath of the Lord of the Glorious Throne, so they went too far.
They harmed the Messenger of God in it, so they were lashed
with disgraces that remain; they were disgraced and exposed.
So there poured upon them stones [as if they were]
showers of rain pouring from the peaks of clouds.

I say: The well-known report and what is recognized among the scholars is that those who were given the hadd were Hassan, Mistah and Hamnah, and no hadd has been heard of for ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy. Abu Dawud narrated from ʿAisha, may God be pleased with her, who said: When my innocence was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up, mentioned that, and recited the Qur'an. When he came down from the pulpit he ordered the two men and the woman, and they were struck their hadd, and he named them: Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah ibn Uthathah and Hamnah bint Jahsh. In the book of at-Tahawi (the text reads): "eighty, eighty." Our scholars said: ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy was not given the hadd because God, Exalted, had prepared for him a great punishment in the Hereafter; if he had been given the hadd in this world, that would have been a reduction of his punishment in the Hereafter and a lightening of it for him. Moreover, God, Exalted, has testified to the innocence of ʿAisha, may God be pleased with her, and to the lie of everyone who accused her, so the purpose of the hadd has been achieved, since its aim is to show the falsehood of the accuser and the innocence of the one accused, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, it is they who, in the sight of God, are the liars﴾. These believers were given the hadd only so that the sin of the slander they had committed would be expiated for them, so that no consequence of it would remain against them in the Hereafter. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the hadd punishments: "They are an expiation for the one upon whom they are carried out", as in the hadith of ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit. It is also possible to say: The hadd of Ibn Ubayy was left out in order to win over his people, to respect his son, and to extinguish the blaze of the feared strife that could have followed from it, for its early signs had already appeared from Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah and his people, as in Sahih Muslim. And God knows best.

The seventh issue: God's saying: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think good of one another and say, "This is an obvious lie"?﴾ This is a rebuke from God, glorified and exalted, to the believers for their thinking when the people of the slander said what they said. Ibn Zayd said: The believers thought that a believer would not commit adultery with his own mother; this was related by al-Mahdawi. Here "lawla" (why not) means "halla" (why did they not). It was also said: The meaning is that the distinguished believing men and women should have judged the matter by their own selves, so that if such a thing seemed unlikely of them, it would be even more unlikely of ʿAisha and Safwan. It was reported that this sound reasoning occurred to Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and his wife. He entered upon her and she said to him: "O Abu Ayyub, have you heard what is being said?" He said: "Yes! And that is a lie! Would you, O Umm Ayyub, do such a thing?" She said: "No, by God!" He said: "Then ʿAisha, by God, is better than you." Umm Ayyub said: "Yes." This act and others like it is what God, Exalted, rebuked the believers for, since not all of them did it.

The eighth issue: God's saying ﴿by their own selves﴾. An-Nahhas said: The meaning of "by their own selves" is "by their brothers." So God made it obligatory upon the Muslims, when they hear a man slander someone and mention him with an ugliness that they do not know him to have, to deny it against him and to call him a liar, and He threatened those who abstain from doing so and those who transmit it.

I say: For this reason the scholars said: This verse is a foundation for the principle that the rank of faith which a person has attained, the status of righteousness which the believer has reached, and the garment of chastity with which the Muslim covers himself, are not removed from him by a report that is merely possible, even if it spreads, when its basis is corrupt or unknown.

The ninth issue: God's saying: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it?﴾ This is a reproach to the people of the slander. "Lawla" here means "halla" (why did they not), i.e., why did they not bring four witnesses for what they alleged of the fabrication. This is a rejection of the first judgment and a referral to the earlier verse on slander.

The tenth issue: God's saying: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, it is they who, in the sight of God, are the liars﴾, meaning: they are liars in the judgment of God. A man may be unable to produce proof while being truthful in his accusation, yet in the judgment of the Law and the outward matter he is a liar, though not in the knowledge of God, Exalted. God only attached the hadd punishments to His ruling which He legislated in this world, not to the requirement of His knowledge which relates to the human being as he truly is. Thus the ruling of the Hereafter is what is built upon that.

I say: What strengthens this meaning and supports it is what al-Bukhari transmitted from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "O people, revelation has ended, and we are now only holding you accountable for what has become apparent to us of your deeds. Whoever shows us good, we grant him security and bring him near, and we have no claim upon his inner intention; God will call him to account for his inner intention. Whoever shows us evil, we do not grant him security nor believe him, even if he says that his inner intention is good." The scholars unanimously agreed that the rulings of this world are based on what is outward, and that inner states are left to God, Mighty and Majestic.

The eleventh issue: God's saying: ﴿And if not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy...﴾ [This refers to verse 10, which is God's saying: "And if not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy, and that God is Forgiving and Wise."] The word "fadl" (bounty) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada') according to Sibawayh, and the predicate is omitted, which the Arabs do not make explicit. The answer to "lawla" is omitted because a similar one was mentioned afterwards. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if not for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy, [it would have] touched you...﴾, meaning: because of what you said about ʿAisha, a great punishment in this world and the Hereafter would have struck you. This is an eloquent rebuke from God, yet with His mercy He concealed it for you in this world, and He will show mercy in the Hereafter to whoever comes to Him in repentance. "Al-ifada" means: taking up in the talk, and it is this that the rebuke fell upon. It is said: "The people plunged into the talk" (afada al-qawm fi'l-hadith), meaning they took up in it.

The twelfth issue: God's saying: ﴿When you received it with your tongues﴾. The reading of Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqaʿ is with a damma on the first letter of "tatalaqqawnahu," a sukun on the lam, and a damma on the qaf, from "al-ilqa'" (casting), and this is a clear reading. Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud read "idh tatalaqqawnahu" from "al-talaqqi," with two taʾs. The majority of the Seven read with one taʾ and clear pronunciation of the dhal without idgham (assimilation), and this too is from "al-talaqqi." Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with idgham of the dhal into the taʾ. Ibn Kathir read with the dhal clearly pronounced and the taʾ assimilated into the taʾ, and this is an uneasy reading, because it requires two consecutive sukuns; it is not like the assimilation in the reading of the one who reads "fala tanajaw. Wa la tanabazu" (Do not confide in one another, nor insult one another by nicknames), because there the alif, a silent letter, intervenes, and since it is a soft vowel letter, that was acceptable there, which is not acceptable with a sukun on the dhal. Ibn Yaʿmur and ʿAisha, may God be pleased with them both, who are the most knowledgeable people in this matter, read "idh talaqqunahu" with a fatha on the taʾ, a kasra on the lam and a damma on the qaf. The meaning of this reading comes from the Arab saying: "Waqa al-rajul yalqu waqlan" when he lied and persisted in it, so they used the transitive verb as evidence for the intransitive. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: In my view, he meant "idh talaqqunahu fihi" (when you were lying about it), so the preposition was omitted and the pronoun attached. Al-Khalil and Abu ʿAmr said: The origin of "al-walq" is haste; it is said: "The camels came hastening" (jaʾat al-ibilu talaq), i.e., they hastened. He said:

When they saw an army upon them that had come by night,
they came with flocks from al-Sham, hastening.
Indeed al-Husayn is slippery and quick to climax,
she brought him, a strong she-camel from al-Sham, hastening.

It is said: "a man who is zalaq and zumlaq," on the pattern of "hudabid," and "zumalaq" and "zumlaq" (with a shadda on the mim), which is one who ejaculates before he has intercourse. The rajaz poet said:

Indeed al-Husayn is zalaq and zumlaq.

Al-walq also means light stabbing. One says "walaqahu yalquhu walqan." It is said: "walaqahu bi'l-sayf walaqat," i.e., blows, so the word is homonymous.

The thirteenth issue: God's saying: ﴿And you say with your mouths﴾, which is intensification, obligation and emphasis. The pronoun in "tahsabunahu" (you consider it) refers to the speech, plunging into it, and spreading it. "Hayyinan" means: slight and easy, not reaching you with any sin.

﴿And it is, in the sight of God, grave﴾, in respect of the burden. This is like his saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of the two graves: "Indeed they are being punished, and they are not being punished for something great", meaning in relation to you.

**Fourteenth:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did you not say, "It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander"? Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it again, if you are believers. And Allah makes the signs clear to you, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ This is a rebuke addressed to all the believers. The meaning is: it was incumbent upon you to disapprove of it, and that none of you should take it up and pass it on from one to another by way of relating and transmitting it. You should also have declared Allah exalted above such a thing occurring from the wife of His Prophet, peace be upon him. And you should have judged this statement to be a slander (buhtan). The reality of buhtan is saying about a person what is not in him, whereas ghiba (backbiting) is saying about a person what is in him. This meaning has been reported in the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Then Allah admonished them against returning to a similar situation. The word "an" (that) is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), with the implied sense of "out of dislike that," or the like.

**Fifteenth:** Allah's words ﴿if you are believers﴾ are a reminder and an emphasis, just as you would say, "It is fitting for you to do such and such, if you are a man."

**Sixteenth:** Allah's words ﴿Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it﴾ refer to Aisha, because "the like of it" can only be a parallel of the accusation concerning the very same person, or concerning one of the same rank as her among the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is because such an act harms the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his honour and his family, and that is disbelief (kufr) on the part of the one who does it.

**Seventeenth:** Hisham ibn Ammar said: I heard Malik say, "Whoever insults Abu Bakr and Umar is to be disciplined, and whoever insults Aisha is to be put to death, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah admonishes you never to repeat the like of it, if you are believers﴾. So whoever insults Aisha has opposed the Qur'an, and whoever opposes the Qur'an is put to death."

Ibn al-Arabi said: The companions of al-Shafi'i said, "Whoever insults Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, is to be disciplined as is done for the rest of the believers. And the words ﴿if you are believers﴾ were not said concerning Aisha, because that [i.e., insulting her] would be disbelief. Rather, it is as he (peace be upon him) said: 'A man does not believe whose neighbour is not safe from his evils.'" And if removing faith in the one who insults Aisha were literal, then removing faith in the statement "An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer" would also be literal.

We reply: It is not as you claim. Rather, the People of the Slander (ahl al-ifk) accused Aisha, the pure one, of indecency, and Allah cleared her. So everyone who insults her with that of which Allah has cleared her is one who denies Allah, and whoever denies Allah is a disbeliever. This is the path of Malik's position, and it is a clear way for people of insight. And if a man insulted Aisha with something other than that from which Allah cleared her, his punishment would be discipline.

**Eighteenth:** Allah's words ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾: that is, that it should spread and become widely known. It is said: "shā'a al-shay'u shuyū'an, wa-shi'an, wa-shi'ānan, wa-shuyū'uh," meaning it became apparent and spread.

﴿Among those who believe﴾: that is, among the chaste men and the chaste women. By this general expression what is meant is Aisha and Safwan, may Allah be pleased with them both. "Al-fāḥisha" (indecency) is an act that is ugly to an extreme degree. It is also said that "al-fāḥisha" in this verse means an evil statement.

﴿For them is a painful punishment in this world﴾: that is, the prescribed punishment (hadd). ﴿And in the Hereafter, the punishment of the Fire﴾: that is, for the hypocrites, so this is specific. We have already explained that the hadd is an expiation (kaffara) for believers. al-Tabari said: its meaning is, if he dies persisting in it without repenting.

**Nineteenth:** Allah's words ﴿And Allah knows﴾: that is, He knows the magnitude of this sin and the recompense for it, and He knows everything.

﴿And you do not know﴾: it has been narrated from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever supports a man among the people in a dispute about which he has no knowledge, he is in the wrath of Allah until he desists from it. And whoever intercedes on behalf of someone so that a prescribed punishment from the punishments of Allah is not carried out, he has truly defied Allah and brought upon himself His wrath, and the curse of Allah follows him until the Day of Resurrection. And whoever spreads a word against a Muslim man, while he is innocent of it, intending to disgrace him with it in this world, it is incumbent upon Allah to cast him into the Fire with it." Then he recited as its confirmation from the Book of Allah: ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾, the verse.

**Twentieth:** Allah's words ﴿O you who have believed, do not follow the steps of Satan﴾: that is, his paths and ways. The meaning: do not travel the road to which Satan calls you. The singular of "khuṭuwāt" is "khuṭwa," which is the distance between the two feet. "Al-khaṭwa" (with a fatḥa) is the verbal noun: one says "khaṭawtu khaṭwatan," and its plural is "khaṭawāt." And "takhaṭṭā ilaynā fulān" (so-and-so stepped over to us), and from this is the hadith that he saw a man stepping over the necks of people on Friday.

The majority of readers recited "khuṭuwāt" with a ḍamma on the ṭā'. ʿĀṣim and al-A'mash read it with sukūn. The majority read "mā zakā" with a light kāf, meaning he was not guided, nor did he accept Islam, nor did he recognise right guidance. It is also said that "mā zakā" means he did not become righteous; one says "zakā yazkū zakā'an," meaning he became righteous. Al-Hasan and Abu Ḥaywa read it with a shaddah, meaning that His purifying you, His cleansing of you and His guidance of you come only through His grace, not through your deeds.

Al-Kisa'i said: "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā tattabiʿū khuṭuwāti al-shayṭān" is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridh), and His words "mā zakā minkum min aḥadin abadan" (none of you would ever have been purified) are the answer to His earlier and second statement: ﴿And if not for the grace of Allah upon you﴾.

**Twenty-first:** Allah's words ﴿And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give﴾, the verse. The most well-known of the reports is that this verse was revealed concerning the story of Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafa, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mistah ibn Uthatha. That was because Mistah was the son of his maternal aunt's daughter, and he was among the poor Emigrants and the Badr veterans. He is Mistah ibn Uthatha ibn ʿAbbad ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manaf. It is also said that his name was Awf, and Mistah was a nickname. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to spend on him because of his poverty and kinship. When the matter of the slander occurred, and Mistah said what he said, Abu Bakr swore that he would not spend on him nor benefit him with any benefit ever. Then Mistah came and made excuses, saying: "I was only frequenting the gatherings of Hassan, and I would listen but not speak." Abu Bakr said to him: "You laughed and took part in what was said." And he passed by his right side (i.e., he swore an oath), and then the verse was revealed.

Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas said: A group of the believers cut off their benefits from everyone who spoke about the slander, and they said: "By Allah, we will not maintain relations with anyone who spoke about the matter of Aisha." So the verse was revealed concerning all of them.

The first (the report about Abu Bakr and Mistah) is more sound. However, the verse includes the Ummah until the Day of Resurrection, in that no one of virtue and wealth should become angry and swear that he will never benefit one who has such a description.

In the authentic report: when Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you﴾, the ten verses, Abu Bakr, who had been spending on Mistah because of his kinship and poverty, said: "By Allah, I will never spend anything on him again after what he said about Aisha." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And let not those of virtue among you and wealth swear not to give﴾, up to His words: ﴿Do you not like that Allah should forgive you?﴾. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah the Exalted. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "By Allah, I truly love that Allah should forgive me." So he returned to Mistah the provision he used to spend on him and said: "I will never withdraw it from him."

**Twenty-second:** In this verse there is evidence that slander (qadhf), even if it is a major sin, does not nullify good deeds, because Allah the Exalted described Mistah after his statement with emigration and faith. The same applies to all the major sins. Nothing nullifies deeds except associating partners with Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65].

**Twenty-third:** Whoever swears an oath not to do something, then sees that doing it is better, should do it and make expiation (kaffara) for his oath, or make expiation for his oath and then do it, as has preceded in Surat al-Ma'ida. The jurists held that whoever swears never to do a sunnah (a recommended practice) or a mandub (commendable act), and makes that permanent, this is a disqualification (jarh) of his testimony. Al-Baji mentioned this in al-Muntaqa.

**Twenty-fourth:** Allah's words ﴿And let not those of virtue﴾: "wa-lā ya'tali" means he swears, its pattern is yaf'ali, from al-alliyya, which is the oath, and from it is the Exalted's words ﴿for those who swear off from their wives﴾ (al-Baqara: 226), which has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqara. A group said its meaning is "yuqassir" (falls short), from your saying "alawtu fī kadhā" when you fell short in it, and from it is the Exalted's words ﴿they do not fall short in harming you﴾ (Ali 'Imran: 118).

**Twenty-fifth:** Allah's words ﴿Do you not like that Allah should forgive you?﴾ are an illustration and an argument: that is, just as you love Allah's pardon for your sins, so likewise you should forgive those beneath you. To this meaning the Prophet's words, peace be upon him, refer: "He who does not show mercy will not be shown mercy."

**Twenty-sixth:** Some scholars said: This is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah the Exalted, in terms of the gentleness of Allah toward the sinful slanderers through this expression. It was also said: the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is His words: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47]. And Allah said in another verse: ﴿Those who believed and did righteous deeds, in gardens of paradise, for them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 22], so this verse explains the great bounty, and the other gives good tidings of it to the believers. Among the verses of hope is His words: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves..."﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and His words: ﴿Allah is Subtle with His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19]. Some of them said: the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5], because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not be content while any one of his Ummah remained in the Fire.

**Twenty-seventh:** Allah's words ﴿that they should give﴾: that is, "an lā yu'tū" (that they should not give), so the "lā" was elided, like the saying of the speaker:

"Fa-qultu yamīnu Allāhi abraḥu qā'idan / wa-law qaṭaʿū ra'sī ladayka wa-awṣālī"

This is the first half of a line of Imru' al-Qays, whose completion is: "Or even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs."

Al-Zajjaj mentioned this. According to the view of Abu Ubayda, there is no need to suppose an elided "lā."

﴿And let them pardon﴾: from "afā al-rab'u," meaning it was effaced, so it is the erasure of the sin, just as the trace of the encampment is effaced.

There are two issues here.

The first concerns the words ﴿al-muhsanat﴾ (ﷺ). Their discussion appeared earlier, in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, pp. 12–20 1. (14)]]. The scholars agreed that the ruling for male *muhsanin* (chaste men) regarding slander is the same as the ruling for female *muhsanat* (chaste women), both by analogy (qiyas, reasoning from a parallel case) and by inference. We explained this at the beginning of the surah, and praise be to Allah. There is disagreement about who is meant by this verse. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it refers specifically to those who slandered 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Others said: it refers to 'A'ishah and all the other wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others. Repentance does not benefit them. As for anyone who slanders other chaste women, Allah has made repentance available to him, because He said: "And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses" up to His words "except those who repent" (160). So Allah made repentance available for these, and did not make it available for those, as al-Dahhak said. It was also said: this threat is for whoever persists in slander and does not repent. It was said: it was revealed about 'A'ishah, but what is meant is every person who has this attribute. It was said: it is general, covering all slanderers of all people, male and female, and the sense would be: "Indeed those who accuse the chaste women (of the believers)," so the masculine and feminine are both included. Al-Nahhas preferred this view.

It was also said: it was revealed about the polytheists of Makkah, because they used to say to a woman when she emigrated: "She only left in order to commit fornication."

The second issue concerns the words ﴿they are cursed in this world and the Hereafter﴾. The scholars said: if the verse is taken to refer to believing slanderers, then "curse" means being distanced (from Allah's mercy and the community), receiving the prescribed punishment (hadd), being shunned and avoided by believers, losing the standing of 'adalah (uprightness of character, which qualifies a person to give testimony), and being removed from good praise on the tongues of believers. According to the view that the verse is specifically about 'A'ishah, these severities apply to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those like him. According to the view that it was revealed about the polytheists of Makkah, there is no discussion needed: they are distanced, and for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment. Whoever embraces Islam, Islam erases what came before it. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: among the best things said in interpreting this verse is that it is general, covering all slanderers of all people, male and female, and the sense would be: "Indeed those who accuse the chaste women (of the believers)," so the masculine and feminine are both included, and likewise in "those who accuse," except that the masculine has been given precedence over the feminine.

Qur'anic reading of the common reciters is with the yā' (yashhadu, "bear witness" in the masculine), and Abū Ḥātim chose it. Al-A'mash, Yaḥyā, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read "yashhadu" with the yā', and Abū 'Ubayd chose it, because the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa'l-majrūr) has come between the noun and the verb. The meaning: on the day when the tongues of some of them will bear witness against others concerning what they used to do of slander (qadhf) and calumny (buhtān). It has also been said: their own tongues will bear witness against them that day for what they spoke. "And their hands and their feet" means: and the limbs (al-jawāriḥ) will speak of what they did in the world.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 25:

﴿On that Day, Allah will pay them their true due, and they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth.﴾ (24:25) That is, their reckoning and their recompense. Mujahid recited: "On that Day Allah will pay them their true due (dinahum al-haqqa)" with "al-haqqu" in the nominative (raf'), taking it as an attribute (na't) of Allah, mighty and majestic. Abu 'Ubayd said: Were it not for disliking to oppose people, the correct reading would be the nominative, so that it is an attribute of Allah, mighty and majestic, and it would agree with the reading of Ubayy, for Jarir ibn Hazim said: "I saw in the Mushaf of Ubayy: 'Yuwaffihimu Allahu al-haqqu dinahum (Allah will pay them, the Truth, their due).'" Al-Nahhas said: This statement of Abu 'Ubayd is not acceptable, because he argued with something that opposes the great majority (al-sawad al-a'zam). Nor is there any proof in it, for even if it is established that it is so in the Mushaf of Ubayy, the reading could be: "Yuwaffihimu Allahu al-haqqa dinahum," with "dinahum" as a substitute (badal) for "al-haqq." According to the reading "dinahumu al-haqqa," "al-haqqa" is an attribute (na't) of "dinahum," and the meaning is good, because Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned the wrongdoers and informed that He will requite them with truth, as He said, mighty and majestic: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ (34:17), because Allah's requital of the disbeliever and the wrongdoer is in truth and justice, and His requital of the doer of good is with goodness and bounty.

(﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾) These are two of His names, glory be to Him. We have mentioned them in more than one place, and especially in the book al-Asna (al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna).

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning is that wicked women are for wicked men, and likewise wicked men are for wicked women, and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women.

Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Ata' and most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: The meaning is that wicked words are for wicked men, and likewise wicked people are for wicked words, and good words are for good people, and good people are for good words. Al-Nahhas said in his book Ma'ani al-Quran: "This is among the best of what has been said about this verse." What supports the soundness of this view is the statement, "Those are cleared of what they say," meaning that Aisha and Safwan are cleared of what the wicked men and wicked women say.

It has also been said that this verse is built upon His saying: "The fornicator marries none but a fornicatress or an idolatress" (24:3). So the wicked women are the adulteresses, and the good women are the chaste, and likewise the good men and the good women. Al-Nahhas also chose this view, and it is the meaning of Ibn Zayd's statement.

"Those are cleared of what they say" refers to the category (jins). It has been said that it refers to Aisha and Safwan, and so the plural is used, as in His saying: "If he has brothers" (4:11), while the intended meaning is two brothers. This was said by al-Farra'. [See vol. 5, p. 72.]

"Cleared" (mubarra'un) means "declared free" (munazzahun) from what they were accused of. Some of the people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq, i.e., careful scholars) said: When Yusuf, peace be upon him, was accused of immorality, Allah cleared him through the tongue of an infant in the cradle. When Maryam was accused of immorality, Allah cleared her through the tongue of her son Isa, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. When Aisha was accused of immorality, Allah cleared her through the Qur'an. So He was not content to clear her by the testimony of an infant or a prophet, until He cleared her with His own speech from slander and calumny.

It is related from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from his grandmother, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I have been given nine things that no woman has been given. Jibril, peace be upon him, came down with my image in his palm when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to marry me. He married me while I was a virgin, and he married no other virgin but me. He (ﷺ) died while his head was in my lap. He (ﷺ) was buried in my house. The angels surrounded my house. The revelation would descend upon him while he was among his family, and they would disperse from him. It would descend upon him while I was with him under his blanket, and it did not separate me from his body. I am the daughter of his khalifa (successor) and his siddiq (truthful companion). My innocence came down from the sky. I was created good, and for a good man. I have been promised forgiveness and a generous provision (rizq karim)," referring to His saying: "For them is forgiveness and a generous provision," which is Paradise.

**The first issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, singled out the children of Adam, whom He honoured and favoured, by giving them dwellings and screening them within them from sight, and by granting them the right to enjoy them in privacy, He forbade the creatures from looking into what is inside from outside or entering them without the permission of their owners. He disciplined them with what pertains to covering them, so that none of them would see another's nakedness (*awrah*).

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever looks into the house of a people without their permission, it is lawful for them to gouge out his eye." The scholars have differed in interpreting this. Some of the scholars said: "This is not to be taken literally. If someone gouges out the eye, he is liable for compensation (*daman*), and the report is abrogated (*mansukh*), having been issued before the revelation of His saying: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]. It may also be that it was stated as a warning (*wa'id*) and not as a binding ruling (*hatm*). A report that contradicts the Book of Allah, the Exalted, may not be acted upon."

The Prophet (ﷺ) would speak words that apparently meant one thing while he intended something else. It is reported that when ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas praised him, he said to Bilal: "Stand up and cut off his tongue," but he only intended by that to give him something, and did not really intend cutting. Likewise, this may be the mention of gouging out the eye, while what is meant is that some action be taken so that he does not look into another's house thereafter. Others said: "There is no compensation for it, nor retaliation (*qisas*)," and this is the correct view, God willing, on the basis of the hadith of Anas, as will come.

**The second issue:** The occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Tabari and others transmitted from ʿAdi ibn Thabit: a woman of the Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am in my house in a state that I do not like anyone to see me in, neither a parent nor a child. A father comes in and enters upon me, and a man of my family keeps entering upon me while I am in that state. What should I do?" Then the verse was revealed. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you think of the inns and dwellings on the roads of Syria that have no one living in them?" So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿There is no sin upon you for entering houses not inhabited﴾ [al-Nur: 29].

**The third issue:** Allah, glorified and exalted is He, extended the prohibition on entering a house that is not yours to a limit, which is *al-istinas*, and that is *al-istidhan* (seeking permission). Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "*Al-istinas* in our view, and Allah knows best, is *al-istidhan*." Likewise in the reading of Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "until you seek permission and greet its people." It was also said that the meaning of *tastanisu* is *tastaʿlimu*, i.e., you make known who is in the house. Mujahid said: by clearing the throat, or by any means possible, and he waits long enough to know that he has been noticed, then he enters after that. Al-Tabari said the same, and from this is His saying: ﴿If you perceive in them sound judgement﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], meaning you know. A poet said:

*She perceived a sound and the cry of the owl frightened her, in the afternoon, when evening was near.*

I say: In the Sunan of Ibn Majah: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba narrated to us, ʿAbd al-Rahim ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Wasil ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu Sawra, from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting (*salam*), so what is *al-istinas*?" He said: "A man speaks with a glorification (*tasbih*), a magnification (*takbir*) and a praise (*tahmid*), clears his throat, and informs the people of the house." I say: This is explicit that *al-istinas* is other than *al-istidhan*, as Mujahid and those who agreed with him said.

**The fourth issue:** It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and some people say from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, that "until you seek companionship" (*hatta tasta'nisu*) is an error or a mistake by the scribe; it is only "until you seek permission" (*hatta tasta'dhinu*). This is not correct from Ibn ʿAbbas or others, for all the codices (*masahif*) of the Muslims have "until you seek companionship" firmly established in them, and consensus (*ijma'*) on it has been established since the time of ʿUthman. It is what may not be opposed. To attribute error and mistake to the scribe regarding a wording on which the Companions unanimously agreed is a statement that is not sound from Ibn ʿAbbas. Allah, mighty and majestic, has said: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Fussilat: 42], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9].

It has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that there is an inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the speech, and the meaning is: "until you greet its people and seek companionship," related by Abu Hatim. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: What negates this view from Ibn ʿAbbas and others is that "seek companionship" is firmly established in meaning and clear in its construction in the speech of the Arabs. ʿUmar said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I seek companionship, O Messenger of Allah?" while ʿUmar was standing at the door of the upper room, the well-known hadith. That requires that he sought companionship with the Prophet (ﷺ). How then would Ibn ʿAbbas err against the Companions of the Messenger in such a matter?

I say: We have mentioned from the hadith of Abu Ayyub that *al-istinas* is only before the greeting, and the verse stands in its own order without any inversion or reordering, and that when one enters, he greets. And Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** The Sunnah regarding seeking permission is three times, and it should not be exceeded. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "Seeking permission is three times. I do not like anyone to exceed them, except one who knows that he was not heard; then I see no harm in repeating it when he is certain he was not heard." The form of seeking permission is for the man to say: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" If he is given permission, he enters; if he is told to return, he leaves; and if he is ignored, he seeks permission three times, then departs after the third time.

We said that the Sunnah is seeking permission three times, not to be exceeded, on the basis of the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, whom he (ʿUmar) employed alongside ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and to which Abu Sa'id al-Khudri testified on behalf of Abu Musa, then Ubayy ibn Ka'b. It is a well-known hadith recorded in the Sahih, and it is an explicit text, for in it: He (ʿUmar) said, that is, ʿUmar: "What prevented you from coming to us?" I said: "I came and greeted at your door three times, but you did not answer me, so I returned." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said: "When one of you seeks permission three times and is not granted it, let him return."

As for what we mentioned regarding the form of seeking permission, it is what Abu Dawud related from Rib'i, who said: A man from the Banu ʿAmir told us: he sought permission to enter upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in a house, and said: "May I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his servant: "Go out to this man and teach him how to seek permission; tell him: say, 'Peace be upon you, may I enter?'" The man heard him and said: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" The Prophet (ﷺ) gave him permission and he entered. Al-Tabari also mentioned it and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a female slave of his called "Rawda": "Say to this one, 'He says: Peace be upon you, may I enter?'" The hadith (continues).

It is also reported that Ibn ʿUmar was afflicted by the heat one day, so he came to the tent of a woman from Quraysh and said: "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" The woman said: "Enter with peace." He repeated, and she repeated. He said to her: "Say, 'Enter.'" She said that, and he entered. He hesitated when she said "with peace," because the wording may mean "with your peace" and not "with your person."

**The sixth issue:** Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: Seeking permission was specified as three times because what is usually spoken, when repeated three times, is heard and understood. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke a word, he would repeat it three times until it was understood from him, and when he greeted a people, he greeted them three times. Since this is the common practice, if permission is not given after three times, it becomes clear that the owner of the house does not wish to grant permission, or perhaps some excuse prevents him from answering that he cannot avoid. So the one seeking permission should depart, because more than that may distress the owner of the house, and persistence may harm him until he is cut off from what he was occupied with. Just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Ayyub when he sought permission from him and he came out in haste, saying: "Perhaps we hurried you..." The hadith (continues).

Ibn Shihab said, narrating from ʿUqayl: As for the Sunnah of the three greetings, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Saʿd ibn ʿUbada and said: "Peace be upon you," and they did not answer. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Peace be upon you," and they did not answer. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then departed. When Saʿd missed his greeting, he knew that he had departed, so Saʿd went out after him until he caught up with him, and said: "And upon you be peace, O Messenger of Allah. We only wished to increase your greetings, and by Allah, we did hear them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then went back with Saʿd until he entered his house. Ibn Shihab said: The greeting was taken as three times from this.

Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated it from al-Awza'i, who said: I heard Yahya ibn Abi Kathir say: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Asʿad ibn Zurara narrated to me, [from Qays ibn Saʿd] (an addition from Sunan Abi Dawud required by the context), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited us at our home and said: "Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah." Saʿd returned the greeting in a faint voice. Qays said: I said: "Will you not give permission to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Leave him, let him increase the greetings upon us..." The hadith (continues). Abu Dawud related it, but it does not contain the statement "Ibn Shihab said: The greeting was taken as three times from this." Abu Dawud said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid and Ibn Sama'a narrated it from al-Awza'i as *mursal* (with a broken chain), without mentioning Qays ibn Saʿd.

**The seventh issue:** It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that people had abandoned acting upon seeking permission. Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: This was due to people taking doors and knocking on them. And Allah knows best. Abu Dawud related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Busr, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to the door of a people, he would not face the door directly, but from its right or left corner, and would say: "Peace be upon you, peace be upon you." That was because the houses did not have curtains on them at that time.

**The eighth issue:** If the door is closed, he may stand wherever he wishes from it and seek permission, and if he wishes he may knock on the door, based on what Abu Musa al-Ash'ari related: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in an orchard in Medina, on the rim (*qaff*) of a well, so he stretched his legs into the well. Abu Bakr knocked on the door, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Give him permission and give him the good news of Paradise." This is how ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad related it, and Salih ibn Kaysan and Yunus ibn Yazid followed him, and they all related it from Abu...

...al-Zinad, from Abu Salama, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Nafi', from Abu Musa." Muhammad ibn Amr al-Laythi differed from them. He narrated it from Abu al-Zinad, from Abu Salama, from Nafi' ibn Abd al-Harith, from the Prophet ﷺ in the same manner. Its first chain is more sound, and Allah knows best.

The Ninth: The manner of knocking is that it should be light, enough to be heard, and one should not be harsh in it. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) reported: "The doors of the Prophet ﷺ were knocked upon with the fingernails." Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Thabit al-Khatib (al-Khatib al-Baghdadi) mentioned it in his Jami'.

The Tenth: The two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with both of them) who said: "I asked permission to enter upon the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: '(Who is this?)' I said: 'I.' The Prophet ﷺ said: '(I, I!)' as if he disliked that." Our scholars said: The Prophet ﷺ disliked it only because the saying "I" does not achieve identification. The rule in this matter is that one should mention his name, as Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and Abu Musa did, because mentioning the name removes the burden of question and answer.

It is established from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was in his upper room (mashruba) and said: "Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. Peace be upon you. May Umar enter?" In Sahih Muslim, Abu Musa came to Umar ibn al-Khattab and said: "Peace be upon you, this is Abu Musa. Peace be upon you, this is al-Ash'ari..." and the hadith continues.

The Eleventh: al-Khatib mentioned in his Jami', from Ali ibn Asim al-Wasiti, who said: "I came to Basra and went to the house of Shu'ba and knocked on the door. He said: 'Who is this?' I said: 'I.' He said: 'O you! I have no friend called "I." ' Then he came out to me and said: 'Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir told me, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: I came to the Prophet ﷺ regarding a need of mine, and I knocked on the door. He said: "(Who is this?)" I said: "I." He said: "(I, I)," for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked my saying this, or his saying this.'"

It is mentioned from Umar ibn Shabba: Muhammad ibn Sallam narrated to us, from his father, who said: "I knocked on the door of Amr ibn Ubayd, and he said to me: 'Who is this?' I said: 'I.' He said: 'None knows the unseen except Allah.'" Al-Khatib said: I heard Ali ibn al-Muhsin al-Qadi relate from some shaykhs that whenever one knocked on his door and he said, "Who is that?", the one at the door would say, "I." The shaykh would say: "I" is a worry (hamm) that knocks.

The Twelfth: Then every people has their customary expression in seeking permission, as al-Khatib narrated with a chain (musnad) from Abu Abd al-Malik, client of Umm Miskin, daughter of Asim ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "My mistress sent me to Abu Hurayra, and he came with me. When he stood at the door he said: 'Andar?' She said: 'Andarun.'" He titled a chapter on it: "Chapter on seeking permission in Persian." It is also mentioned from Ahmad ibn Salih, who said: "Al-Darawardi, who was from the people of Isfahan, settled in Medina, and he used to say to the man who wished to enter: 'Andarun?' So the people of Medina gave him the nickname al-Darawardi."[[He is Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad ibn Ubayd ibn Abi Ubayd. (See his biography in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib.)]]

The Thirteenth: Abu Dawud narrated from Kalada ibn Hanbal that Safwan ibn Umayya sent him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with milk, a young gazelle (jadaya), and cucumbers (dagha'is),[[al-Jadaya: the male and female young of gazelles when they reach six or seven months, like a kid of goats. The dagha'is are cucumbers, singular dagbus. It is said they are a plant that grows at the roots of thymam, which is boiled in vinegar and oil and eaten.]] while the Prophet ﷺ was in the upper part of Mecca. He entered without giving the greeting, and he said: "(Go back and say: As-salamu alaykum.)" This was after Safwan ibn Umayya had embraced Islam. Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does not begin with the greeting, do not give him permission." Ibn Jurayj mentioned: Ata' informed me, who said: I heard Abu Hurayra say: "If a man says, 'May I enter?' without greeting, say: 'No,' until he brings the key." I said: "As-salamu alaykum?" He said: "Yes." It is related that a man came to Hudhayfa, looked into the house, and said: "As-salamu alaykum, may I enter?" Hudhayfa said: "As for your eye, you have entered; as for your rear, you have not entered!"

The Fourteenth: Among what enters this chapter is what Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A man's messenger to a man is his permission," meaning that when he is sent to him, he has been given permission to enter. This is clarified by his saying, peace be upon him: "When one of you is invited [to a meal[[Addition from Sunan Abi Dawud.]]] and the messenger comes with him, that is permission for him." Abu Dawud also narrated it from Abu Hurayra.

The Fifteenth: If the eye meets the eye, then the greeting becomes binding, and seeing him is not considered permission for you to enter upon him. When you have fulfilled the right of the greeting, because you are the one arriving upon him, you say: "May I enter?" If he gives you permission, [enter]; otherwise, return.

The Sixteenth: All these rulings apply only to a house that is not yours. As for your own house in which you dwell, if your family is in it, there is no permission required for them, except that you greet when you enter. Qatada said: "When you enter your house, greet your family, for they have more right to your greeting than anyone." If your mother or your sister is with you in it, they should be told: "Clear your throat and stamp your foot until they become aware of your entrance," because there is no formality (hishma) between you and your family. As for the mother and the sister, they may be in a state in which you would not like to see them. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik said: "A man should seek permission to enter upon his mother and sister when he wishes to enter upon them." Ata' ibn Yasar narrated that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I seek permission to enter upon my mother?" He said: "Yes." He said: "I serve her." He said: "Seek permission to enter upon her." He repeated it three times. He said: "Would you like to see her naked?" He said: "No." He said: "Then seek permission to enter upon her." Al-Tabari mentioned it.

The Seventeenth: If one enters his own house and no one is in it, our scholars said: He says, "Peace be upon us from our Lord, the good and blessed greetings, to Allah belongs peace." Ibn Wahb narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ, but its chain is weak. Qatada said: "When you enter a house in which there is no one, say: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah,' for one is commanded to do so." He said: "It has been mentioned to us that the angels return the greeting to them." Ibn al-Arabi said: "The sound view is to abandon the greeting and the seeking of permission in this case, and Allah knows best." I say: Qatada's statement is good.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 28:

There are four issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you find no one therein﴾. The pronoun in "you find therein" refers to the houses which belong to others. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he said: the meaning of His saying, "But if you find no one therein," is: there is no property of yours in them (lam yakun lakum fihā matā'). Al-Tabari declared this interpretation weak, and indeed it is extremely weak. It seems that Mujahid held that uninhabited houses may only be entered without permission if the one entering has property in them.

He also took the word "matā'" (property) to mean the household goods, namely the rugs and clothing. All of this is weak. The sound view is that this verse is connected with what precedes it and with the hadiths. The implied meaning is: O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you seek permission and greet their occupants. If you are given permission, enter; otherwise, return, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) did with Sa'd, and Abu Musa did with Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. "But if you find no one therein who gives you permission, do not enter them until you are given permission." Al-Tabari transmitted through a chain going back to Qatadah, who said: A man from the Muhajirun said: I sought to understand this verse all my life, and I did not attain it: that I ask permission to enter upon one of my brothers, and he says to me, "Go back," and I go back, and I am content, because of His saying, exalted is He: "That is purer for you."

The second: Whether the door is closed or open, because the Law has closed it through the prohibition of entering until permission from his Lord opens it. Rather, he is obligated to come to the door and seek permission in a manner whereby he does not look into the house, neither in his approach nor in his turning away. Our scholars have related from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Whoever fills his eyes with the inner courtyard of a house has committed sin (faseqa)." It is related in the Sahih from Sahl ibn Sa'd that a man looked through a hole in the door of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a comb (midraa) with which he was combing his head. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "If I knew that you were looking, I would have stabbed you in the eye with it. Permission was only ordained for the sake of sight." It is related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man looks at you without permission, and you strike him with a pebble (hadhafa) and blind his eye, there is no blame upon you."

The third: Once it is established that permission is a condition for entering a dwelling, it is permissible [to seek it] from the young and the old. Anas ibn Malik, while still below the age of puberty, used to ask permission to enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and likewise the Companions with their sons and their young servants, may Allah be pleased with them. More elaboration on this will come at the end of the surah, if Allah wills.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾. This is a warning to those who spy upon houses and seek to enter them unawares for the purpose of sin, and to look at what is not lawful and not permissible, and to others who fall into what is forbidden.

There are two issues here.

The first: it is reported that when the verse about seeking permission (al-isti'dhan) was revealed, some people became overly scrupulous about the matter. They would not go to any place, whether ruined or inhabited, without greeting and asking permission. Then this verse was revealed, and God permitted in it that permission need not be sought for every house that no one lives in, because the reason for seeking permission is only to avoid exposing what is private (al-hurumat). When the reason is removed, the ruling is removed with it.

The second: the scholars differed over what is meant by these houses. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Qatada and Mujahid said: they are the inns (al-fanadiq) on the roads used by travelers. Mujahid said: no one lives in them; rather they are endowed (mawqufa) so that every wayfarer (ibn sabil) may take shelter in them, and "in them is provision for you" means enjoyment of their benefit. It is also reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya that what is meant is the houses of Makkah, and this is supported by the statement of Malik. This is according to the view that they are not owned as private property, that people share in them, and that Makkah was taken by force (ʿanwatan). Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi said: they are the shops of the covered markets (hawanit al-qaysariyyat). Al-Sha'bi said: because they bring their goods and place them in them, and they call out to people, "Come here!" ʿAta' said: what is meant is the ruins into which people enter to relieve themselves, and in this too there is provision. Jabir ibn Zayd said: "provision" does not mean equipment (al-jihaz), but whatever other need is met: a dwelling where a people stop by night or day, or a ruin one enters to fulfil a need, or a house one looks at; this is provision, and all the benefits of this world are provision. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: this is a good explanation from the words of one of the imams of the Muslims, and it agrees with the language. In Arabic usage, al-mata' means benefit, and from it comes the phrase amta'a Allah bika (may God let you benefit from you). And from it is the Qur'anic phrase ﴿فَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49], "then provide for them."

I say: Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi also chose this view and said: As for one who interprets al-mata' as all kinds of benefit, he has matched the detailed explanation and brought the decisive one. He made clear that whoever enters these places does so for the benefit he gains from them: the seeker of knowledge enters the khankat, which are the madrasas, to seek knowledge; the resident enters the khanat, which are the fanatiq, that is the fanadiq; the buyer enters the shop (dukkan) to buy; and the one who needs to relieve himself enters the latrine (khala') for the need. Each comes to the place in its proper way and through its proper door. As for the statement of Ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi, it is [a view that is] weak. This is because the houses of the qaysariyyat are protected by people's property, and by consensus (bi-ijma') they are not open to everyone who wishes to enter; no one enters them except one whom their owner permits, and indeed their owners are appointed to keep people out.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 30:**

There are seven issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾ (30). Having mentioned covering (the private parts), He connected to it what relates to it concerning the matter of looking. It is said: *ghadda basarahu yaghuddubu ghaddan* (he lowered his gaze). The poet said:

*So lower your glance, for you are of Numayr,*
*You have reached neither Ka'b nor Kilab.*

And 'Antarah said:

*I lower my glance whenever my neighbour appears to me,*
*until she conceals her dwelling-place from my neighbour.*

God, the Exalted, did not mention what the gaze is to be lowered from, or what the private parts are to be guarded from, but this is known by custom, and what is meant is the forbidden, not the permitted. In al-Bukhari: "Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan said to al-Hasan, 'The women of the non-Arabs uncover their chests and heads?' He said: 'Turn your gaze away. God, the Exalted, says: *Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts*.'" Qatadah said: "(They should lower their gaze) from what is not lawful for them." And ﴿Say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ [al-Nur: 31] — *khaa'inat al-a'yun* (the treachery of the eyes) [from [[addition from Sahih al-Bukhari.]]] is looking at what has been forbidden.

**The second issue:** His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿from their gaze﴾ (30). The word "min" (from) is superfluous (*za'idah*), like His saying: ﴿so none of you could hold back from Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47] [[see vol. 18, p. 276.]]. It has also been said that "min" is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*), because some looking is permitted. It has also been said: *al-ghadd* means reduction; it is said *ghadda fulan min fulan*, meaning he lowered him, i.e., diminished him. So when the eye is not permitted to perform its function, it is lowered and diminished. Thus "min" is attached to the verb *ghadd* (lower), and is neither partitive nor superfluous. [[In b and k: "min".]]

The eye is the greatest gate to the heart, and the most frequented of the senses' routes to it, and in proportion to this, falling (into sin) through it is frequent. Therefore warning against it is obligatory, and lowering it is obligatory with respect to all prohibited things and everything that fear of temptation is feared from. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware of sitting on the roads." They said: "O Messenger of God, we have no choice but to sit in our gatherings and talk in them." He said: "If you refuse except the gathering, then give the road its right." They said: "And what is the right of the road, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Lowering the gaze, refraining from harm, returning the greeting, enjoining good and forbidding evil." Narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri; recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Prophet ﷺ also said to 'Ali: "Do not follow a glance with another glance, for the first is yours, but the second is not yours." Al-Awza'i narrated, saying: Haroun ibn Ri'ab told me that Ghazwan and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari were on one of their military expeditions, when a slave-girl was uncovered, and Ghazwan looked at her. He raised his hand and slapped his eye until it swelled [[*nafarat al-'ayn* means the eye and other limbs swelled and became inflamed.]]. He said: "You are indeed a glancer at what harms you and does not benefit you." Then he met Abu Musa and asked him, and he said: "You wronged your eye. Ask God's forgiveness and repent, for it is entitled to the first glance, and what follows is upon it." Al-Awza'i said: Ghazwan had mastered himself, so he did not laugh until he died, may God be pleased with him.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away." This strengthens the view of those who say that "min" is partitive, because the first glance is not within one's control, so it does not fall under the obligation of accountability, since its occurrence cannot be intended, and therefore it is not acquired, and one is not held accountable for it. Hence the partitive sense is required. But this was not said regarding the private parts, because they are within one's control.

Al-Sha'bi disliked that a man should continue to gaze at his daughter, his mother or his sister, and his time was better than our time! It is forbidden for a man to look at a woman who is *dhat mahram* (within the prohibited degrees) with a lustful gaze that he repeats. [[In k: *muharram*.]]

**The fourth issue:** His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and guard their private parts﴾ (30), that is, they should cover them from being seen by one who is not lawful to them. It is said: "and guard their private parts" (30) means from fornication (*zina*). According to this view, if one said "from their private parts" [i.e., in other than the Qur'an], it would be permissible. The correct view is that all of this is intended and the wording is general. Bahz ibn Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah al-Qushayri narrated from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, what of our private parts: what may we uncover of them and what should we conceal?' He said: 'Guard your private part except from your wife or what your right hand possesses.' He said: 'What about a man with a man?' He said: 'If you are able that no one sees it, then do so.' I said: 'What about a man who is alone?' He said: 'God is more worthy that one should be shy before Him than before people.'"

'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, mentioned the Messenger of God ﷺ and her situation with him, saying: "I never saw that from him, nor did he see that from me."

**The fifth issue:** By this verse the scholars explicitly prohibited entering the bathhouse (*hammam*) without a loincloth (*mi'zar*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "The best thing a man spends is a dirham he gives to the bathhouse in privacy." And it is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas that he entered the bathhouse while in the state of *ihram* at al-Juhfah. Thus entering is permitted for men with a loincloth, and likewise for women out of necessity, such as washing after menstruation, postpartum bleeding, or an illness that affects them. The better and more excellent course for them is to wash in their homes if that is possible. Ahmad ibn Mani' narrated to us: al-Hasan ibn Musa narrated to us: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us: Zabban narrated to us, from Sahl ibn Mu'adh, from his father, from Umm al-Darda', that she heard her say: "The Messenger of God ﷺ met me as I came out of the bathhouse, and he said: 'From where, O Umm al-Darda'?' She said: 'From the bathhouse.' He said: 'By the One in whose hand is my soul, there is no woman who removes her clothes in other than the house of one of her mothers, except that she tears away every veil between her and the Merciful, Mighty and Majestic.'"

Abu Bakr al-Bazzar narrated from Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Beware of a house called the bathhouse." They said: "O Messenger of God, it cleanses the dirt?" He said: "Then cover yourselves." Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq said: This is the most authentic chain of narration on this topic, except that people transmit it as *mursal* from Tawus. As for what Abu Dawud recorded on this topic regarding prohibition and permission, nothing from it is sound due to the weakness of its chains; likewise what al-Tirmidhi recorded.

I say: As for entering the bathhouse in these times, it is forbidden for people of virtue and religion, because ignorance has overcome people, and they make it easy for themselves: when they enter the bathhouse, they throw off their loincloths, until one sees a handsome man with gray hair standing upright in the middle of the bathhouse and outside it, uncovered of his private part, holding his thighs together, and no one objects to him. This is a matter among men, so how about among women! Especially in the Egyptian lands, where their bathhouses are empty of the partitions that screen them from people's eyes. There is no power and no might except with God, the Most High, the Mighty!

**The sixth issue:** The scholars said: If one covers himself, then he should enter according to ten conditions.

The first: He should not enter except with the intention of treatment or with the intention of purifying himself from *al-ruhda'* (the sweat following fever).

The second: He should choose times of privacy or times when few people are present.

The third: He should cover his private part with a thick (*safiq*) loincloth [*safiq*: strong, well-woven; in k: *dayyiq* (narrow), which is not correct].

The fourth: His gaze should be on the ground, or he should face the wall, so that his gaze does not fall upon what is forbidden.

The fifth: He should change, gently, whatever he sees of wrongdoing. He says: "Cover yourself, may God cover you!"

The sixth: If someone rubs him, he should not allow him to reach his private part, from the navel to the knee, except his wife or his slave-girl. It has been disputed whether the two thighs are part of the private part or not.

The seventh: He should enter it for a known fee, either by agreement or by the custom of people.

The eighth: He should pour water to the extent of need.

The ninth: If he cannot enter it alone, he should agree with people who guard their religion to rent it [i.e., to rent the bath for them].

The tenth: He should remember Hell through it.

If he is unable to do all of this, then he should cover himself and strive to lower his gaze. Al-Tirmidhi, Abu 'Abd Allah, mentioned in *Nawadir al-Usul*, from the hadith of Tawus, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Beware of a house called the bathhouse." It was said: "O Messenger of God, it takes away the dirt and reminds one of the Fire?" He said: "If you must do it, then enter it covered."

He also recorded from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "What an excellent house is the bathhouse, which a Muslim man enters—for when he enters it, he asks God for Paradise and seeks refuge in Him from the Fire—and what an evil house is the bridal house, which a man enters." That is because it makes him desire this world and makes him forget the Hereafter.

Abu 'Abd Allah said: This is for the heedless. God has made this world, with what it contains, a cause for remembrance for the heedless, so that they may remember their Hereafter through it. As for the people of certainty, the Hereafter has become before their eyes. So there is no bathhouse that disturbs him, nor a bridal house that tempts him. The world, with its two kinds and types, has been reduced to dust beside the Hereafter, so much so that all the bounties of this world in their eyes are like crumbs of food from a great table, and all the hardships of this world in their eyes are like the killing with which a criminal is punished, or a wrongdoer who deserved execution or crucifixion, among all the punishments of the people of this world.

**The seventh issue:** His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿That is purer for them﴾ (30), that is: lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts is purer in religion and further from the filth of sins.

(Indeed God is Aware) — that is, Knowing.

(of what they do) (30) — a threat and a warning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 31 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And tell the believing women to lower their gaze, and guard their private parts, and not to display their adornment﴾ up to His saying: ﴿except what [normally] appears of it﴾. On this there are twenty-three issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And tell the believing women﴾. Here Allah, glorified and exalted is He, singled out the females with the address for emphasis, although His saying "Tell the believers" would suffice, since it is a general statement that includes both male and female believers, as is the case with every general address in the Qur'an. The doubling appears in "yaghuddunna" (they should lower) but does not appear in "yaghuddu" (they should lower; masculine plural), because the final radical of the verb in the second is quiescent while in the first it is vowelled, and both are in the jussive position as a response (jawab). He began with lowering the gaze before guarding the private parts, because the gaze is the scout (ra'id) of the heart, just as fever is the scout of death. Some poets took up this meaning and said:

Do you not see that the eye is the heart's scout,
so the two eyes become attached, and the heart becomes attached.

In a report (khabar): "The glance is one of the arrows of Iblis, poisoned; whoever lowers his gaze, Allah will bequeath to him sweetness in his heart." Mujahid said: When a woman comes forward, Satan sits on her head and adorns her for the one who looks; when she turns away, he sits on her buttocks and adorns her for the one who looks. And on the authority of Khalid ibn Abi Imran, who said: Do not follow a glance with another glance, for a servant may glance once and his heart is corrupted [[al-naghl (with vowel): corruption. And naghila al-adim means the hide rotted and decayed in tanning, so it is spoiled and ruined.]] by it, just as the hide is corrupted, and so it cannot be benefited from. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded the believing men and believing women to lower their gaze from what is not lawful. It is not lawful for a man to look at a woman, nor for a woman to look at a man, for her attachment to him is like his attachment to her, and her desire for him is like his desire for her. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably attain: the two eyes commit adultery, and their adultery is the gaze..." the hadith. Al-Zuhri said concerning the gaze at a girl who has not menstruated among women: It is not proper to look at any part of them by one whose looking at them is desired, even if she is a little girl. Ata disliked looking at the slave girls who are sold in Makkah, unless one intends to buy. In the two Sahihs, from him (ﷺ), that he turned the face of al-Fadl away from the woman of Khath'am when she asked him, while al-Fadl began to look at her [[In al-Bukhari: "From Ibn Abbas, who said: al-Fadl was riding behind the Prophet (ﷺ) when a woman from Khath'am came, and al-Fadl began to look at her and she looked at him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) began to turn al-Fadl's face to the other side. She said: The obligation of Allah has reached my father, an old man who cannot remain steady on the mount; may I perform the Hajj on his behalf? He said: Yes."]]. He (ﷺ) also said: "Jealousy is from faith, and madha' is from hypocrisy." Al-mida' is that a man gathers together women and men, then leaves them so that some of them engage in madha' with one another, derived from al-madhy. It is also said: it is the sending of men to women, from their saying: "I sent the mare to pasture" (madhaytu al-faras), when I let her loose to graze. Every male is one who emits madhy, and every female is one who emits qadhy. So it is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to display her adornment except to one to whom it is lawful, or to one to whom she is forbidden permanently, for he is safe from his nature being stirred toward her because of the despair of attaining her.

The second: Al-Tirmidhi related, from Nabhan, the freedman of Umm Salamah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her and to Maymunah, when Ibn Umm Maktum entered upon them: "Veil yourselves." They said: "He is blind." He said: "Are you two blind? Do you not see him?" If it is said: this hadith is not authentic according to the transmitters, because its narrator from Umm Salamah is Nabhan her freedman, and he is one whose hadith is not used as proof. And even if it is authentic, that was a strictness from him (ﷺ) upon his wives because of their sanctity, just as the matter of the veil was made stricter for them, as Abu Dawud and other imams indicated. The meaning of the sound, established hadith remains: that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Fatimah bint Qays to observe her 'iddah in the house of Umm Sharik, then said: "That is a woman whom my companions frequent; observe your 'iddah at the house of Ibn Umm Maktum, for he is a blind man; you may put off your clothing and he will not see you." We say: Some scholars have used this hadith as evidence that a woman may look at a man at what it is not permissible for a man to look at in a woman, such as the head and the earring-hanging, but not the awrah. Accordingly, this specifies the generality of His saying, "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze," and "min" will be partitive (li-l-tab'id), as it is in the verse before it. Ibn al-Arabi said: He commanded her to move from the house of Umm Sharik to the house of Ibn Umm Maktum only because that was more fitting for her than remaining in the house of Umm Sharik, since Umm Sharik's house was frequented by many visitors, so many would see her, whereas in the house of Ibn Umm Maktum no one would see her; so restraining her gaze from him was closer and more fitting. Thus she was granted this concession, and Allah knows best.

The third: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded women not to display their adornment to onlookers, except what He excepted from the onlookers in the rest of the verse, out of caution against temptation. Then He excepted what [normally] appears of the adornment. People differed about the extent of that. Ibn Mas'ud said: the apparent adornment is the garments. Ibn Jubayr added the face. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also, and Ata and al-Awza'i said: the face, the two palms and the garments. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: the apparent adornment is kohl, bracelets, dye (khidab) up to half the forearm [[In J, T and K: "al-siyaq" (the context). The correct reading is "al-dhira'" (the forearm), as will come.]], earrings, al-fatakh [[al-fatakh (with two fathas, plural of fatkhah): large rings worn on the hands.]], and the like. It is permissible for a woman to display these to everyone who enters upon her among people. Al-Tabari mentioned from Qatadah concerning the meaning of "half the forearm" a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and another report from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day, when she has menstruated (idha 'arakat [['arakat al-mar'ah: she menstruated]]), to show anything except her face and her hands up to here," and he grasped half the forearm.
