Ibn Atiyyah said: It appears to me from the wording of the verse that the woman is commanded not to display, and to strive in concealing everything that is adornment; the exception occurs regarding what appears through the necessity of movement in what is unavoidable, or the setting right of a matter and the like. So what appears in this manner, of what necessity brings forth in women, is the excused. I say: This is a good opinion, except that since the face and the two palms are generally those that customarily and in worship (as in prayer and Hajj) are exposed, it is fitting that the exception refers to them. This is indicated by what Abu Dawud related from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: that Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wearing thin garments, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from her and said to her: "O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not proper that anything be seen of her except this," and he pointed to his face and his two palms. This is stronger from the side of caution, and out of regard for the corruption of people; so a woman should not display of her adornment except what appears of her face and her two palms, and Allah is the Granter of success, there is no lord besides Him. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad, one of our scholars, said: If a woman is beautiful and temptation is feared from her face and palms, it is incumbent upon her to cover that; and if she is an old woman or ugly, it is permissible for her to uncover her face and palms.

The fourth: Adornment is of two kinds: natural (khilqiyyah) and acquired (muktasabah). The natural is her face, for it is the origin of adornment and the beauty of creation and the meaning of animality, because of what it contains of benefits and the paths of knowledge. As for acquired adornment, it is what a woman strives at in beautifying her creation, such as garments, jewelry, kohl and dye. From it is His saying, exalted is He: "Take your adornment" [[Refer to vol. 7 p. 188 and following.]] [al-A'raf: 31]. The poet said:

They take their adornment, the finest you see,
and when they are without it, they are the best of the unadorned.

The fifth: Of adornment there is the apparent and the concealed. What appears is permissible always for all people, whether mahram or strangers, and we have already mentioned what the scholars have on this. As for what is concealed, it is not lawful to display it except to those whom Allah, exalted is He, named in this verse, or those who take their place. Differences arose about the anklet (siwar). Aisha said: it is among the apparent adornment, because it is on the hands. Mujahid said: it is among the concealed adornment, because it is outside the palms and is only on the forearm. Ibn al-Arabi said: As for dye, it is among the concealed adornment if it is on the two feet.

The sixth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests (juyub)﴾. The majority read the lam, which is the lam of command, with sukun. Abu Amr, in the narration of Ibn Abbas, read it with kasra according to the original form, because the original of the lam of command is kasr, and the kasra was dropped due to its heaviness; its sukun is only due to the sukun of "'add" and "fakhdh." "Yadribna" is in the jussive position by the command, except that it was built on one state, following the perfect verb according to Sibawayh. The occasion of this verse was that women in that era, when they covered their heads with khimar, which are the maqani'[[the head-coverings]], they would let them hang behind the back. Al-Naqqash said: as the Nabat do, so the throat, the neck and the ears remained uncovered; Allah, exalted is He, commanded that the khimar be drawn over the chests (juyub). The manner of that is that the woman strikes her khimar over her chest so as to cover her breast. Al-Bukhari related from Aisha that she said: May Allah have mercy on the first emigrant women (nisa' al-muhajirat); when "And let them draw their head-coverings over their chests" was revealed, they split their izars and covered themselves with them. And Hafsah bint her brother Abd al-Rahman, may Allah be pleased with them, entered upon Aisha wearing a head-covering that showed her neck and what was beyond it, so she tore it off her and said: "It is only that what is thick and conceals should be drawn."

The seventh: Al-khumur is the plural of khimar, which is what a woman covers her head with; from it come "ikhtamarat al-mar'ah" and "takhammarat," and she is of good khumrah (complexion/appearance). Al-juyub is the plural of al-jayb, which is the place of the opening in a robe (dir') and a shirt (qamis), and it is from al-jawb, which is cutting. The well-known reading is with a damma on the jim in "juyubihinna." Some Kufans read it with kasra because of the ya', like their reading of such in "buyut" and "shuyukh." The early grammarians do not permit this reading and say: "bayt" and "buyut" like "fals" and "fulus." Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible on the basis that the damma is replaced by a kasra. As for what is narrated from Hamzah of combining damma and kasra, it is impossible; no one can pronounce it except by indicating what is not permissible. Muqatil said: "'ala juyubihinna" means "over their chests," that is, over the places of their openings.

**Eighth:** This verse indicates that the *jayb* (the opening or neckline of a garment) is only at the chest of the garment. The *juyub* (openings) in the clothing of the early generation (*al-salaf*, may God be pleased with them) were likewise, as women in our land of al-Andalus and the people of the Egyptian region, men, children and others still make them. Al-Bukhari, may God have mercy on him, titled a chapter "The Chapter on the Opening of the Shirt at the Chest and Other Than That," and cited the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ gave the example of the miser and the one who gives charity as like two men wearing coats of iron, whose hands had been pulled tight to their breasts and their collarbones... (the hadith, which has already been mentioned in full [[See vol. 10, p. 250.]]). In it: Abu Hurayrah said: "I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ, with his two fingers, point like this at his opening, and if you had seen him widen it, it would not widen." [[The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: you would have been amazed.]] This shows you that the opening of the Prophet's garment, peace be upon him, was at his chest, because if it had been at his shoulder, his hands would not have been pulled tight to his breasts and collarbones. This is a good inference.

**Ninth:** The words of God Most High: ﴿except to their husbands﴾. *Al-ba'l* in the speech of the Arabs means the husband and also the master. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Jibril: "When a slave woman gives birth to her *ba'l*," meaning her master. This is an indication of the abundance of concubines through the abundance of conquests, so children are born from slave women, and each mother is freed by her child, and it is as if her master, who granted her freedom, were the one who did so, since the freedom came to her from his cause. This was said by Ibn al-Arabi. I say: From this is also his saying, peace be upon him, concerning Maria: "Her child has freed her," where freedom is attributed to him. This is among the best interpretations of this hadith. And God knows best.

**Issue:** The husband and the master see the adornment of the woman, and more than the adornment, since every part of her body is lawful to him for pleasure and for looking. For this reason it begins with the husbands, because their gaze falls on something greater than this. God Most High said: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy﴾ [[See p. 105 of this part.]] [al-Mu'minun: 5-6].

**Tenth:** The people differ over whether a man may look at a woman's private part, on two views. The first: it is permitted, because if he is allowed to take pleasure in it, then looking is more fitting. It is also said: it is not permitted, based on the statement of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, when describing her situation with the Messenger of God ﷺ: "I never saw that from him, nor did he see that from me." The first view is more sound, and this [prohibition] is understood as a matter of good manners. This was said by Ibn al-Arabi. Ashhab, one of our scholars, said: He may lick it with his tongue. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: As for the husband and the master, he may look at the whole body and the outer part of the private region, but not the inner part. Likewise, a wife may look at the private parts of her husband, and a slave woman at those of her master. I say: It has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Looking at the private part causes *al-tamas*," that is, blindness, meaning for the one who looks. It is also said that a child born between them will be born blind. And God knows best.

**Eleventh:** When God Most High mentioned the husbands and began with them, He followed with those within the prohibited degrees (*dhu al-mahram*) and made them equal in the display of adornment, but their ranks differ according to what is in human souls. There is no doubt that the uncovering before a father and a brother is more cautious than the uncovering before the son of her husband. The ranks of what is displayed to them differ, so what is displayed to the father is not what may be displayed to the son of the husband. Al-Qadi Isma'il reported from al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both, that they did not consider the mothers of the believers (the wives of the Prophet) to be among those who may be seen. Ibn 'Abbas said: Their seeing them is lawful. Isma'il said: I think al-Hasan and al-Husayn held this view because the sons of the husbands were not mentioned in the verse concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, which is His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers﴾ [[See vol. 14, p. 231.]] [al-Ahzab: 55]. In Surat al-Nur He said: "And not to reveal their adornment except to their husbands," and so on. Ibn 'Abbas relied on this verse, while al-Hasan and al-Husayn relied on another verse.

**Twelfth:** The words of God Most High: ﴿or the sons of their husbands﴾ mean the male sons of the husbands. It includes the sons of the sons, however low they go, whether males or females, such as the sons of sons and the sons of daughters. Likewise the fathers of the husbands and the grandfathers, however high they go, from the male line: the fathers of fathers and the fathers of mothers. Likewise their sons, however low they go. Likewise the sons of daughters, however low they go, so the sons of sons and the sons of daughters are equal in this. Likewise their brothers, who are of the same father and mother or of one of the two kinds. Likewise the sons of brothers and the sons of sisters, however low they go, whether male or female, such as the sons of the sons of brothers and the sons of the daughters of sisters. All of this is in the sense of what is forbidden in marriage, because that is according to the meanings of birth, and these are mahram relatives. It was already mentioned in [al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 105 and what follows.]]]. The majority hold that the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle are like the rest of the mahram relatives in permitting them to look at what is permitted for those relatives. The verse does not mention fosterage, which is like lineage, as was already mentioned. According to al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah, the paternal uncle and maternal uncle are not mahram relatives. 'Ikrimah said: He did not mention them in the verse because they follow their sons.

**Thirteenth:** The words of God Most High: ﴿or their women﴾ mean the Muslim women. This includes believing slave women, and it excludes the women of polytheists, from the people of the dhimma and others. So it is not lawful for a believing woman to uncover any part of her body in front of a polytheist woman, unless she is her slave woman, and this is His saying: ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾. Ibn Jurayj, 'Ubadah ibn Nusayy and Hisham al-Qari disliked that a Christian woman kiss a Muslim woman or see her private part, and they interpreted "or their women" accordingly. 'Ubadah ibn Nusayy said: 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, wrote to Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah: "It has reached me that the women of the people of the dhimma enter the bathhouses with the women of the Muslims, so prevent that and stop it, for it is not lawful for a dhimmi woman to see the nakedness [[The *mariyya* of a woman: what is bared and uncovered of her.]] of a Muslim woman." He said: At that point Abu 'Ubaydah stood up, made an earnest supplication and said: "Any woman who enters the bathhouse without an excuse, wanting only to whiten her face, may God blacken her face on the day when faces turn white." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: It is not lawful for a Muslim woman to be seen by a Jewish or Christian woman, lest she describe her to her husband. On this question there is disagreement among the jurists. If the unbelieving woman is a slave of a Muslim woman, it is permitted for her to look at her mistress, but other than that is not, because the bond of guardianship between the people of Islam and the people of disbelief is severed, and because of what we have mentioned. And God knows best.

**Fourteenth:** The words of God Most High: ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾. The apparent meaning of the verse includes male and female slaves, Muslim and People of the Book. This is the view of a group of scholars, and it is the apparent position of 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn 'Abbas said: There is no harm in a male slave looking at the hair of his mistress. Ashhab said: Malik was asked, "Does a woman remove her headscarf in front of a eunuch?" He said: "Yes, if he is her slave or the slave of someone else. But as for a free man, no." And if he is an adult male, a *wagh* [[*al-wagh*: a lowly man who serves for the sake of his stomach. It is also said: one of weak intellect.]] whom she owns, with no dignity or appearance, then he may look at her hair. Ashhab said, Malik said: "It is not permissible for a child or a wife's slave to enter the lavatory of a man," and God Most High said: "or what your right hands possess." Ashhab reported from Malik: "The lowly boy may look at the hair of his mistress, but I do not like it for the slave of a husband." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "Let not this verse deceive you: ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾; it refers only to the female slaves, not the male slaves." Al-Sha'bi disliked that a male slave look at the hair of his mistress. This is also the view of Mujahid and 'Ata'. Abu Dawud related from Anas that the Messenger of God ﷺ came to Fatimah with a slave whom he had given her. He said: Fatimah had a garment which, when she covered her head with it, did not reach her feet, and when she covered her feet with it, did not reach her head. When the Prophet ﷺ saw what she was experiencing because of that, he said: "There is no harm upon you; he is only your father and your slave."

**Fifteenth:** The words of God Most High: ﴿or male attendants who have no physical desire﴾. "That is, those without need. *Al-irbah* means need. One says: *aribtu kadha aribu araban*. *Al-irb*, *al-irbah*, *al-ma'rabah* and *al-arab* all mean need, and the plural is *ma'arib*, meaning needs. From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And for him there are other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], and it has been mentioned [[See vol. 11, p. 187.]]. Tarafah said:

*When a man says "ignorance," "sin," and "obscenity,"*
*He advances one day, then his needs are lost.*

The commentators differed over the meaning of His words, "or male attendants who have no physical desire" (ghayri ulī al-irbah). It was said: he is the fool who has no need of women. It was also said: he is the imbecile (al-ablah). It was said: he is the man who follows a people, eats with them, and benefits from them, being weak and indifferent to women and feeling no desire for them. It was said: he is the impotent man (al-innin). It was said: he is the eunuch (al-khasi). It was said: he is the effeminate man (al-mukhannath). It was said: he is the elderly man, and the child who has not yet reached maturity. All of these opinions are close in meaning, and they converge on one who has no understanding and no drive by which he would become attentive to matters concerning women. It was with this description that Hit al-Mukhannath was among the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)'s household. When he heard from him what he heard describing the beauty of a woman, Badiyah bint Ghaylan, he ordered that he be veiled from them. Muslim, Abu Dawud, Malik in al-Muwatta', and others transmitted his hadith from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah.

Abu 'Umar said: 'Abd al-Malik ibn Habib related from Habib, the scribe of Malik, who said: I said to Malik: "Sufyan added to the hadith of the daughter of Ghaylan: (that an effeminate man called Hit...), but Hit is not in your book?" Malik said: "He is right; it is so. The Prophet (ﷺ) banished him to al-Himan, which is a place near Dhu al-Hulayfah, on the left side of its mosque." Habib said: I also said to Malik: "Sufyan said in the hadith: when she sits, she spreads out [[meaning she becomes like a tent-dome from her fat and bulk. Ibn al-Athir said: that is, she spreads her legs because of the largeness of her thighs (her private part), as if he likened her to a leather tent.]], and when she speaks, she sings." Malik said: "He is right; it is so."

Abu 'Umar said: What Habib, the scribe of Malik, reported from Sufyan, that he said in the hadith, meaning the hadith of Hisham ibn 'Urwah, "that an effeminate man called Hit," is not known from any of his transmitters from Hisham, neither Ibn 'Uyaynah nor anyone else. He did not say it in the continuous text of the hadith ("an effeminate man called Hit"); rather, he mentioned it from Ibn Jurayj after the completion of the hadith. Likewise, his report from Sufyan that he said in the hadith: "when she sits she spreads, and when she speaks she sings," is not something Sufyan or anyone else said in the hadith of Hisham ibn 'Urwah. This wording is found only in the narration of al-Waqidi. What is strange is that he relates it from Sufyan and relates from Malik that it is so, so it became a narration from Malik, yet no one transmitted it from Malik except Habib, nor did anyone else mention it from Sufyan. And Allah knows best. Habib, the scribe of Malik, is abandoned in hadith (matruk al-hadith), weak according to all of them; his hadith is not written down and what he brings is not regarded.

Al-Waqidi and al-Kalbi mentioned that Hit the effeminate man said to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayyah al-Makhzumi, who was the paternal brother of Umm Salamah, and whose mother was 'Atikah, the paternal aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was in the house of his sister Umm Salamah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was listening: "If Allah grants you victory over al-Ta'if, then take Badiyah bint Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi, for she comes forward with four [folds] and turns back with eight [[meaning: she presents four folds of flesh and turns back with eight folds of flesh. Al-'Ukun and al-A'kan are what is folded and bent of the belly flesh from fatness.]], along with a mouth like camomile; when she sits she spreads, and when she speaks she sings; between her legs is like a turned-over vessel [[meaning: large in her thighs (her private part) and her mound, as if it were an overturned vessel.]]." And she is as Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

She captivates the glance while she is heedless,
as if her face were tinged with the blood of its bloom [[He says: whoever looks at her is captivated in his gaze and sight and distracted from looking at anyone else, while she is heedless and unconcerned. Al-Taraf (with a dammah then a sukun, here vocalized for the requirements of the verse) means the flowing of blood. In the commentary on the Diwan of Qays: "He meant that in her complexion, along with whiteness, there is a yellowness, and that is the most beautiful."]]
between the varied forms of women, her build is moderate, neither heavy-boned nor lean. [[Al-Shukul: the kinds. Qasd: neither large nor thin. Al-Jiblah: the coarse one, from jabal (like farah), so he is jabl and jibl. Al-Qadaf: thinness and scarcity of flesh.]]
She sleeps out of the greatness of her state, and when she
rises slowly, she nearly breaks.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You have certainly gazed at her too intently, O enemy of Allah!" Then he expelled him from Madinah to al-Himan. He said: When al-Ta'if was conquered, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf married her, and she bore him Buraymah, according to the report of al-Kalbi. Hit remained in that place until the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away. When Abu Bakr became caliph, he was spoken to about him, but he refused to return him. When 'Umar became caliph, he was spoken to about him, but he refused. Then 'Uthman was spoken to about him later. It was also said: he had grown old, weak, and in need, so he was permitted to enter each Friday, ask, and then return to his place. He said: Hit was a client (mawla) of 'Abd Allah ibn [Abi] Umayyah al-Makhzumi, and he also had a slave-singer named Tuways [[Tuways was a nickname that came to dominate him; his name was 'Isa ibn 'Abd Allah, a client of the Banu Makhzum. He was the first to sing Arabic songs in Madinah, and the first to introduce effeminacy there.
(See his biography in al-Aghani, vol. 3, p. 37, Dar al-Kutub edition.)]] as well, and from that he acquired effeminacy.

Abu 'Umar said: It is said "Badiyah" with a ya' and "Badinah" with a nun, and the correct form according to them is with a ya', which is the view of most of them, and likewise al-Zubayri mentioned it with a ya'.

Sixteenth issue: He described the Successors (al-tabi'in) with "ghayr," because the Successors are not specifically intended as individuals, so the word functions like an indefinite noun. "Ghayr" does not become purely indefinite, so it is permissible for it to function as an adjective (wasf) for a definite noun. If you wish, you may say it is a substitute (badal). The discussion of it is like the discussion of "ghayr al-maghdubi 'alayhim" (not of those who earned Your anger) [[See vol. 1, p. 149.]] [al-Fatihah: 7]. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "ghayra" with a fatha, making it an exception: that is, they reveal their adornment to the Successors except those among them who have physical desire. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: and those who follow them, being incapable of them; this was said by Abu Hatim. The one it refers to is the masculine pronoun in "al-tabi'in."

Seventeenth issue: His words, "or the children (al-tifl)" [[Allah says: "or children who have not yet attained knowledge of women's private matters"]]: "al-tifl" is a collective noun with the meaning of the plural; the evidence for this is that it is described with "alladhina" (who). In the Mushaf of Hafsah (a codex), it reads "al-atfal," in the plural. It is said: a tifl is one who has not yet reached the age of puberty (ihtilam). "Yazhharu" means they become aware of through intercourse, i.e., they do not uncover their private parts for intercourse because of their youth. It was also said: they have not reached the age of being able to desire women. It is said: "zahartu 'ala kadha" means I came to know it, and "zahartu 'ala kadha" means I overcame him. The majority read the waw in "'awrat" with a sukun, because the movement on the waw is burdensome. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas [[In B and K: Ibn 'Amir.]] that the waw is read with a fatha, like jafnah and jafanat. Al-Farra' related that this is the dialect of Qays: "'awarat" with a fatha on the waw. Al-Nahhas said: this is the analogical form, because it is not an adjective, as you say: jafnah and jafanat. However, the sukun is better in "'awrat" and similar words, because when the waw is vowelled and the letter before it is vowelled, it becomes an alif; if this were said, the meaning would be lost.

Eighteenth issue: The scholars differed over the obligation to cover what lies between the navel and the knees [[as in the text]], or rather what lies other than the face and the two palms, on two views. The first: it is not obligatory, because there is no legal obligation upon it, and this is the sound view. The second: it is obligatory, because he may feel desire and she may also feel desire; if he reaches puberty, his ruling is the ruling of the adult regarding the obligation of covering. Similar to him is the old man whose desire has ceased; this too is disputed on two views, just as with the child. The sound view is that the prohibition remains; this was said by Ibn al-'Arabi.

Nineteenth issue: The Muslims agreed that the two private parts are 'awrah for both men and women, and that the entire woman is 'awrah except her face and her two hands, though they differed concerning these two. Most scholars said regarding a man: from his navel to his knee is 'awrah, which may not be seen. The discussion of this has been fully given in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 172.]].

Twentieth issue: The people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: the 'awrah of a woman in the presence of her slave is from the navel to the knee. Ibn al-'Arabi said: It seems they supposed she was a man or supposed he was a woman, while Allah has prohibited a woman absolutely from being looked at for gaze or pleasure; then He excepted pleasure for spouses and those their right hands possess; then He excepted adornment for twelve persons, the slave among them. So what concern is that to us? This is a corrupt opinion and a view far from correctness. Some people interpreted His words, "or those their right hands possess," as referring to female slaves only, not male slaves, among them Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. How can they be understood as male slaves and then be attached to women? This is very far-fetched! [Ibn al-'Arabi said [[from K.]]] It has also been said that the implied sense is: "or those their right hands possess, of men who are not possessors of physical desire, or the attendant men who lack desire," meaning the men; this was related by al-Mahdawi.

Twenty-first issue: His words, "and let them not strike their feet" [[Allah says: "and let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they hide of their adornment"]]: that is, a woman should not strike her foot when she walks in order to make the sound of her anklet heard. Making the sound of adornment audible is like revealing adornment and worse, and the purpose is concealment. Al-Tabari related through al-Mu'tamir, from his father, that he said: a Hadrami claimed that a woman had two silver anklets and had made a bead of carnelian [[al-Bur'ah: the anklet, and every ring of a bracelet or earring.]], and she placed it on her leg. She passed by a group of people and struck the ground with her foot, so the anklet struck the carnelian bead and made a sound, and this verse was revealed. The hearing of this adornment stirs desire more than its display; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

Twenty-second issue: Whoever does this among women out of joy in her ornaments, it is disliked. Whoever does this among women in order to display herself and to expose herself to men, it is forbidden and blameworthy. Likewise, whoever strikes with his sandal among men: if he does so out of amazement, it is forbidden, for self-admiration is a major sin; and if he does so to display himself, it is not permissible.

Twenty-third issue: Makki, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no verse in the Book of Allah with more pronouns than this one; it contains twenty-five pronouns for the believing women, both in the genitive and the nominative.

His words, "And turn to Allah in repentance all together, O believers" [[Allah says: "And turn to Allah in repentance all together, O believers, that you may be successful."]]: In this there are two issues.

The first: His words, "And turn in repentance," is an imperative. There is no disagreement among the community regarding the obligation of repentance, and that it is a definite and binding duty. The discussion of it has already passed in al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 90.]] and elsewhere, so there is no point in repeating it. The meaning: repent to Allah, for you are not free from heedlessness and shortcoming in fulfilling the rights of Allah, so do not abandon repentance in any state.

The second: The majority read "ayyuhah" with a fatha on the ha'. Ibn 'Amir read it with a dammah, and its basis is that the ha' is made part of the word itself, so that the case-ending of the vocative falls on it. Abu 'Ali strongly weakened this and said: the final letter of the noun is the second ya' of "ayy," so what is vowelled with a dammah should be the final letter of the noun; if it were permissible to vowel the ha' here because it is attached to the word, it would be permissible to vowel the mim in "Allahumma" because it is attached to the word in a long speech. The correct position is that when a reading has been authentically transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), there is nothing for us but to hold belief in its linguistic soundness, since the Qur'an is the proof. Al-Farra' recited:

O restless heart, of persistent breath,
desist from the fair, white women with dark lips.

Al-la'as: the color of the lip when it tends slightly toward blackness, and that is considered attractive; one says: a lip that is la'sa', youths and women who are la's.

Some stop on "ayyuh," and some stop on "ayyuha" with the alif, because the cause of its deletion in connected speech is only its being vowelless and the vowellessness of the lam; when there is a pause, that cause disappears and the alif returns, just as the ya' returns when you pause on "muhilli" in His words, "not violating the sanctity of game" [[See vol. 6, p. 31.]] [al-Ma'idah: 1]. This same disagreement that we mentioned is also found in "ya ayyuha al-sahir" [[See vol. 16, p. 96.]] and in "ayyuha al-thaqalan" [[See vol. 17, p. 168.]].

**First issue:** This address is part of the category of covering (one's chastity) and righteousness. That is, marry off those among you who have no spouse, for it is a path to chastity. The address is to the guardians (awliya'). It was also said to be addressed to the husbands, but the sound view is the first, because if it meant the husbands, it would have said *wa-nkihu* without the hamza, and the alif would be an alif of connection (*alif al-wasl*). This is evidence that a woman may not marry herself off without a guardian, and this is the view of most scholars. Abu Hanifa said: if a previously married woman or a virgin marries herself off without a guardian, and her matchmaker is suitable for her, it is permissible. This has already been discussed fully in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 3, p. 72].

**Second issue:** The scholars differed on this matter in three views. Our scholars (the Malikis) said: the ruling varies according to the state of the believer: whether he fears falling into sin (*al-'anat*), whether he lacks patience, whether he is strong enough to be patient, and whether the fear of falling into sin has left him. If he fears ruin in his religion or his worldly life, or both, then marriage is obligatory. If he fears nothing and his situation is unrestricted, al-Shafi'i said: marriage is permissible (*mubah*). Malik and Abu Hanifa said: it is recommended (*mustahabb*). Al-Shafi'i relied on the argument that it is the fulfilment of a desire, so it is permissible, like eating and drinking. Our scholars relied on the sound hadith: "Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."

**Third issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿al-ayama minkum﴾ [the unmarried among you] refer to those men and women who have no spouses. Its singular is *ayyim*. Abu 'Amr said: *ayama* is an inverted form of *ayayima*. The lexicographers agree that *ayyim* originally means a woman who has no husband, whether a virgin or previously married. Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and others related this. The Arabs say: "*ta'ayyamat al-mar'ah*" when a woman remains without marrying.

In the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I and a woman with darkened cheeks (*sap'a' al-khaddayn*) [Al-sap': blackness and paleness. He meant that she gave herself up and abandoned adornment and luxury until her complexion paled and darkened, remaining (unmarried) for the sake of her children after the death of her husband.] who has remained a widow for the sake of her young children until they reach maturity or God enriches them from His bounty, will be in Paradise like these two," [and he pointed with his two fingers].

And the poet said:

*"If you marry, I will marry; and if you remain unmarried, I will remain unmarried,
Even though I am more worthy than you to remain unmarried."*

It is also said: *ayyim* among the people (*ayyim bayna al-a'immah*). The woman has become *ayyim* (*amat hiya*), and I have become *ayyim* (*imtu ana*). The poet said:

*"I have become unmarried, until every companion blamed me,
Hoping for Salma that she would become unmarried as I have."*

Abu 'Ubayd said: one says *rajulun ayyim* (a man) and *imra'atun ayyim* (a woman), but this is mostly used for women, and for men it is figurative. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

*"By God, the excellence of the sons of 'Al... among them is the unmarried and the married."*

Some said: this verse abrogates (*nasikhah*, i.e., *naskh*, abrogation of a ruling by a later one) the ruling of the Exalted's words: ﴿The adulterous woman none marries except an adulterer or an idolater, and that is forbidden to the believers﴾ [An-Nur: 3]. We have explained this at the beginning of the surah, praise be to God.

**Fourth issue:** The intended meaning of the Exalted's words "*wa-ankihu al-ayama minkum*" [Marry off the unmarried among you] [See p. 167 of this part] is free women and free men. Then He explained the ruling for slaves, saying: ﴿and the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves﴾. Al-Hasan read: "*wa-al-salihina min 'ibadikum*" [the righteous among your male servants], and *'abid* is a collective noun. Al-Farra' said: it is permissible to read *wa-imaa'akum* [and your female slaves] in the accusative, referring it to *al-salihin* (the righteous), meaning the males and the females. *Al-salah* (righteousness) means faith.

It was also said: the meaning is that the desire should be to marry off slaves and female slaves when they are righteous, and so it is permissible to marry them, but there is no encouragement or recommendation for it, just as He said: ﴿So write a contract of manumission for them if you know any good in them﴾ [An-Nur: 33]. Then manumission is permitted even if it is not known that the slave has any good in him, but the address came in the context of encouragement and recommendation, and manumission is only recommended for one in whom there is good.

**Fifth issue:** Most scholars hold that a master may compel his male slave and female slave to marry. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and others. Malik said: that is not permitted if it causes harm. Something similar is related from al-Shafi'i. Then he said: a master may not compel a slave to marry. Al-Nakha'i said: they used to compel the slaves to marry and would lock the doors upon them.

The companions of al-Shafi'i held: the slave is a responsible person (*mukallaf*), so he is not compelled to marry, because being responsible indicates that the slave is complete in terms of his humanity; slavery applies to him only regarding what is the master's right, namely ownership of the body and its benefit. Unlike the female slave, the master has a right of ownership over her genitals so that he may enjoy them. As for the slave's genitals, he has no right in them, and for this reason the mistress is not permitted to her slave. This is the main argument of the people of Khurasan and Iraq. Their main argument also includes divorce, since the slave owns it by virtue of owning his marriage contract.

Our scholars' great point is that the slave's ownership was overtaken by the master's ownership, and for this reason he does not marry except with his master's permission, by consensus. Marriage and its related matters are only among the matters of public interest, and the interest of the slave is entrusted to the master, who sees it and provides it to the slave.

**Sixth issue:** The Exalted's words: ﴿If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty﴾. The discourse returns to free people: that is, do not refrain from marrying because of the poverty of the man or the woman. ﴿If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty.﴾ This is a promise of wealth for those who marry seeking the pleasure of God and protecting themselves from His disobedience.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Seek wealth through marriage," and he recited this verse. 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "I am amazed at one who does not seek wealth through marriage, when God the Exalted has said: ﴿If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty﴾." This meaning was also related from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both).

From the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him): the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three whose help is due from God: the one who strives in the way of God, the one who marries seeking chastity, and the slave who seeks to purchase his freedom (*mukatab*) seeking to pay (his price)." Related by Ibn Majah in his *Sunan*.

If it is said: we find that one who marries is not made wealthy, we say: it does not necessarily follow that this is permanent; even if it happened for a single moment, the promise would be true. It was also said: "He will enrich him" means he will enrich the soul (*nafs*). In the sound hadith: "Wealth is not having abundant goods; true wealth is the wealth of the soul." It was also said: this is not a promise that never fails; rather, the meaning is that wealth comes and goes, so hope for wealth. It was said: the meaning is "God will enrich them from His bounty if He wills," like His words: ﴿so He will remove that to which you call Him, if He wills﴾ [Al-An'am: 41] [See vol. 6, p. 423], and His words: ﴿He extends provision to whomever He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura: 12] [See vol. 9, p. 318 onward]. It was also said: the meaning is "If they are poor in need of marriage, God will enrich them through what is lawful, so that they may refrain from adultery."

**Seventh issue:** This verse is evidence for marrying off the poor. One should not say, "How can I marry when I have no wealth?" For his provision is upon God. The Prophet (ﷺ) married off a woman who came to him offering herself to him to a man who had nothing but a single garment. After that, she has no right to annul the marriage on account of his inability to provide, because she entered it knowingly. Annulment for inability is only applicable when she entered the marriage while he was wealthy and then he became poor, or poverty arose after the marriage, because hunger cannot be endured, as our scholars said.

Al-Naqqash said: this verse is an argument against those who say that the judge separates the spouses if the husband is poor and unable to provide maintenance, because God the Exalted said: "God will enrich them," and did not say "they should be separated." This is a weak deduction. This verse is not a ruling regarding one who is unable to provide maintenance; it is only a promise of enrichment for one who marries a poor person. As for one who married while wealthy and then became unable to provide maintenance, the two shall be separated. God the Exalted said: ﴿But if they separate, God will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [An-Nisa': 130] [See vol. 5, p. 404].

The gifts of God the Exalted are to be hoped for in every state, and He has promised them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 33–34 (part 1 of 4):**

God the Exalted says: ﴿And let those who find no means of marriage keep themselves chaste until God enriches them from His bounty.﴾ In it are four issues.

**The first issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿And let those who﴾. The address is to one who controls his own affairs, not to one whose reins are in another's hand, for that person is led by the one who controls him to whatever he sees fit, like the one under guardianship [[from K.]]. This is unanimous. As for the female slave and the male slave, it is one of the two opinions of the scholars.

**The second issue:** "Istaʿfaf" (keep oneself chaste) is on the pattern of istafʿala, and its meaning is seeking to be chaste. God the Exalted, by this verse, commands everyone for whom marriage is impossible, and who does not find it by any means that is impossible for him [[in K.: "yuʿdhar" (is impossible)]], to keep himself chaste. Then, since the most common obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth, He promised enrichment from His bounty, so that He provides him with what he marries with, or he finds a woman who is content with a small dowry, or the desire for women leaves him. Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Three are all owed by God, the Mighty and Majestic, to help them: the one who strives in the way of God, the one who marries seeking chastity, and the slave who seeks to pay for his freedom (mukatab)." 

**The third issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿who find no means of marriage﴾, meaning the means (ṭawl) for marriage, so the modifier is omitted. It has also been said: marriage here means what the woman is married with of dowry and maintenance, just as "al-liḥāf" is the name of what one wraps oneself in, and "al-libās" is the name of what is worn. According to this view, there is no omission in the verse. This was said by a group of exegetes (tafsir, explanation of the Qur'an). What led them to this view is God's saying: ﴿until God enriches them from His bounty﴾, so they thought that the one commanded to keep chaste is only the one who lacks the wealth with which he would marry. In this view there is a restriction of those commanded to keep chaste, and that is weak. Rather, the command to keep chaste applies to everyone for whom marriage is impossible, by whatever means it is impossible, as we have already stated. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Whoever's soul yearns for marriage, if he finds the means, then it is recommended for him to marry. If he does not find the means, then he must keep chaste, and if that is possible even by fasting, then fasting is for him a castration (wijaʾ) [[al-wijāʾ, with a kasra, means castration; that is, fasting cuts off desire as castration does]], as came in the sound report. Whoever's soul does not yearn for marriage, it is better for him to devote himself to the worship of God the Exalted. And in a report: "The best of you is the light one (al-khafif al-ḥādhdh) who has no family and no children." [[al-ḥādhdh: the one whose state is explained by what follows it.]] The permissibility of marrying female slaves when one cannot afford a free woman has already been mentioned in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 136 onward]], and praise be to God. Since God did not make a rank between chastity and marriage, this indicates that whatever is other than these two is forbidden. The ownership of the right hand does not fall under this, because by another text it is permitted, namely God's saying: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, so there was an addition in it. What remains under prohibition is masturbation, against Ahmad's view. [[the text here ends the first verse's discussion]]

Likewise, temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) is excluded from it by its abrogation (naskh), and this was already mentioned at the beginning of "al-Mu'minun" [[see p. 10 onward of this part]].

God the Exalted says: ﴿And those among your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾. In it are sixteen issues.

**The first issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿And those who seek﴾. "Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative position. According to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, it is in the accusative position by an implied verb, because after it there is a command. Since slaves and female slaves were mentioned previously, it was connected to that: if the slave seeks a written deed of manumission, then it is recommended to write it for him, because he may intend by the contract to become independent, earn, and marry when he wishes, and so it will be more chaste for him. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza called Subh, or Subayh, who asked his master to make a contract of manumission with him, but he refused. So God the Exalted revealed this verse, and Huwaytib made a contract with him for a hundred dinars and remitted twenty dinars from it, and he paid them, and he was killed at Hunayn in battle. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri and related by al-Naqqash. Makki said: he was Subayh the Copt, the slave of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. In general, God the Exalted commanded all believers that whoever among them has a slave, and the slave seeks a contract of manumission, and his master knows good in him, then he should make the contract with him.

**The second issue:** "al-kitab" and "al-mukatabah" are the same. It is a form of mutual action (mufa'ala), which can only occur between two parties, because it is a contract between the master and his slave. One says: kataba yukatibu kitaban and mukatabah, just as one says: qatala qitalan and muqatalah. So "al-kitab" in the verse is a verbal noun like "al-qital," "al-jilad," and "al-difaʿ." It has also been said: "al-kitab" here is the well-known writing in which a thing is written, because when they made a contract with the slave, they wrote for him and for themselves a document concerning that. So the meaning is that they seek the manumission which is written in the document, and so it is given to them.

**The third issue:** The meaning of mukatabah in the Shari'a is that a man makes a contract with his slave for a sum of money which he pays him in installments, and when he pays it, he is free. It has two states. The first: the slave seeks it and the master agrees; this is the absolute sense of the verse and its apparent meaning. The second: the slave seeks it and the master refuses. In this there are two opinions. The first, held by ʿIkrima, ʿAta', Masruq, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, and a group of the people of the apparent meaning (Zahiriyya), is that this is obligatory upon the master. The scholars of the regions said: this is not obligatory. Whoever held it obligatory relied on the absolute command, and the imperative form (afʿal) in its absolute sense indicates obligation until another proof comes indicating otherwise. This was related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tabari chose it. Dawud also argued that Sirin, the father of Muhammad ibn Sirin, asked Anas ibn Malik for a contract of manumission, and he was his master, but Anas refused. So ʿUmar raised the whip against him and recited: ﴿write it for them if you know any good in them﴾, and Anas made the contract with him. Dawud said: ʿUmar would not raise the whip against Anas concerning what is permissible for him not to do. The majority held that there is a consensus that if the slave asked him to sell him to another, he would not be bound to do so, and he could not be compelled, even if the price was doubled for him. Likewise, if he said to him: free me, or make me a mudabbar, or marry me, he would not be bound to do so by consensus. Therefore the contract of manumission is likewise, because it is an exchange, and it is not valid except by mutual consent. As for their saying that the absolute command implies obligation, it is correct, but only when it is free of an indicator that turns it away from obligation. Here the command is conditioned on knowing good in him, so the obligation is attached to a hidden matter, namely the master's knowledge of his good character. And if the slave says: make a contract with me, and the master says: I do not know any good in you, and that is a hidden matter, then the master is to be referred to and relied upon in it. And this is strong in its field.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed concerning God's saying: ﴿good﴾ (khayran). Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAta' said: wealth. Mujahid said: wealth and the ability to pay. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: religion and trustworthiness. Malik said: I heard some people of knowledge say it is the strength to earn and to pay. The same was related from al-Layth, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i. ʿUbayda al-Salmani said: establishing the prayer and goodness [[the word "and goodness" may be superfluous; perhaps "good" here means the rest of the praiseworthy qualities]]. Al-Tahawi said: the view of whoever says it is wealth is not valid according to us, because the slave is the property of his master, so how could he have property of his own? The meaning according to us is: if you know in them religion and truthfulness, and you know that they deal with you as those who are devoted to fulfilling for you what is owed by them of the contract, and truthfulness in dealing, then make a contract with them. Abu ʿUmar said: whoever does not say that good here means wealth denies that one can say "if you know wealth in them," for one only says: "I knew in him good, uprightness, and trustworthiness," and one does not say: "I knew in him wealth"; one says: "I knew wealth with him."

I say: The hadith of Barira refutes the view of whoever says that good is wealth, as will come.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning making a contract with one who has no craft. Ibn ʿUmar disliked making a contract with his slave if he had no craft, and he would say: do you order me to eat people's filth? Something similar was related from Salman al-Farisi. Hakim ibn Hizam related: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to ʿUmayr ibn Saʿd: "As for what follows: it has reached me from you that Muslims are making contracts with their slaves for the sake of begging from people." Al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq disliked it, while Malik, Abu Hanifa, and al-Shafi'i permitted it. It was related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that Ibn al-Tayyah, his muezzin, said to him: "Shall I make a contract when I have no property?" He said: "Yes." Then he urged people to give charity to me, and they gave me what exceeded my contract, and I went to ʿAli and he said: "Put it toward the freeing of necks." It has been related from Malik that making such a contract is disliked, and that a female slave who has no craft, making a contract with her is disliked because of the corruption it leads to. But the proof is in the Sunna, not in what contradicts it. The Imams related from ʿA'isha, may God be pleased with her, who said: Barira came to me and said: "My family made a contract with me for nine ounces in nine years, one ounce each year, so help me..." [[the hadith in full]]. This is evidence that a master may make a contract with his slave while the slave has nothing with him. Do you not see that Barira came to ʿA'isha to inform her that she had made a contract with her family and asked her to help her? That was at the beginning of her contract, before she had paid anything from it. Likewise Ibn Shihab related from ʿUrwa that ʿA'isha informed him that Barira came seeking her help with her contract, and she had not yet paid anything of her contract. Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud related it. In this is evidence for the permissibility of making a contract with a female slave who has no skill, no craft, and no property. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not ask whether she had earnings, or lasting work [[wasiba: lasted]], or property. Had this been obligatory, he would have asked about it so that the ruling would fall upon it, for he was sent as one who clarifies and teaches (ﷺ). And in this hadith is something indicating that whoever interprets God's saying: ﴿if you know any good in them﴾ as meaning wealth has not given a good interpretation, and that the good mentioned is strength to earn together with trustworthiness. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** A contract may be made for a small amount of wealth or a large amount, and it may be in installments (anjum), according to the hadith of Barira. There is no disagreement among the scholars about this, and praise be to God. So if he makes a contract with him for a thousand dirhams and does not mention a term, it is divided into installments...

she him according to his earning, even if the master dislikes it. Al-Shafi'i said: it must have a term, and its minimum is three installments (anjum). They differed when it falls due in a single installment. Most scholars permit it in a single installment. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted in a single installment, and it is never permitted as a deferred-free immediate contract; rather that is a manumission on a condition, as if he said: "When you pay such-and-such, you are free," and it is not a kitabah (contract of manumission).

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the scholars and the early generation differed about an immediate kitabah on two views, and the opinion of our scholars differed accordingly. The sounder view on reflection is that kitabah is deferred, as the report concerning it came in the hadith of Barirah when she made a kitabah with her people for nine awaq, one uqiyyah every year, and as the Companions did. For this reason it was called kitabah, because it is written down and witnessed upon. Thus the name and the report agree, and the meaning supports them, for if he makes the property immediate while the slave has something, it is property of a settlement (muqata'ah) and a contract of settlement, not a contract of kitabah.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if he makes a kitabah for property that is immediate, it is manumission for property, and it is not a kitabah. Others among our companions permitted an immediate kitabah and named it qita'ah (settlement), and this is the analogical view, because the deferral in it is only a respite for the slave to earn. Do you not see that if the one bound by installments brought it before its due date, the master would be obliged to accept it and hasten the freeing of the mukatab?

The Kufans said that an immediate kitabah is permitted. I say: no explicit text from Malik about an immediate kitabah has been transmitted, and the companions say it is permitted and call it qita'ah. As for al-Shafi'i's statement that it is not permitted for fewer than three installments, it is not correct, because if it were correct it would be permitted for another to say: it is not permitted for fewer than five installments, since five was the least number of installments in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the case of Barirah, and the Prophet ﷺ knew of it and judged in it, so the correct proof is more deserving.

Al-Bukhari narrated from 'A'ishah that Barirah came to her seeking help with her kitabah, and upon her were five awaq, which were divided into installments over five years... the hadith. Thus said al-Layth from Yunus from Ibn Shihab from 'Urwah from 'A'ishah: "and upon her were five awaq, which were divided into installments over five years." Abu Usamah said from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: Barirah came and said: "I made a kitabah with my people for nine awaq..." the hadith. The apparent meaning of the two reports is a contradiction, except that the hadith of Hisham is preferable for its continuity (ittisal) and the break in the hadith of Yunus, due to the statement of al-Bukhari: "and al-Layth said: Yunus narrated to me," and because Hisham is more firm in the hadith of his father and his grandfather than others. And Allah knows best.

Seventh: the mukatab remains a slave as long as anything of the kitabah money remains upon him, due to his (peace be upon him) saying: "The mukatab is a slave as long as there remains upon him from his kitabah a single dirham." Abu Dawud narrated it from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather. And it is also narrated from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whichever slave makes a kitabah for a hundred dinars, and pays it all except ten dinars, he is a slave." This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Dawud and al-Tabari. And this was narrated from Ibn 'Umar through several channels, and from Zayd ibn Thabit, 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah, without difference among them, may Allah be pleased with them. It was also narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Qasim, Salim and 'Ata' said likewise. Malik said: every one we encountered in our city used to say so. There is another view narrated from 'Ali that when he pays half, he is a debtor (gharim), and al-Nakha'i said likewise. This was also narrated from 'Umar, but the chain from him that the mukatab is a slave as long as a dirham remains upon him is better than the chain from him that when the mukatab pays half, there is no bondage upon him, as said by Abu 'Umar. And from 'Ali also: he is freed to the extent of what he has paid. And also from him: manumission takes effect in him with the first installment he pays. Ibn Mas'ud said: when he pays a third of the kitabah, he is a freed debtor (gharim 'atiq), and this is the view of Shurayh. And from Ibn Mas'ud: if the kitabah were two hundred dinars and the value of the slave were one hundred dinars, and the slave paid the hundred which is his value, he is freed; and this is also the view of al-Nakha'i. A seventh view: when he pays three quarters and a quarter remains, he is a debtor and does not return to being a slave; this was said by 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, related by Ibn Jurayj from him. It is related from some of the early scholars that by the very contract of kitabah he is free, and he is a debtor for the kitabah and never returns to bondage. This view is refuted by the hadith of Barirah for its authenticity from the Prophet ﷺ. And in it is clear evidence that the mukatab is a slave; had it not been so, Barirah would not have been sold, and had there been any freedom in it he would not have permitted its sale, for it is an agreed-upon sunnah that a free person is not sold. Likewise the kitabah of Salman and Juwayriyah, for the Prophet ﷺ ruled for all of them that they remained in bondage until they paid the kitabah. And it is a proof for the majority that the mukatab is a slave as long as anything remains upon him. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib debated Zayd ibn Thabit about the mukatab; Zayd said to 'Ali: "Would you stone him if he committed adultery, or accept his testimony if he testified?" 'Ali said: "No." Zayd said: "He is a slave as long as anything remains upon him." And al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The mukatab is freed of him to the extent of what he has paid, the prescribed punishment is applied to him to the extent of what he has paid, and he inherits to the extent of what has been freed of him." Its chain is sound. This is a proof for what was narrated from 'Ali, and it is strengthened by what Abu Dawud narrated from Nabhan, the mukatab of Umm Salamah, who said: I heard Umm Salamah say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "If one of you has a mukatab and he has what he can pay, let her veil herself from him." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: a hasan sahih hadith. However, it may be that it was an address to his wives, taking the precaution and piety regarding them, as he said to Sawdah: "Veil yourself from him," although he had judged her to be his sister, and as he said to 'A'ishah and Hafsah: "Are you two blind? Do you not see him?" meaning Ibn Umm Maktum, although he said to Fatimah bint Qays: "Observe your 'iddah at the house of Ibn Umm Maktum." This meaning has already been discussed.

Eighth: The scholars agreed that when one of the installments of the mukatab falls due, or two, or all of his installments, and the master refrains from demanding it and leaves him in his state, the kitabah is not dissolved as long as both remain upon that.

Ninth: Malik said: the slave has no right to incapacitate himself if he has apparent property; and if no property appears for him, that is up to him. Al-Awza'i said: he is not enabled to incapacitate himself if he is strong enough to pay. Al-Shafi'i said: he may incapacitate himself, whether property is known for him or strength for kitabah or not; so when he says, "I have become incapable and I annul the kitabah," that is up to him. Malik said: if the mukatab becomes incapable, whatever his master received from him before incapacity is lawful for him, whether it was from his earnings or from charity given to him. As for what was given to help him free his neck, if it did not suffice for his kitabah, each one who helped him has the right to recover what he gave, or the mukatab must make them lawful for him. And if they gave charity not for the freeing of his neck, then if he becomes incapable, it is lawful for his master, even if his freedom was completed by it and some surplus remained. If it was for the purpose of freeing, he returns it to them proportionally, or they make it lawful for him. All of this is the school of Malik as related by Ibn al-Qasim. Most scholars said: what the master received from him as kitabah, and what remains in his hand after his incapacity from charity or otherwise, belongs to his master, and it is lawful for him to take all of it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and a report from Shurayh. Al-Thawri said: the master spends what he gave on the freeing of necks; this is the view of Masruq and al-Nakha'i, and a report from Shurayh. A group said: what the master received from him is his, and what remains in his hand after incapacity is his, not his master's; this is the view of some who held that the slave owns property. Ishaq said: what was given during the kitabah is returned to its owners.

Tenth: The hadith of Barirah, through its differing chains and wordings, implies that a sale occurred involving Barirah after an earlier kitabah. People differed regarding the sale of a mukatab on account of this. Al-Bukhari titled a chapter "The sale of the mukatab if he consents." Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Dawudi held that it is permitted to sell him for manumission if the mukatab consents to the sale even if he is not incapable, and Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr approved this; Ibn Shihab, Abu al-Zinad and Rabi'ah said likewise, except that they said: because his consent to the sale is an incapacity on his part. Malik, Abu Hanifah and their companions said: the sale of the mukatab is not permitted as long as he is a mukatab until he becomes incapable, and the sale of his kitabah is not permitted in any case; this is the view of al-Shafi'i in Egypt, while in Iraq he said: his sale is permitted, but the sale of his kitabah is not permitted. Malik permitted the sale of the kitabah: if the buyer pays it, he is freed, otherwise he is a slave of the buyer of the kitabah. Abu Hanifah prohibited this because it is a sale involving gharar. Al-Shafi'i's view on this varied between prohibition and permission. A group said: the sale of the mukatab is permitted on condition that he continues in his kitabah; if he pays, he is freed and his walaʼ belongs to the one who bought him, and if he becomes incapable, he is a slave to him. This was said by al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', al-Layth, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Al-Awza'i said: the mukatab is not sold except for manumission, and it is disliked to sell him before his incapacity; this is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq. Abu 'Umar said: the hadith of Barirah indicates the permissibility of selling the mukatab when he consents to the sale and is not incapable of paying an installment that has fallen due upon him, unlike the view of one who claimed that the sale of

The mukatab (a slave who has contracted to purchase his freedom) may not be sold except when he is unable to pay. Barirah did not report that she had become unable to pay an installment, nor did she say that an installment had fallen due to her, and the Prophet ﷺ did not say to her, "Are you unable, or has an installment fallen due to you?" Had the sale of a mukatab or mukatabah been permissible only upon inability to pay what had fallen due, the Prophet ﷺ would have asked her whether she was unable, and he would not have permitted the purchase until he knew that she was unable, even to pay a single installment that had fallen due to her. In the report of al-Zuhri, she had not paid anything of her kitabah (contractual manumission). I know of no proof on this matter more sound than this hadith of Barirah, and nothing has been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ that contradicts it, nor is there in any of the reports any indication that she was unable.

Those who prohibited the sale of the mukatab relied on several matters. Among them, they said that the kitabah mentioned had not been concluded, and that her saying "I made a kitabah with my family" means that she negotiated with them concerning it, and they fixed its amount and term but did not conclude it. The apparent meaning of the hadiths is contrary to this when their context is considered. It has also been said that Barirah became unable to pay, so she and her family agreed to dissolve the kitabah, and then the sale was valid. However, this can only be upheld according to the view of those who say that the inability of the mukatab does not require the ruling of a judge when the slave and the master agree upon it, since the right does not go beyond the two of them. This is the well-known school of thought. Sahnun said: a ruling of the sultan (ruler) is necessary, and he feared only that the two might collude to abandon the right of Allah, the Exalted.

What indicates the soundness of the view that she was unable is what has been transmitted: that Barirah came to Aishah seeking her help in her kitabah, and she had not paid anything of it. Aishah said to her: "Return to your family; if they wish that I pay your kitabah on your behalf, I will do so." The apparent meaning of this is that all or part of her kitabah became due from her, because nothing of the rights is paid except what has become due to be demanded, and Allah knows best.

These interpretations are the most plausible of what they have, and in them there is a flaw that we have explained. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I know of no proof for one who says that it is not permissible for him to sell the mukatab, except that he says perhaps Barirah was unable." Al-Shafi'i said: "The most apparent of its meanings is that the owner of the mukatab may sell him."

Eleventh issue: When the mukatab pays his kitabah, he is freed, and he does not need a fresh manumission from the master. Likewise, his children who were born to him from his female slave during his kitabah are freed by his freeing and enslaved by his enslavement, because the child of a person from his female slave has the same status as him, by analogy with the free person. Likewise, the child of a mukatabah. If they had a child before the kitabah, that child does not enter into the kitabah except by a condition.

Twelfth issue: The words (and give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you) are a command to the masters to assist them in the wealth of the kitabah, either by giving them something from what is in their hands, meaning the hands of the masters, or by remitting something of the kitabah wealth. Malik said: something is remitted from the mukatab from the last of his kitabah. Ibn Umar remitted five thousand out of thirty-five thousand. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, considered it good that this should be a quarter of the kitabah. Al-Zahrawi said: this was transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan considered a third of it good. Qatadah said: a tenth of it. Ibn Jubayr said: he remits something from it, without setting a limit, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, and al-Thawri considered it good. Al-Shafi'i said: "Something" is the least thing that falls under the name of "a thing," and the master is compelled to it, and the judge rules concerning it against the heirs if the master dies.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarded this command as recommendation, and he did not see a fixed amount for the remission. Al-Shafi'i relied on the unrestricted form of the command in His words "and give them," and he held that the conjunction of an obligatory matter with a recommended one is known in the Qur'an and the language of the Arabs, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct and giving to relatives﴾ [An-Nahl: 90], and what is similar to it. Ibn al-Arabi said: Ismail ibn Ishaq al-Qadi also mentioned this before him, saying that al-Shafi'i made the giving obligatory and the kitabah non-obligatory, so he made the origin non-obligatory and the branch obligatory, and this has no parallel, so it became a bare claim. If it is said: it is like marriage, which is not obligatory, but once it is concluded its rulings become binding, among them the mut'ah (compensatory gift). We say: according to us, the mut'ah is not obligatory, so there is no point for the followers of al-Shafi'i. Uthman ibn Affan made a kitabah with his slave and swore that he would not remit anything from it... in a long hadith.

I say: al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Buraydah said that the address in His words "and give them" is to all people, that they should give charity to the mukatabin and assist them in ransoming their necks. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to the rulers, that they should give the mukatabin their share from the zakat funds, and this is what His words "and for the slaves" (At-Tawbah: 60) encompass. According to these two views, the master of the mukatab does not have the right to remit anything from his mukatab. The evidence for this is that if he had wanted to remit some of the installments of the kitabah, he would have said: "Remit for them such and such."

Thirteenth issue: If we say that the address is to the masters, then Umar ibn al-Khattab considered that this should be from the first of his installments, hastening to good, fearing that he might not live to see the last of them. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others considered that the remission should be from the last installment. The reason for this is that if he remits from the first installment, the slave may perhaps become unable, and then he and his property return to the master, and so the remission returns to him, and it resembles charity. This is the view of Abdullah ibn Umar and Ali. Mujahid said: he leaves for him from each installment. Ibn al-Arabi said: what is stronger in my view is that it should be at the end, because remission is always in the final parts of debts.

Fourteenth issue: If the mukatab is sold for the purpose of manumission, with his consent after the kitabah, and his seller receives the price, it is not obligatory for him to give the mukatab anything of the price, whether he sold him for manumission or for other than manumission. This is unlike a master to whom a mukatab pays his kitabah, and he gives him something from it, or remits from its last installment an installment or whatever he wishes, in accordance with what Allah commanded in His Book, because the Prophet ﷺ did not command the owners of Barirah to give her anything of what they had received, even though they had sold her for manumission.

Fifteenth issue: They differed concerning the description of the contract of kitabah. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: its description is that the master says to his slave: "I have made a kitabah with you for such and such an amount of wealth, in such and such installments; when you pay it, you are free," or he says to him: "Pay me a thousand in ten installments and you are free." The slave says: "I have accepted," and similar words. Whenever he pays it, he is freed. Likewise, if the slave says: "Make a kitabah with me," and the master says: "I have done so," or "I have made a kitabah with you." Ibn al-Arabi said: this is not binding, because the wording of the Qur'an does not require it, and the situation bears witness to it. If he mentions it, that is good, and if he omits it, it is known and does not need to be stated. The issues of this chapter and its branches are many, and we have mentioned a body of its principles, in which there is sufficiency for one who restricts himself to them, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

Sixteenth issue: Concerning the inheritance of the mukatab, the scholars differed on it in three views. The school of Malik holds that if the mukatab dies and leaves property more than what remains of his kitabah, and he has children who were born during his kitabah, or for whom he made a kitabah, they inherit what remains of the property after the settlement of his kitabah, because their ruling is like his ruling. They are obliged to strive for what remains of his kitabah if he left no property. They are not freed except by his freeing. If he had paid on their behalf, he would not have recovered it from them, because they are freed through him, so they have the better claim to his inheritance, since they are equal to him in all his circumstances.

The second view: his entire kitabah is paid on his behalf from his property, and he is treated as though he had died free, and all his children inherit from him, whether those who were free before his death, or those for whom he made a kitabah, or those who were born during his kitabah, because they are all equal in freedom once their kitabah has been settled on their behalf. This view was transmitted from Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, and among the Successors from Ata', al-Hasan, Tawus and Ibrahim. Fuqaha' of Kufa, Sufyan al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy, also said this, and Ishaq adopted it.

The third view: if the mukatab dies before he has paid all his kitabah, then he has died a slave, and all the property he leaves behind belongs to his master, and none of his children inherit from him, neither the free ones nor those who were with him in the kitabah, because when he died before paying all his kitabah, he died a slave, and his property belongs to his master, so his manumission after his death is not valid, since it is impossible for a slave to be freed after his death. His children for whom he made a kitabah, or who were born during his kitabah, must strive for the remainder of the kitabah, and the share of his portion is dropped from it for them. If they pay, they are freed, because they were included in it as followers of their father; if they do not pay, they are enslaved. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also said it, and it is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Zayd ibn Thabit, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Zuhri and Qatadah.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity﴾. It was transmitted from Jabir ibn Abdullah and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy. He had two slave girls, one called Mu'adhah and the other Musaykah, and he would compel them to fornication and beat them for it, seeking wages and the gain of children. They complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and the verse was revealed concerning him and concerning whoever did his deed among the hypocrites. Mu'adhah was the mother of Khawlah, who disputed with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir: a slave girl of Abdullah ibn Ubayy called Musaykah and another called Umaymah, and he used to compel them to fornication, so they complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution," up to His words: "Forgiving, Merciful."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 33–34 (part 4 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿if they desire chastity﴾, refers to the slave-girls. This is because when the slave-girl desires chastity, it is then possible and conceivable that the master may be compelling her, and it is possible to forbid compulsion. But if the slave-girl does not desire chastity, it is not conceivable to say to the master, "Do not compel her," because compulsion cannot be conceived of in her case while she is desirous of fornication. So this is a matter concerning masters and slave-girls in such a state.

Ibn al-'Arabi alluded to this meaning, saying: "God, exalted is He, only mentioned the woman's desire for chastity because that is what depicts compulsion. As for when she herself is eager for fornication, compulsion cannot be conceived of, so grasp this." This consideration escaped many of the exegetes. Some of them said that His saying, "if they desire chastity," refers to the unmarried women (al-ayama). Al-Zajjaj and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, meaning: "And marry the unmarried women and the righteous among your servants, if they desire chastity." And some of them said: this condition in His saying "if they desire" is cancelled (mulgha), and similar to that of what is weak, and God is the Granter of success. That is, the thing that the slave-girl earns by her private part, and the child is enslaved and sold. It was also said: the fornicator used to ransom his child from the one he had fornicated with by a hundred camels, which he would hand over to her master.

﴿And whoever compels them﴾, that is, subdues them, ﴿then indeed God, after their compulsion, is Forgiving﴾ toward them, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them.

Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn Jubayr read "lahunna ghafur" with the addition of "lahunna" (for them).

The discussion of compulsion has already passed in [al-Nahl [see vol. 10, p. 180 and following]], and praise be to God. He, exalted is He, enumerated for the believers His blessings in what He sent down to them of the clear verses [in K: "al-nayyirat", and what He struck of parables], and in it He struck for them parables of the nations that passed away, so that they may be guarded against what those people fell into.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 33–34 (part 1 of 4):**

God the Exalted says: ﴿And let those who find no means of marriage keep themselves chaste until God enriches them from His bounty.﴾ In it are four issues.

**The first issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿And let those who﴾. The address is to one who controls his own affairs, not to one whose reins are in another's hand, for that person is led by the one who controls him to whatever he sees fit, like the one under guardianship [[from K.]]. This is unanimous. As for the female slave and the male slave, it is one of the two opinions of the scholars.

**The second issue:** "Istaʿfaf" (keep oneself chaste) is on the pattern of istafʿala, and its meaning is seeking to be chaste. God the Exalted, by this verse, commands everyone for whom marriage is impossible, and who does not find it by any means that is impossible for him [[in K.: "yuʿdhar" (is impossible)]], to keep himself chaste.
