Then, since the most common obstacle to marriage is lack of wealth, He promised enrichment from His bounty, so that He provides him with what he marries with, or he finds a woman who is content with a small dowry, or the desire for women leaves him. Al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Three are all owed by God, the Mighty and Majestic, to help them: the one who strives in the way of God, the one who marries seeking chastity, and the slave who seeks to pay for his freedom (mukatab)." 

**The third issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿who find no means of marriage﴾, meaning the means (ṭawl) for marriage, so the modifier is omitted. It has also been said: marriage here means what the woman is married with of dowry and maintenance, just as "al-liḥāf" is the name of what one wraps oneself in, and "al-libās" is the name of what is worn. According to this view, there is no omission in the verse. This was said by a group of exegetes (tafsir, explanation of the Qur'an). What led them to this view is God's saying: ﴿until God enriches them from His bounty﴾, so they thought that the one commanded to keep chaste is only the one who lacks the wealth with which he would marry. In this view there is a restriction of those commanded to keep chaste, and that is weak. Rather, the command to keep chaste applies to everyone for whom marriage is impossible, by whatever means it is impossible, as we have already stated. And God knows best.

**The fourth issue:** Whoever's soul yearns for marriage, if he finds the means, then it is recommended for him to marry. If he does not find the means, then he must keep chaste, and if that is possible even by fasting, then fasting is for him a castration (wijaʾ) [[al-wijāʾ, with a kasra, means castration; that is, fasting cuts off desire as castration does]], as came in the sound report. Whoever's soul does not yearn for marriage, it is better for him to devote himself to the worship of God the Exalted. And in a report: "The best of you is the light one (al-khafif al-ḥādhdh) who has no family and no children." [[al-ḥādhdh: the one whose state is explained by what follows it.]] The permissibility of marrying female slaves when one cannot afford a free woman has already been mentioned in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 136 onward]], and praise be to God. Since God did not make a rank between chastity and marriage, this indicates that whatever is other than these two is forbidden. The ownership of the right hand does not fall under this, because by another text it is permitted, namely God's saying: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾, so there was an addition in it. What remains under prohibition is masturbation, against Ahmad's view. [[the text here ends the first verse's discussion]]

Likewise, temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a) is excluded from it by its abrogation (naskh), and this was already mentioned at the beginning of "al-Mu'minun" [[see p. 10 onward of this part]].

God the Exalted says: ﴿And those among your slaves who seek a deed of manumission, write it for them if you know any good in them﴾. In it are sixteen issues.

**The first issue:** God the Exalted says: ﴿And those who seek﴾. "Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative position. According to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, it is in the accusative position by an implied verb, because after it there is a command. Since slaves and female slaves were mentioned previously, it was connected to that: if the slave seeks a written deed of manumission, then it is recommended to write it for him, because he may intend by the contract to become independent, earn, and marry when he wishes, and so it will be more chaste for him. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza called Subh, or Subayh, who asked his master to make a contract of manumission with him, but he refused. So God the Exalted revealed this verse, and Huwaytib made a contract with him for a hundred dinars and remitted twenty dinars from it, and he paid them, and he was killed at Hunayn in battle. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri and related by al-Naqqash. Makki said: he was Subayh the Copt, the slave of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. In general, God the Exalted commanded all believers that whoever among them has a slave, and the slave seeks a contract of manumission, and his master knows good in him, then he should make the contract with him.

**The second issue:** "al-kitab" and "al-mukatabah" are the same. It is a form of mutual action (mufa'ala), which can only occur between two parties, because it is a contract between the master and his slave. One says: kataba yukatibu kitaban and mukatabah, just as one says: qatala qitalan and muqatalah. So "al-kitab" in the verse is a verbal noun like "al-qital," "al-jilad," and "al-difaʿ." It has also been said: "al-kitab" here is the well-known writing in which a thing is written, because when they made a contract with the slave, they wrote for him and for themselves a document concerning that. So the meaning is that they seek the manumission which is written in the document, and so it is given to them.

**The third issue:** The meaning of mukatabah in the Shari'a is that a man makes a contract with his slave for a sum of money which he pays him in installments, and when he pays it, he is free. It has two states. The first: the slave seeks it and the master agrees; this is the absolute sense of the verse and its apparent meaning. The second: the slave seeks it and the master refuses. In this there are two opinions. The first, held by ʿIkrima, ʿAta', Masruq, ʿAmr ibn Dinar, al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, and a group of the people of the apparent meaning (Zahiriyya), is that this is obligatory upon the master. The scholars of the regions said: this is not obligatory. Whoever held it obligatory relied on the absolute command, and the imperative form (afʿal) in its absolute sense indicates obligation until another proof comes indicating otherwise. This was related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tabari chose it. Dawud also argued that Sirin, the father of Muhammad ibn Sirin, asked Anas ibn Malik for a contract of manumission, and he was his master, but Anas refused. So ʿUmar raised the whip against him and recited: ﴿write it for them if you know any good in them﴾, and Anas made the contract with him. Dawud said: ʿUmar would not raise the whip against Anas concerning what is permissible for him not to do. The majority held that there is a consensus that if the slave asked him to sell him to another, he would not be bound to do so, and he could not be compelled, even if the price was doubled for him. Likewise, if he said to him: free me, or make me a mudabbar, or marry me, he would not be bound to do so by consensus. Therefore the contract of manumission is likewise, because it is an exchange, and it is not valid except by mutual consent. As for their saying that the absolute command implies obligation, it is correct, but only when it is free of an indicator that turns it away from obligation. Here the command is conditioned on knowing good in him, so the obligation is attached to a hidden matter, namely the master's knowledge of his good character. And if the slave says: make a contract with me, and the master says: I do not know any good in you, and that is a hidden matter, then the master is to be referred to and relied upon in it. And this is strong in its field.

**The fourth issue:** The scholars differed concerning God's saying: ﴿good﴾ (khayran). Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAta' said: wealth. Mujahid said: wealth and the ability to pay. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: religion and trustworthiness. Malik said: I heard some people of knowledge say it is the strength to earn and to pay. The same was related from al-Layth, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i. ʿUbayda al-Salmani said: establishing the prayer and goodness [[the word "and goodness" may be superfluous; perhaps "good" here means the rest of the praiseworthy qualities]]. Al-Tahawi said: the view of whoever says it is wealth is not valid according to us, because the slave is the property of his master, so how could he have property of his own? The meaning according to us is: if you know in them religion and truthfulness, and you know that they deal with you as those who are devoted to fulfilling for you what is owed by them of the contract, and truthfulness in dealing, then make a contract with them. Abu ʿUmar said: whoever does not say that good here means wealth denies that one can say "if you know wealth in them," for one only says: "I knew in him good, uprightness, and trustworthiness," and one does not say: "I knew in him wealth"; one says: "I knew wealth with him."

I say: The hadith of Barira refutes the view of whoever says that good is wealth, as will come.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning making a contract with one who has no craft. Ibn ʿUmar disliked making a contract with his slave if he had no craft, and he would say: do you order me to eat people's filth? Something similar was related from Salman al-Farisi. Hakim ibn Hizam related: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to ʿUmayr ibn Saʿd: "As for what follows: it has reached me from you that Muslims are making contracts with their slaves for the sake of begging from people." Al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq disliked it, while Malik, Abu Hanifa, and al-Shafi'i permitted it. It was related from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that Ibn al-Tayyah, his muezzin, said to him: "Shall I make a contract when I have no property?" He said: "Yes." Then he urged people to give charity to me, and they gave me what exceeded my contract, and I went to ʿAli and he said: "Put it toward the freeing of necks." It has been related from Malik that making such a contract is disliked, and that a female slave who has no craft, making a contract with her is disliked because of the corruption it leads to. But the proof is in the Sunna, not in what contradicts it. The Imams related from ʿA'isha, may God be pleased with her, who said: Barira came to me and said: "My family made a contract with me for nine ounces in nine years, one ounce each year, so help me..." [[the hadith in full]]. This is evidence that a master may make a contract with his slave while the slave has nothing with him. Do you not see that Barira came to ʿA'isha to inform her that she had made a contract with her family and asked her to help her? That was at the beginning of her contract, before she had paid anything from it. Likewise Ibn Shihab related from ʿUrwa that ʿA'isha informed him that Barira came seeking her help with her contract, and she had not yet paid anything of her contract. Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud related it. In this is evidence for the permissibility of making a contract with a female slave who has no skill, no craft, and no property. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not ask whether she had earnings, or lasting work [[wasiba: lasted]], or property. Had this been obligatory, he would have asked about it so that the ruling would fall upon it, for he was sent as one who clarifies and teaches (ﷺ). And in this hadith is something indicating that whoever interprets God's saying: ﴿if you know any good in them﴾ as meaning wealth has not given a good interpretation, and that the good mentioned is strength to earn together with trustworthiness. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** A contract may be made for a small amount of wealth or a large amount, and it may be in installments (anjum), according to the hadith of Barira. There is no disagreement among the scholars about this, and praise be to God. So if he makes a contract with him for a thousand dirhams and does not mention a term, it is divided into installments...

she him according to his earning, even if the master dislikes it. Al-Shafi'i said: it must have a term, and its minimum is three installments (anjum). They differed when it falls due in a single installment. Most scholars permit it in a single installment. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permitted in a single installment, and it is never permitted as a deferred-free immediate contract; rather that is a manumission on a condition, as if he said: "When you pay such-and-such, you are free," and it is not a kitabah (contract of manumission).

Ibn al-'Arabi said: the scholars and the early generation differed about an immediate kitabah on two views, and the opinion of our scholars differed accordingly. The sounder view on reflection is that kitabah is deferred, as the report concerning it came in the hadith of Barirah when she made a kitabah with her people for nine awaq, one uqiyyah every year, and as the Companions did. For this reason it was called kitabah, because it is written down and witnessed upon. Thus the name and the report agree, and the meaning supports them, for if he makes the property immediate while the slave has something, it is property of a settlement (muqata'ah) and a contract of settlement, not a contract of kitabah.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: if he makes a kitabah for property that is immediate, it is manumission for property, and it is not a kitabah. Others among our companions permitted an immediate kitabah and named it qita'ah (settlement), and this is the analogical view, because the deferral in it is only a respite for the slave to earn. Do you not see that if the one bound by installments brought it before its due date, the master would be obliged to accept it and hasten the freeing of the mukatab?

The Kufans said that an immediate kitabah is permitted. I say: no explicit text from Malik about an immediate kitabah has been transmitted, and the companions say it is permitted and call it qita'ah. As for al-Shafi'i's statement that it is not permitted for fewer than three installments, it is not correct, because if it were correct it would be permitted for another to say: it is not permitted for fewer than five installments, since five was the least number of installments in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the case of Barirah, and the Prophet ﷺ knew of it and judged in it, so the correct proof is more deserving.

Al-Bukhari narrated from 'A'ishah that Barirah came to her seeking help with her kitabah, and upon her were five awaq, which were divided into installments over five years... the hadith. Thus said al-Layth from Yunus from Ibn Shihab from 'Urwah from 'A'ishah: "and upon her were five awaq, which were divided into installments over five years." Abu Usamah said from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: Barirah came and said: "I made a kitabah with my people for nine awaq..." the hadith. The apparent meaning of the two reports is a contradiction, except that the hadith of Hisham is preferable for its continuity (ittisal) and the break in the hadith of Yunus, due to the statement of al-Bukhari: "and al-Layth said: Yunus narrated to me," and because Hisham is more firm in the hadith of his father and his grandfather than others. And Allah knows best.

Seventh: the mukatab remains a slave as long as anything of the kitabah money remains upon him, due to his (peace be upon him) saying: "The mukatab is a slave as long as there remains upon him from his kitabah a single dirham." Abu Dawud narrated it from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather. And it is also narrated from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whichever slave makes a kitabah for a hundred dinars, and pays it all except ten dinars, he is a slave." This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Dawud and al-Tabari. And this was narrated from Ibn 'Umar through several channels, and from Zayd ibn Thabit, 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah, without difference among them, may Allah be pleased with them. It was also narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Qasim, Salim and 'Ata' said likewise. Malik said: every one we encountered in our city used to say so. There is another view narrated from 'Ali that when he pays half, he is a debtor (gharim), and al-Nakha'i said likewise. This was also narrated from 'Umar, but the chain from him that the mukatab is a slave as long as a dirham remains upon him is better than the chain from him that when the mukatab pays half, there is no bondage upon him, as said by Abu 'Umar. And from 'Ali also: he is freed to the extent of what he has paid. And also from him: manumission takes effect in him with the first installment he pays. Ibn Mas'ud said: when he pays a third of the kitabah, he is a freed debtor (gharim 'atiq), and this is the view of Shurayh. And from Ibn Mas'ud: if the kitabah were two hundred dinars and the value of the slave were one hundred dinars, and the slave paid the hundred which is his value, he is freed; and this is also the view of al-Nakha'i. A seventh view: when he pays three quarters and a quarter remains, he is a debtor and does not return to being a slave; this was said by 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, related by Ibn Jurayj from him. It is related from some of the early scholars that by the very contract of kitabah he is free, and he is a debtor for the kitabah and never returns to bondage. This view is refuted by the hadith of Barirah for its authenticity from the Prophet ﷺ. And in it is clear evidence that the mukatab is a slave; had it not been so, Barirah would not have been sold, and had there been any freedom in it he would not have permitted its sale, for it is an agreed-upon sunnah that a free person is not sold. Likewise the kitabah of Salman and Juwayriyah, for the Prophet ﷺ ruled for all of them that they remained in bondage until they paid the kitabah. And it is a proof for the majority that the mukatab is a slave as long as anything remains upon him. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib debated Zayd ibn Thabit about the mukatab; Zayd said to 'Ali: "Would you stone him if he committed adultery, or accept his testimony if he testified?" 'Ali said: "No." Zayd said: "He is a slave as long as anything remains upon him." And al-Nasa'i narrated from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The mukatab is freed of him to the extent of what he has paid, the prescribed punishment is applied to him to the extent of what he has paid, and he inherits to the extent of what has been freed of him." Its chain is sound. This is a proof for what was narrated from 'Ali, and it is strengthened by what Abu Dawud narrated from Nabhan, the mukatab of Umm Salamah, who said: I heard Umm Salamah say: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: "If one of you has a mukatab and he has what he can pay, let her veil herself from him." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: a hasan sahih hadith. However, it may be that it was an address to his wives, taking the precaution and piety regarding them, as he said to Sawdah: "Veil yourself from him," although he had judged her to be his sister, and as he said to 'A'ishah and Hafsah: "Are you two blind? Do you not see him?" meaning Ibn Umm Maktum, although he said to Fatimah bint Qays: "Observe your 'iddah at the house of Ibn Umm Maktum." This meaning has already been discussed.

Eighth: The scholars agreed that when one of the installments of the mukatab falls due, or two, or all of his installments, and the master refrains from demanding it and leaves him in his state, the kitabah is not dissolved as long as both remain upon that.

Ninth: Malik said: the slave has no right to incapacitate himself if he has apparent property; and if no property appears for him, that is up to him. Al-Awza'i said: he is not enabled to incapacitate himself if he is strong enough to pay. Al-Shafi'i said: he may incapacitate himself, whether property is known for him or strength for kitabah or not; so when he says, "I have become incapable and I annul the kitabah," that is up to him. Malik said: if the mukatab becomes incapable, whatever his master received from him before incapacity is lawful for him, whether it was from his earnings or from charity given to him. As for what was given to help him free his neck, if it did not suffice for his kitabah, each one who helped him has the right to recover what he gave, or the mukatab must make them lawful for him. And if they gave charity not for the freeing of his neck, then if he becomes incapable, it is lawful for his master, even if his freedom was completed by it and some surplus remained. If it was for the purpose of freeing, he returns it to them proportionally, or they make it lawful for him. All of this is the school of Malik as related by Ibn al-Qasim. Most scholars said: what the master received from him as kitabah, and what remains in his hand after his incapacity from charity or otherwise, belongs to his master, and it is lawful for him to take all of it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and their companions, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and a report from Shurayh. Al-Thawri said: the master spends what he gave on the freeing of necks; this is the view of Masruq and al-Nakha'i, and a report from Shurayh. A group said: what the master received from him is his, and what remains in his hand after incapacity is his, not his master's; this is the view of some who held that the slave owns property. Ishaq said: what was given during the kitabah is returned to its owners.

Tenth: The hadith of Barirah, through its differing chains and wordings, implies that a sale occurred involving Barirah after an earlier kitabah. People differed regarding the sale of a mukatab on account of this. Al-Bukhari titled a chapter "The sale of the mukatab if he consents." Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Dawudi held that it is permitted to sell him for manumission if the mukatab consents to the sale even if he is not incapable, and Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr approved this; Ibn Shihab, Abu al-Zinad and Rabi'ah said likewise, except that they said: because his consent to the sale is an incapacity on his part. Malik, Abu Hanifah and their companions said: the sale of the mukatab is not permitted as long as he is a mukatab until he becomes incapable, and the sale of his kitabah is not permitted in any case; this is the view of al-Shafi'i in Egypt, while in Iraq he said: his sale is permitted, but the sale of his kitabah is not permitted. Malik permitted the sale of the kitabah: if the buyer pays it, he is freed, otherwise he is a slave of the buyer of the kitabah. Abu Hanifah prohibited this because it is a sale involving gharar. Al-Shafi'i's view on this varied between prohibition and permission. A group said: the sale of the mukatab is permitted on condition that he continues in his kitabah; if he pays, he is freed and his walaʼ belongs to the one who bought him, and if he becomes incapable, he is a slave to him. This was said by al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', al-Layth, Ahmad and Abu Thawr. Al-Awza'i said: the mukatab is not sold except for manumission, and it is disliked to sell him before his incapacity; this is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq. Abu 'Umar said: the hadith of Barirah indicates the permissibility of selling the mukatab when he consents to the sale and is not incapable of paying an installment that has fallen due upon him, unlike the view of one who claimed that the sale of

The mukatab (a slave who has contracted to purchase his freedom) may not be sold except when he is unable to pay. Barirah did not report that she had become unable to pay an installment, nor did she say that an installment had fallen due to her, and the Prophet ﷺ did not say to her, "Are you unable, or has an installment fallen due to you?" Had the sale of a mukatab or mukatabah been permissible only upon inability to pay what had fallen due, the Prophet ﷺ would have asked her whether she was unable, and he would not have permitted the purchase until he knew that she was unable, even to pay a single installment that had fallen due to her. In the report of al-Zuhri, she had not paid anything of her kitabah (contractual manumission). I know of no proof on this matter more sound than this hadith of Barirah, and nothing has been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ that contradicts it, nor is there in any of the reports any indication that she was unable.

Those who prohibited the sale of the mukatab relied on several matters. Among them, they said that the kitabah mentioned had not been concluded, and that her saying "I made a kitabah with my family" means that she negotiated with them concerning it, and they fixed its amount and term but did not conclude it. The apparent meaning of the hadiths is contrary to this when their context is considered. It has also been said that Barirah became unable to pay, so she and her family agreed to dissolve the kitabah, and then the sale was valid. However, this can only be upheld according to the view of those who say that the inability of the mukatab does not require the ruling of a judge when the slave and the master agree upon it, since the right does not go beyond the two of them. This is the well-known school of thought. Sahnun said: a ruling of the sultan (ruler) is necessary, and he feared only that the two might collude to abandon the right of Allah, the Exalted.

What indicates the soundness of the view that she was unable is what has been transmitted: that Barirah came to Aishah seeking her help in her kitabah, and she had not paid anything of it. Aishah said to her: "Return to your family; if they wish that I pay your kitabah on your behalf, I will do so." The apparent meaning of this is that all or part of her kitabah became due from her, because nothing of the rights is paid except what has become due to be demanded, and Allah knows best.

These interpretations are the most plausible of what they have, and in them there is a flaw that we have explained. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I know of no proof for one who says that it is not permissible for him to sell the mukatab, except that he says perhaps Barirah was unable." Al-Shafi'i said: "The most apparent of its meanings is that the owner of the mukatab may sell him."

Eleventh issue: When the mukatab pays his kitabah, he is freed, and he does not need a fresh manumission from the master. Likewise, his children who were born to him from his female slave during his kitabah are freed by his freeing and enslaved by his enslavement, because the child of a person from his female slave has the same status as him, by analogy with the free person. Likewise, the child of a mukatabah. If they had a child before the kitabah, that child does not enter into the kitabah except by a condition.

Twelfth issue: The words (and give them of the wealth of Allah which He has given you) are a command to the masters to assist them in the wealth of the kitabah, either by giving them something from what is in their hands, meaning the hands of the masters, or by remitting something of the kitabah wealth. Malik said: something is remitted from the mukatab from the last of his kitabah. Ibn Umar remitted five thousand out of thirty-five thousand. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, considered it good that this should be a quarter of the kitabah. Al-Zahrawi said: this was transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan considered a third of it good. Qatadah said: a tenth of it. Ibn Jubayr said: he remits something from it, without setting a limit, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, and al-Thawri considered it good. Al-Shafi'i said: "Something" is the least thing that falls under the name of "a thing," and the master is compelled to it, and the judge rules concerning it against the heirs if the master dies.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarded this command as recommendation, and he did not see a fixed amount for the remission. Al-Shafi'i relied on the unrestricted form of the command in His words "and give them," and he held that the conjunction of an obligatory matter with a recommended one is known in the Qur'an and the language of the Arabs, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct and giving to relatives﴾ [An-Nahl: 90], and what is similar to it. Ibn al-Arabi said: Ismail ibn Ishaq al-Qadi also mentioned this before him, saying that al-Shafi'i made the giving obligatory and the kitabah non-obligatory, so he made the origin non-obligatory and the branch obligatory, and this has no parallel, so it became a bare claim. If it is said: it is like marriage, which is not obligatory, but once it is concluded its rulings become binding, among them the mut'ah (compensatory gift). We say: according to us, the mut'ah is not obligatory, so there is no point for the followers of al-Shafi'i. Uthman ibn Affan made a kitabah with his slave and swore that he would not remit anything from it... in a long hadith.

I say: al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Buraydah said that the address in His words "and give them" is to all people, that they should give charity to the mukatabin and assist them in ransoming their necks. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the address is to the rulers, that they should give the mukatabin their share from the zakat funds, and this is what His words "and for the slaves" (At-Tawbah: 60) encompass. According to these two views, the master of the mukatab does not have the right to remit anything from his mukatab. The evidence for this is that if he had wanted to remit some of the installments of the kitabah, he would have said: "Remit for them such and such."

Thirteenth issue: If we say that the address is to the masters, then Umar ibn al-Khattab considered that this should be from the first of his installments, hastening to good, fearing that he might not live to see the last of them. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others considered that the remission should be from the last installment. The reason for this is that if he remits from the first installment, the slave may perhaps become unable, and then he and his property return to the master, and so the remission returns to him, and it resembles charity. This is the view of Abdullah ibn Umar and Ali. Mujahid said: he leaves for him from each installment. Ibn al-Arabi said: what is stronger in my view is that it should be at the end, because remission is always in the final parts of debts.

Fourteenth issue: If the mukatab is sold for the purpose of manumission, with his consent after the kitabah, and his seller receives the price, it is not obligatory for him to give the mukatab anything of the price, whether he sold him for manumission or for other than manumission. This is unlike a master to whom a mukatab pays his kitabah, and he gives him something from it, or remits from its last installment an installment or whatever he wishes, in accordance with what Allah commanded in His Book, because the Prophet ﷺ did not command the owners of Barirah to give her anything of what they had received, even though they had sold her for manumission.

Fifteenth issue: They differed concerning the description of the contract of kitabah. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: its description is that the master says to his slave: "I have made a kitabah with you for such and such an amount of wealth, in such and such installments; when you pay it, you are free," or he says to him: "Pay me a thousand in ten installments and you are free." The slave says: "I have accepted," and similar words. Whenever he pays it, he is freed. Likewise, if the slave says: "Make a kitabah with me," and the master says: "I have done so," or "I have made a kitabah with you." Ibn al-Arabi said: this is not binding, because the wording of the Qur'an does not require it, and the situation bears witness to it. If he mentions it, that is good, and if he omits it, it is known and does not need to be stated. The issues of this chapter and its branches are many, and we have mentioned a body of its principles, in which there is sufficiency for one who restricts himself to them, and Allah is the One who grants success in guidance.

Sixteenth issue: Concerning the inheritance of the mukatab, the scholars differed on it in three views. The school of Malik holds that if the mukatab dies and leaves property more than what remains of his kitabah, and he has children who were born during his kitabah, or for whom he made a kitabah, they inherit what remains of the property after the settlement of his kitabah, because their ruling is like his ruling. They are obliged to strive for what remains of his kitabah if he left no property. They are not freed except by his freeing. If he had paid on their behalf, he would not have recovered it from them, because they are freed through him, so they have the better claim to his inheritance, since they are equal to him in all his circumstances.

The second view: his entire kitabah is paid on his behalf from his property, and he is treated as though he had died free, and all his children inherit from him, whether those who were free before his death, or those for whom he made a kitabah, or those who were born during his kitabah, because they are all equal in freedom once their kitabah has been settled on their behalf. This view was transmitted from Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, and among the Successors from Ata', al-Hasan, Tawus and Ibrahim. Fuqaha' of Kufa, Sufyan al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Hasan ibn Salih ibn Hayy, also said this, and Ishaq adopted it.

The third view: if the mukatab dies before he has paid all his kitabah, then he has died a slave, and all the property he leaves behind belongs to his master, and none of his children inherit from him, neither the free ones nor those who were with him in the kitabah, because when he died before paying all his kitabah, he died a slave, and his property belongs to his master, so his manumission after his death is not valid, since it is impossible for a slave to be freed after his death. His children for whom he made a kitabah, or who were born during his kitabah, must strive for the remainder of the kitabah, and the share of his portion is dropped from it for them. If they pay, they are freed, because they were included in it as followers of their father; if they do not pay, they are enslaved. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal also said it, and it is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Zayd ibn Thabit, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Zuhri and Qatadah.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity﴾. It was transmitted from Jabir ibn Abdullah and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy. He had two slave girls, one called Mu'adhah and the other Musaykah, and he would compel them to fornication and beat them for it, seeking wages and the gain of children. They complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and the verse was revealed concerning him and concerning whoever did his deed among the hypocrites. Mu'adhah was the mother of Khawlah, who disputed with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir: a slave girl of Abdullah ibn Ubayy called Musaykah and another called Umaymah, and he used to compel them to fornication, so they complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution," up to His words: "Forgiving, Merciful."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 33–34 (part 4 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿if they desire chastity﴾, refers to the slave-girls. This is because when the slave-girl desires chastity, it is then possible and conceivable that the master may be compelling her, and it is possible to forbid compulsion. But if the slave-girl does not desire chastity, it is not conceivable to say to the master, "Do not compel her," because compulsion cannot be conceived of in her case while she is desirous of fornication. So this is a matter concerning masters and slave-girls in such a state.

Ibn al-'Arabi alluded to this meaning, saying: "God, exalted is He, only mentioned the woman's desire for chastity because that is what depicts compulsion. As for when she herself is eager for fornication, compulsion cannot be conceived of, so grasp this." This consideration escaped many of the exegetes. Some of them said that His saying, "if they desire chastity," refers to the unmarried women (al-ayama). Al-Zajjaj and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, meaning: "And marry the unmarried women and the righteous among your servants, if they desire chastity." And some of them said: this condition in His saying "if they desire" is cancelled (mulgha), and similar to that of what is weak, and God is the Granter of success. That is, the thing that the slave-girl earns by her private part, and the child is enslaved and sold. It was also said: the fornicator used to ransom his child from the one he had fornicated with by a hundred camels, which he would hand over to her master.

﴿And whoever compels them﴾, that is, subdues them, ﴿then indeed God, after their compulsion, is Forgiving﴾ toward them, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them.

Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn Jubayr read "lahunna ghafur" with the addition of "lahunna" (for them).

The discussion of compulsion has already passed in [al-Nahl [see vol. 10, p. 180 and following]], and praise be to God. He, exalted is He, enumerated for the believers His blessings in what He sent down to them of the clear verses [in K: "al-nayyirat", and what He struck of parables], and in it He struck for them parables of the nations that passed away, so that they may be guarded against what those people fell into.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 35 (part 1 of 3):

Allah's words: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth...﴾ [the verse]. Al-nur (light) in the speech of the Arabs means the lights perceived by sight. It is used metaphorically for meanings that are sound and clear, so one says of a speech that it "has light" (kalam lahu nur). From this comes "the clear book" (al-kitab al-munir), and from it the words of the poet:

A lineage as if upon it, from the sun of forenoon, is light, and from the dawn's cleft, a pillar.

People also say: "So-and-so is the light of the land," and "the sun and moon of the age." And he said:

For you are a sun, and the kings are stars.

[This is the first half of a verse by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani from a qasida in praise of al-Nu'man, whose second half is: "When she rises, no star appears among them."]

Another said:

Why did you not choose from among the lands a destination: the moon of the tribes, Khalid ibn Yazid?

Another said:

When Abdullah travels from Marw for a single night, its light and its beauty have departed with him.

It is permissible, then, to say that Allah, the Exalted, has light in the sense of praise, because He brought things into existence, and the light of all things originates from Him, and from Him they proceed. He, glory be to Him, is not one of the perceptible lights, exalted far above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation. Hisham al-Jawaliqi and a group of the Mujassima said: "He is light, not like lights, and a body, not like bodies." All of this is impossible for Allah, the Exalted, by reason and by transmission, as is known in its place in the science of kalam. Moreover, their statement is self-contradictory: their saying "a body" or "light" is a judgment about Him in its literal reality, while their saying "not like lights and not like bodies" negates what they had affirmed of corporeality and light, and that is contradictory. Its verification belongs to the science of kalam. What led them into this were apparent texts they followed, among them this verse, and his saying, peace be upon him, when he rose at night to pray: "O Allah, to You be praise; You are the light of the heavens and the earth." He, peace be upon him, also said when he was asked, "Did you see your Lord?": "I saw light." And other hadiths besides these.

The scholars differed in the interpretation of this verse. It was said: the meaning is that by Him and by His power their lights shine, their affairs are set straight, and their creations stand. The speech here is an approximation for the understanding, as one says: "The king is the light of the people of the land," meaning that by him the order of their affairs and the welfare of the whole are sustained, because his affairs proceed upon the paths of rectitude. So it is a metaphor when said of the king, but it is a pure reality when said of the attributes of Allah, since He is the One who originated the existent things and created the intellect as a guiding light, because the manifestation of existent things through it occurs just as the manifestation of visible things occurs through light. Blessed and exalted is He; there is no lord other than Him. This was the view of Mujahid, al-Zuhri and others. Ibn Arafa said: that is, the One who illuminates the heavens and the earth. Likewise said al-Dahhak and al-Qarazi, as they say: "So-and-so is our helper (ghiyath), that is, our aider," and "So-and-so is my provision (zad), that is, my provider." Jarir said:

You are for us light, rain, protection, and a plant for whoever hopes for your generosity, and moisture.

That is, possessing foliage. Mujahid said: the one who manages the affairs in the heavens and the earth. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya said: the adorner of the heavens with the sun, the moon and the stars, and the adorner of the earth with the prophets, the scholars and the believers. Ibn Abbas and Anas said: the meaning is that Allah is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth. The first interpretation is more comprehensive in its meanings and more sound with respect to the figurative sense, namely the description of His signs which He casts into the heart of the believer, and signs are called light. Allah the Exalted has named His Book light, saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [an-Nisa: 174]. And He named His Prophet light, saying: ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15]. This is because the Book guides and makes clear, and likewise the Messenger. The attribution to Allah, the Exalted, is that He establishes the indication, makes it clear, and sets it down.

The verse may bear another meaning, in which there is no matching of a part of the likeness with a part of the thing likened, but the comparison is made as a whole to a whole. That is, it means: the likeness of the light of Allah, which is His guidance and His perfection of the making of every creature, and His radiant proofs in general, is like this whole light which you yourselves make of this description, which is the most eloquent description of light among men. So the likeness of Allah's light in clarity is like this one, which is your ultimate, O mankind. The niche (mishkah) is the recess in the wall that does not pass through; Ibn Jubayr and the majority of the exegetes said so. It is the most gathering of light, and the lamp within it gives more illumination than it would elsewhere. Its origin is a container into which a thing is placed. The mishkah is a vessel of leather, like a bucket, into which water is cooled, and it is of the form mif'alah, like al-miqra (the bowl from which a guest is fed) and al-misfah (the strainer). The poet said:

As if his two eyes were two niches in a stone, split apart by the beaks of chisels.

[This line is transmitted in another version in Kitab al-Sina'atayn by Abu Hilal al-Askari, where it is attributed to Abu Zubayd. The version there is: "As if his two eyes were in two hollows of a rock, cleft... " The waqab is a hollow in the rock where water gathers; qaydan means split apart; al-manaqir is the singular minqar, an iron tool like an axe with which one chips the rock and other things.]

It was said: the mishkah is the pillar of the lamp in which the wick is. Mujahid said: it is the lamp itself. He said "in a glass" because it is a transparent body, and the lamp within it is brighter than it would be outside glass. The misbah (lamp) is the wick with its fire, that is, in its illumination and light. This may bear two meanings: either that it is so by means of the lamp, or that it is so in itself, by its purity and the excellence of its substance. This second interpretation is more eloquent in the cooperation toward light. Al-Dahhak said: the bright star (al-kawkab al-durri) is Venus. [The phrase] "from the oil of a tree" means the tree's oil, the noun being elided. The blessed tree is the one that is cultivated, and the olive is among the greatest of fruits in growth, and so is the pomegranate. Observation supports this. The verse of Abu Talib lamenting Musafir ibn Abi Amr ibn Umayya ibn Abd Shams:

Would that I knew, Musafir ibn Abi Amr... and "would that" is a phrase the grieving one says.

Blessed is the stranger dead, as the sapling of the pomegranate and the olive are blessed.

It was said: among their blessing is that their branches bear leaves from their base up to their top. Ibn Abbas said: in the olive tree there are benefits: it is used to light lamps, it is a condiment, an ointment, and a tanning agent, and a fuel, burned with its wood and its dregs; there is nothing in it without some benefit, even the ash of it is used to wash silk (al-ibrisam, an arabized word with three forms, meaning silk). It is the first tree that grew in the world, and the first tree that grew after the Flood, and it grows in the dwellings of the prophets and in the holy land. Seventy prophets invoked blessing upon it, among them Ibrahim, and among them Muhammad (ﷺ), for he said: "O Allah, bless the oil and the olive." He said it twice. [In al-Hadith al-Dhahabi/ Musnad al-Darimi, traced back to the Prophet: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."]

The scholars differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither eastern nor western﴾. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah and others said: the eastern is the one that the sun strikes when it rises but not when it sets, because it has a screen. The western is its opposite. Or it is a tree in an open desert, uncovered from the earth, with nothing shielding it from the sun, and this is best for its oil. It is therefore not purely eastern, so as to be called eastern, nor purely western, so as to be called western, but it is both eastern and western. Al-Tabari said, from Ibn Abbas: it is a tree within a grove that surrounds it, so it is uncovered neither from the east nor from the west. Ibn Atiyya said: this statement is not sound from Ibn Abbas, because the fruit with this description would spoil, and that is observed in existence. Al-Hasan said: this tree is not of the trees of this world; it is only a parable that Allah the Exalted struck for His light, and had it been in this world it would have been either eastern or western. Al-Tha'labi: The Qur'an has made clear that it is of the trees of this world, because it is a substitution (badal) for "the tree," and He says "an olive tree." Ibn Zayd said: it is of the trees of Syria, for the trees of Syria are neither eastern nor western, and the trees of Syria are the best of trees, and it is the blessed land. "Eastern" is an attribute of "olive tree," and "neither" does not intervene between the attribute and the thing described; "nor western" is conjoined to it.

Allah's words: ﴿its oil would almost shine even if no fire touched it﴾ is an exaggeration of its excellence, its clarity and its quality.

(نُورٌ عَلى نُورٍ) That is, the light of the lamp, the light of the glass, and the light of the oil gathered together in the niche, so that there is light upon light. These lights were confined within the niche, so that they became as bright as can be. Likewise, the proofs of Allah the Exalted are clear: they are proof after proof and admonition after admonition, such as His sending of the messengers and His sending down of the scriptures, and admonitions that are repeated for one who has sound reasoning. Then the Exalted mentioned His guidance by His light for whomever He wills among His servants, and He mentioned His favour to the servants in coining parables, so that they may take heed and reflect in a way that leads to faith.

Abdullah ibn Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a and Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "Allahu nur" with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the waw. The commentators differed about the antecedent of the pronoun in "nurihi" (His light). Ka'b al-Ahbar and Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning the likeness of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn al-Anbari said: "Allahu nuru as-samawati wal-ard" (Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth) is a good place to pause (waqf hasan), and then one begins with "mathalu nurihi ka-mishkatin fiha misbah" (the likeness of His light is as a niche in which is a lamp) in the sense of the light of Muhammad (ﷺ). Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Jubayr also, and al-Dahhak said: it refers to the believers. In the recitation of Ubayy it is "mathalu nuri al-mu'minin" (the likeness of the light of the believers). It is also narrated that in his recitation it is "mathalu nuri al-mu'min" (the likeness of the light of the believer), and it is narrated that in it is "mathalu nuri man amana bihi" (the likeness of the light of one who believed in Him). Al-Hasan said: it refers to the Qur'an and faith. Ibn Atiyya said: on these views one stops at His saying "wal-ard" (and the earth).

Ibn Atiyya said: in these views the pronoun refers to something not previously mentioned, and there is a comparison of a part of the likeness with a part of the thing likened. For the one who says that the thing likened is Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the view of Ka'b al-Ahbar, the messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the niche or his chest, the lamp is prophethood and what is connected to it of his conduct [in another reading, "his knowledge"] and his guidance, the glass is his heart, the blessed tree is the revelation, and the angels are the messengers of Allah to him, and the means connected to him. The oil is the proofs, the evidences, and the signs contained in the revelation. And for the one who says that the thing likened is the believer, which is the view of Ubayy, the niche is his chest, the lamp is faith and knowledge, the glass is his heart, and its oil is the proofs and wisdom contained in it. Ubayy said: he, in the best condition, walks among people like a living man walking among the graves of the dead. And for the one who says that the thing likened is the Qur'an and faith, the sense of the speech is: the likeness of His light, which is faith in the chest of the believer, in his heart, is like a niche, that is, like this sentence. This view is not a comparison in the same way as the first two, because the niche does not correspond to faith.

A group said: the pronoun in "nurihi" refers to Allah the Exalted. This is the view of Ibn Abbas as mentioned by al-Tha'labi, al-Mawardi and al-Mahdawi, and its meaning has been mentioned previously. On this view one does not stop at "al-ard." Al-Mahdawi said: the "ha" is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the sense is: Allah is the guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth; the likeness of His guidance in the hearts of the believers is as a niche. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. Likewise Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Hasan said that the "ha" is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud used to recite it: "mathalu nurihi fi qalbi al-mu'min ka-mishkatin" (the likeness of His light in the heart of the believer is as a niche). Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: as for others than these two, they did not recite it in this way in the revelation, though they agreed with them in interpretation that this is the light of the believer's heart, and its confirmation in another verse is His saying: ﴿Is one whose chest Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar 39:22]. The earlier scholars argued: it is not permissible for the "ha" to be for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because the light of Allah has no limit.

Al-Kisa'i, as narrated from him by Abu Umar al-Duri, inclined the alif of "mishkat" and pronounced the kaf before it with a kasra. Nasr ibn Asim read "zujajatin" with a fatha on the zay, and "al-zujajatu" likewise; this is a dialectal form.

Ibn Amir and Hafs from Asim read "durriyyun" with a damma on the dal and a shadda on the ya'. This reading has two possible explanations: either the star is ascribed to pearl (durr) because of its whiteness and clarity, or its original form is "durri'un" with a hamza, on the pattern fu'ayyil from the verb "daraʾa" meaning to repel, and the hamza was softened. The great stars whose names are unknown are called "al-darari" without a hamza, so perhaps they softened the hamza, and the origin is from "dar'" which is repelling. Hamza and Abu Bakr from Asim read "durri'un" with the hamza and a long vowel, which is fu'ayyil from "dar'," in the sense that some of its light repels others. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Amr read "durri'un" with a kasra on the dal and the hamza, from "dar'" and "daf'" (repelling), like "sikkir" and "fisiq" (intensive forms). Sibawayh said: that is, some of its light repels other parts of its light because of its brilliance.

Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubayd strongly criticised the reading of Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i, because he interpreted it from "daraʾtu" meaning "I repelled," that is, a star moving from horizon to horizon. If the interpretation is as he interpreted, the speech would have no benefit, and this star would have no distinction over most stars. Do you not see that one does not say "a human being of the children of Adam came to me"? One should not interpret for men like Abu Amr and al-Kisa'i, with their knowledge and eminence, such a distant interpretation. Rather, the interpretation for them is what is narrated from Muhammad ibn Yazid, that their meaning is: a star moving forcefully with light, as one says "indara'a al-hariq" (the fire spread) if it spread. This is a sound interpretation of this reading. Sa'id ibn Mas'ada related that one says: "dara'a al-kawkabu bi-daw'ihi" (the star repelled with its light) when its light extended and rose. Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "daraʾa 'alayna fulan yadraʾu duru'an" means he appeared suddenly. From this comes "kawkabun durri'un," on the pattern fi'il, like "sikkir" and "khimmir," because of the intensity of its blazing and its shining. The star has indeed "daraʾa" (appeared) "duru'an." Abu Amr ibn al-Ala said: I asked a man from Sa'd ibn Bakr, of the people of Dhat Irq: "What do you call this large star?" He said: "al-durri." He was one of the most eloquent of people.

Al-Nahhas said: as for the reading of Hamza, all the linguists said it is a solecism and not permissible, because there is no noun in the speech of the Arabs on the pattern fi'il (fu'ayyil). Abu Ubayd objected to this and argued for Hamza, saying: it is not fi'il but fu'ul, like "subbuh," and the waw was changed to ya', as they said "utiy" (from "utuww"). Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: this objection and argument is among the greatest and most severe errors, because this is absolutely impermissible; and if what he said were permissible, one would say "subbih" for "subbuh," and no one says that. "Utiy" is not of this type, and the difference between them is clear and evident, because "utiy" is either the plural of "ati" (rebellious), in which case the substitution is obligatory, since plurals are subject to change, and the waw is not a final radical in nouns when preceded by a damma. Since before this waw there is a sakin (quiescent letter) and before the sakin there is a damma, and the sakin is not a strong barrier, a kasra was substituted for the damma and the waw was changed to ya'. And if "utiy" is singular, then the waw would be more appropriate, and it would be permissible to change it because it is final; but the waw in fu'ul is not final, so it may not be changed.

Al-Jawhari said: Abu Ubayd said: if you put a damma on the dal you say "durriyyun," which is ascribed to pearl (durr), on the pattern fu'liyy, and you do not put a hamza on it, because there is no fu'ayyil in the speech of the Arabs. As for the readers who put a hamza, they meant fu'ul like "subbuh," and it was found heavy because of the many dammas, so part of it was returned to kasra. Al-Akhfash related from some people: "duri'un" from "daraʾtuhu" (I repelled it), with the hamza, and he made it on the pattern fa'\u0000'ayyil with an open first letter. He said: that is from its brilliance. Al-Tha'labi said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Abu Raja' read "durri'un" with a fatha on the dal and the hamza. Abu Hatim said: this is an error, because there is no fa'ayyil in the speech, and if it is authentically transmitted from them, then they are a proof.

(يُوقَدُ) Shayba, Nafi, Ayyub, Sallam, Ibn Amir, the people of Syria, and Hafs read "yuqadu" with a damma on the ya', a light qaf, and a damma on the dal. Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Abu Ja'far, and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala al-Basri read "tawaqqada" with a fatha on all its letters and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Hatim and Abu Ubayd preferred this. Al-Nahhas said: these two readings are close in meaning, because both refer to the lamp, and it is more fitting for this description, because it is what gives light and shines, while the glass is only its container. "Tawaqqada" is the past tense of "tawaqqada yatawaqqadu," and "yuqadu" is the future of "aqada yuqidu." Nasr ibn Asim read "tuqadu," and the original form in his reading is "tatawaqqadu," with one of the two taʾs deleted because the other indicates it. The Kufans read "tuqadu" with a taʾ, meaning the glass. These two readings are based on the feminine gender of the glass.

(مِنْ شَجَرَةٍ مُبارَكَةٍ زَيْتُونَةٍ لَا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلا غَرْبِيَّةٍ) The discussion of this has already been given.

(يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نارٌ نُورٌ عَلى نُورٍ) This is read with the feminine form for "nar" (fire). Abu Ubayd claimed that he knew of no other reading than this. Abu Hatim related that al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik, from Ibn Abbas, that he read: "wa-law lam tamsashu nar" with a ya'. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: the masculine form is because the feminine here is not real, and this is the way with the feminine in his view.

Ibn Umar said: the niche is the interior of Muhammad (ﷺ), the glass is his heart, and the lamp is the light which Allah the Exalted placed in his heart, "yuqadu min shajaratin mubarakatin" (it is kindled from a blessed tree), that is, its origin is from Abraham, and he is its tree. Allah the Exalted kindled in the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) the light as He placed it in the heart of Abraham (peace be upon him). Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the niche is Abraham, the glass is Ishmael, and the lamp is Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all. Allah called him a lamp just as He called him a lamp-light (siraj), when He said: ﴿And as one who calls to Allah by His permission, and as a shining lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:46]. It is kindled from a blessed tree, which is Adam (peace be upon him); blessing was placed in his offspring, and many prophets and saints came from him. It was also said: the tree is Abraham (peace be upon him), whom Allah called blessed because most of the prophets were from his loins.

(لَا شَرْقِيَّةٍ وَلا غَرْبِيَّةٍ) That is, he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but was a hanif, a Muslim. He said this because the Jews pray facing the west, before sunset, and the Christians pray facing the east.

(يَكادُ زَيْتُها يُضِيءُ) That is, the excellent qualities of Muhammad (ﷺ) almost appear to people before Allah the Exalted revealed to him.

Light upon light: a prophet from the descendants of a prophet. Al-Dahhak said: He likened ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib to the *mishkāt* (niche) and ʿAbd Allāh to the *zujājah* (glass lamp chimney), and the Prophet ﷺ to the *miṣbāḥ* (lamp) that was in their hearts. So he inherited prophethood from Abraham. "From a blessed tree": that is, the tree of piety, good pleasure, and the lineage of guidance and faith. It is a tree whose root is prophethood, whose branch is *muruwwah* (manliness and integrity), whose boughs are *tanzīl* (revelation), whose leaves are *ta'wīl* (interpretation), and whose attendants are Gabriel and Michael.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī said: "It is a strange matter that some jurists said this is a parable which God, exalted is He, struck for Abraham, Muhammad, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and his son ʿAbd Allāh. The *mishkāt* is the *kuwwa* (niche) in the language of Abyssinia. So ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib is likened to the *mishkāt*, in which is the *qindīl* (lamp), which is the *zujājah* (glass). ʿAbd Allāh is likened to the *qindīl*, which is the *zujājah*. Muhammad is like the *miṣbāḥ*, meaning from their loins, and it is as if he were a shining star, which is Jupiter." "Kindled from a blessed tree": meaning the inheritance of prophethood from Abraham, peace be upon him, is the blessed tree, meaning the *ḥanīfiyyah* (pure monotheism), neither eastern nor western, neither Jewish nor Christian. "Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it": he says, Abraham would almost speak with inspiration before it was revealed to him. "Light upon light": Abraham, then Muhammad ﷺ.

Al-Qāḍī said: "All of this is a departure from the apparent meaning, and there is no objection to a person extending himself in interpreting a parable."

I say: The same applies to all the other opinions, because they are not connected to the verse, except the first opinion. The verse means that this is a parable God, exalted is He, struck for His light. It is not possible to strike a parable for His exalted light to alert His creation except through some of His creation, because creatures, due to their limitations, understand only through themselves and from themselves. Had it not been so, none would know God except God alone. This was said by Ibn al-ʿArabī.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: This is a parable of God's light and His guidance in the heart of the believer, as pure oil almost glows before fire touches it. If fire touches it, its light increases. Likewise, the heart of the believer almost acts upon guidance before knowledge comes to it. When knowledge comes to it, guidance is increased to guidance upon guidance, and light upon light, like the saying of Abraham before knowledge reached him: ﴿This is my lord﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 25], before anyone informed him that he had a Lord. When God informed him that He was his Lord, his guidance increased. ﴿His Lord said to him: "Submit." He said: "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:131].

Whoever said this is a parable of the Qur'an in the heart of the believer said: Just as this lamp is used for light and does not diminish, so the Qur'an is used for guidance and does not diminish. So the lamp is the Qur'an, the glass is the heart of the believer, the niche is his tongue and understanding, and the blessed tree is the tree of revelation.

﴿Its oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it﴾: the proofs of the Qur'an almost become clear even if it were not recited.

﴿Light upon light﴾: meaning the Qur'an is a light from God, exalted is He, for His creation, along with the proofs and signs which He established for them before the revelation of the Qur'an. Thus they increased in light upon light.

Then He informed that this mentioned light is rare, and that none attains it except those whom God wills to guide. So He said: ﴿God guides to His light whom He wills. And God presents parables for people﴾, meaning He clarifies the likenesses, bringing them near to understanding.

﴿And God is Knowing of all things﴾, meaning of the one who is guided and the one who is astray.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Jews said: "O Muhammad, how does God's light pass through the sky?" So God, exalted is He, struck this parable for His light.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 1 of 5):**

Allah the Exalted says:
﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; He is exalted therein morning and evening. Men whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah and establishing prayer and giving zakah﴾. In it there are nineteen issues:

The first: His saying, ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾. The ba' in "buyūt" (bayūt) may be pronounced with a damma or a kasra, and this has already been discussed [[See vol. 2, p. 346.]].

Scholars differed about the fa' (i.e., the word "fī") in His saying "fī". It is said that it is connected to "miṣbāḥ" (lamp). It is also said that it is connected to "yusabbiḥu lahu" (glorifies Him), and according to this interpretation one stops at "ʿAlīm" (All-Knowing).

Ibn al-Anbari said: I heard Abu al-ʿAbbas say: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) for the lamp, the glass and the star, as if he said: "and it is in houses."

And al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Muhammad ibn ʿAli said: "fī buyūtin" is separate, as if he is saying: Allah is in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised. And accordingly, reports have come: "Whoever sits in the mosque, he sits with his Lord."

Likewise what came in a report, related from the Torah: "When the believer walks to the mosque, Allah, blessed is His name, says: My servant has visited Me, and it is incumbent upon Me to host him, and I will not be content to host him with anything less than Paradise."

Ibn al-Anbari said: If "fī" is connected to "yusabbiḥu," or raising for "al-rijāl," it is good to stop at His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

And al-Rummani said: it is connected to "yūqadu," and accordingly one does not stop at "ʿAlīm."

If it is said: what is the explanation when the houses are connected to "yūqadu," regarding the singular "miṣbāḥ" and "mishkāt" and the plural "buyūt"? There would not be one niche except in one house.

It is said: this is from the shifting mode of address (al-khiṭāb al-mutalawwin), which begins with the singular and ends with the plural, like His saying ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 147 onward.]] [al-Ṭalāq: 1], and similar.

It is also said: it returns to each one of the houses.

It is also said: it is like His saying ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 304.]] [Nūḥ: 16], whereas it is in only one of them.

People differed about the meaning of "the houses" here, into five views:

The first: they are the mosques specifically dedicated to Allah the Exalted for worship, and they give light to the people of heaven as the stars give light to the people of earth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan.

The second: they are the houses of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), also from al-Hasan.

The third: they are the houses of the Prophet ﷺ, also from Mujahid.

The fourth: they are all the houses, said by ʿIkrimah.

His saying "in which He is glorified morning and evening" strengthens the view that they are the mosques.

A fifth view: they are the four mosques which none built except a prophet: the Kaʿbah, the house of Jericho (Arīḥā), the Mosque of Madinah and the Mosque of Quba, said by Ibn Buraydah.

This has already been mentioned in "Barā'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 260.]].

I say: the most apparent is the first view, due to what Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who said:
"Whoever loves Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, let him love me; and whoever loves me, let him love my companions; and whoever loves my companions, let him love the Qur'an; and whoever loves the Qur'an, let him love the mosques, for they are the courtyards of Allah and His houses. Allah has permitted their raising and blessed them. They are blessed and their people are blessed; they are protected and their people are protected. They are in their prayers, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is in their needs; they are in their mosques and Allah is behind them."

The second: His saying "Allah has permitted to be raised" (adhina Allahu an turfa'a). "Adhina" means He commanded and decreed. The true meaning of permission (idhn) is knowledge and enablement without prohibition; if it is accompanied by command and urging, it is stronger.

"Turfa'a" (is raised): it is said its meaning is built and elevated, said by Mujahid and ʿIkrimah.

From this is His saying ﴿And when Abraham raised the foundations of the House﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 120.]] [al-Baqarah: 127]. And He ﷺ said: "Whoever builds a mosque from his wealth, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise."

There are many hadiths in this meaning urging the building of mosques.

Al-Hasan al-Basri and others said: the meaning of "turfa'a" is that it is magnified, its status is raised, and it is purified from impurities and filth. In a hadith: "The mosque shrinks from impurity as the skin shrinks from fire."

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "Whoever removes harm from the mosque, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise."

It is also related from ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to make mosques in neighborhoods, and that they be purified and perfumed.

The third: If we say the meaning is their construction, is it then to be decorated and carved?

Scholars differed on this: some disliked it and others permitted it.

Hammad ibn Salamah related from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Anas, and Qatadah from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Hour will not come until people boast about mosques." Abu Dawud recorded it.

In al-Bukhari, Anas said: "They will boast about them, then they will not frequent them except a little." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You will surely decorate them as the Jews and Christians decorated [their places of worship]."

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah related in Nawadir al-Usul from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you decorate your mosques and adorn your Qur'ans, then destruction is upon you."

Those who permitted it argued that it contains the magnification of mosques, and Allah commanded their magnification in His saying "in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised," meaning magnified.

It is related from ʿUthman that he built the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ with teak (sāj) [[Sāj: a very large tree that does not grow in the land of India; a strong wood which the earth hardly decays.]] and beautified it.

Abu Hanifah said: there is no harm in decorating mosques with gold leaf.

It is related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz that he decorated the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ and exerted himself in its construction and adornment, during his governorship before his caliphate, and no one objected to this.

It is mentioned that al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik spent on the construction and adornment of the Mosque of Damascus the equivalent of the land tax of Syria three times.

And it is related that Solomon, son of David, peace be upon them both, built the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis and exerted himself in its adornment.

The fourth: From what mosques must be protected and kept clean of are foul odors, evil speech, and other things, as we will explain, and this is part of their magnification.

It is authentically narrated from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said during the Battle of Tabuk: "Whoever eats of this tree—meaning garlic—let him not approach the mosques."

In the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Whoever eats of this herb—garlic." And at another time he said: "Whoever eats onions, garlic and leeks, let him not approach our mosque, for the angels are harmed by what harms the children of Adam."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his sermon: "Then, O people, you eat two plants, and I do not regard them except as foul: these are onion and garlic. I have seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he found their smell on a man in the mosque, order that he be taken out to al-Baqiʿ. Whoever eats them, let him kill their smell by cooking them." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih.

The scholars said: if the reason for expelling him from the mosque is that he is harmed by it, then by analogy, anyone whose neighbors in the mosque are harmed by him—by being sharp-tongued and abusive toward them, or having a foul smell that does not leave him due to his poor trade, or a harmful defect such as leprosy and the like—

and whatever harms people, they have the right to expel it as long as the cause is present in it, until it disappears.

Likewise, one avoids the gathering of people wherever it is for prayer or other things, such as gatherings of knowledge, feasts and similar, from eating garlic and what is in its meaning, of what has an offensive smell that harms people.

For this reason he combined onion, garlic and leeks, and informed that these are things by which one is harmed.

Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I witnessed our shaykh Abu ʿUmar Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him, issue a ruling regarding a man whose neighbors complained about him and agreed that he harmed them in the mosque with his tongue and hand. It was consulted about him, and he ruled that he be expelled from the mosque and kept away from it, and that he not attend the prayer with them, since there was no way, given his madness and aggression, to be safe from him. One day I discussed his affair with him, demanded evidence for what he had ruled, and debated the matter with him. He cited the hadith about garlic and said: "In my view, his harm is greater than eating garlic, and his companion is prevented from attending congregation in the mosque."

I say: In the transmitted reports (al-athar al-mursalah) it says: "A man may tell a lie, and the angel moves away from the stench of his breath."

Accordingly, whoever is known for lying and for speaking falsehood is expelled, for that causes harm.

The fifth: Most scholars hold that all mosques are equal, based on the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.

Some of them said: the prohibition was specifically about the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because of Jibril, peace be upon him, and his descent in it, and because of his saying in the hadith of Jabir: "let him not approach our mosque."

The first view is more sound, because he mentioned the attribute in the ruling, namely mosquehood, and mentioning an attribute in a ruling is a causal indication.

Al-Tha'labi related with his chain from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will come with the mosques of the world as if they were white she-camels whose legs are of ambergris, whose necks are of saffron, whose heads are of musk, and whose reins are of green chrysolite. Their riders are the muezzins who lead them, their imams drive them, and their worshippers hold on to them. They will pass through the open plains of the Resurrection like a flash of lightning. The people of the assembly will say: 'These are noble angels and sent prophets!' It will be called out: 'These are not angels nor prophets, but they are the people of the mosques and those who guard the prayers from the community of Muhammad ﷺ.'"

In the revelation: ﴿Only he who believes in Allah builds up the mosques of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 90.]] [al-Tawbah: 18]. This is general for every mosque.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosque, bear witness that he is a believer." Indeed Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Only he who believes in Allah and the Last Day builds up the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. This has already been mentioned.

The sixth: Mosques are also to be protected from buying and selling and all occupations, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to the man who called out about the red camel [[That is, whoever finds my lost camel, the red one, and calls me to it.]]: "May you not find it. Mosques were only built for what they were built for."

Muslim recorded it from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Buraydah from his father, that when the Prophet ﷺ finished the prayer, a man stood and said: "Who called out about the red camel?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "May you not find it. Mosques were only built for what they were built for."

This indicates that the original principle is that nothing other than prayers, remembrance of Allah and recitation of the Qur'an is to be done in the mosque.

Likewise it came explained in a hadith from Anas, who said: While we were in the mosque with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a Bedouin came and began to urinate in the mosque. The companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Stop! Stop!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not interrupt him; leave him." So they left him until he finished urinating. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and said to him:

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 2 of 5):**

"Indeed, these mosques are not fit for any of this urine or filth; they are only for the remembrance of God, prayer, and the recitation of the Qur'an."
Or as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said.
He said:
He ordered a man from the people, and he came with a bucket of water and poured it [[al-shann: pouring that is intermittent, i.e., sprinkling it over the spot in scattered drops]] over it.
Muslim recorded it.
And among what indicates this from the Book is the saying of the Truth (God): "And His name is mentioned therein."
And his saying (ﷺ) to Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami:
"Indeed, these mosques [[In Sahih Muslim: "Indeed, this prayer..."]] are not fit for any of the speech of people; they are only for glorification (tasbih), magnification (takbir), and the recitation of the Qur'an."
Or as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said.
The hadith in its entirety was recorded by Muslim in his Sahih, and that is sufficient for you. And Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) heard the voice of a man in the mosque and said:
"What is this voice? Do you know where you are?"
Khalaf ibn Ayyub was sitting in his mosque, and his servant came to him asking him about something. He stood up, left the mosque, and answered him. He was asked about that, and he said:
"I have not spoken in the mosque with worldly speech since such-and-such time, so I disliked speaking today."

The Seventh: al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he forbade reciting poetry in the mosque, and buying and selling in it, and that people form circles on Friday before the prayer. He said: "And on this subject there are reports from Buraida, Jabir, and Anas. The hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr is a hasan hadith." Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) said: "I saw Muhammad [[In al-Tirmidhi: "Ahmad"]] and Ishaq, and he mentioned others besides them, arguing with the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb." And a group of the people of knowledge disliked buying and selling in the mosque, and Ahmad and Ishaq held this view. It is related that Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, came upon a people buying and selling in the mosque, so he made his garment into a whip [[al-mikhraq: a cloth wrapped up and used to strike children with, one against another]], then began to chase them, striking them and saying: "O sons of vipers! You have taken the mosques of God as marketplaces! This is the market of the Hereafter."

I say: Some of our companions disliked teaching children in mosques, and considered it to be a form of buying and selling. This applies when it is done for a wage. If it were without a wage, it would still be prohibited for another reason, namely that children do not guard themselves against filth and dirt, which leads to the mosques not being kept clean, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that they be cleaned and perfumed.
