It was also said: they will be turned over on the embers of Hell, as in the saying of Allah: "The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire" [al-Ahzab: 66], and "We will turn their hearts and their eyes" [al-An'am: 110], according to those who understand the meaning as their being turned over on the flames of the Fire. It was also said: they will be turned by being scorched by the Fire once and burned to ripeness another time. It was also said: the turning of the hearts is their throbbing (wajib), and the turning of the eyes is looking with them toward the directions of terrors.

To reward them with the best of what they did: He mentioned the reward for good deeds and did not mention the reward for evil deeds, although He does recompense for them, for two reasons. First, the verse is an encouragement, so it confined itself to mentioning the desire. Second, it describes a people among whom major sins do not occur, so their minor sins are forgiven.

And increase them from His bounty: this may have two meanings. First, what He multiplies of a good deed to ten times its like. Second, what He bestows out of grace without any recompense.

And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning: that is, without calling him to account for what He gave him, since His giving has no end. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the building of the Mosque of Quba. ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha attended and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has the one who builds mosques prospered?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha." He said: "And prayed in them standing and sitting?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha." He said: "And did not spend the night except prostrating to Allah?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha. Refrain from saj' (rhymed prose, a rhythmic style of speech), for no servant has been given anything worse than fluency of the tongue."

Mentioned by al-Mawardi.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 1 of 5):**

Allah the Exalted says:
﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; He is exalted therein morning and evening. Men whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah and establishing prayer and giving zakah﴾. In it there are nineteen issues:

The first: His saying, ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾. The ba' in "buyūt" (bayūt) may be pronounced with a damma or a kasra, and this has already been discussed [[See vol. 2, p. 346.]].

Scholars differed about the fa' (i.e., the word "fī") in His saying "fī". It is said that it is connected to "miṣbāḥ" (lamp). It is also said that it is connected to "yusabbiḥu lahu" (glorifies Him), and according to this interpretation one stops at "ʿAlīm" (All-Knowing).

Ibn al-Anbari said: I heard Abu al-ʿAbbas say: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) for the lamp, the glass and the star, as if he said: "and it is in houses."

And al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Muhammad ibn ʿAli said: "fī buyūtin" is separate, as if he is saying: Allah is in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised. And accordingly, reports have come: "Whoever sits in the mosque, he sits with his Lord."

Likewise what came in a report, related from the Torah: "When the believer walks to the mosque, Allah, blessed is His name, says: My servant has visited Me, and it is incumbent upon Me to host him, and I will not be content to host him with anything less than Paradise."

Ibn al-Anbari said: If "fī" is connected to "yusabbiḥu," or raising for "al-rijāl," it is good to stop at His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

And al-Rummani said: it is connected to "yūqadu," and accordingly one does not stop at "ʿAlīm."

If it is said: what is the explanation when the houses are connected to "yūqadu," regarding the singular "miṣbāḥ" and "mishkāt" and the plural "buyūt"? There would not be one niche except in one house.

It is said: this is from the shifting mode of address (al-khiṭāb al-mutalawwin), which begins with the singular and ends with the plural, like His saying ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 147 onward.]] [al-Ṭalāq: 1], and similar.

It is also said: it returns to each one of the houses.

It is also said: it is like His saying ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 304.]] [Nūḥ: 16], whereas it is in only one of them.

People differed about the meaning of "the houses" here, into five views:

The first: they are the mosques specifically dedicated to Allah the Exalted for worship, and they give light to the people of heaven as the stars give light to the people of earth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan.

The second: they are the houses of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), also from al-Hasan.

The third: they are the houses of the Prophet ﷺ, also from Mujahid.

The fourth: they are all the houses, said by ʿIkrimah.

His saying "in which He is glorified morning and evening" strengthens the view that they are the mosques.

A fifth view: they are the four mosques which none built except a prophet: the Kaʿbah, the house of Jericho (Arīḥā), the Mosque of Madinah and the Mosque of Quba, said by Ibn Buraydah.

This has already been mentioned in "Barā'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 260.]].

I say: the most apparent is the first view, due to what Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who said:
"Whoever loves Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, let him love me; and whoever loves me, let him love my companions; and whoever loves my companions, let him love the Qur'an; and whoever loves the Qur'an, let him love the mosques, for they are the courtyards of Allah and His houses. Allah has permitted their raising and blessed them. They are blessed and their people are blessed; they are protected and their people are protected. They are in their prayers, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is in their needs; they are in their mosques and Allah is behind them."

The second: His saying "Allah has permitted to be raised" (adhina Allahu an turfa'a). "Adhina" means He commanded and decreed. The true meaning of permission (idhn) is knowledge and enablement without prohibition; if it is accompanied by command and urging, it is stronger.

"Turfa'a" (is raised): it is said its meaning is built and elevated, said by Mujahid and ʿIkrimah.

From this is His saying ﴿And when Abraham raised the foundations of the House﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 120.]] [al-Baqarah: 127]. And He ﷺ said: "Whoever builds a mosque from his wealth, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise."

There are many hadiths in this meaning urging the building of mosques.

Al-Hasan al-Basri and others said: the meaning of "turfa'a" is that it is magnified, its status is raised, and it is purified from impurities and filth. In a hadith: "The mosque shrinks from impurity as the skin shrinks from fire."

Ibn Majah related in his Sunan from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah said: "Whoever removes harm from the mosque, Allah builds for him a house in Paradise."

It is also related from ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to make mosques in neighborhoods, and that they be purified and perfumed.

The third: If we say the meaning is their construction, is it then to be decorated and carved?

Scholars differed on this: some disliked it and others permitted it.

Hammad ibn Salamah related from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Anas, and Qatadah from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Hour will not come until people boast about mosques." Abu Dawud recorded it.

In al-Bukhari, Anas said: "They will boast about them, then they will not frequent them except a little." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You will surely decorate them as the Jews and Christians decorated [their places of worship]."

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah related in Nawadir al-Usul from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you decorate your mosques and adorn your Qur'ans, then destruction is upon you."

Those who permitted it argued that it contains the magnification of mosques, and Allah commanded their magnification in His saying "in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised," meaning magnified.

It is related from ʿUthman that he built the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ with teak (sāj) [[Sāj: a very large tree that does not grow in the land of India; a strong wood which the earth hardly decays.]] and beautified it.

Abu Hanifah said: there is no harm in decorating mosques with gold leaf.

It is related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz that he decorated the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ and exerted himself in its construction and adornment, during his governorship before his caliphate, and no one objected to this.

It is mentioned that al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik spent on the construction and adornment of the Mosque of Damascus the equivalent of the land tax of Syria three times.

And it is related that Solomon, son of David, peace be upon them both, built the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis and exerted himself in its adornment.

The fourth: From what mosques must be protected and kept clean of are foul odors, evil speech, and other things, as we will explain, and this is part of their magnification.

It is authentically narrated from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said during the Battle of Tabuk: "Whoever eats of this tree—meaning garlic—let him not approach the mosques."

In the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Whoever eats of this herb—garlic." And at another time he said: "Whoever eats onions, garlic and leeks, let him not approach our mosque, for the angels are harmed by what harms the children of Adam."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his sermon: "Then, O people, you eat two plants, and I do not regard them except as foul: these are onion and garlic. I have seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he found their smell on a man in the mosque, order that he be taken out to al-Baqiʿ. Whoever eats them, let him kill their smell by cooking them." Muslim recorded it in his Sahih.

The scholars said: if the reason for expelling him from the mosque is that he is harmed by it, then by analogy, anyone whose neighbors in the mosque are harmed by him—by being sharp-tongued and abusive toward them, or having a foul smell that does not leave him due to his poor trade, or a harmful defect such as leprosy and the like—

and whatever harms people, they have the right to expel it as long as the cause is present in it, until it disappears.

Likewise, one avoids the gathering of people wherever it is for prayer or other things, such as gatherings of knowledge, feasts and similar, from eating garlic and what is in its meaning, of what has an offensive smell that harms people.

For this reason he combined onion, garlic and leeks, and informed that these are things by which one is harmed.

Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: I witnessed our shaykh Abu ʿUmar Ahmad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him, issue a ruling regarding a man whose neighbors complained about him and agreed that he harmed them in the mosque with his tongue and hand. It was consulted about him, and he ruled that he be expelled from the mosque and kept away from it, and that he not attend the prayer with them, since there was no way, given his madness and aggression, to be safe from him. One day I discussed his affair with him, demanded evidence for what he had ruled, and debated the matter with him. He cited the hadith about garlic and said: "In my view, his harm is greater than eating garlic, and his companion is prevented from attending congregation in the mosque."

I say: In the transmitted reports (al-athar al-mursalah) it says: "A man may tell a lie, and the angel moves away from the stench of his breath."

Accordingly, whoever is known for lying and for speaking falsehood is expelled, for that causes harm.

The fifth: Most scholars hold that all mosques are equal, based on the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.

Some of them said: the prohibition was specifically about the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because of Jibril, peace be upon him, and his descent in it, and because of his saying in the hadith of Jabir: "let him not approach our mosque."

The first view is more sound, because he mentioned the attribute in the ruling, namely mosquehood, and mentioning an attribute in a ruling is a causal indication.

Al-Tha'labi related with his chain from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will come with the mosques of the world as if they were white she-camels whose legs are of ambergris, whose necks are of saffron, whose heads are of musk, and whose reins are of green chrysolite. Their riders are the muezzins who lead them, their imams drive them, and their worshippers hold on to them. They will pass through the open plains of the Resurrection like a flash of lightning. The people of the assembly will say: 'These are noble angels and sent prophets!' It will be called out: 'These are not angels nor prophets, but they are the people of the mosques and those who guard the prayers from the community of Muhammad ﷺ.'"

In the revelation: ﴿Only he who believes in Allah builds up the mosques of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 90.]] [al-Tawbah: 18]. This is general for every mosque.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosque, bear witness that he is a believer." Indeed Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Only he who believes in Allah and the Last Day builds up the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. This has already been mentioned.

The sixth: Mosques are also to be protected from buying and selling and all occupations, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to the man who called out about the red camel [[That is, whoever finds my lost camel, the red one, and calls me to it.]]: "May you not find it. Mosques were only built for what they were built for."

Muslim recorded it from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Buraydah from his father, that when the Prophet ﷺ finished the prayer, a man stood and said: "Who called out about the red camel?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "May you not find it. Mosques were only built for what they were built for."

This indicates that the original principle is that nothing other than prayers, remembrance of Allah and recitation of the Qur'an is to be done in the mosque.

Likewise it came explained in a hadith from Anas, who said: While we were in the mosque with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a Bedouin came and began to urinate in the mosque. The companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Stop! Stop!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not interrupt him; leave him." So they left him until he finished urinating. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and said to him:

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 2 of 5):**

"Indeed, these mosques are not fit for any of this urine or filth; they are only for the remembrance of God, prayer, and the recitation of the Qur'an."
Or as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said.
He said:
He ordered a man from the people, and he came with a bucket of water and poured it [[al-shann: pouring that is intermittent, i.e., sprinkling it over the spot in scattered drops]] over it.
Muslim recorded it.
And among what indicates this from the Book is the saying of the Truth (God): "And His name is mentioned therein."
And his saying (ﷺ) to Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami:
"Indeed, these mosques [[In Sahih Muslim: "Indeed, this prayer..."]] are not fit for any of the speech of people; they are only for glorification (tasbih), magnification (takbir), and the recitation of the Qur'an."
Or as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said.
The hadith in its entirety was recorded by Muslim in his Sahih, and that is sufficient for you. And Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) heard the voice of a man in the mosque and said:
"What is this voice? Do you know where you are?"
Khalaf ibn Ayyub was sitting in his mosque, and his servant came to him asking him about something. He stood up, left the mosque, and answered him. He was asked about that, and he said:
"I have not spoken in the mosque with worldly speech since such-and-such time, so I disliked speaking today."

The Seventh: al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he forbade reciting poetry in the mosque, and buying and selling in it, and that people form circles on Friday before the prayer. He said: "And on this subject there are reports from Buraida, Jabir, and Anas. The hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr is a hasan hadith." Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) said: "I saw Muhammad [[In al-Tirmidhi: "Ahmad"]] and Ishaq, and he mentioned others besides them, arguing with the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb." And a group of the people of knowledge disliked buying and selling in the mosque, and Ahmad and Ishaq held this view. It is related that Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon them both, came upon a people buying and selling in the mosque, so he made his garment into a whip [[al-mikhraq: a cloth wrapped up and used to strike children with, one against another]], then began to chase them, striking them and saying: "O sons of vipers! You have taken the mosques of God as marketplaces! This is the market of the Hereafter."

I say: Some of our companions disliked teaching children in mosques, and considered it to be a form of buying and selling. This applies when it is done for a wage. If it were without a wage, it would still be prohibited for another reason, namely that children do not guard themselves against filth and dirt, which leads to the mosques not being kept clean, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that they be cleaned and perfumed. He said: "Keep your children and your insane away from your mosques, and the drawing of your swords, the enforcement of your punishments, the raising of your voices, your disputes, and perfume them on Friday, and place purifiers at their doors." Its chain includes al-Ala' ibn Kathir al-Dimashqi, mawla of the Banu Umayya, who is weak according to them; Abu Ahmad ibn Adi al-Jurjani, the hafiz, mentioned him.

Abu Ahmad also mentioned, from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him), who said: "I prayed the afternoon prayer with Uthman, Commander of the Believers, and he saw a tailor in a corner of the mosque and ordered him to be removed. It was said to him: 'O Commander of the Believers, he sweeps the mosque, closes its doors, and sometimes sprinkles it.' Uthman said: 'I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Keep your craftsmen away from your mosques."'" This is a non-preserved hadith; its chain includes Muhammad ibn Mujib al-Thaqafi, who is abandoned in hadith.

I say: What has been reported with this meaning, even if its chain is weak, is sound in meaning, and what we mentioned before indicates its soundness. Al-Tirmidhi said: "Some of the Successors (tabi'un) from among the people of knowledge have related a concession regarding buying and selling in the mosque." And it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) in more than one hadith a concession regarding reciting poetry in the mosque.

I say: As for reciting poetry, there is disagreement about it: some forbid it absolutely, and some permit it absolutely, but the preferable view is detailed: one should look at the poetry. If it calls for praise of God the Mighty and Majestic, or of His Messenger (ﷺ), or defends them, as was the poetry of Hassan, or if it includes encouragement to good, admonition, and asceticism regarding this world and contentment with little of it, then it is good in the mosques and elsewhere, like the saying of the speaker:

"Circle, O soul, that I may aim for the One, the Eternal Refuge,
And leave me; I seek nothing but my Lord, the One.
He is my intimate and my companion; leave the people,
For you will not find any refuge other than Him."
[[From the meter ramal, and its recitation: "Circle, O soul, that I may aim for the one, the eternal refuge."]]

What is not of this kind is not permitted, because poetry in most cases is not free of indecency, falsehood, and adorning with falsehood. And even if it is free of that, the least of what it contains is idle talk and nonsense, while the mosques are pure of such things, because of His saying, Exalted is He: "In houses which God has permitted to be raised." And it may be permissible to recite in the mosque, like the saying of the speaker:

"Like the stallion of the sand-dune, the dew strikes it,
The dew rises upon its back and drips down."
[[Al-adhab (with fatha and the unpointed dal): what is swept by sand. It is said: its side which is soft and adjoins the rough ground. Singular and plural are the same.]]

And like the saying of another:

"When the sky falls upon the land of a people,
We graze upon it, even if they are angry."

This kind, even if it contains no praise or commendation, is permissible, because it is free of indecency and falsehood. The mention of permissible poetry and other poetry, with what is sufficient, will come, God willing, in "The Poets." Al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, from Aisha (may God be pleased with her), who said: "Poets were mentioned in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: 'It is speech: its good is good and its bad is bad.'" On this subject there are also reports from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, Abu Hurayra, and Ibn Abbas from the Prophet (ﷺ), mentioned in the Sunan.

I say: The companions of al-Shafi'i transmit this statement from al-Shafi'i, and that no one else said it, and it seems they did not come across the hadiths on this matter. And God knows best.

The Eighth: As for raising the voice, if it is for a benefit to the one raising his voice, he is answered with the opposite of his intention, due to the hadith of Barira mentioned earlier, and the hadith of Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever hears a man announcing a lost item in the mosque, let him say: 'May God not return it to you, for the mosques were not built for this.'" Malik and a group went this way, so they disliked raising the voice in the mosque, whether in knowledge or otherwise. Abu Hanifa and his companions, and Muhammad ibn Maslama from our companions, permitted raising the voice in disputes and knowledge. They said: "Because they cannot avoid it." This contradicts the apparent meaning of the hadith, and their saying "they cannot avoid it" is disputed. Rather, they can avoid it for two reasons: first, by constantly maintaining dignity and reverence, and by keeping this in mind and guarding against its opposite. Second, if they are unable to do that, they should take a place specifically for it, as Umar did when he built an open area called al-Butayha, and said: "Whoever wishes to make noise or recite poetry in the mosque of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), let him go out to this open area." This indicates that Umar disliked reciting poetry in the mosque, and that is why he built al-Butayha outside it.

The Ninth: As for sleeping in the mosque, for one who is in need of it, whether a man or a woman, from among strangers and those who have no home, it is permissible, because in al-Bukhari, and Abu Qilaba said, from Anas: "A group from Ukl came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and they stayed in the Suffa [[A shaded place at the far end of the Prophet's Mosque where the needy would take shelter]]." Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said: "The companions of the Suffa were poor." And in the two Sahihs, from Ibn Umar, that he used to sleep while he was a young unmarried man with no family, in the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ). The wording of al-Bukhari: he gave a chapter heading "The Sleep of a Woman in the Mosque" and included the hadith of Aisha about the story of the black woman [[Al-sawda': a black woman from among the Arab tribe of Lahha, whose people accused her of stealing a shoulder-belt, and they began to search her until they searched her private parts. She said: "By God, I was standing with them when a kite passed and dropped it among them..." Then she came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and embraced Islam, and she had a tent in the mosque... See Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Mosques).]], whose people accused her of the shoulder-belt. Aisha said: "She had a tent in the mosque, or a small room..." [[Al-khiba': a tent of wool or fur. Al-hafsh (with kasra on the ha and sukun on the fa): a small house.]] ... the hadith. It is said: Ata ibn Abi Rabah's lodging in the mosque was for forty years.

The Tenth: Muslim related from Abu Humayd or from Abu Usayd, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him say: 'O God, open for me the doors of Your mercy,' and when he leaves, let him say: 'O God, I ask You of Your bounty.'" Abu Dawud recorded it likewise, except that he added after his saying "When one of you enters the mosque": "let him greet the Prophet (ﷺ) [[In Sunan Abi Dawud: "let him greet upon the Prophet (ﷺ)"]] and pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then let him say: 'O God, open for me...'" The hadith. Ibn Majah related from Fatima, daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the mosque, he said: 'In the name of God, and peace be upon the Messenger of God. O God, forgive me my sins and open for me the doors of Your mercy.' And when he left, he said: 'In the name of God, and blessings be upon the Messenger of God. O God, forgive me my sins and open for me the doors of Your mercy and Your bounty.'" It has also been related from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and say: 'O God, open for me the doors of Your mercy,' and when he leaves, let him greet the Prophet (ﷺ) and say: 'O God, protect me from the accursed Satan.'" Abu Dawud related from Haywa ibn Shurayh, who said: "I met Uqba ibn Muslim and said to him: 'It has reached me that you narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he entered the mosque he said: "I seek refuge in God the Mighty, in His noble face, and His ancient authority, from the accursed Satan."' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When he says that, Satan says: "He has been protected from me for the rest of the day."'"

The Eleventh: Muslim related from Abu Qatada that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'as before he sits." And from him, he said: "I entered the mosque while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting among the people, so I sat down. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'What prevented you from praying two rak'as before you sat?' I said: 'O Messenger of God, I saw you sitting and the people sitting.' He said: 'When one of you enters the mosque, let him not sit until he has prayed two rak'as.'" The scholars said: "He (ﷺ) gave the mosque a distinction that sets it apart from all other houses, which is that one should not sit until one has prayed." And the majority of scholars [[In MS K: "the jurists"]] hold that the command to pray is for recommendation and encouragement.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 3 of 5):

Dawud (al-Zahiri) and his companions held that this is obligatory, but this is false. If the matter were as they said, it would be forbidden for one in a state of minor ritual impurity (hadath al-asghar) to enter the mosque until he performs wudu', and, as far as I know, no one holds this view. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: Ibrahim ibn Yazid related from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Salama, from Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs. And when one of you enters his house, let him not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs, for Allah will place good in his house because of his two rak'ahs." This implies equating the mosque with the house. It is said in reply: this addition regarding praying two rak'ahs upon entering the house has no basis, as al-Bukhari stated. What is authentic on this matter is the hadith of Abu Qatada which has preceded it in Muslim. This Ibrahim, as far as I know, had no narrators from him except Sa'd ibn Abd al-Hamid, and I know of no other hadith from him besides this one. So said Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq.

Twelfth issue: Sa'id ibn Zabban related: my father told me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Abu Hind, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Tamim (i.e., al-Dari) brought from Syria to Madina lamps, oil and muqut (ropes). When he reached Madina, it coincided with the night of Friday. He ordered a boy called Abu al-Bazzad, who stood up, tied the muqut, hung the lamps, poured water and oil into them, and placed wicks in them. When the sun set, he ordered Abu al-Bazzad to light them, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to the mosque and found them shining. He said: "Who did this?" They said: "Tamim al-Dari, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "You have illuminated Islam; may Allah illuminate you in this world and the Hereafter. Indeed, if I had a daughter, I would have married her to you." Nawfal ibn al-Harith said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have a daughter called al-Mughira bint Nawfal, so do with her as you wish." So he married him to her.

Zabban (with a fatha on the za' and the ba', and its shadda, with one dot beneath it) is a name borne by Sa'id alone. He is Abu Uthman Sa'id ibn Zabban ibn Qa'id ibn Zabban ibn Abi Hind. This Abu Hind was a client of the Banu Bayada, the cupper of the Prophet (ﷺ) [[So in manuscripts B and K, and this is the correct reading.]]. And al-Muqut is the plural of al-Miqat, which is the rope, as if it were a metathesis of al-qimat. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Majah related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The first to light lamps in the mosques was Tamim al-Dari. It was also related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever lights a lamp in a mosque, the angels and the bearers of the Throne will continue to send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him as long as that light remains in it, and even if he sweeps the dust of the mosque, he will be rewarding the wide-eyed houris." The scholars said: It is recommended that the house in which the Qur'an is recited be illuminated by hanging lamps and setting up candles in it, and that the lighting in the mosques be increased in the month of Ramadan.

Thirteenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Glorified in them morning and evening by men﴾. The scholars differed concerning the description of those who glorify Allah. It was said: they are those who watch over the command of Allah, seeking His pleasure, whom no matter of worldly affairs distracts from the prayer and the remembrance of Allah. Many of the Companions said: this verse was revealed concerning the people of the markets who, when they heard the call to prayer, left every occupation and hastened. Salim ibn Abd Allah saw the people of the markets as they were coming to the prayer, and said: "These are the ones whom Allah meant by His saying: ﴿Neither trade nor sale distracts them from the remembrance of Allah﴾." This was also related from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abd Allah ibn Amir, Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr from him), and al-Hasan read "yusabbaha lahu fiha" with a fatha on the ba', in the passive form whose subject is not named. Nafi', Ibn Umar, Abu Amr and Hamza read "yusabbihu" with a kasra on the ba', and so Abu Amr also related from Asim. Whoever reads "yusabbaha" with a fatha on the ba' has two possible meanings. The first: that "rijal" is in the nominative by a hidden verb indicated by the apparent one, meaning: "men glorify Him in it," and in this case one stops at "al-asal." Sibawayh mentioned something similar, and he recited:

"Let Yazid be wept for by a humble one who seeks a lawsuit, and by one who is struck by what the calamities bring down."

The meaning is: a humble one weeps for him. On this basis you say: "Zayd was struck, Amr," meaning: "Amr struck him." [[The author of al-Khizana disputed its speaker and attributed it to Nahshal ibn Hari. This line is one of a number of verses in an elegy for his brother Yazid, whose opening is:
"By my life, if Yazid ibn Nahshal has become a corpse, the winds blow over him..."
And his saying "dara'" is from al-di'a, which is submission and humbling. "Al-mukhtabit" is the one who asks you without any acquaintance between you two, and he means here the needy. "Tutih" means goes away or perishes. "Al-tawa'ih" is the plural of mutiha, which means those that cast down. "Al-hasha" is what is in the belly. "Hadith," with a fatha on the jim and the tha', is the grave. "Al-rawamih" are the blowing days.]]

The other meaning: "rijal" is in the nominative as the subject of an inceptive sentence, and the predicate is "fi buyutin," meaning: in houses which Allah has permitted to be raised, men [glorify Him]. "Yusabbihu lahu fiha" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "turfa'a," as if he said: "that they be raised, glorified for Him in them." In this interpretation one does not stop at "al-asal." Whoever reads "yusabbihu" with a kasra on the ba' does not stop at "al-asal," because "yusabbihu" is a verb of "rijal," and the verb requires its subject, with no hidden pronoun in it. The discussion of "bil-ghuduwwi wal-asal" has already been made at the end of al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 355 onward.]]. And praise belongs to Allah alone.

Fourteenth issue: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿yusabbihu lahu fiha﴾. It was said: its meaning is "yusalli" (he prays). Ibn Abbas said: every glorification (tasbih) in the Qur'an is a prayer, and this is indicated by His saying: "morning and evening," meaning: at dawn and in the evening. Most of the exegetes said: He meant the obligatory prayers. Al-ghuduw is the dawn prayer, and al-asal is the noon and afternoon prayers and the two evening prayers, since the name al-asal comprises them.

Fifteenth issue: Abu Dawud related from Abu Umama that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever leaves his house in a state of purity to an obligatory prayer, his reward is like the reward of the pilgrim in ihram. And whoever leaves to the glorification of the forenoon (duha), not intending by it anything but that, his reward is that of the one who performs 'umrah. And a prayer following a prayer, with no idle talk between them, is a record in 'Illiyyin." [[An addition from Sunan Abi Dawud.]]

And he (al-Tabarani) related from Buraydah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Give good news to those who walk in darkness to the mosques, of perfect light on the Day of Resurrection." And in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever goes to the mosque in the morning or in the evening, Allah prepares for him a welcome in Paradise every time he goes in the morning or in the evening." Among the additions not found in the authentic collection (is): "Just as if one of you were to visit someone whose visit he loves, he would strive to honour him." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Muslim also related from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then walks to one of the houses of Allah to fulfil one of the obligations of Allah, one of his steps erases a sin and the other raises a degree." And from him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man's prayer in congregation exceeds his prayer in his house and his prayer in his market by twenty-some degrees, because when one of them performs wudu' and does it well, then comes to the mosque, he does not step out except

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 36–38 (part 4 of 5):

Except for prayer. He intends nothing but prayer, so he does not take a single step without being raised a degree for it and having a sin removed from him by it, until he enters the mosque. When he enters the mosque, he is in prayer for as long as the prayer is what holds him back, and the angels send blessings upon one of you as long as he remains in the place where he prayed. They say: "O Allah, have mercy on him. O Allah, forgive him. O Allah, accept his repentance," so long as he does not harm anyone there and does not break wind there. (In another narration: "What is 'breaking wind'?" He said: "Passing wind silently or audibly.")

Hakim ibn Zurayq said: It was said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "Is attending a funeral more beloved to you, or sitting in the mosque?" He said: "Whoever prays over a funeral has one qirat (a unit of reward), and whoever witnesses its burial has two qirats. But sitting in the mosque is more beloved to me, because the angels say: 'O Allah, forgive him. O Allah, have mercy on him. O Allah, accept his repentance.'"

It is also narrated from al-Hakam ibn Umayr, a companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Be in this world as strangers, take the mosques as your homes, train your hearts to tenderness, increase your reflection and weeping, and let not your desires lead you astray. You build what you will not live in, you gather what you will not eat, and you hope for what you will not attain."

Abu al-Darda' said to his son: "Let the mosque be your house, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Indeed the mosques are the houses of the God-fearing, and whoever makes the mosques his house, Allah the Exalted guarantees him comfort, ease, and passage over the Sirat.'"

Abu Sadiq al-Azdi wrote to Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab: "Keep to the mosques and cling to them, for it has reached me that they were the gatherings of the prophets."

Abu Idris al-Khawlani said: "The mosques are the gatherings of the noble among people."

Malik ibn Dinar said: "It has reached me that Allah, blessed and exalted, says: 'I am about to punish My servants, but then I look at those who frequent the mosques, the companions of the Qur'an, and the young of Islam, and My anger subsides.'"

It is narrated from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "In the last era there will be men who come to the mosques and sit in them in circles, their talk being of this world and its love. So do not sit with them, for Allah has no need of them."

Ibn al-Musayyab said: "Whoever sits in a mosque is in fact sitting with his Lord, so his duty is to say nothing but good."

What has passed regarding the glorification and sanctity of mosques is sufficient [see vol. 8, p. 90]. Some scholars have gathered fifteen points on this matter, saying: "Among the sanctity of the mosque is that one greets upon entering if people are seated there. If no one is in the mosque, he says: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah. And that he prays two rak'ahs before sitting down. And that he does not buy or sell in it, nor draw a sword or arrow in it, nor seek a lost item in it, nor raise his voice in it except for the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, nor speak in it of worldly matters, nor step over people's necks, nor dispute over a place, nor crowd anyone in the row, nor pass in front of one who is praying, nor spit in it, nor clear his throat in it, nor blow his nose in it, nor crack his fingers, nor fidget with any part of his body. And that it is kept free of impurities, children, and the insane, and of the carrying out of prescribed punishments (hudud). And that he frequently remembers Allah the Exalted and does not neglect Him." When he does these things, he has fulfilled the right of the mosque, and the mosque becomes a protection for him and a fortress against the accursed Satan.

And in a report: "A mosque lifted its people up to heaven, complaining of them to Allah because of the worldly talk they engaged in there."

Al-Daraqutni narrated from 'Amir al-Sha'bi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the signs of the approach of the Hour: the crescent moon will be seen early (qabalan) [Ibn al-Athir said: 'That is, it is seen as soon as it rises, because of its size and clarity, rather than being searched for. It is with a fatha on the qaf and the ba'.'] and it will be said that it is for two nights; mosques will be used as thoroughfares; and sudden death will become widespread."

This is transmitted by 'Abd al-Kabir ibn al-Mu'afa from Sharik, from al-'Abbas ibn Dhurayh, from al-Sha'bi, from Anas. Others transmit it from al-Sha'bi as a mursal (a report whose chain omits a companion), and Allah knows best.

Abu Hatim said: "'Abd al-Kabir ibn Mu'afa is thiqah (trustworthy). He was counted among the Abdal [The Abdal are a group of the righteous through whom Allah sustains the earth: forty in Syria and thirty in the rest of the lands. None of them dies without another taking his place, which is why they are called abdal. The singular of abdal is 'abd' or 'badal'. Ibn Duraid said: the singular is 'badil'.]."

In al-Bukhari, from Abu Musa, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever passes through any of our mosques or markets carrying arrows, let him hold their points, so that he does not injure a Muslim with his hand."

Muslim narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Spitting in the mosque is a sin, and its expiation is burying it."

And from Abu Dhar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The deeds of my community were displayed to me, both their good and their bad. I found among the good deeds the removal of harm from the road, and I found among the bad deeds the phlegm left in the mosque unburied."

Abu Dawud narrated from al-Faraj ibn Fudala, from Abu Sa'd [In the original manuscripts it reads: "from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri," which is an error, because al-Faraj ibn Fudala did not narrate from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri but from Abu Sa'd al-Himyari, and this Abu Sa'd was a companion of Wathila ibn al-Asqa'.] al-Himyari, who said: "I saw Wathila ibn al-Asqa' in the mosque of Damascus spit on the mat and then rub it with his foot. He was asked: 'Why did you do this?' He said: 'Because I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do it.'" Al-Faraj ibn Fudala is weak. Furthermore, there was no mat in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The correct report is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spat on the ground and rubbed it with his left sandal, and perhaps Wathila intended this, but then took it to mean the mat.

The sixteenth issue: When Allah said "men" and singled them out for mention, this indicates that women have no share in the mosques, since the Friday prayer (jumu'ah) and congregational prayer (jama'ah) are not obligatory for them, and that their prayer in their homes is better. Abu Dawud narrated from 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A woman's prayer in her house is better than her prayer in her courtyard, and her prayer in her inner room is better than her prayer in her house."

The seventeenth issue: the words of Allah, "neither trade nor sale distracts them," meaning: do not occupy them.

"From the remembrance of Allah." Trade was singled out for mention because it is the greatest thing a person busies himself with away from prayer. If it is asked: "Why is sale mentioned again when trade includes it?" The answer is: by trade he meant buying, as indicated by "nor sale." A parallel is the saying of Allah: "And when they see trade or amusement, they scatter to it" [al-Jumu'ah: 11]. This was said by al-Waqidi. Al-Kalbi said: "The merchants (tujjar) are the importers who travel, and the sellers (ba'a) are those who stay in place."

"From the remembrance of Allah." Its interpretation has been disputed. 'Ata' said: it means attendance at prayer. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the obligatory prayer. It was also said: it means the call to prayer (adhan), as mentioned by Yahya ibn Salam. It was also said: it means remembering Him by His beautiful names, that is, affirming His oneness and glorifying Him. The verse was revealed concerning the people of the markets, as said by Ibn 'Umar. Salim said: "'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar passed by the market when they had closed their shops and stood up to pray in congregation, and he said: 'It was concerning them that this was revealed: "Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts..."' to the end of the verse." Abu Hurayra said, from the Prophet ﷺ: "They are those who travel through the earth seeking Allah's bounty." It was also said: two men lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, one of whom was a seller, and when he heard the call to prayer, if the scale was in his hand he would throw it down without setting it down properly, and if it was on the ground he would not lift it. The other was a blacksmith who made swords for trade. When his hammer was on the anvil he would leave it resting there, and if he had raised it, he would throw it behind his back when he heard the adhan. So Allah the Exalted revealed this, as praise for both of them and for everyone who followed their example.

The eighteenth issue: the words of Allah, "and the establishment of prayer." This indicates that what is meant by "from the remembrance of Allah" is other than prayer, since otherwise it would be repetition. One says: "aqama al-salat iqamatan" (he established prayer). The original form was iqwaman, and the movement of the waw was transferred to the qaf, so the waw became an alif, and since an unvowelled alif followed it, one of them was dropped. The ha' was kept so that they would not drop it and cause the word to be defective. When it is in the construct state (idafa), the noun in the construct takes the place of the ha', so it is permissible to drop it. If it is not in the construct, it is not permissible to drop it. Do you not see that you say: "wa'ada 'idatan" (he promised a promise) and "wazana zinatan" (he weighed a weight), so it is not permissible to drop the ha', because you have dropped a waw, since the original was wa'ada wi'datan and wazana wizunatan. If you put it in the construct, the ha' is dropped. Al-Farra' recited:

"Indeed the companions have hastened the separation and departed,
and they broke their promise, the promise they had made."

He means 'idata, and dropped the ha' when it was in the construct.

It is narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will bring the mosques of the world, as if they were white camels whose legs are of ambergris, whose necks are of saffron, whose heads are of musk, and whose reins are of green emerald. Their pillars and their muezzins lead them, their imams drive them, and their worshippers cling to them. They will pass over the plains of the Resurrection like a flash of lightning. The people of the gathering will say: 'These are near angels or sent prophets.' It will be called out: 'These are neither angels nor prophets, but they are the people of the mosques, and those who guard the prayers, from the community of Muhammad ﷺ.'"

It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A time will come upon people when nothing of Islam will remain but its name, and nothing of the Qur'an but its outline. They will adorn their mosques, but they will be ruined in terms of the remembrance of Allah. The worst people of that time will be their scholars. From them the trial emerges, and to them it returns." He means that they know, but do not act upon the obligations of what they know.

The nineteenth issue: the words of Allah, "and the giving of zakat." It was said: it means the obligatory zakat, as said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: zakat here means obedience to Allah and sincerity, since not every believer has wealth.

"They fear a Day in which hearts and eyes will be turned about": that is the Day of Resurrection.

"In which hearts and eyes will be turned about": meaning from its terror and the fear of destruction. Taqallub means change. What is meant is the hearts and eyes of the disbelievers. The turning of the hearts is their being torn from their places up to the throats, so they neither return to their places nor leave. As for the turning of the eyes, it is their becoming blue after being black, and blind after seeing. It was also said: the hearts turn between hope for salvation and fear of destruction, and the eyes look to see from which direction their books will be given, and to which direction they will be led. It was also said: the hearts of doubters turn away from what they were upon of doubt, and likewise their eyes, when they see certainty. This is like the saying of Allah: "We removed your veil, so your sight today is sharp" [Qaf: 22]. What they used to see as error in this world, they will see as guidance, but that will not benefit them in the Hereafter. It was also said: they will be turned over on the embers of Hell, as in the saying of Allah: "The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire" [al-Ahzab: 66], and "We will turn their hearts and their eyes" [al-An'am: 110], according to those who understand the meaning as their being turned over on the flames of the Fire. It was also said: they will be turned by being scorched by the Fire once and burned to ripeness another time. It was also said: the turning of the hearts is their throbbing (wajib), and the turning of the eyes is looking with them toward the directions of terrors.

To reward them with the best of what they did: He mentioned the reward for good deeds and did not mention the reward for evil deeds, although He does recompense for them, for two reasons. First, the verse is an encouragement, so it confined itself to mentioning the desire. Second, it describes a people among whom major sins do not occur, so their minor sins are forgiven.

And increase them from His bounty: this may have two meanings. First, what He multiplies of a good deed to ten times its like. Second, what He bestows out of grace without any recompense.

And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning: that is, without calling him to account for what He gave him, since His giving has no end. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the building of the Mosque of Quba. ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha attended and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has the one who builds mosques prospered?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha." He said: "And prayed in them standing and sitting?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha." He said: "And did not spend the night except prostrating to Allah?" He said: "Yes, O Ibn Rawaha. Refrain from saj' (rhymed prose, a rhythmic style of speech), for no servant has been given anything worse than fluency of the tongue."

Mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a qi'ah﴾. When He struck the example of the believer, He struck the example of the disbeliever. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah ibn Abd Shams, who used to practise asceticism (yatarahhabu), seeking the religion (mutalammisan lil-din). When the Prophet (ﷺ) emerged, he disbelieved. Abu Sahl said: It concerns the People of the Book. Al-Dahhak said: It concerns the good deeds of the disbeliever, such as maintaining the ties of kinship and benefiting neighbours.

Al-sarab (mirage) is what is seen at midday in the intensity of the heat, like water in the deserts, clinging to the ground. Al-al (the shimmer) that appears in the forenoon is like water, except that it rises above the ground until it seems to be between the earth and the sky. The sarab was named sarab because it saraba, i.e. flows like water. It is said: sarab al-fahl, meaning it went off and walked on the earth. The al is also called sarab, and it occurs only in the wilderness and in heat, so the thirsty one is deceived by it. The poet said:

So I became like one who spills what is in his waterskin, for the shimmering of a mirage atop a hard hill.

Another said:

When we restrained war, their covenants were like the gleam of a mirage shining in the desert.

Imru' al-Qays said:

Did I not wear out the riding-camels through every desert, tall of stature, gleaming with mirage?

[[In the originals: "tawil al-tul"; the correction is from the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays. Al-Amq means tall. The minister Abu Bakr Asim ibn Ayyub (commentator on the Diwan) said: In the line there is what is asked about from the viewpoint of Arabic grammar, namely the idafa of "amq" to "tul". It is supposed to be an idafa of a thing to itself, because amq is tall, and it is not as is supposed; rather it is like your saying: "distant distance".]]

Al-qi'ah is the plural of al-qa', like jirah and jar. Al-Harawi said this. Abu Ubaydah said: qi'ah and qa' are one and the same; this was related by al-Nahhas. Al-qa' is the land that is spread out and wide and has no vegetation, and in it the mirage occurs. The original meaning of al-qa' is the low place where water settles, its plural being qi'an. Al-Jawhari said: al-qa' is the level part of the land; its plurals are aqwu', aqwa', and qi'an. The waw became ya' because of the kasrah before it. Al-qi'ah is like al-qa', and it too is from the waw. Some say it is a plural.

(Yahsabuhu al-zam'an): that is, the thirsty one.

(Ma'an): that is, he thinks the mirage is water.

(Hatta idha ja'ahu lam yajiduhu shay'an): of what he estimated, and he finds a land with no water in it. This is an example God exalted struck for the disbelievers, who rely on the reward of their deeds; when they come before God, exalted is He, they find the reward of their deeds nullified by disbelief. That is, they find nothing, just as the owner of the mirage finds only a land with no water in it, so he perishes or dies.

(Wa-wajada Allah 'indahu): that is, he finds God lying in wait.

(Fa-waffahu hisabahu): that is, the recompense for his deed. Imru' al-Qays said:

So he turned back fleeing, hastening, and he was certain that he would meet the reckoning.

It is said: he found God's promise of recompense for his deed. It is also said: he found God's command at His gathering, and the meanings are close. It was also read "biqi'at" (in the plural). Al-Mahdawi said: The alif may be a lengthened vowel from the fatha of the 'ayn. It may also be like rajul 'izah and 'izhah, for the man who does not approach women. It may also be the plural of qi'ah, and in that case the ta' is pronounced in both pause and continuation. It is related from Nafi', Ibn Ja'far and Shaybah that they read "al-zaman" without hamz, whereas the well-known reading from them has the hamz. It is said: zami'a yazma'u zama'an fahuwa zam'an, and if you soften the hamza you say: al-zaman. As for His saying, "And those who disbelieve": it is the subject (mubtada'), "a'maluhum" is a substitute (badal) for "alladhina kafaru", that is, and the deeds of those who disbelieve are like a mirage, so the modifier (al-mudaf) has been omitted.

**Allah's words: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea﴾.** He, exalted is He, gave another parable for the disbelievers, meaning: their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, or like darkness. Al-Zajjaj said: "If you wish, give the parable of the mirage, and if you wish, give the parable of the darknesses. The *aw* (أَوْ, "or") here is for permissibility (*ibahah*), as was stated earlier concerning ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 215.]] [Al-Baqarah: 19]." Al-Jurjani said: "The first verse concerns the deeds of the disbelievers, and the second concerns their disbelief. Disbelief is linked to their deeds because disbelief is also one of their deeds. Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 282.]] [Al-Baqarah: 257], meaning from disbelief to faith." Abu Ali said: "*Aw kaZulumat* means *aw ka-dhi zulumat* (or like one possessing darknesses), and Allah's words ﴿when he brings out his hand﴾ indicate this omitted noun, so the pronoun refers back to the omitted noun." Al-Qushayri said: "According to al-Zajjaj, the parable applies to the deeds of the disbelievers; according to al-Jurjani, to the disbelief of the disbeliever; and according to Abu Ali, to the disbeliever himself." Ibn Abbas, in one narration, said: "This is the parable of the disbeliever's heart."

**(In a deep sea)**: It is said that *lujjiy* is a relative adjective derived from *lujjah*, which is the sea whose bottom cannot be reached. *Lujjah* is the greatest mass of water, and its plural is *lujaj*. One says *iltajja al-bahr* when its waves clash with each other. From this is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever boards the sea when it is *iltajja*, the protection (*dhimmah*) is cleared from him." *Iltajja al-amr* means the matter became great and confused. Allah's words ﴿he took it for a deep water (*lujjah*)﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 208.]] [An-Naml: 44] mean: it has depth. *Lajjajat al-safinah* means the ship plunged into the *lujjah* (with a *damma* on the *lam*). As for *al-lajjah* (with a *fatha* on the *lam*), it means the voices of people; one says: "I heard the *lajjat* of the people," meaning their voices and clamor. Abu al-Najm said:

*"Fi lajjatin amsik Fulanan 'an Ful"*

*Iltajjat al-aswat* means the voices mixed together and grew loud.

**(There covers it a wave)**: meaning, that deep sea is covered by a wave.

**(Above it a wave)**: meaning, above the wave there is a wave, and above this second wave there is a cloud. Thus the fear of the wave, the fear of the wind, and the fear of the cloud combine. It is also said that the meaning is: a wave covers it, followed after it by another wave, so the waves follow one another until it is as if some of them are above others. This is most frightening when its waves follow closely and draw near. Above this wave is a cloud. It increases fear in two respects: first, it has covered the stars by which one is guided; second, the wind that arises with the cloud and the rain that falls from it.

**(Darknesses, some above others)**: Ibn Muhaysin and al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read *sahabu zulumatin* with *idafah* (annexation) and the genitive. Qunbul read *sahab* with tanwin and *zulumatin* in the genitive with tanwin. The rest read it in the nominative with tanwin. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads *min fawqihi sahabu zulumatin* with *idafah*, it is because the cloud rises at the time of these darknesses, so it is annexed to them, just as one says *sahab rahmah* when it rises at the time of rain. Whoever reads *sahabun zulumatin*, puts *zulumatin* in the genitive as an emphasis of the first *zulumat*, or as a substitute (*badal*) for it, and *sahab* is the subject (*mubtada'*) while *min fawqihi* is the predicate. Whoever reads *sahabun zulumatun*, *zulumatun* is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: "these are darknesses" or "this is darknesses." Ibn al-Anbari said: "*min fawqihi mawj* is not a complete pause, because his words *min fawqihi sahab* are a relative clause describing the wave. The stop on his words *min fawqihi sahab* is good, and then you begin with *zulumat ba'duha fawqa ba'd*, meaning: they are darknesses, some above others." It is related from the people of Makkah that they read *zulumat* in the sense of *aw ka-zulumatin zulumat ba'duha fawqa ba'd* (or like darknesses, darknesses some above others). According to this view, it is not good to stop at *al-sahab*.

Then it has been said: by these darknesses is meant the darkness of the cloud, the darkness of the waves, the darkness of the night, and the darkness of the sea, so whoever is in these darknesses sees nothing, not even a star. It has also been said: by the darknesses is meant hardships, that is, hardships some above others. It has further been said: by the darknesses is meant the deeds of the disbeliever; by the deep sea, his heart; by the wave above the wave, what covers his heart of ignorance, doubt and bewilderment; and by the cloud, the rust (*rayn*), the sealing and the stamping upon his heart. This meaning is related from Ibn Abbas and others, meaning he does not see with his heart the light of faith, just as the one in the darknesses of the sea, when he brings out his hand, scarcely sees it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "The disbeliever moves about in five darknesses: his speech is darkness, his deed is darkness, his entrance is darkness, his exit is darkness, and his final destination on the Day of Resurrection is into the darknesses of the Fire, and what an evil destination."

**(When he brings out his hand)**: meaning, the one who looks.

**(He scarcely sees it)**: meaning, because of the intensity of the darknesses. Al-Zajjaj and Abu Ubaydah said: the meaning is "he did not see it and he almost did not," and this is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan. The meaning of *lam yakad* is: he did not hope to see it. Al-Farra' said: *kada* here is a filler (*silah*), meaning he did not see it, just as you say *ma kidtu a'rifuhu* (I did not know him). Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is he saw it only after great effort, just as you say *ma kidtu arakaSa min al-zulmah* (I could hardly see you in the darkness), and he saw it after despair and hardship. It has been said: its meaning is that he came close to seeing but did not see, as one says: *kada al-'arus yakunu amiran* (the bride almost became a princess), *kada al-na'am yatir* (the ostrich almost flew), and *kada al-muntali yakunu rakiban* (the one wearing shoes almost became a rider). Al-Nahhas said: "The most correct of the views on this is that the meaning is: he did not come near to seeing it. So when he did not come near to seeing it, he did not see it, neither a distant seeing nor a near seeing."

**(And whomever Allah does not give a light)**: whereby he may be guided, the affairs become dark upon him. Ibn Abbas said: meaning, whoever Allah does not grant a religion, has no religion; and whoever Allah does not grant a light by which he walks on the Day of Resurrection, will not be guided to Paradise, as in His words: ﴿and He will give you a light by which you walk﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 266.]] [Al-Hadid: 28]. Al-Zajjaj said: this refers to the world, and the meaning is: whomever Allah does not guide, will not be guided. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: it was revealed concerning Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, who used to seek religion in the pre-Islamic period, and wore woolen garments (*al-musuh*), and then disbelieved in Islam. Al-Mawardi said: it was revealed concerning Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, who used to practice asceticism in the pre-Islamic period, wear wool and seek religion, and then disbelieved in Islam. I say: both of them died as disbelievers, so it is not unlikely that they are the intended ones in the verse, along with others. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Jahsh, who had embraced Islam and emigrated to the land of Abyssinia, and then became a Christian after his Islam.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned: Anas said, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, created me from a light, and created Abu Bakr from my light, and created Umar and Aisha from the light of Abu Bakr, and created the believers of my community from the light of Umar, and created the believing women of my community from the light of Aisha. Whoever does not love me and love Abu Bakr, Umar and Aisha, then he has no light." Then it was revealed: ﴿And whomever Allah does not give a light, for him there is no light﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verses 41–42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah glorify whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds in flight?﴾ When He mentioned the clarity of the signs, He increased the proof and the clear evidences, and He made clear that His created things, by their variation, indicate that they have a Maker capable of perfection. So to Him belongs the sending of the messengers, and He has sent them and supported them with miracles, and they informed of Paradise and Hellfire. The address in "Have you not seen" is to the Prophet ﷺ, and its meaning is "Do you not know," and the intended meaning is everyone.

(That Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens) from the angels.

(And the earth) from the jinn and mankind.

(And the birds in flight) Mujahid and others said: prayer is for humans, and glorification is for the rest of creation. Sufyan said: for birds there is a prayer in which there is no bowing nor prostration. It was also said: their beating of their wings is a prayer, and their voices are glorification, related by al-Naqqash. It was also said: glorification here is what is seen in the created thing of the traces of craftsmanship. The meaning of "ṣāffāt" is those whose wings are spread out in the air. The majority read "wal-ṭayru" in the nominative, as a conjunction with "man" (whoever). Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "wal-ṭayra" (in the accusative) with the meaning of "together with the birds." Al-Nahhas said: I heard him give the example "qumtu wa-Zaydan" with the meaning "I stood with Zayd." He said: this is better than the nominative. He said: if you say "qumtu anā wa-Zaydun" (I stood, I and Zayd), the nominative is better, and the accusative is permissible.

(Each has indeed known its prayer and its glorification) It is permissible that the meaning is: each one, Allah has indeed known its prayer and its glorification, i.e., He knows the prayer of the one who prays and the glorification of the one who glorifies. In this respect, the accusative of "kullun" is permissible according to the Basrans and the Kufans, by supposing a verb that is explained by what follows it. It has been said: the meaning is that every one who prays and glorifies has known the prayer of himself and the glorification that he was charged with. Some people read "kullun qad ʿulima ṣalātuhu wa-tasbīḥuhu" (in the passive), without naming the agent. Some grammarians mentioned that some of them read "kullun qad ʿallama ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu," so it is permissible that its supposition is: each one has been taught by Allah its prayer and its glorification. It is also permissible that the meaning is: each one has taught others its prayer and its glorification, i.e., the prayer of itself, and the teaching, which is conveying understanding, is then the intended specific meaning, because among people there are those who have not taught. It is also permissible that the meaning is: each one from whom the one who derives inference has derived, and he expressed inference by teaching; this was said by al-Mahdawi. The prayer here means glorification, and it was repeated for emphasis, like His saying "He knows the secret and the private talk." Prayer is sometimes called glorification; this was said by al-Qushayri.

(And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return) It has preceded in more than one place.

So to Him belongs the sending of the messengers, and He has sent them and supported them with miracles, and they informed of Paradise and Hellfire. The address in "Have you not seen" is to the Prophet ﷺ, and its meaning is "Do you not know," and the intended meaning is everyone.

(That Allah is glorified by whoever is in the heavens) from the angels.

(And the earth) from the jinn and mankind.

(And the birds in flight) Mujahid and others said: prayer is for humans, and glorification is for the rest of creation. Sufyan said: for birds there is a prayer in which there is no bowing nor prostration. It was also said: their beating of their wings is a prayer, and their voices are glorification, related by al-Naqqash. It was also said: glorification here is what is seen in the created thing of the traces of craftsmanship. The meaning of "ṣāffāt" is those whose wings are spread out in the air. The majority read "wal-ṭayru" in the nominative, as a conjunction with "man" (whoever). Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read "wal-ṭayra" (in the accusative) with the meaning of "together with the birds." Al-Nahhas said: I heard him give the example "qumtu wa-Zaydan" with the meaning "I stood with Zayd." He said: this is better than the nominative. He said: if you say "qumtu anā wa-Zaydun" (I stood, I and Zayd), the nominative is better, and the accusative is permissible.

(Each has indeed known its prayer and its glorification) It is permissible that the meaning is: each one, Allah has indeed known its prayer and its glorification, i.e., He knows the prayer of the one who prays and the glorification of the one who glorifies. In this respect, the accusative of "kullun" is permissible according to the Basrans and the Kufans, by supposing a verb that is explained by what follows it. It has been said: the meaning is that every one who prays and glorifies has known the prayer of himself and the glorification that he was charged with. Some people read "kullun qad ʿulima ṣalātuhu wa-tasbīḥuhu" (in the passive), without naming the agent. Some grammarians mentioned that some of them read "kullun qad ʿallama ṣalātahu wa-tasbīḥahu," so it is permissible that its supposition is: each one has been taught by Allah its prayer and its glorification. It is also permissible that the meaning is: each one has taught others its prayer and its glorification, i.e., the prayer of itself, and the teaching, which is conveying understanding, is then the intended specific meaning, because among people there are those who have not taught. It is also permissible that the meaning is: each one from whom the one who derives inference has derived, and he expressed inference by teaching; this was said by al-Mahdawi. The prayer here means glorification, and it was repeated for emphasis, like His saying "He knows the secret and the private talk." Prayer is sometimes called glorification; this was said by al-Qushayri.

(And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the final return) It has preceded in more than one place.

God Almighty says: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds﴾. He mentions another of His proofs, meaning: have you not seen with the eyes of your heart?

(He drives clouds) means He drives them wherever He wills. The wind drives the clouds, and the cow drives (*tuzji*) her calf, meaning she herds it. From this comes *zajā al-kharāj yazjū zajā'an* (mamdūdan, with a long vowel), meaning the tax became easy to collect. Al-Nabigha said:

*Indeed I came to you from my family and my homeland,*
*driving the remnant of a soul in which there is no breath left.*

He also said:

*A night traveler at the Pleiades' rising journeyed with him,*
*while the north wind drove over him the frozen cold.*

(Then He gathers it together) means He gathers it when it spreads out, so that it grows stronger, joins together and becomes dense. The basic form of *al-ta'lif* (gathering) takes a hamza, and one says *ta'allafa*. It is also read *yu'allifu* with a *waw* for lightness. *Al-sahāb* (the cloud) is singular in form, but its meaning is plural, which is why He says ﴿He produces the clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12]. *Bayn* (between) is used only with two or more, so how is *baynahu* (between it) permissible? The answer is that *baynahu* here refers to a collection of clouds, just as you say *al-shajar qad jalastu baynahu* (I sat among the trees), because it is a plural, and the pronoun is returned to the word's form. This was stated by al-Farra'. Another answer is that the cloud is singular, but it is permissible to say *baynahu* because it contains many pieces, as in the line:

*...between al-Dukhūl and Ḥawmal.*

Here *bayn* is placed with *al-Dukhūl*, which is singular, because it includes several places. Similarly you say *mā ziltu adūru bayn al-Kūfa* (I kept wandering around in Kufa), because Kufa has many places. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. Al-Asma'i claimed that this is not permissible, and the line was transmitted as:

*...between al-Dukhūl and Ḥawmal.*

(Then He makes it piled up) means gathered, one part riding upon another, as in His saying ﴿And if they should see a fragment of the sky falling, they would say, "A layered cloud"﴾ [al-Tūr: 44]. *Al-Rakm* is the gathering of a thing. One says *rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu rakman* when he gathers it and throws part of it upon part. *Irtakama al-shay'* and *tarākama* mean it became gathered. *Al-Rukma* is gathered mud. *Al-Rukām* is sand piled up, and likewise clouds and what resembles them. *Murtakam al-ṭarīq* (with a fatḥah on the kāf) is its main road.

(So you see the rain coming out from its midst) There are two opinions about *al-wadq*. The first is that it means lightning. This was said by Abu al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, and from it is the poet's saying:

*We raised a dust cloud, and they came out from it,*
*like the coming out of the rain from the gaps of the cloud.*

The second is that it means rain. This was said by the majority, and from it is the poet's saying:

*No cloud has poured its rain,*
*and no land has brought forth its herbage as it has.*

Imru' al-Qays said:

*Their tears are a downpour, a flood, a heavy rain,*
*a pouring, a continuous flow, and a dripping.*

It is said: *waddaqat al-sahāba fa-hiya wādiqa* (the cloud rained, so it is raining), and *wadaqa al-maṭar yadiqu wadqan*, meaning it dripped. *Waddaqtu ilayhi* means I drew near to him. In the proverb: *wadaqa al-'ayr ilā al-mā'* (the donkey drew near to the water), meaning it approached it. It is used for one who submits to something out of eagerness for it. *Al-mawdi'* is a place of rain. *Waddaqtu [bihi] wadqan* means I became familiar with him. It is said of a female animal with hooves when she desires the stallion: *waddaqat tadiqu wadqan*, *awdaqat*, and *istawdaqat*. A female donkey is *wadūq*, a mare is *wadūq*, and *wadīq* as well, and there is *bihā widāq*. *Al-wadīqa* is intense heat. *Khilāl* is the plural of *khalal*, like *al-jabal* and *al-jibāl*. It means its gaps and the exits of the rain from it. It has already been mentioned in *al-Baqara* [vol. 2, pp. 12–20] that Ka'b said: "The cloud is the sieve of the rain. Were it not for the cloud, when the water descends from the sky, it would ruin what falls upon the earth." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Abu al-'Aliyah read *min khilālihi* in the singular. One says *kuntu fī khilāl al-qawm*, meaning in their midst.

(And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in it) It is said: Allah created in the sky mountains of hail, and He sends down hail from them. There is an implied element here, meaning He sends down hail from mountains of hail, so the object is omitted. Similar to this is the view of al-Farra', since his estimate is: *min jibāl barad* (from mountains of hail), so the mountains for him are the hail. *Barad* is in the genitive position, and according to his view the meaning must be *min jibālin baradin fīhā*, with the word *jibāl* carrying tanwīn. It is also said that Allah created in the sky mountains in which there is hail, so the estimate is: "and He sends down from the sky, from mountains in which there is hail." Here *min* is a *ṣila* (a superfluous particle). It is also said that the meaning is: He sends down from the sky the quantity of mountains, or like mountains, of hail to the earth. In that case the first *min* indicates the starting point (*ghāya*), since the descent begins from the sky; the second indicates partition (*tab'īd*), since hail is part of the mountains; and the third indicates specification of the kind (*tabyīn al-jins*), since the kind of those mountains is hail. Al-Akhfash said: *min* in *al-jibāl* and *barad* are both superfluous in both positions, and *al-jibāl* and *al-barad* are in the accusative position, meaning He sends down from the sky hail that is like mountains. And Allah knows best.

(So He strikes with it whom He wills and turns it away from whom He wills) Its striking becomes a punishment, and its turning away a blessing. This has already passed in *al-Baqara* [vol. 1, p. 218] and *al-Ra'd* [vol. 9, p. 298], that whoever says when he hears the thunder: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels from fear of Him," three times, will be protected from what might happen from that thunder.

(The flash of its lightning nearly takes away the sight) meaning the light of that lightning that is in the cloud (nearly takes away the sight) because of the intensity of its glare and brightness. Al-Shammakh said:

*And when it raised its light, no one could see its brightness*
*except the one with sharp sight.*

Imru' al-Qays said:

*Its light shines, or the lamps of a monk,*
*who has spent the olive oil on the twisted wick.* [*al-Salīṭ*: oil; *al-dhibāl*: plural of *dhubāla*, which is the wick.]

So *al-sanā* (with a short vowel, *maqṣūr*) is the light of lightning. *Al-sanā* is also a plant used for medicine. *Al-sanā'* (with a long vowel, *mamdūd*) means height. Talha ibn Musarrif read *sanā'* with a long vowel, for emphasis on the intensity of light and clarity, so the name of nobility is applied to it. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-sanā* (*maqṣūr*) is the flash, and when it is of nobility and lineage, it is *mamdūd* (with a long vowel). Both have one origin, which is the flashing. Talha ibn Musarrif read *sanā' burqihi*. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is the plural of *burqa*. Al-Nahhas said: *al-burqa* is a measure of lightning, and *al-barqa* is one single flash. Al-Jahdari and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read *yudhhibu bil-abṣār* with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the hā', from *al-idhhāb*, and the bā' in *bil-abṣār* is then an extra superfluous particle. The rest read *yadhhabu bil-abṣār* with a fatḥah on the yā' and the hā', and the bā' indicates attachment (*ilṣāq*). Lightning is a sign of the density of the cloud, a herald of the strength of the rain, and a warning of the descent of thunderbolts.

This was said by al-Naqqash. It is also said: their alternation is by the variation of what is decreed in them of good and evil, benefit and harm.

(Indeed in that) meaning in what we have mentioned of the alternation of night and day, and the states of rain, summer and winter, (is surely a lesson) meaning a consideration (for those of vision) meaning for people of insight among My creation.
