Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 45–46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah created every moving creature from water﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-Allahu khaliqu kulli" with the genitive construction (idafah). The rest read "khalaqa" as a verb. It has been said: both meanings in the two readings are sound. Allah, mighty and majestic, has informed of two matters, and it should not be said in this case that one of the two readings is more correct than the other. It has also been said: "khalaqa" refers to a specific thing, whereas "khaliq" is used in a general sense, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿the Creator, the Originator﴾ [al-Hashr: 24].[[See vol. 18, p. 48.]] In the specific sense: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1].[[See vol. 6, p. 383.]] Likewise: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾ [al-A'raf: 189].[[See vol. 7, p. 337.]] Thus it must be that: "And Allah created every moving creature from water." The "dabbah" is every living thing that crawls on the face of the earth, from the animals; one says "dabba yadibbu, fa-huwa dabb," and the "ha'" is for emphasis (intensification). This was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah.[[See vol. 2, p. 196.]] The phrase "from water" does not include the jinn and the angels in this, because we have not witnessed them, and it has not been established that they were created from water; rather, in the Sahih (it is reported) that "the angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from fire."[[In k: "from".]] This has been mentioned earlier.[[See vol. 10, p. 23 onward.]]

The exegetes said: "from water" means from a drop (nutfah). Al-Naqqash said: it means the seminal fluid of males. The majority of theologians said: it means that the make-up of every animal contains water, just as Adam was created from water and clay. On this basis is understood the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to the old man who asked him during the Battle of Badr: "From whom are you two?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We are from water." The hadith. Others said: the jinn and the angels are not excluded; rather every living creature was created from water, and fire was created from water, and wind was created from water, since the first thing Allah, mighty and majestic, created of the world was water, and then from it He created everything.

I say: The correctness of this is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Of them is one that walks on its belly﴾. Walking on the belly applies to snakes, fish, worms and the like; walking on two legs applies to humans and birds when they walk; and four applies to the rest of the animals. In the codex of Ubayy there is: "and of them is one that walks on more," which includes by this addition all animals, such as crabs and insects; but it is a Qur'an that was not established by consensus. However, al-Naqqash said: the statement mentioned only what walks on four instead of mentioning what walks on more, because the support of all animals is on four, which is the basis of their walking, and the multiplicity of legs in some of them is an addition to their creation, which such an animal does not need in its walking to all of them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent meaning is that those many legs are not futile, but the animal needs them in its movement, and all of them move in its activity.[[In k: "move and act."]] Some said: there is nothing in the Book that prevents walking on more than four, since it did not say that none of them walks on more than four. It has been said that there is an implied elision: "and of them is one that walks on more than four," as occurs in the codex of Ubayy. And Allah knows best.

The word "dabbah" includes those who have reason and those who do not; those who have reason are given precedence when they are combined with those who do not, because they are the addressees and those obligated to worship, and therefore He said "of them" (minhum). And He said "one that walks" (man yamshi), indicating by the difference (in movement) the existence of the Creator: that is, were it not that for all of them there is a Creator who chooses, they would not differ, but would be of one kind. This is like His saying: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4].[[See vol. 9, p. 281.]]

(﴿He creates what He wills; indeed Allah is over all things﴾) of what He wills to create (﴿Competent﴾).

(﴿We have certainly sent down distinct signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾) its explanation has preceded in more than one place.

Others said: the jinn and the angels are not excluded; rather every living creature was created from water, and fire was created from water, and wind was created from water, since the first thing Allah, mighty and majestic, created of the world was water, and then from it He created everything.

I say: The correctness of this is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Of them is one that walks on its belly﴾. Walking on the belly applies to snakes, fish, worms and the like; walking on two legs applies to humans and birds when they walk; and four applies to the rest of the animals. In the codex of Ubayy there is: "and of them is one that walks on more," which includes by this addition all animals, such as crabs and insects; but it is a Qur'an that was not established by consensus. However, al-Naqqash said: the statement mentioned only what walks on four instead of mentioning what walks on more, because the support of all animals is on four, which is the basis of their walking, and the multiplicity of legs in some of them is an addition to their creation, which such an animal does not need in its walking to all of them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent meaning is that those many legs are not futile, but the animal needs them in its movement, and all of them move in its activity.[[In k: "move and act."]] Some said: there is nothing in the Book that prevents walking on more than four, since it did not say that none of them walks on more than four. It has been said that there is an implied elision: "and of them is one that walks on more than four," as occurs in the codex of Ubayy. And Allah knows best.

The word "dabbah" includes those who have reason and those who do not; those who have reason are given precedence when they are combined with those who do not, because they are the addressees and those obligated to worship, and therefore He said "of them" (minhum). And He said "one that walks" (man yamshi), indicating by the difference (in movement) the existence of the Creator: that is, were it not that for all of them there is a Creator who chooses, they would not differ, but would be of one kind. This is like His saying: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4].[[See vol. 9, p. 281.]]

(﴿He creates what He wills; indeed Allah is over all things﴾) of what He wills to create (﴿Competent﴾).

(﴿We have certainly sent down distinct signs, and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾) its explanation has preceded in more than one place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger and we have obeyed"﴾. He means the hypocrites (munafiqun). They say with their tongues, "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger," without certainty (yaqin) and without sincerity (ikhlas).

(And we have obeyed) meaning: and they say [it], and they are liars.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away after that, and those are not believers.﴾

There are four issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah) in this.

The first is His saying, ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾. Al-Tabari and others said: A man among the hypocrites, named Bishr, had a dispute over a piece of land with a Jew. The Jew invited him to seek judgment before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but the hypocrite was in the wrong and refused, saying, "Muhammad is biased against us. Let us have Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf judge between us." So the verse was revealed concerning him. It was also said that it was revealed concerning al-Mughirah ibn Wa'il of the Banu Umayyah, who had a dispute with Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, over water and land. Al-Mughirah refused to take Ali to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for judgment and said, "He hates me." Then the verse was revealed. Al-Mawardi mentioned this. The verse says "that he may judge" (li-yahkuma) and not "that they may judge" (li-yahkuma, dual), because the one meant is the Messenger (ﷺ). Allah is mentioned first to magnify Him and to open the speech.

The second is His saying, ﴿But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly﴾. That is, obedient and submissive, because they know that he (peace be upon him) judges with the truth. It is said: "Fulan complied with (adhana) the judgment of Fulan, complying (yudh'inu) with complete compliance (idh'anan)." Al-Naqqash said: "mudh'inin" means submissive. Mujahid said: hastening. Al-Akhfash and Ibn al-A'rabi said: acknowledging.

(﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾) means doubt and suspicion.

(﴿Or do they have doubt?﴾) means: has doubt arisen in them about his prophethood and his justice?

(﴿Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them?﴾) means: that he will deviate in judgment and be unjust. The interrogative form is used because it is stronger in rebuke and more eloquent in blame, as in Jarir's words in praise:

"Are you not the best of those who have ridden the mounts,
and the most generous of all people in filling the bellies with wine?"

(﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾) means: the obstinate, the disbelievers, because they turn away from the judgment of Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: judgment belongs to the Muslims when the case is between a mu'ahid (a non-Muslim party bound by a treaty) and a Muslim, and the dhimmis (non-Muslims under the protection of the Muslim state) have no right in it. If it is between two dhimmis, the matter is left to them. If they come to the qadi (judge) of Islam, he may judge if he wishes, or turn away if he wishes, as was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Ma'idah.

The fourth issue: this verse is evidence for the obligation of answering the summons of a judge, because Allah, glory be to Him, censured those who were called to His Messenger to judge between them and their opponent with the worst censure, saying, ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease?﴾ and the rest of the verse. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: It is obligatory upon everyone who is summoned to the court of a judge to respond, unless it is known that the judge is a sinner, or there is enmity between the plaintiff and the defendant. Al-Zahrawi transmitted with a chain of narration from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is summoned by his opponent to a judge among the judges of the Muslims and does not respond, he is a wrongdoer and has no right." Al-Mawardi also mentioned this. Ibn al-Arabi said: This hadith is false. As for his saying "he is a wrongdoer," that is a sound statement; but as for his saying "he has no right," that is not sound. It may be that he means he is upon other than the truth.
