Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 51:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning: to the Book of Allah and the judgement of His Messenger.

(That they say: "We hear and we obey.") Ibn 'Abbas said: He informed of the obedience of the Muhajirun and the Ansar, even if that was in what they disliked. That is, this is their saying, whereas these people, had they been believers, would have said, "We hear and we obey." So the word "qawl" (saying) is put in the accusative as the predicate of kana (was), and its subject is in His saying "an yaqulu" (that they say), as in: ﴿And their only saying was that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147]. It has also been said: "innama qawlu al-mu'minin" (the saying of the believers), with kana being a filler in the speech, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ [Maryam: 29]. Ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "liyahkuma baynahum" with the verb in the passive form, the agent not named. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib recited "innama kana qawlu" with the qawl in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ — concerning what He commands, there is a ruling (ḥukm).

(And fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him) Ḥafs read "wa-yattaqhi" with the qaf silent, on the intention of jazm (the apocopate, or jussive, mood), and the poet said:

"Whoever keeps his duty (yattaqi), then Allah is with him, and the provision of Allah comes morning and evening."

The rest read it with a kasra, because its jazm is by deleting its last letter. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr made the ha' silent. Ya'qub, and Qalun from Nafi', and al-Bistiyy from Abu 'Amr and Ḥafs, weakened the kasra (ikhtilas, a brief, truncated vowel). The rest pronounced the kasra of the ha' in full (ishbaa').

(Then it is those who are the triumphant) Aslam reported that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) [[from k.]] was standing in the mosque of the Prophet ﷺ when a man from the landlords of the Romans was standing over his head, saying: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." So 'Umar said to him: "What is your affair [[in k.: ma shanuk aslamta. Probably an addition by a copyist.]]?" He said: "I have embraced Islam for Allah." He said: "Is there a cause for this?" He said: "Yes! I read the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and many books of the prophets, and I heard a captive reciting a verse of the Qur'an that combined everything in the earlier books, so I knew that it was from Allah, and I embraced Islam." He said: "What is this verse?" He said: the saying of Him, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ — in the obligatory duties — "and His Messenger" — in the sunnahs — "and fears Allah" — concerning what has passed of his life — "and keeps his duty to Him" — concerning what remains of his life — "then it is those who are the triumphant." The triumphant is one who is saved from the Fire and admitted into Paradise. Then 'Umar said: The Prophet ﷺ said: (I have been given jawami' al-kalim (concise, comprehensive speech).)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾

It returns to the mention of the hypocrites (munafiqun). When He had shown their aversion to the judgment of the Prophet ﷺ, they came to him and said: "By Allah, if you were to order us to leave our homes, our women and our wealth, we would leave; and if you ordered us to fight (jihad), we would fight." So this verse was revealed, meaning: they swore by Allah that they would go out with you in the future and would obey. "With their most emphatic oaths" means: with the utmost of what they were able to swear. Muqatil said: whoever swears by Allah has exerted himself in the oath. The explanation of this has already passed in "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 62.]]. "Jahd" (jahd, utmost effort) is in the accusative according to the manner of the verbal noun (masdar), its implied sense being: a strong oath.

(Say: "Do not swear;")

Here the statement is complete.

(obedience is known.)

That is: your obedience is better for you than your oaths, or let there be among you obedience that is known (ma'ruf) and a speech that is known, with sincerity of heart, and there is no need for oaths. Mujahid said: the meaning is, "Your obedience is already known, and it is lying and denial." That is, what is known of you is lying, not sincerity.

(Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.)

[That is,] of your obedience in word and your opposition in deed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 54:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, with sincere obedience and abandoning hypocrisy.

(But if you turn away) meaning: if you turn away (tatawallaw), with one of the two taa's elided. What indicates this is that after it comes "wa-alaykum" and not "wa-alayhim."

(Then upon him is only that with which he has been charged) meaning: the conveying of the message.

(And upon you is only that with which you have been charged) meaning: obedience to him, related from Ibn Abbas and others.

(And if you obey him, you will be guided) He made being guided conditional upon obeying him.

(And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance) meaning: the conveying (al-tabligh) (al-mubin), the clear [message].

Revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is the view of Malik. It is also said that the occasion of this verse was that some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) complained of the hardship of fighting the enemy, and of the fear they felt for themselves, and that they could not put down their weapons. So the verse was revealed.

Abu al-Aliyah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained in Makkah for ten years after revelation came to him, in fear, he and his Companions, calling to Allah secretly and openly. Then he was commanded to emigrate (hijrah) to Madinah, and they were there in fear, morning and evening in arms. A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, will there not come a day upon us when we are safe and can put down our weapons?" He, peace be upon him, said: (You will not wait but a little while until a man among you sits in the great assembly, squatting, with no iron upon him.) And this verse was revealed, and Allah made His Prophet victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, and they put down their weapons and were secure.

Al-Nahhas said: In this verse there is a proof of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, fulfilled that promise.

Al-Dahhak said in the book of al-Naqqash: This [verse [[from manuscript K.]]] includes the caliphate of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, because they were the people of faith and did righteous deeds. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (The caliphate after me will be thirty years.)

Ibn al-Arabi in his book of rulings (Ahkam) adopted this view and preferred it, and said: Our scholars said: this verse is a proof of the caliphate of the four rightly-guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, and that Allah appointed them as successors, and was pleased with their trustworthiness, and that they were upon the religion which He approved for them, because no one has surpassed them in virtue up to this day. So the matter was settled for them, they upheld the governance of the Muslims, and they defended the boundaries of the religion. Thus the promise was fulfilled through them, and if this promise was not for them, it was fulfilled, was carried out through them, and came upon them, then for whom would it be? No one like them has come after them up to this day, nor will there be anyone like them after that. May Allah be pleased with them.

Al-Qushayri transmitted this view from Ibn Abbas. They argued with what Safinah, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), narrated, saying: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: (The caliphate after me will be thirty years, then it will become kingship.) Safinah said: Count against yourself [[an addition from Ibn al-Arabi. The address is to Sa'id ibn Hamdan, the narrator of the hadith from Safinah.]] the caliphate of Abu Bakr as two years, the caliphate of Umar as ten, the caliphate of Uthman as twelve years, and the caliphate of Ali as six.

Others said: This is a promise to the entire Ummah concerning the rule of the whole earth under the word of Islam, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: (The earth was folded up for me, so I saw its eastern and western parts, and the kingdom of my Ummah will reach what was folded up for me of it.) Ibn Atiyyah chose this view in his tafsir, where he said: The correct view regarding the verse is that it concerns the appointing of the community as successors, and their being appointed as successors is that He gives them dominion over the lands and makes them its people, as happened in al-Sham, Iraq, Khurasan and the Maghrib.

Ibn al-Arabi said: We say to them: this is a general promise concerning prophethood, the caliphate, establishing the call, and the generality of the Shari'ah. The promise is fulfilled in each person according to his measure and his condition, even among the muftis, judges and imams. There is no place for the caliphate in which this noble promise is fulfilled except through those caliphs who preceded. Then he mentioned an objection and its resolution, the meaning of which is: If it is said that this matter is only valid for Abu Bakr alone, since Umar and Uthman were killed by treachery, and Ali was disputed in the caliphate. We say: Security does not include safety from death by any means. As for Ali, his engagement in war did not nullify security, and the condition of security is not the removal of war; its condition is that a person possesses himself by his own choice, not as the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were in Makkah. Then he said at the end of his speech: The reality of the situation is that they were subdued and then became dominant, they were sought after and then became the seekers, and this is the extreme of security and honour.

I say: This condition was not specific to the four rightly-guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them, so that they should be singled out from the generality of the verse. Rather, all the Muhajirun (emigrants) shared in this, and others besides them. Do you not see the Quraysh's incitement of the Muslims at Uhud and other battles, and especially the Trench, until Allah, Exalted, informed about all of them, saying: ﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you thought about Allah assumptions. There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10-11] [[see vol. 14, p. 144.]]. Then Allah turned back the disbelievers, who gained no good, and He secured the believers and gave them as inheritance their land, their homes and their wealth. This is what is meant by His saying: "He will surely make them successors in the land." And His saying: "as He made successors those before them" refers to the Children of Israel, when Allah destroyed the tyrants in Egypt and gave them as inheritance their land and their homes, and He said: ﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inheritors of the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 137] [[see vol. 7, p. 272.]]. Thus were the Companions oppressed and fearful, then Allah, Exalted, gave them security, established them and gave them dominion. So it is correct that the verse is general for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), not specific, since specification can only be by a report from one whose word must be accepted, and from the established principle is adherence to the generality (of the text).

Concerning the meaning of the exchange of their fear for security, it is also reported that when his Companions said: "Will there not come upon us a day when we are safe and can put down our weapons?", the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, peace be upon him: (You will not wait but a little, until a man among you sits in the great assembly, squatting, with no iron upon him.) And he (ﷺ) said: (By Allah, Allah will surely complete this affair, until a rider travels from San'a to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah and the wolf for his sheep, but you are hasty.) Muslim recorded it in his Sahih, and it was as the Prophet (ﷺ) had informed. So the verse is a miracle of prophethood, because it is a report of what would come to be, and it came to be.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the land﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it means the land of Makkah, because the Muhajirun asked Allah for this, and they were promised as the Children of Israel were promised. This was said by al-Naqqash. The second: the lands of the Arabs and non-Arabs. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is the correct view, because the land of Makkah is forbidden to the Muhajirun. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (But the wretched one is Sa'd ibn Khawlah.) The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pitied him because he died in Makkah. He also said in the Sahih: (The emigrant may stay in Makkah for three days after completing his rites.)

The lam in "la-yastakhlifannahum" is the answer to an implied oath, since the promise is a speech. Its meaning: Allah said to those who believed and did righteous deeds, "By Allah, He will surely make them successors in the land, and will make them its kings and its inhabitants."

(As He made successors those before them) means the Children of Israel: He destroyed the tyrants in Egypt and al-Sham and gave them their land and their homes. The recitation of the majority is "kama istakhlafa" with a fatha on the ta and the lam, in keeping with "wa'ada" and "la-yastakhlifannahum". Isa ibn Umar, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from Asim recited "istukhlifa" with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the lam, as a passive verb.

(And He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them) which is Islam, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and this has already been discussed [[see vol. 6, p. 63.]]. Sulaym ibn Amir narrated from al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: (There is no house of stone or clay on the face of the earth but that Allah will cause the word of Islam to enter it, by the honour of the honoured or the humiliation of the humiliated: as for their honour, He will make them of its people; and as for their humiliation, they will submit to it.) Al-Mawardi cited this as evidence for those who said that the meaning of "the land" is the lands of the Arabs and non-Arabs, which is the second view mentioned above.

(And He will surely replace them) Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr recited it with a lightened form, from "abdala". This is the recitation of al-Hasan and the choice of Abu Hatim. The rest recited it with a doubled letter, from "baddala", which is the choice of Abu Ubayd, because it occurs more in the Qur'an. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿There is no change in the words of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 64], and He said: ﴿And when We replace a verse﴾ [al-Nahl: 101], and similar. Both are dialects. Al-Nahhas said: Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related from al-Farra' who said: Asim and al-A'mash recited "wa-la-yubaddilannahum" with doubling. This is an error from Asim, and he mentioned after it an even greater error, namely that he related from all other people the lightened form. Al-Nahhas said: Ahmad ibn Yahya claimed that there is a difference between the doubled and the lightened forms, and that it is said: "baddaltuhu" means I changed it, and "abdaltuhu" means I removed it and put something else in its place. Al-Nahhas said: This view is correct, as you say: "Abdil li hadha al-dirham", meaning remove it and give me another. And you say: "Qad baddalta ba'dana", meaning you changed after us. However, one of them may be used in place of the other, and what he mentioned is the more common. This has already passed in "al-Nisa'" [[see vol. 5, p. 425.]], praise be to Allah. We also mentioned in Surah "Ibrahim" the evidence from the Sunnah that "baddala" means the removal of the thing [[see vol. 9, p. 382.]], so consider it there. It was also recited: ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better﴾ [al-Qalam: 32], lightened and doubled.

(They worship Me) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while they worship Allah with sincerity. It may also be a new sentence in the manner of praising them.

(They associate nothing with Me) On this there are four views. First: they do not worship any god other than Me, related by al-Naqqash. Second: they do not show off their worship of Me to anyone. Third: they do not fear other than Me, said by Ibn Abbas. Fourth: they do not love other than Me, said by Mujahid.

(And whoever disbelieves after that) meaning after these blessings. What is meant is ingratitude for the blessing. Since Allah, Exalted, said: (Those are the defiantly disobedient.) The one who disbelieves in Allah is defiantly disobedient after this favour and before it.
Already mentioned, so he repeated the command to worship as emphasis.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 57:

His saying, Exalted is He: (Let not those who disbelieve suppose [that they can escape]) — this is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and a promise of victory. The common reading is "taḥsabanna" with a ta' (addressing the Prophet), while Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and Abū Ḥaywah read "yaḥsabanna" with a ya' (third person), meaning: let not those who disbelieve suppose themselves to be those who can escape Allah on earth, because al-ḥusbān (supposing) transitively takes two objects. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿAlī said: it is permissible for the verb to have the Prophet ﷺ as its subject, i.e., "let not Muhammad suppose that those who disbelieve are those who can escape on earth." Then "alladhīna kafarū" is the first object, and "muʿjizīna" is the second object. On the first view, "alladhīna kafarū" is the subject, "anfusahum" is the first object (elided, intended), and "muʿjizīna" is the second object.

Al-Nahhas said: I know of no grammarian among the people of Arabic, whether from Basra or Kufa, who does not criticise the reading of Ḥamzah. Some of them say it is a grammatical error (laḥn), because "yaḥsabanna" has come with only one object. Among those who said this was Abū Ḥātim. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is weak, but he permitted it despite its weakness, on the basis that the first object is elided, as we have explained.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān say about this reading: "alladhīna kafarū" stands in the accusative position. He said: the meaning would be "and let not the disbeliever suppose that those who disbelieve are those who can escape on earth." I say: this agrees with what al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿAlī said, except that the subject there is the Prophet ﷺ, whereas in this view it is the disbeliever. Muʿjizīna means fāʾitīn (those who escape).

(And their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the destination) — i.e., the place of return.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):**

It contains eight issues (masa'il). [[So in K. This is what is found.]]

**The first issue:** The scholars said: this verse is specific (khassah), and the one before it is general (ammah), because He said: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. Then He specified here, saying: "Let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission." So in this verse He specified some of those who must ask permission. Likewise, the statement in the first verse is interpreted as general for all times. In this verse some times are specified, so no servant or slave-girl enters, whether it is the morning or a time of undress, except after asking permission.

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Asma' bint Marthad. An adult male servant of hers entered upon her, so she complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. It is also said that the cause of its revelation was the entry of Mudlij upon 'Umar, and this will come.

**The second issue:** The scholars differed about the meaning of the Exalted's words "Let ... ask your permission" (li-yasta'dhinkum), in six opinions.

The first: it is abrogated (mansukhah) [the term *mansukh* means abrogated by *naskh* (abrogation)]. This was said by Ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Jubayr.

The second: it is recommended (nadb) and not obligatory. This was said by Abu Qilabah, who said: They were ordered to do this only out of consideration for them.

The third: it refers to women. This was said by Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami. Ibn 'Umar said: it concerns men only, not women. This is the fourth opinion.

The fifth: that was obligatory at a time when they had no locks and no doors, and if the situation returned, the obligation would return. This was related by al-Mahdawi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The sixth: it is muhkamah (not abrogated) and binding, applying to both men and women. This is the view of most scholars, including al-Qasim, Jabir ibn Zayd and al-Sha'bi. The weakest of these is the view of al-Sulami, because *alladhina* (those who) is not used for women in the Arabic language; rather, for women one uses *allati* and *allawati*. The view of Ibn 'Umar is regarded favourably by the people of reasoning, because *alladhina* is used for men in Arabic. Although it is permissible for women to be included with them, that happens only by evidence, and the speech is to be taken in its apparent sense. However, its chain includes Layth ibn Abi Sulaym. [[In Tahdhib al-Tahdhib: "Ibn Hibban said: he became confused in his old age, so he would reverse chains and raise mursal reports, and would narrate from reliable transmitters what was not part of their narrations. Al-Bazzar said: he was like one of the worshippers, except that confusion befell him, so his narrations became disordered ... etc."]]

As for the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Dawud related from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid, who heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "It is a verse which most people have not been commanded to act upon: the verse of asking permission. Indeed, I order this slave-girl of mine to ask permission to enter upon me." Abu Dawud said: 'Ata' related it in the same way from Ibn 'Abbas, "He orders it." 'Ikrimah related that a group of people from Iraq said: "O Ibn 'Abbas, what do you think about this verse, in which we are commanded with what we are commanded, and no one acts upon it?" [the phrase "anyone" (ahad) is added from Sunan Abi Dawud. In K: "and we do not act upon it."] — the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those among you who have not reached puberty, three times: before the dawn prayer, and when you take off your clothes at midday, and after the night prayer. Three times of nakedness (awrat) for you. There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these, as you go about attending to one another." Abu Dawud said: al-Qa'nabi recited up to "All-Knowing, All-Wise." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed Allah is Forbearing and Merciful toward the believers; He loves concealment. The people had no curtains for their houses, nor canopies [[al-hijal: plural of hijlah (with vowelling), a tent-like chamber covered with cloth, having large buttons.]]. Often a servant, a child or a man's orphan girl would enter, and the man would be with his wife. So Allah commanded them to ask permission during those times of nakedness. Then Allah brought them curtains and good provision, and I have not seen anyone acting upon that since." [the word "since" (ba'd) is added from Sunan Abi Dawud. In K: "and we do not act upon it."]

I say: this is a good text (matn), and it refutes the view of Sa'id and Ibn Jubayr, because there is no evidence in it for abrogation of the verse, but rather that it applied in a particular situation and then that situation ended. If a situation like that situation returns, its ruling remains as it was. Indeed, its ruling is still established today in many homes of Muslims in the desert, the open country and similar places.

Waki' related from Sufyan, from Musa ibn Abi 'A'ishah, from al-Sha'bi, concerning "O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission," that he said: "It is not abrogated." I said: "People do not act upon it." He said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the One sought for help."

**The third issue:** Some scholars said: asking permission three times is derived from the saying of the Exalted: "O you who believe, let those whom your right hands possess ask your permission, and those among you who have not reached puberty, three times." Yazid [[So in B. In K, H, and A: Yazid. This has no basis.]] said: "Three times, meaning three occasions." He said: "So the Qur'an came concerning the slaves and the children, and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning all of them."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: What he said of this, although it may have some basis, is not known from the scholars in the interpretation of the verse he cited. What most of them hold regarding "three times" is that it means three times (occasions). The mention of these in it confirms the soundness of this view: "before the dawn prayer, and when you take off your clothes at midday, and after the night prayer."

**The fourth issue:** Allah, Mighty and Majestic, taught His servants in this verse that the slaves, since they have no sexual desire, and the children who have not reached puberty but have understood the meanings of uncovering and similar matters, should ask permission to enter upon their families at these three times. These are the times when people's custom leads to uncovering and to being constantly unclothed. Before dawn is the time of ending sleep, leaving sleepwear and putting on daytime clothes. The time of the qa'ilah (midday rest) is also a time of undressing, which is midday, because the day becomes visible then, when its light is high and its heat intense. After the night prayer is the time of undressing for sleep. So uncovering is common at these times.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a young man from the Ansar called Mudlij to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab at midday to summon him. He found him asleep, having locked the door upon himself. The boy knocked on the door and called to him, and entered. 'Umar woke and sat up, and some part of him became uncovered. 'Umar said: "I wish that Allah had forbidden our children, our women and our servants from entering upon us at these hours without permission." Then he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found that this verse had been revealed, so he fell down in prostration in gratitude to Allah. It is Meccan.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and those among you who have not reached puberty﴾, meaning those among your free persons who have not had wet dreams. This was said by Mujahid. Isma'il ibn Ishaq related that he used to say: "Let those who have not reached puberty among those whom your right hands possess ask your permission," with inversion of order, and that the verse concerns the female slaves. [[So in the manuscripts of the original. It is evident that there is a gap in the expression.]]

The majority read the lam with a damma (*al-hulm*). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read it with a sukun because the damma is heavy, and Abu 'Amr used to regard that reading favourably. "Three times" (thalatha marrat) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), because they were not commanded to ask permission three times, but were commanded to ask permission at three occasions. The temporal sense in "three" is clear: before the dawn prayer, and when you take off your clothes at midday, and after the night prayer. Its meaning has already passed. It is not necessary to ask permission three times at every time.

**(Three times of nakedness for you):** The majority of the Seven read "thalathu awrat" with *thalath* in the nominative. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "thalatha" with the accusative, as an apposition (badal) to the adverbial phrase in His saying "three times." Abu Hatim said: "The accusative is weak and rejected." Al-Farra' said: "The nominative is more beloved to me." He said: "I chose the nominative because the meaning is: these matters are three times of nakedness." The nominative, according to al-Kisa'i, is by way of the subject (ibtida'), and its predicate is what follows it; he did not mention a returning pronoun, but stated it explicitly as a subject. He said: "The awrat are the times in which nakedness occurs, except that he read it with the accusative." The accusative has two views. One is that it is governed by His saying "three times," and for this reason al-Farra' regarded it as unlikely. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "let them ask your permission during the times of three nakedness," so the governing noun is omitted and the noun in the genitive is put in its place.

"Awrat" is the plural of 'awrah. Its regular form in the sound language is that it comes in the pattern *fa'alat* (with fatha on the 'ayn), like *jafnah* and *jafanat*, and similar. In the defective (weak-letter) forms they used a sukun on the 'ayn, like *bayda* and *bayda't*, because a fatha there would lead to its weak-letter change, so it was not given a fatha for that reason. As for the saying of the poet:

*Abu Bayda'at goes out and returns, swift to pursue,*
*Gentle in wiping the two shoulders, tender in his wiping.* [[So in the Lisan, under the root "bayd." What is in the manuscripts of the original is:
*Abu Bayda'at goes out or sets off early,
Eager, with provision and without needing a supplier.*
This verse is by al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, and the correct recitation is:
*From the family of Mayyah, a traveller goes out or sets off ... etc.*]]
it is anomalous (shadh).

**The sixth issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these﴾, meaning in entering without asking permission, even if you are in a state of lightly dressed domestic clothing.

"Tawwafun" (going about) means "they are tawwafun." Al-Farra' said: like your saying in speech: "They are only your servants and those who go about attending to you." Al-Farra' permitted the accusative "tawwafin," because it is indefinite, while the pronoun in "'alaykum" is definite. The Basrans do not permit it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) of the two pronouns, the one in "'alaykum" and the one in "ba'dukum," because the governing elements differ. And it is not permissible to say "I passed by Yazid and I alighted upon 'Amr, the two intelligent ones," as an adjective for both of them. So the meaning of "tawwafun 'alaykum" is: they go about attending to you, and you go about attending to them. From this is the hadith about the cat (hadith: a report of the Prophet's words or deeds): "It is only among those who go about among you, male or female." [[His saying "or female" (aw al-tawwafat) may be a doubt on the part of the narrator. It may also be that he (ﷺ) said it, meaning that this animal is either one of the male roamers or the female roamers (from al-Baji).]]

So He prohibited, during the three times of nakedness, their entering upon us, because the reality of 'awrah is everything that has no barrier before it. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed (awrah)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 13], meaning easy for entry. Thus He made clear the cause that requires permission, which is privacy during a time of nakedness, so obeying it became required and its abrogation became impossible. Then He lifted the sin by His saying: "There is no sin upon you or upon them beyond these, as you go about attending to one another," meaning: some of you go about attending to others.

**(Thus Allah makes the verses clear to you):** The kaf (thus) is in the accusative position, meaning: Allah makes His verses clear to you, the verses that indicate His acts of worship, with a clarification like the way He makes these matters clear to you.

(وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ) This has already been discussed [see vol. 1, p. 287].

The seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and after the prayer of ʿIshāʾ﴾. He means the ʿAtama (the night prayer, here meaning ʿIshāʾ).

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your prayer. Indeed, it is the ʿIshāʾ, but they call it the ʿAtama because of milking camels." In another narration: "Indeed, in the Book of Allah it is the ʿIshāʾ, and they call it the ʿAtama because of the milking of camels."

In al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Abū Barzah: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to delay the ʿIshāʾ. Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) delayed the ʿIshāʾ. This indicates the first ʿIshāʾ (i.e., the earlier-named prayer, the one that is called ʿIshāʾ in the Book of Allah).

In the Ṣaḥīḥ: "He prayed it," meaning the ʿAṣr, "between the two ʿishāʾs," the Maghrib and the ʿIshāʾ.

In the Muwaṭṭaʾ and elsewhere: "If they knew what is in the ʿAtama and the Ṣubḥ, they would come to them even crawling."

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, on the authority of Jābir ibn Samurah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray the prayers roughly like your prayers, but he would delay the ʿAtama slightly after your prayer, and he would shorten the prayer.

Qāḍī Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī said: These are conflicting reports, and it is not known from them which came first and which came later by dating. His prohibition, peace be upon him, against calling the Maghrib "ʿishāʾ" and against calling the ʿIshāʾ "ʿatama" is established, so there is no rejecting it on the basis of the sayings of the Companions, let alone of others.

Ibn ʿUmar used to say: Whoever says "the prayer of al-ʿAtama" has committed a sin.

Ibn al-Qāsim said: Mālik said: "And after the prayer of ʿIshāʾ" — Allah named it the prayer of ʿIshāʾ, so the Prophet (ﷺ) loved that it be named by what Allah the Exalted named it, and that a person teach it to his family and children. One should not say "ʿatama" except when addressing someone who does not understand.

Ḥassān [ibn Thābit] [a note from another manuscript] has said:
"She always had a companion in her meadows, camels and sheep,
So leave this aside, but who is the gentle one who keeps me awake when the ʿIshāʾ has passed?"

It has been said: this prohibition against following the Bedouins in calling the ʿIshāʾ "ʿatama" was only so that it would not be diverted from what Allah the Exalted named it in His Book when He said: "And after the prayer of ʿIshāʾ." So it is a prohibition of guidance toward what is better, not a prohibition of the forbidden kind, and it does not mean that calling it "ʿatama" is impermissible. Do you not see that it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) himself used that name for it, and that Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, permitted calling it by that name?

It has also been said: he only forbade this to keep this noble, religious act of worship free from being called by a term that is the name of a worldly act, namely the milking that they used to do at that time and which they called "ʿatama." This is supported by his saying: "for they call it ʿatama because of the milking of camels."

The eighth issue: Ibn Mājah related in his Sunan: ʿUthmān ibn Abī Shaybah told us, Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh told us, from ʿUmārah ibn Ghaziyyah, from Anas ibn Mālik, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever prays in congregation for forty nights, never missing the first rak'ah of the ʿIshāʾ prayer, Allah will write for him by it freedom from the Fire."

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, on the authority of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays the ʿIshāʾ in congregation, it is as if he stood in prayer for half the night, and whoever prays the Fajr in congregation, it is as if he stood in prayer the whole night."

Al-Dāraquṭnī related in his Sunan, from Subayʿ or Tubayʿ, from Kaʿb, who said: Whoever performs wuḍūʾ and does it well, prays the late ʿIshāʾ, then prays four rakʿahs after it, completing their bowing and prostrations, and knows what he recites in them, they will be for him like the Night of Power.

Al-Hasan recited "al-ḥulm" (الْحُلْمَ), dropping the ḍamma because of its heaviness. The meaning is that the children were commanded to seek permission during the three times mentioned, and that they were permitted to act otherwise at other times, as we have mentioned. Then God, exalted is He, commanded in this verse that when they reach puberty (al-ḥulm) they should follow the ruling of men regarding seeking permission at every time. This is an explanation from God, mighty and majestic is He, of His rulings and a clarification of what is lawful and unlawful. He said, "fa-l-yastadhinū" (فَلْيَسْتَأْذِنُوا) and did not say "fa-l-yastadhinūkum." In the first instance He said, "li-yastadhinkumu" (لِيَسْتَأْذِنْكُمُ) because the children are not addressed and are not under obligation.

Ibn Jurayj said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ, "And when the children among you reach puberty, then let them seek permission," and he said: "It is obligatory upon people that they seek permission when they have reached puberty, whether they are free or slaves."

Abu Ishaq al-Fazari said: I asked al-Awzaʿi, "What is the limit of the child who seeks permission?" He said: "Four years old." He said: "He should not enter upon a woman until he seeks permission."

And al-Zuhri said (this is in some copies: "Wa-qālahu" [[as in K.]]): that is, a man should seek permission before entering upon his mother, and this verse was revealed concerning this meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 60:

There are five issues in this.

The First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the women past child-bearing﴾. Al-qawa'id (the women past child-bearing), its singular is qa'id, without a ta' marbuta (the feminine ending ha'), so that its omission indicates that it refers to the sitting of old age, just as they say: imra'ah hamil (a pregnant woman) without the ha', to indicate that it is the carrying of pregnancy. The poet said:

"Even if what is in her belly were among women, / who have conceived, though the qawa'id are barren (ʿuqr)."

And in other usage they say: qa'idah fi baytiha (a woman sitting in her house), and hamilah ʿala zahriha (a woman carrying on her back), with the ha'. Al-qawa'id also means the foundations of the house, its singular being qa'idah, with the ha'.

The Second: Al-qawa'id are the old women (al-ʿujjaz) who have ceased from activity because of age, and have ceased from bearing children and from menstruation. This is the saying of most of the scholars. Rabi'ah said: they are those whom, when you see them, you find repulsive because of their age. Abu ʿUbaydah said: those who have ceased from bearing children. But this is not sound, because a woman may cease from bearing children while still being a source of enjoyment. This was said by al-Mahdawi.

The Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they put aside their outer garments, not displaying adornment﴾. The qawa'id are singled out for this because people's desires turn away from them, since no man seeks them. So what was not permitted to others was permitted to them, and the burden of the strict covering, which is wearisome for them, was removed from them.

The Fourth: Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy and Ibn ʿAbbas recited: "an yada'na min thiyabihinna" (that they put down some of their garments), with the addition of "min" (some). Ibn ʿAbbas said: this is the jilbab (outer cloak). It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud: "min jalabibihinna" (from their outer cloaks). The Arabs say: imra'ah wadi' (a woman who has put aside her head-covering), for the woman who has grown old and put down her khimar (head-covering). Some people said: the elderly woman who has despaired of marriage, if her hair shows there is no harm; according to this it is permissible for her to put down the khimar. The correct view is that she is like the young woman in covering, except that the elderly woman may put down the jilbab which is worn over the dir' (shift) and the khimar. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jubayr and others.

The Fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿not displaying adornment﴾, that is, not revealing and not exposing themselves to view with adornment so that they may be looked at, for that is among the most ugly things and furthest from the truth. Tabarruj (display) is uncovering and showing oneself to the eyes, and from it comes: "buruj mushayyadah" (fortified towers). And buruj of the sky and of the walls, meaning there is no barrier between them and what would conceal them.

It was said to ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "O Mother of the Believers, what do you say about dyeing (khidab), coloring (sibagh), amulets (tama'im), the two earrings, the anklet, a gold ring, and thin garments?" She said: "O assembly of women, your case is the case of one woman. Allah has permitted you adornment, not displaying yourselves to those who are not permitted to see you, [that is], the forbidden ones (muharram)." ʿAta' said: this applies within their houses; when she goes out it is not permitted for her to put down the jilbab. According to this, "not displaying themselves" means not going out of their houses. And according to this it follows that when she is in her house there is no need for a jilbab over the dir', and this is far-fetched, except when a stranger (ajnabi) enters upon her.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned that the modesty of all of them, their abstention from putting aside garments and their adherence to what is required of young women, is better and more excellent for them. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa an yata'affafna" (and that they restrain themselves) without the sin.

Then it was said: among tabarruj is that a woman wears two thin garments which describe her body.

The sound narration from Abu Hurayrah says: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Two types of the people of the Fire I have not seen: a people who have whips like the tails of cows with which they strike people, and women who are clothed yet naked, enticing and enticed, their heads like the humps of the Bukht camels, leaning. They will not enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance, though its fragrance is found from such and such a distance." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: He made them "clothed" because garments are upon them, and described them as "naked" because when the garment is thin it describes them and reveals their charms, and that is forbidden. I say: this is one of the two interpretations of the scholars regarding this meaning. The second is that they are clothed in garments but naked of the garment of piety about which Allah, exalted is He, said: "And the garment of piety, that is best."

And they recited:

"When a man does not wear garments of piety, / he turns about naked even if he is clothed.
And the best garment of a man is obedience to his Lord, / and there is no good in one who disobeys Allah."

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "While I was sleeping, I saw people being presented to me, wearing shirts, some of which reached to the breasts and some less than that. And ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab passed by, wearing a shirt that he was dragging." They said: "How did you interpret that, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The religion." So his ﷺ interpretation of the shirt as religion is taken from His saying, exalted is He: "And the garment of piety, that is best." The Arabs use garments as a metaphor for virtue and chastity, as their poet said:

"The garments of the Banu ʿAwf are pure and clean..."
[This is the first half of a line of Imru' al-Qays, whose second half in his Diwan is: "and their faces at the gatherings are bright."]

And the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿUthman: "Allah will clothe you with a shirt; if they want you to take it off, do not take it off." He expressed caliphate by the shirt, and this is a well-known good metaphor. I say: this interpretation is the more correct of the two, and it is the most fitting for them in these times, especially the young women, for they adorn themselves and go out displaying themselves, so they are clothed in garments yet naked of piety in reality, outwardly and inwardly, since they reveal their adornment and do not care who looks at them; rather that is their intention, and this is observed in existence among them. If they had any piety, they would not do that, and no one would know what is there. What strengthens this interpretation is what is mentioned in the description of them in the rest of the hadith: "their heads like the humps of the Bukht." The Bukht is a kind of camel with large bodies and large humps; he likened their heads to them because of the locks of their hair which they raise up on the middle of their heads. This is observed and known, and the one who looks at them is blameworthy.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have left after me no trial more harmful to men than women." Related by al-Bukhari.

**Its Eleventh Issues:** There are eleven issues concerning it.

**The first:** The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿There is no blame upon the blind man﴾. The scholars differed in interpreting this verse, giving eight opinions. The closest of them concerns whether it is abrogated (*mansukhah*), abrogating (*nasikhah*), or definitive (*muhkamah*). These are three opinions.

The first is that it is abrogated, from His words "nor upon yourselves" to the end of the verse. This was said by Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, who said: "This is something that has ended. In the early days of Islam, their doors had no locks, and the curtains were lowered. A man might come, enter the house while hungry, and no one would be there, so Allah the Mighty and Majestic permitted him to eat from it. Then locks were placed on the houses, and it became unlawful for anyone to open them. So this ended and was discontinued." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let no one milk another's livestock except with his permission..." This hadith was transmitted by the Imams.

The second is that it is abrogating. This was said by a group. Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed, 'O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth by false means' [[See vol. 2, p. 337.]], the Muslims said: 'Allah the Mighty and Majestic has forbidden us to consume one another's wealth by falsehood, and food is among the best of wealth. So it is not lawful for any of us to eat at the house of another.' The people refrained from that. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: 'There is no blame upon the blind man'... to '...or that of which you hold the keys.'" He said: "This refers to a man who appoints another to manage his estate." I say: This Ali ibn Abi Talhah was a client (*mawla*) of the Banu Hashim, who settled in Syria. He was known as Abu al-Hasan, and it is said Abu Muhammad. His father's name was Abi Talhah Salim. His tafsir (*tafsir*, commentary) has been criticized, and it is said that he never met Ibn Abbas, and Allah knows best.

The third is that it is definitive (*muhkamah*). This was said by a group of scholars whose views are followed, among them Said ibn al-Musayyab and Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah ibn Masud. Al-Zuhri narrated from Urwah, from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Muslims used to join the expeditions (*yu'bun fi al-nafir*) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they would hand over their keys to their disabled companions (*dam'na*) and say: 'If you are in need, then eat.' But they would say: 'We only took it from them without their full consent.' So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed: 'Nor upon yourselves, that you eat from your own houses or the houses of your fathers...' to the end of the verse."

Al-Nahhas said: "*Yu'bun*" means they go out all together on the military campaigns. It is said: "The sons of so-and-so mobilized against the sons of so-and-so" when they came against them with all of them. Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said "the sons of so-and-so mobilized in emigration (*jala'*)," so that no one remained in their land. And "the horse came with full stride and full power (*ruk'*, *'ayb*)," meaning with the utmost of what it had. In the hadith: "For the nose, when its cutting is complete (*istu'iba jad'uhu*), the blood money is due," meaning when nothing of it is left. *Istiab* of a thing means its complete removal. It is said: "A house is *wa'ib* when it is spacious and can contain everything placed in it." The *dam'a* are the disabled; their singular is *damin* (*zamin*).

Al-Nahhas said: This opinion is among the most excellent of what has been related concerning the verse, because it contains reports from the Companions and the Successors that the verse was revealed concerning a specific matter.

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a coherent statement, for it concerns their staying behind from jihad while their wealth remained in their hands. But His words "or that of which you hold the keys" contradict it, so this opinion is very far-fetched. Rather, the preferred view is that Allah lifted the hardship from the blind man in matters that depend on sight in the duty imposed, and from the lame man in matters that require walking, and from actions that are impossible because of lameness, and from the sick man in matters where illness affects its exemption, such as fasting, the conditions and pillars of prayer, jihad, and the like. Then he said, further clarifying: "And there is no blame upon you in eating from your houses." This is a correct meaning and a clear, beneficial explanation, supported by the Law and reason, and there is no need to rely on transmitted reports to explain the verse.

I say: Ibn Atiyyah pointed to this, saying: "The apparent meaning of the verse and the spirit of the Law indicate that hardship is lifted from them in everything that their excuse compels them to, and their intention requires them to perform the most complete, while their excuse requires that they perform the lesser. So hardship is lifted from them in this."

As for what people have said about this hardship here, that is: 

**The second:** Ibn Zayd said: It refers to hardship in the campaign, meaning there is no blame upon them for delaying. The words of Allah the Exalted "nor upon yourselves" to the end of the verse form a separate meaning from the first.

Another group said: The whole verse concerns food. They said: The Arabs and the people of Medina, before the Prophethood (*mab'ath*), used to avoid eating with people who had disabilities. Some of them did this out of disgust at the wandering of the blind man's hand, the spreading out of the lame man's posture, and the smell and ailments of the sick. These were ignorant (*jahiliyyah*) character traits and arrogance, so the verse was revealed announcing (their permissibility).

Others did this out of scruple toward those with disabilities, as they fell short of the level of the healthy in eating, because the blind cannot see, the lame cannot compete, and the sick are weak. So the verse was revealed permitting eating with them.

Ibn Abbas said, in the book of al-Zahrawi: The people of disabilities scrupled to eat with others because of their disabilities, so the verse was revealed permitting them.

It is also said: When a man brought people with disabilities to his house and found nothing in it, he would take them to the houses of his relatives. The people with disabilities were reluctant about this, so the verse was revealed.

**The third:** His words "nor upon yourselves." This is the beginning of a statement, meaning: nor upon you, O people. When the addressed and the non-addressed were combined, the addressed was given precedence so that the speech would be coherent. He mentioned the houses of relatives but omitted the houses of children. The exegetes said: That is because they are included in His words "in your houses," since a man's son's house is his own house, and in a report (*khabar*): "You and your wealth belong to your father." And because He mentioned the relatives afterward but did not mention the children.

Al-Nahhas said: Some people objected to this view, saying: "This is an imposition upon the Book of Allah. Rather, the apparent preference is that the son should not be excluded from these." The argument from what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), "You and your wealth belong to your father," is not strong, because this hadith is weak, and even if it were authentic, it would not be a proof, since the Prophet (ﷺ) may have known that the wealth of that addressed person belonged to his father.

It has been said that the meaning is: "You belong to your father, and your wealth is yours," with "your wealth" as a subject: "and your wealth belongs to you." This cuts off the inheritance between father and son.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: The words of Allah the Exalted "nor upon yourselves that you eat from your houses" are as if He were saying: "Your dwellings in which your families and your children are." So the family and children have there something that this man, to whom the dwelling belongs, has provided for them. There is no blame upon him for eating with them from that food. Or the wife and child have there something of their own possession, and there is no blame upon him in that.

**The fourth:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts﴾. Some scholars said: This applies when they have given him permission for that. Others said: Whether they have given him permission or not, he may eat, because the kinship between them is itself a permission from them, since in that kinship there is tenderness, and people's souls allow this tenderness so that this one may eat from their property and be pleased by it when they know.

Ibn al-Arabi said: He permitted us to eat by reason of kinship without seeking permission, provided the food is freely available. But if it is kept safe (*mahzun*) from them, it is not lawful for them to take it, nor may they go beyond to storing it, nor to what is not food, even if it is not kept safe from them, except with their permission.

**The fifth:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or that of which you hold the keys﴾. This means what you have stored and what has come into your possession. The greatest part of this is what a man possesses in his house and under his lock. This is the interpretation of al-Dahhak, Qatada, and Mujahid. According to the majority of the exegetes, the agents, slaves, and hired workers are included in the verse. Ibn Abbas said: It refers to a man's agent over his estate and his keeper over his wealth, so it is lawful for him to eat from what he is entrusted with. Ma'mar narrated from Qatada, from Ikrimah, who said: "When a man holds the key, he is a keeper, so there is no harm in his eating a small amount."

Ibn al-Arabi said: The keeper may eat from what is stored by consensus (*ijma'*). This applies when he has no wage. But if he has a wage for the storing, it is unlawful for him to eat.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mulliktum* (with a *damma* on the *mim*, a *kasra* on the *lam*, and a shadda). He also read *mafatihahu* with a *ya* between the *ta* and the *ha*, as the plural of *miftah* (key); this was discussed in *al-An'am* [[See vol. 7, p. 1.]]. Qatada read *miftahahu* in the singular. 

Ibn Abbas said: This verse was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Amr, who went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a campaign and left Malik ibn Zayd in charge of his family. When he returned, he found him exhausted, asked him about his condition, and he said: "I was scrupulous about eating from your food without your permission." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

**The sixth:** The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿or your friend﴾. *Sadiq* (friend) is used in the sense of the plural, as is *'aduw* (enemy). Allah the Exalted said: "For they are an enemy to me" [al-Shu'ara: 77]. Jarir said:

*They called to desire, then shot our hearts*
*With arrows of enemies, while they are friends.*

The friend is one whose affection toward you is genuine and whose affection you return genuinely. Then it was said: this ruling has been abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) by His words: ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], and by His exalted words: ﴿But if you find no one in them, do not enter them﴾ [al-Nur: 28], and by the Prophet's saying (peace be upon him): "The property of a Muslim man is not lawful except with his good-hearted consent." [[See vol. 14, p. 223.]]

It was also said: the ruling is *muhkam* (firm, not abrogated), and this is the more sound view. Muhammad ibn Thawr reported from Ma'mar, who said: "I entered the house of Qatadah and saw dates in it, so I began to eat them. He said: 'What is this?' I said: 'I saw dates in your house and ate them.' He said: 'You did well.' Allah the Exalted says: ﴿or your friends﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning His words "or your friends," that he said: "If you enter the house of your friend without consulting him, there is no harm in that."

Ma'mar said: "I said to Qatadah: 'Shall I not drink from this *hibb*?' [[The *hibb* (with an unpointed initial h): a large jar or earthen vessel. Ibn Duraid said: it is that in which water is placed, and it was not given a name.]] He said: 'You are my friend! Then what is this asking permission?'"

The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to enter the orchard of Abu Talhah, known as Bayruha [[See the discussion of its vowelling in Yaqut's *Mu'jam al-Buldan*.]], and drink from its good water without his permission, according to what our scholars have said. They said: water is owned by its people. If it is permissible to drink from the water of a friend without his permission, then it is permissible to eat from his fruits and his food when one knows that his heart is pleased with this, because of its triviality and the slightness of its cost, or because of the affection between them. In this sense belongs the feeding of Umm Haram to the Prophet (peace be upon him) when he slept at her house, because it is generally the case that the food in a house belongs to the man, and that the wife's hand in such matters is only a loan. All of this applies so long as eating is not taken as a *khubnah* [[The *khubnah*: the fold of a waistwrap or the edge of a garment, i.e., one does not take food into his garment.]], and he does not intend thereby to protect his property, and the food is trivial and small.

The seventh point: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in this verse joined the friend with the pure and firm kinship, because the nearness of affection is intimate. Ibn 'Abbas said in the book of al-Naqqash: "The friend is firmer than kinship. Do you not see the cry of the inhabitants of Hell: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a close friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100-101]." I say: for this reason, in our school, the testimony of a friend for his friend is not accepted, just as the testimony of a relative for his relative is not accepted. The explanation of this and its reason has passed in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 410 onward.]]. In the proverb: "Which of them is dearer to you, your brother or your friend?" He said: "My brother, if he is also my friend."

The eighth point: His words, exalted be He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for eating together or separately﴾. It was said: this was revealed concerning the tribe of Layth ibn Bakr, who were a clan of Kinanah. A man among them would not eat alone, and would remain hungry for days until he found someone to eat with him. From this is the saying of one of the poets:

*When you prepare provisions, seek for them a companion to eat with,*
*For I will not eat it alone.*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this custom was inherited among them from Abraham (peace be upon him), for he would not eat alone. Some Arabs, when they had a guest, would not eat unless they ate with their guest. So the verse came explaining the sunnah of eating and removing every practice contrary to it from the customs of the Arabs, and permitting for the one eating alone what had been prohibited among the Arabs, drawing them toward the nobility of character, while going to excess in obligating it. The bringing of a companion to eat is indeed good, but not so that it becomes forbidden to eat alone.

The ninth point: His words: ﴿together or separately﴾. "Jami'an" (together) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). "Ashtatan" is the plural of *shatt*, and *shatt* is a verbal noun meaning dispersal; one says: "The people *shatta*," i.e., they dispersed. Al-Bukhari, in his *Sahih*, gave a chapter heading: "Chapter: There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick," [citing] the verse, and [also] "*al-nahd*" and "gathering." What our scholars intended in this chapter is the permissibility of eating together even if their circumstances differ in eating. The Prophet (peace be upon him) sanctioned this, and it became a custom among groups invited to food in pooled provisions (*nahd*), at banquets, and during shortage on journeys. Whatever keys you hold through trust, kinship, or friendship, you may eat with a relative or a friend, or alone.

*Al-nahd* is what companions gather of money or food in equal measure of expense, which they spend among themselves; they have *tanahadu* (pooled), according to Sahib al-'Ayn. Ibn Duraid said: it is said of this: "The people pooled the thing among themselves." Al-Harawi said: in the hadith of al-Hasan: "Bring out your *nahd*, for it is greater in blessing and better for your characters." *Al-nahd* is what a company brings forth at the time of pooling, which is dividing the expense equally on a journey and otherwise. The Arabs say: "Bring your *nahd*," with a kasra on the nun.

Al-Muhallab said: pooled food is not set out for eaters on the basis that they eat equally; rather each eats according to his appetite, and one man may eat more than another. It has been said that abandoning it is more like scrupulousness (*wara'*). If the company gathers each day at the food of one of them, that is better than *nahd*, because they only pool so that each of them may contribute from his own property, and then one does not know, perhaps one of them holds back from his property while another eats more than his share. And if they are one day at this one's and another day at that one's, without any condition, then they are merely guests, and a guest eats with good heart from what is presented to him.

Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani said: the origin of *nahd* was that the people, while travelling, one of them would go ahead to the stopping-place, slaughter and prepare the food, then come to them; then he would go ahead again to the stopping-place and do the same. They said: "What you do, we all wish to do the like of. So come, let us set between us something by which none of us is favoured over another." So they set up *nahd* among themselves. The righteous, when they pooled, would strive that the best of them give more than what his companions contributed; and if they were not content with this from him, once they knew he had done it, he did it in secret apart from them.

The tenth point: His words (Exalted is He): ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good. Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, that you may understand﴾. The interpreters differed as to which houses He intended. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan said: He meant the mosques, and the meaning is: greet those in them from among your guests [[So in MS K, and it is the more likely reading. In the other manuscripts: "your guests."]]. If there is no one in the mosques, the greeting is for a person to say: "Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah." It was also said: one says "Peace be upon us," intending the angels, then says: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." 'Abd al-Razzaq reported: Ma'mar informed us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), concerning His words, "So when you enter houses, greet one another," the verse, that he said: "When you enter the mosque, say: Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah."

It was also said: the meaning of "houses" is inhabited houses, i.e., greet one another. This was said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas as well, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah. They said: uninhabited houses are included in this, and a person greets himself in them by saying: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." Ibn al-'Arabi said: the view that the ruling is general regarding houses is the sound one, and there is no evidence for specification; He spoke in absolute terms so that every house, whether belonging to another or to oneself, would fall under this generality. So when one enters another's house, he asks permission, as has preceded; and when he enters his own house, he greets, as came in the report: "He says: Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." This was related from Ibn 'Umar. This applies when the house is empty; if it has its people and servants in it, he says: "Peace be upon you." If it is a mosque, he says: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." Ibn 'Umar interpreted the empty house in this way. Ibn al-'Arabi said: What I choose, when the house is empty, is that greeting is not obligatory, for if what is intended is the angels, the angels never leave the servant in any state. But when you enter your house, it is recommended for you to mention Allah by saying: "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah." This has preceded in *Surat al-Kahf* [[See vol. 10, p. 406.]].

Al-Qushayri, regarding His words "So when you enter houses," said: "The more apparent view is that this is general for entering every house. If there is a Muslim resident in it, he says: 'Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings.' If there is no resident in it, he says: 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.' If there is in the house someone who is not a Muslim, he says: 'Peace be upon those who follow the guidance,' or 'Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah.'"

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad reported, saying: Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm wrote to me, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam told us, saying: Ibn Wahb told us, saying: Ja'far ibn Maysarah told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: "When you enter houses, greet their people and mention the name of Allah, for when one of you greets upon entering his house and mentions the name of Allah over his food, the devil says to his companions: 'You have no lodging here, nor supper.' But when one of you does not greet upon entering and does not mention the name of Allah over his food, the devil says to his companions: 'You have gained lodging and supper.'"

I say: this hadith is established in meaning, raised (*marfu'*) from the hadith of Jabir, which Muslim recorded. In the book of Abu Dawud, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, who said: the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: "When a man enters his house, let him say: 'O Allah, I ask You for the best of entering and the best of leaving; in the name of Allah we enter, and in the name of Allah we leave, and upon Allah our Lord we rely.' Then let him greet his family."

The eleventh point: His words: ﴿a greeting﴾ is a verbal noun (*masdar*), because His words "greet" (*fa-sallimu*) mean "then greet with a greeting" (*fa-hayyu*). He described it as blessed because in it is supplication and the drawing of the Muslim's affection toward him. He described it also as good because its hearer finds it good. The *kaf* in His words "Thus" (*kadhalika*) is the *kaf* of comparison. And "that" (*dhalika*) is a reference to these sunan; i.e., just as He has made clear to you the sunnah of your religion in these matters, so He makes clear to you all that you need in your religion.

**The verse:** ﴿Only those are believers who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter requiring assembly, they do not leave until they have asked his permission.﴾ There are two issues concerning it.

**The first issue: His saying, ﴿Only those are believers﴾**

"Innama" (إِنَّمَا, "only") in this verse indicates restriction. The meaning is: the faith of one who believes in Allah and His Messenger is not complete and not perfected unless he listens to the Messenger without objecting when the Messenger wants to complete a matter, and he does not wish to spoil it by absenting himself at the time of the gathering, and the like. In the beginning of the surah Allah stated that He sent down "clear signs," and the revelation was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus He concluded the surah by emphasizing the obligation to follow him, peace be upon him, so that it would be known that his commands are like the commands of the Qur'an.

**The second issue: What is the "matter requiring assembly"?**

It has been disputed what the "matter requiring assembly" is. It was said: it refers to what the leader (imam) needs of gathering the people for the announcement of a benefit, such as establishing a sunnah in the religion, or for instilling fear in an enemy by their gathering, and for wars. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾ [Al-Imran: 159].[[See vol. 4, p. 250.]] So when there is a matter whose benefit and harm affect them all, he gathers them for consultation about it. The imam whose permission is awaited is the imam of command (imam al-imara), so no one may leave for an excuse except with his permission. When he leaves with his permission, the bad suspicion is removed from him.

Makhul and al-Zuhri said: the Friday prayer (al-Jumu'a) is among the matters requiring assembly. The prayer leader (imam al-salat) should be asked for permission when the imam of command has appointed him, if the one seeking permission is seen by him.

Ibn Sirin said: "They used to ask the imam for permission while he was on the pulpit. When this became frequent, Ziyad said: 'Whoever puts his hand over his mouth, let him leave without permission.'" This was in Medina, to the extent that Sahl ibn Abi Salih had a nosebleed on a Friday and asked the imam for permission.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that permission be sought from the commander of command, who occupies the seat of prophethood, because he may have an opinion on detaining that man for a matter of the affairs of the religion. As for the prayer leader alone, it is not for him to decide this, because he is an agent over a part of the parts of the religion on behalf of the one who occupies the seat of prophethood.

It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning the digging of the trench (al-khandaq) when the Quraysh came, led by Abu Sufyan, and the Ghatafan, led by Uyayna ibn Hisn. The Prophet (ﷺ) dug the trench around Medina, and that was in Shawwal of the fifth year after the Hijra. The hypocrites would slip away stealthily from the work and offer false excuses. Ashhab and Ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated similarly from Malik, and Muhammad ibn Ishaq also said likewise.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to return during the expedition of Tabuk, and he granted it to him and said: "Go, for by Allah you are not a hypocrite," intending by this to make the hypocrites hear it.

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) asked permission for the 'umra (lesser pilgrimage), and when he granted it, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Hafs, do not forget us in your righteous supplication."

I say: the first view is the sound one, because it encompasses all the statements. Ibn al-Arabi chose what was mentioned concerning the revelation of the verse from Malik and Ibn Ishaq, and that the ruling is specific to war. He said: "Two matters clarify this. The first is His saying in another verse: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, covering one another﴾ [An-Nur: 63]. The hypocrites used to hide behind one another, leave the congregation, and abandon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah commanded all of them that none of them should leave until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grants him permission, and by this his faith is made evident. The second is His saying: 'they do not leave until they have asked his permission.' What permission is there for one who has become impure (ḥadath) while the imam is delivering the sermon? The imam has no choice in preventing him or keeping him." And He has said: "﴿So grant permission to whomever you wish of them﴾," which shows by that that it is specific to war.

I say: the view that the ruling is general is more preferable, higher, better, and loftier.

**﴿So grant permission to whomever you wish of them﴾**

The Prophet (ﷺ) had the choice: if he wished, he could grant permission, and if he wished, he could refuse. Qatada said: His saying "﴿So grant permission to whomever you wish of them﴾" has been abrogated (naskh, "abrogation" of a ruling by a later revelation) by His saying: ﴿May Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [At-Tawba: 43], meaning, for their leaving the congregation, if you knew they had an excuse.

**﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾**

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 63:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like the calling of some of you to others.﴾ It means: do not shout from afar, "O Abu al-Qasim!" Rather, honour him, as He said in Surat al-Hujurat: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Hujurat: 3], to the end of the verse.[[See vol. 16, p. 328.]] Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: the meaning is, say "O Messenger of Allah" gently and softly, and do not say "O Muhammad" harshly. Qatadah said: He commanded them to show him honour and reverence. Ibn 'Abbas said: Do not expose yourselves to the supplication of the Messenger against you by angering him, for his supplication is binding.

(﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind others.﴾) Al-tasallul and al-insilal mean going out. Al-liwadh derives from al-mula dhah, which is to conceal yourself behind something for fear of being seen by someone. The hypocrites used to slip away from the Friday prayer. "Liwadhan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "hiding behind one another" (mutalawidhin), that is, one of them takes cover behind another, joining him in order to hide from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because nothing was heavier upon the hypocrites than the day of Friday and attending the sermon. This was related by al-Naqqash, and the discussion of it has already passed. It was also said: they used to slip away during jihad, turning back from it, each hiding behind the other. Al-Hasan said: "liwadhan" means fleeing from jihad. From this is the saying of Hassan:

And Quraysh flees from us, hiding behind one another... they did not stand firm, and their wisdom was light.

Its waw was kept sound because it is vowelled in "lawadha." One says: lawadha yulawidhu mulawadhatan and liwadhan, and ladha yaludhu [lawdhan] and liyadhan, where the waw changed into a ya' because of the kasra before it, following "ladha" in its weak form. When it is the verbal noun of fa'ala, it is not made weak, because fa'ala cannot be made weak.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾. By this verse the jurists argued that a command implies obligation. Its argument is that Allah, blessed and exalted, warned against opposing His command and threatened punishment for it with His saying: (lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment befall them). Therefore opposing Him is forbidden, and obeying His command is obligatory. Here "fitnah" means killing, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ata': earthquakes and terrors. Ja'far ibn Muhammad: an unjust ruler set over them. It was also said: the sealing of the hearts due to the ill omen of opposing the Messenger. As for the pronoun in "amrihi," it was said that it refers to the command of Allah, the Exalted, as said by Yahya ibn Sallam; and it was said that it refers to the command of His Messenger, peace be upon him, as said by Qatadah. The meaning of "yukhalifuna 'an amrihi" is that they turn away from his command. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: "'an" in this position is superfluous. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: it is not superfluous, and the meaning is: they oppose after his command, as in the saying:

... did not hold back from excess (from the Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays; the full line is: "And she comes forth with the crumbs of musk upon her bed, sleeping until midday, not restraining herself from excess.")

From this is His saying: ﴿So he transgressed against the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], meaning after the command of his Lord. "An" is in the position of the accusative governed by "yahdhar." According to most grammarians, "hadhira zaydan" is not permitted, while it is permitted with "an," because the particles of genitive are dropped with it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 24, verse 64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Verily, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, in creation and in ownership.

(He knows that in which you are) so He will recompense you for it. Here "yaʿlamu" (He knows) carries the meaning of "ʿalima" (He knew).

(And the Day they are returned to Him) after the address had been in the second person, it turned to a report in the third person; this is called khiṭāb al-talwīn (the shifting of address).

(Then He will inform them of what they did) meaning He will tell them of their deeds and recompense them for them.

(And Allah is Knowing of all things) of their deeds and their states. The surah is concluded with what it contained of tafsir, and praise be to Allah for the facilitation.

Completed, by the grace of Allah the Exalted, the twelfth part of the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi, to be followed, God willing, by the tenth part, whose beginning is the surah "al-Furqan."

Its editor, Abu Ishaq Ibrahim Atfayyish, the thirteenth part.
